** Canonical document identity and provenance

This document specifies the candidate R5 Gesso unified design as an intended
end-state, not a claim that the current implementation already satisfies its
requirements. Canonical R4 remains the preservation baseline until a complete
cross-part requirements and acceptance audit explicitly accepts R5.

The published design retains twelve ordered parts. During review, a part may be
maintained as smaller numbered editorial source sections (for example, 01.01
and 01.02) assembled mechanically into that published part. These fragments
have no independent normative status. The candidate remains =r5-draft= until
its assembly, cross-references, and requirement changes have been reviewed; it
does not implicitly supersede R4.

Historical source plans remain provenance. They do not carry independent
normative revision identities inside this specification.

The principal source lineage is:

| <45> | <55> |
| Source | Revision / role |
|--------+-----------------|
| Gesso Choreography Design | v4.5; foundational choreography semantics |
| Gesso Provable Hardening Plan | v7.376; compositional rejection and proof direction |
| Gesso/HumanHelp Biff 2 Migration Plan | native Biff 2 substrate and lifecycle integration |
| Gesso/HumanHelp Preflight Recovery Plan | v662; no-silent-downgrade and production-path closure |
| Gesso Unified Design | canonical r2; prior consolidation |
| Gesso Unified Design | canonical r3; earlier predecessor |
| Gesso Unified Design | canonical r4; direct predecessor and preservation baseline |
| Gesso Unified Design Revision and Validation Plan | plan revision 2; r3 review discipline |

Historical plans explain the origin of the design. The reviewed R4 assembly is
the preservation reference for this R5 proposal. Existing obligations are
retained when their wording is consolidated; a requirement is not deleted just
because its original example or paragraph was removed. Each significant R4
omission must be classified as preserved elsewhere, deliberately superseded, or
unresolved for repair. A change in implementation does not by itself change a
requirement, and an implementation restriction does not become a design
restriction merely because it made one proving experiment tractable.

This specification describes the intended architecture from zero. It does not
classify features as implemented or unfinished, prescribe patches to a current
checkout, or treat a passing implementation test as a normative decision.
Implementation-specific remediation belongs in a separate document.

*** Revision scope

Candidate R5 specifies the semantic, construction, runtime, acceptance, and
assurance boundaries of Gesso as one coherent architecture. Its requirements remain owned
by the sections that define them; this summary is a navigation aid.

The revision emphasizes:

- the full host language within checked managed application construction;
- explicit contracts for opaque computations, with assumptions preserved through
  every dependent guarantee;
- typed semantic transitions, derived obligations, and controlled realization
  of admitted effects;
- backend contracts supported by versioned qualification and adversarial
  conformance evidence;
- owner-relative admission for asynchronous events, including shared events;
- scope-preserving acquisition requirements and precisely stated resource bounds;
- independent required-capability acceptance alongside assembly closure and
  production-path enforcement;
- participant-relative command uncertainty after local retirement or lost delivery;
- explicit HumanHelp adoption policy and testable product outcomes;
- production/formal correspondence classified by the evidence actually supplied;
- a single normative home for each obligation, with examples that preserve it;
- connected reference realizations and controlled defects on production paths.

Unresolved product choices remain explicit. A completion claim that depends on
one of those choices is unavailable until the choice and its acceptance
conditions are specified. Generic Gesso semantics do not silently choose
HumanHelp business policy.

** Purpose

This document specifies the intended end-state design of Gesso choreography,
proof, execution, application assembly, and its use by HumanHelp.

The goal is not merely to provide a convenient syntax for distributed state
machines.  Gesso should provide a useful correctness boundary for distributed
application operations.  It should make coherent programs straightforward to
express, malformed programs difficult to assemble, and contradictions visible
as early and as locally as the available information permits.

The central design target is:

#+begin_quote
A Gesso application may still express a coherent but domain-wrong business
rule, but it should be difficult to assemble a structurally contradictory
distributed program that appears to work.
#+end_quote

Gesso therefore distinguishes two very different failure classes.

A *well-formed but domain-wrong* program may express the wrong policy while
remaining internally coherent.  For example, an application may validly encode
a rule that an Organization chose incorrectly.  Gesso cannot infer product
intent merely from syntax.

A *malformed* program contradicts its own declared semantic structure.  Examples
include:

- a role consuming a fact it cannot know;
- a browser affordance naming an operation that has no projected realization;
- an operation requiring authority that no trusted server path can establish;
- a provisional trajectory with no permitted resolution or recovery path;
- a projected plan whose required semantic dependency no longer matches the
  certified dependency used to produce it;
- a lifecycle operation silently degrading to a weaker ordinary request because
  required semantic metadata is absent;
- a proof or diagnostic artifact being accepted as runtime authority;
- a stale callback mutating a newer execution merely because both refer to the
  same logical DOM target.

Those are framework-recognizable contradictions and must be rejected when the
applicable supported checker has the information needed to establish them.
Diagnostics must identify the violated obligation and its owning boundary.

A computation being outside the supported proof fragment is a different matter.
It is not thereby malformed or prohibited. Ordinary Clojure remains available
within checked construction, with precisely stated interfaces, effects, and
assumptions. The framework must distinguish an invalid construction from an
unproved proposition and from an explicitly accepted asserted contract.


The distinction is easier to see in a small but nontrivial application slice.
Suppose an expense system models submitted expenses and a current approval
policy. The following code is illustrative rather than a frozen public API, but
it shows the amount of semantic structure Gesso should be able to reason about
without requiring the application author to reproduce framework internals.

#+begin_src clojure
(def Money
  [:int
   {:min 0
    :max 9007199254740991
    :semantic/type :money/usd-cents}])

(def Expense
  [:map
   [:expense/id uuid?]
   [:expense/employee-id uuid?]
   [:expense/department keyword?]
   [:expense/amount Money]
   [:expense/status
    [:enum :draft
           :submitted
           :approved
           :rejected
           :needs-finance]]])

(def ApprovalPolicy
  [:map
   [:policy/department keyword?]
   [:policy/manager-limit Money]
   [:policy/finance-threshold Money]])

(defrule manager-may-approve?
  {:inputs {:expense Expense
            :policy ApprovalPolicy}
   :returns :boolean}
  [:and
   [:= [:expense/status :expense] :submitted]
   [:= [:expense/department :expense]
       [:policy/department :policy]]
   [:< [:expense/amount :expense]
       [:policy/manager-limit :policy]]])

(defrule needs-finance?
  {:inputs {:expense Expense
            :policy ApprovalPolicy}
   :returns :boolean}
  [:and
   [:= [:expense/status :expense] :submitted]
   [:>= [:expense/amount :expense]
        [:policy/finance-threshold :policy]]])

;; Suppose this is what the Organization actually intends.
(def accounting-policy
  {:policy/department :accounting
   :policy/manager-limit 50000
   :policy/finance-threshold 50000})
#+end_src

This introductory =defrule= form, with expressions such as
=[:expense/status :expense]=, is *schematic application-authoring notation*,
not an expression admitted by Part IX's closed =[:read reader-id]= rule grammar.
The baseline Part IX grammar also does not directly admit an arbitrary
=Money= nominal value or infer its semantics from a Malli metadata key.
A supported frontend must validate the source interfaces and provide a checked
elaboration into the admitted typed-rule/reader semantics, with any required
nominal codec or registered extension. Otherwise a selected checked-rule
profile rejects the unsupported form or retains an expressly permitted opaque
contract with its premises; it must not pretend to type-check or execute an
unknown operator as part of the closed proof language. No specific =defrule=
constructor or elaborator is asserted to exist by this example.

Here =Money= *illustrates* an intended nominal semantic type backed by
nonnegative, exactly represented integer USD cents. The schema and rule
declarations must cross their construction checks before downstream code
treats them as admitted semantic interfaces; a metadata key or a Var name
does not itself admit them. The maximum is part of the example's intended
portable numeric profile. Arithmetic must preserve that bound or return a
declared failure; a JavaScript floating-point approximation must not silently
replace exact monetary semantics. A different currency or decimal profile
needs its own declared encoding and operations. Malli shape validation alone
does not establish nominal semantic identity.

Now imagine that the application author accidentally changes only the policy
data:

#+begin_src clojure
(def accounting-policy
  {:policy/department :accounting
   :policy/manager-limit 500000
   :policy/finance-threshold 500000})
#+end_src

The program may still be perfectly coherent. =500000= is a valid amount in
this USD-cent representation: $5,000 rather than $500.
The rule is well typed. The operation may project correctly. The authoritative
transaction may apply the rule exactly as declared. Gesso has no basis for
inventing the unstated product intention that the limit should have been
=50000= cents.

Contrast that with a malformed rule whose own semantic structure is
contradictory:

#+begin_src clojure
(defrule malformed-manager-rule
  {:inputs {:expense Expense
            :policy ApprovalPolicy}
   :returns :boolean}
  [:and
   ;; A status enum is not an ordered monetary value.
   [:< [:expense/status :expense]
       [:policy/manager-limit :policy]]

   ;; A money value is not a status variant.
   [:= [:expense/amount :expense]
       :submitted]])
#+end_src

Once a supported frontend has admitted the nominal types and *checked* an
elaboration of these schematic expressions to Part IX's typed reader grammar,
the checker has enough information to reject their incompatible operand
categories before the rule enters choreography or a model operation. If
elaboration is unsupported, the correct first result is an unsupported-source
diagnostic, not a fabricated successful type check or a claimed proof of these
particular operand mismatches. When the typed terms actually have been
admitted, an illustrative diagnostic can identify both the location and
the expected semantic categories:

#+begin_src clojure
{:error/type :gesso.rule/type-error
 :rule       'malformed-manager-rule
 :at         [:and 0]
 :operator   :<
 :left       {:type [:enum :draft :submitted :approved
                     :rejected :needs-finance]
              :source [:expense/status :expense]}
 :right      {:type :money/usd-cents
              :source [:policy/manager-limit :policy]}
 :required   {:operator :<
              :operands [:ordered :ordered]}}

{:error/type :gesso.rule/type-error
 :rule       'malformed-manager-rule
 :at         [:and 1]
 :operator   :=
 :left       {:type :money/usd-cents
              :source [:expense/amount :expense]}
 :right      {:type [:enum-value :submitted]}
 :required   {:operator :=
              :operands [:same-semantic-category
                         :same-semantic-category]}}
#+end_src

The diagnostic map shapes are illustrative output, not the public error API
or independent evidence that a real checker ran. The distinction is the
foundational one this document relies on everywhere else: the first
application can be wrong because humans chose the wrong coherent policy.
The second is malformed under the intended typed semantics because its own
declarations do not compose. Admission of its concrete authoring syntax and
proof of the checker implementation remain separate obligations.
Later examples apply the same distinction to knowledge, authority, browser
ownership, application assembly, and proof evidence.

#+LATEX: \newpage

The choreography system should provide the following broad properties:

- one global choreography describes an allowed distributed interaction;
- the global choreography crosses checked construction before execution, with
  the supported semantic judgments established and accepted assumptions retained;
- the choreography is projected into actor-local machines;
- local machines execute independently in Clojure and ClojureScript;
- actors acquire justified knowledge through declared provenance paths such as
  inputs, communication, authoritative observation, deterministic derivation,
  and explicit trusted assertion;
- authoritative model transitions remain atomic at their model transaction
  boundaries;
- clients may hold explicit provisional state without confusing it with
  authoritative state;
- actors may temporarily observe different frontiers of an evolving world;
- where convergence is required, the protocol provides a path toward justified
  knowledge of the relevant authoritative facts;
- durable application facts normally rendezvous through model authority rather
  than requiring direct client-to-client delivery;
- browser-local concerns such as continuity remain implementation concerns
  rather than becoming distributed truth;
- sleeping, reconnecting, stale, or incompatible browser projections have a
  defined recovery path rather than being assumed compatible forever;
- browser actors are treated as adversarial participants that may replace or
  modify every byte of client JavaScript and protocol state;
- authoritative security never depends on an honest browser projection;
- portable choreography and browser-adapter semantics are explicit transition
  systems suitable for machine-checked reasoning;
- the production browser adapter uses the same semantic transition model that
  is checked or proved rather than independently reimplementing a paper model;
- HTMX remains responsible for the ordinary declarative browser lifecycle it
  already owns;
- Gesso-owned browser effects remain behind a narrow explicit boundary;
- verification and projection produce one canonical executable artifact plus
  separate optional proof and diagnostic artifacts;
- proof or diagnostic artifacts cannot participate in runtime semantic
  decisions;
- whole-application assembly checks the correspondence between the semantic
  operation, projected plan, browser artifact, transport, trusted server
  capability, authoritative operation, settlement/progression, and permitted
  authoritative reacquisition;
- safety properties called proved identify their checked derivations or sound
  exhaustive/refinement arguments; asserted contracts and tested properties
  remain separately identified;
- tests remain essential for trusted assumptions, implementation
  correspondence, real browsers, external libraries, operational behavior, and
  application policy.

The design should make downstream application code easier to reason about even
when Gesso itself becomes substantially more sophisticated.

Correctness, explicit boundaries, debuggability, strong guarantees, and clear
repair paths are more important than minimizing implementation size.

#+LATEX: \newpage

** Full-language application logic and checked construction
:PROPERTIES:
:CUSTOM_ID: req-full-language-construction
:END:

Gesso supports ordinary Clojure application logic. Functions, recursion,
collections, libraries, and computations outside a decidable or supported proof
fragment remain available. The checked rule language is a reasoning
representation, not the boundary of the application programming language.

The normal application path is checked managed construction. An application
does not move to an unmanaged second architecture because one policy predicate
or computation is opaque to a prover. Its operation identities, contracts,
authority boundaries, effects, settlement, and recovery still compose through
the same admission system.

Full-language support is relative to the declared execution target. A
JVM-specific Clojure function does not become browser-executable merely because
its interface can be serialized. Server logic may remain behind a public model
operation; a portable or browser-local realization must separately satisfy its
target contract. Projection preserves the declared placement and communication
boundaries rather than pretending to translate arbitrary host code.

An opaque implementation exports a semantic contract. The contract states the
input and output meanings, relevant preconditions and postconditions, permitted
effects, and the assumptions on which dependent reasoning relies. Claims of
purity, determinism, termination, or bounded resource use are required only when
the enclosing guarantee depends on them. Their evidence must then be explicit.
No such property follows merely from the function's name or declared result type.

There are three complementary ways to establish a needed property:

- derive it from supported semantic definitions and checked inference rules;
- enforce an instance-specific premise at the appropriate runtime boundary;
- accept a named asserted contract under the applicable admission policy and
  retain it in every dependent claim.

These mechanisms may be combined within one operation. An opaque business
predicate need not prevent proof that a transition preserves an unrelated
field, that a command identifier survives retries, or that a retired execution
cannot mutate a replacement owner. A conclusion that depends on that predicate
implementing the intended policy remains conditional on its contract.

*** Ordinary Clojure behind an explicit semantic interface

The following sample Organization policy requires the helper to hold the skills
listed for the Request's category and requires claiming to be enabled. This is
an illustrative policy for the example, not a mandatory HumanHelp product rule.
HumanHelp's actual policy remains application-owned.

#+begin_src clojure
(defn organization-allows?
  [{:keys [organization membership request]}]
  (let [policy (:organization/policy organization)
        required (get-in policy
                         [:skills-by-category (:request/category request)]
                         #{})
        held (set (:membership/skills membership))]
    (and (= :enabled (:claim policy))
         (every? #(contains? held %) required))))

(def organization-claim-policy-contract
  {:contract/id :organization/claim-policy
   :inputs {:organization Organization
            :membership Membership
            :request Request}
   :returns :boolean
   :state-inputs #{:organization/policy
                   :membership/skills
                   :request/category}
   :effects #{}
   :meaning
   {:true-iff [:and
               [:policy/claim-enabled]
               [:membership/holds-required-category-skills]]}})

(def organization-claim-policy-binding
  {:contract organization-claim-policy-contract
   :implementation #'organization-allows?
   :assertions
   [{:id :organization/policy-implementation-contract
     :proposition [:implementation/refines-contract
                   :organization/claim-policy]
     :owner :humanhelp/model-maintainer}
    {:id :organization/policy-effect-contract
     :proposition [:implementation/has-no-undeclared-effects
                   :organization/claim-policy]
     :owner :humanhelp/model-maintainer}]})
#+end_src

The two symbolic policy clauses refer to the displayed policy meaning: claiming
is enabled, and every required category skill is held. The contract vocabulary
and binding syntax are illustrative. Admission must resolve each symbol and
schema, validate its interface, and bind the assertions to the exact contract,
implementation realization, and applicability scope. Merely placing an
assertion map next to a function is not admission.

The framework can check declared argument/result categories and the surrounding
operation's use of them. It can evaluate the function on bound current inputs.
It must not label the implementation's policy correctness or lack of hidden
effects proved solely because those declarations are well formed.

For this effect-free contract, the declared state inputs determine which
authoritative facts must be protected when its result is used to authorize a
new commit. Data obtained before submission is suitable only when the commit
mechanism validates all relevant dependencies or recomputes the decision under
an equivalent atomic contract. A caller assertion that a pre-read is current
does not close that race.

An effectful computation instead declares its effects and their realization
boundaries. External service calls, clocks, randomness, mutable process state,
and asynchronous completion must not be hidden inside a contract claiming
deterministic evaluation over supplied values. Full-language support permits
these operations; their semantics and assumptions remain explicit.

*** A small authoring surface and a richer internal representation

Application authors provide domain meaning and genuine implementation choices.
Gesso derives the information it can derive soundly, including references,
footprints for supported expressions, obligations, and evidence dependencies.
Generated artifacts must be independently validated at their required boundary.

For opaque code, a declared effect or read footprint is an explicit contract,
not automatically an exact static analysis result. The assembly must retain
the evidence or assumption that connects it to the implementation. Where a
managed capability or candidate validator enforces a narrower property, that
property can have stronger evidence without upgrading the rest of the contract.

Ordinary authors must not have to write theorem-prover languages, proof DAGs,
transitive certificate maps, or hand-maintained copies of derivable metadata.
Proof-producing elaboration and dedicated checking belong inside Gesso.
Explicit data and ordinary functions are the canonical authoring basis; helper
macros may improve ergonomics but must not define a competing semantic system.

** Design priority and dependency direction

Gesso is organized around a strict distinction between semantic truth,
distributed coordination, physical realization, and evidence about that
realization.

At the highest level:

| Layer | Responsibility |
|-------+----------------|
| Domain model | Own business meaning and authoritative state transitions |
| Public model operations | Expose admitted operations and their contracts |
| Global choreography | Coordinate operations and participant knowledge |
| Role projections | Derive actor-local machines from the choreography |
| Executable plans | Carry canonical executable semantics and identities |
| Runtime realization | Perform declared effects through adapters and transport |

Evidence flows alongside this path:

Declarations export normalized semantic interfaces. Checking derives and
validates their obligations. Certificates, proof sidecars, and explanations
record the resulting judgments, evidence, and premises.

Evidence may justify acceptance of an executable artifact, but evidence does not
become an executable authority channel.

That distinction separates *admission evidence* from *runtime authority*.

A certificate, derivation, proof sidecar, exact artifact digest, preflight
report, or other assurance artifact may establish that an =ExecutablePlan= was
constructed from the declared semantics, depends on the expected semantic
interfaces, satisfies the checks claimed for it, and is therefore eligible to
run.  Once admitted, however, that evidence does not grant the running program
new principals, permissions, authoritative facts, capabilities, branch
discriminators, or current authorization.

For example, a certificate may establish:

#+begin_quote
A new incorporation of this Claim command can occur only through a declared
path requiring its current claim-authority premise. A compatible replay reaches
its recorded result through a separately declared disclosure-authority check.
#+end_quote

The certificate does not establish:

#+begin_quote
This particular HTTP request is currently made by principal P and P is currently
authorized to claim Request R.
#+end_quote

Those concrete premises still come from trusted authentication, current model
state, runtime authorization, and other declared runtime boundaries.


A fuller HumanHelp Claim slice makes that separation visible in code. The
operation is defined once and reused by later assembly and view examples.
The declaration syntax is illustrative; its distinctions are required.

#+begin_src clojure
(def ClaimInput
  [:map [:request/id uuid?]])

(def claimable-rule
  {:rule/id :request/new-claim-allowed
   :inputs {:principal Principal
            :arguments ClaimInput
            :request Request
            :membership Membership
            :organization Organization}
   :returns :boolean
   :expression
   [:and
    [:= [:request/id :request] [:request/id :arguments]]
    [:= [:membership/user-id :membership] [:user/id :principal]]
    [:= [:membership/organization-id :membership]
        [:request/organization-id :request]]
    [:= [:organization/id :organization]
        [:request/organization-id :request]]
    [:= [:request/status :request] :open]
    [:= [:membership/status :membership] :active]
    [:no-conflicting-active-primary-assignment :request]
    [:call :organization/claim-policy
     {:organization :organization
      :membership :membership
      :request :request}]]})

(def claim-request
  {:operation/id :request/claim
   :actor :helper
   :input ClaimInput
   :entry-knowledge [[:knows? :helper [:request/id]]]

   :invocation
   {:requires [:authenticated-principal :admitted-command-binding]
    :model-operation :request/claim}

   :new-incorporation
   {:guard claimable-rule
    :policy-binding organization-claim-policy-binding
    :transition
    {:request {:status :claimed}
     :primary-assignment
     {:effect :establish-active-primary
      :request [:request/id :arguments]
      :helper :authenticated-principal}
     :preserve [:unrelated-request-fields
                :unrelated-assignment-facts]}
    :atomic-with [:command/result-record
                  :required-durable-publication-intent]

   :repetition
   {:binding [:operation :semantic-arguments :principal :authority-scope]
    :requires :command/result-disclosure-authority
    :result :permitted-recorded-outcome
    :incorporate-again? false}

   :effect
   [:model/invoke :request/claim
    {:request-id [:request/id :arguments]
     :principal :authenticated-principal
     :command-id :gesso/command-id}]

   :provisional
   {:view :request/claiming
    :owner :gesso/execution-id
    :correlate :gesso/command-id}

   :settlement
   {:accepted
    {:learns [:command/recorded-success :gesso/command-id]
     :reacquire [:request/card [:request/id :arguments]]}
    :rejected
    {:learns [:command/typed-rejection :gesso/command-id]
     :reacquire [:request/card [:request/id :arguments]]}
    :unknown
    {:recover [:request/reconcile-claim
               {:request-id [:request/id :arguments]
                :command-id :gesso/command-id}]}}})
#+end_src

=:actor= describes a semantic participant position; it does not authenticate a
browser. Schema names denote admitted domain interfaces. Their relationship
fields are shown explicitly so that a same-shaped Membership or Organization
cannot be substituted merely because it is active or has a permissive policy.
An implementation may establish these bindings through checked acquisition
contracts, explicit guards, or both; the obligation is not optional.

This declaration is a *semantic sketch*, not a parsed Part IX rule or an
available Gesso constructor. In particular, its field-path forms, the
=:no-conflicting-active-primary-assignment= condition, and =[:call ...]=
are not operators in Part IX's closed reader-based rule grammar. To make a
typed-rule claim, Gesso must use that grammar with a supported, checked
elaboration from the source meaning. Otherwise those obligations remain
explicit opaque contracts with their applicable implementation premises.
Neither a familiar-looking vector nor arbitrary host evaluation can substitute
for rule checking. The illustration does not assert that such an elaborator
already exists.

The Organization policy call represents the contract defined above. Its
interface and result category can be checked, but policy correctness and
effect behavior remain conditional on its named implementation assertions
unless stronger corresponding evidence is supplied.

This is the self-Claim variant: the trusted actor is also the intended helper.
Reassign and manager-assisted Claim require separate actor/target-helper
authorization and eligible Membership conditions. Real helper responsibility
belongs to the production RequestAssignment model, not a fabricated
=:request/helper= field. The transition sketch describes a Request status change
and establishment of an active primary assignment under the appropriate
relationship and absence/uniqueness guards. It does not define physical
RequestAssignment fields or XTDB lowering. Those belong to the public production
model and its qualified authoritative realization, with a complete frame and
durable publication intent.

The guard belongs to new incorporation. It is not a precondition for recognizing
an already incorporated command. Otherwise a successful retry would be rejected
because its own first incorporation changed the Request from open to claimed.
Disclosure of a recorded result has its own current authorization policy; it
must not be confused with permission to perform a new claim.

Verification of the declaration produces claim-specific evidence. For example:

| Proposition | Required evidence and scope |
|-------------+-----------------------------|
| The new-claim guard is well typed | Dedicated semantic checking over its declared inputs and policy-call interface |
| New incorporation requires the guard and excludes a competing primary assignment | A checked reachability/transition argument over the admitted operation semantics and protected assignment relations |
| Role projection does not create Claim authority | A checked distributed-admissibility/projection judgment over the supported semantics; current authority still requires trusted enforcement |
| Compatible replay does not incorporate again | A checked command-protocol argument, conditional on the authoritative command-record contract |
| Replay disclosure requires its own authority | Checked semantic requirement plus concrete runtime enforcement |
| The declaration covers accepted, rejected, and unknown settlements | Exhaustive checking over that finite declared outcome set |
| The policy implementation realizes its contract | The named assertion unless stronger corresponding evidence is supplied |

These are separate judgments. A certificate may collect them only with their
actual evidence, scope, and premises. Merely emitting the table as a map does
not establish any row. A rule checker cannot decide whether Alice's future
Membership is active, and a plan proof cannot by itself establish that an
independently written handler enforces its declared guard.

A trusted invocation boundary binds the concrete caller and passes the command
to the public authoritative model operation:

#+begin_src clojure
(defn invoke-claim!
  [{:keys [session now] :as ctx}
   {:request/keys [id] :gesso/keys [command-id]}]
  (let [principal (auth/current-principal! session)]
    ;; The admitted model binding validates the command envelope and owns
    ;; replay, current disclosure permission, and new-incorporation guards.
    (request-model/claim!
      (assoc ctx :biff.fx/now now :principal principal)
      {:request-id id :command-id command-id})))
#+end_src

The context is supplied through the admitted server binding. The principal does
not come from the command body. The public model operation must establish the
relationship between the principal and the Membership it uses, rather than
trust a browser-supplied helper identifier.

*** Claim command identity, replay, and uncertainty

Before the command's first possible submission, its command boundary allocates
a stable =:gesso/command-id=. Its allocation may be local or use an earlier
trusted issuance protocol. Allocating the bytes is separate from establishing
their trusted binding. At the authoritative boundary, authentication and command
admission establish or validate the operation, canonical semantic arguments,
principal, and authority scope to which the identity is bound. The binding must
be compatible with the admitted operation version. Browser-carried bytes alone
confer no authority.

A retry preserves that command identity. A new transport attempt has a new
transport-request identity, and a new presentation execution has its own
execution and resource-instance identities. Neither changes which command is
being reconciled.

The public =request-model/claim!= operation checks for a compatible recorded
command before interpreting the Request as a new claim. It validates the
recorded binding and current permission to disclose the result. A permitted
successful replay returns the recorded success without another transition,
including when the Request is now claimed or has subsequently changed again.
Incompatible identity reuse is rejected without disclosing another principal's
record or outcome.

For new incorporation, the Request identity and state, the principal's active
Membership, the Organization identity and policy, the absence of a conflicting
active primary assignment, and every relevant relationship or predicate
dependency are protected by the same atomic contract as the Request/assignment
changes, successful command-result record, and required durable publication
intent. A pre-read may prepare a candidate; it cannot replace commit-time
protection of those facts.

Two attempts can both initially observe no command record. If one commits and
the other's guard fails, the failing attempt must use the command protocol to
determine whether the same command was incorporated concurrently. It must not
report a fresh domain rejection merely because its attempt lost a race.
Similarly, absence observed at one read basis does not establish that an
outstanding attempt cannot later commit. Part IV owns the authoritative
resolution, retry, retention, and terminal-rejection contracts.

Part IV distinguishes model outcomes =:committed=, =:rejected=,
=:already-incorporated=, and =:commit-unknown=. This example presents
=:accepted=, =:rejected=, or =:unknown= to the participant:

| Model outcome | Presentation settlement |
|---------------+-------------------------|
| =:committed= | =:accepted= when permitted successful command evidence is delivered |
| =:rejected= | =:rejected= when an authoritative typed rejection for the applicable command scope is delivered |
| =:already-incorporated= | The permitted recorded result; recorded success maps to =:accepted= without a second transition |
| =:commit-unknown= | =:unknown= until authorized outcome evidence resolves it |

A delivery failure may leave the participant uncertain even after a commit.
Conversely, accepted command evidence establishes that the command succeeded at
its recorded point; it does not establish that the Request is still owned by
that helper at every later observation. Current presentation comes from an
authorized acquisition with its own basis and scope. Reading a currently
claimed Request does not by itself identify the command that claimed it.

The assembly checks these mappings and the required acquisition/reconciliation
paths. Acquisitions still enforce current read permission and must represent
denial, absence, or an unavailable dependency under their declared contracts.
Neither accepted nor rejected settlement grants a new right to read the card.

An admitted Claim plan may have strong structural and transition guarantees
while remaining conditional on a policy assertion, an authentication boundary,
or a qualified backend contract. Production correspondence must establish which
realization enforces those requirements. A certificate cannot manufacture the
principal, Membership, Request state, Organization policy, or current authority.
Sending it back from the browser adds no authority.

#+LATEX: \newpage

The two decisions remain separate:

| Stage | Basis of the decision |
|-------+-----------------------|
| Artifact admission | Appropriate proof, checking, and preflight evidence under the admission policy |
| Concrete execution | The admitted runtime semantics and current trusted premises |
| Authority decision | The applicable principal, resource, policy, scope, and current state |

The following inference is forbidden:

#+begin_quote
A certificate says "valid", so the runtime grants authority, accepts a current
fact, or selects a semantic branch without establishing its required premises.
#+end_quote

This applies more broadly than authorization.  Assurance evidence must not
secretly decide which role the current user has, which principal is
authenticated, whether a current authoritative fact is true, whether a stale
basis is acceptable, which settlement is canonical, or what transaction should
commit.

A separately declared runtime credential, observation receipt, or other evidence
protocol may supply a runtime premise only through its own trusted validation
contract, with its subject, scope, applicability, and authorization meaning made
explicit. That is a distinct runtime input category. It does not turn a proof
sidecar, build report, or matching artifact hash into authority.

Proof and diagnostic sidecars are therefore runtime-nonsemantic.  Running the
same =ExecutablePlan= with or without a matching read-only sidecar must produce
the same semantic transitions and abstract effects, modulo diagnostics.
Evidence explains or justifies why an executable was accepted; it does not
become a bearer capability or an alternate semantic control path.

The dependency direction is intentional:

- application business meaning belongs in application models;
- choreography coordinates use of public model semantics;
- projection derives local behavior from the global choreography;
- runtime code executes projected behavior;
- proof/checking artifacts explain why construction was accepted;
- physical browser, network, database, and process mechanisms realize declared
  effects under explicit assumptions.

A lower layer must not acquire higher-level meaning merely because doing so
would make an implementation convenient. For example:

- a DOM node does not become a semantic Request merely because it has an id;
- a web node does not become Request authority merely because it handles the
  request;
- a browser-supplied principal id does not become authenticated identity because
  it has the expected shape;
- a map with =:verified? true= does not become a verified choreography;
- a matching hash does not establish the truth of the proposition represented
  by the hashed artifact;
- a Live invalidation does not establish the changed authoritative fact;
- a rendered button does not confer authorization to execute its operation.

#+LATEX: \newpage

** Normative language

This design uses the following terms deliberately.

- *MUST* or *must* identifies a correctness requirement of the intended design.
- *MUST NOT* or *must not* identifies behavior that would violate the intended
  correctness boundary.
- *SHOULD* or *should* identifies the ordinary design path.  Deviations require
  a concrete reason and must preserve the relevant invariants.
- *MAY* or *may* identifies an implementation freedom that does not change the
  semantic contract.
- *proved* is reserved for mechanically established properties under named
  assumptions.
- *verified* may also describe a mechanically checked closed construction whose
  result is not claimed as a theorem over an explicitly formalized semantic
  relation.  The result classification must remain precise.
- *trusted* does not mean "probably correct."  It means the proposition is
  outside the proof currently being claimed and is accepted as an explicit
  assumption.

A green test suite never silently upgrades a tested property into a proved
property.

A successful schema validation never silently upgrades a value into trusted
authority.

A valid certificate identity never silently upgrades the certificate's claims
into truth unless an appropriate checker has accepted the certificate under the
premises and evidence classification attached to those claims.

*** Interpretation of examples and implementation freedom

Examples illustrate the enclosing contract. Their concrete syntax is
illustrative unless the owning section explicitly defines it as the required
public or wire representation. Their stated required behavior must still obey
the normative invariants.

Examples using symbolic operators must identify their semantic contract and
whether they denote checked expressions, runtime premises, opaque calls, or
inspection output. Unknown operators and unresolved references are construction
errors; illustrative syntax is not permission to accept arbitrary forms.

An abbreviated diagram does not waive an authorization, admission, scope,
ownership, or outcome-attribution condition merely because the diagram omits
that step. Worked examples must identify consequential policy choices instead
of silently selecting behavior that the specification leaves open.

The implementation may choose a representation or mechanism where the design
allows alternatives. It must state which supported contract was chosen and
provide evidence appropriate to the resulting claim. Implementation freedom
does not permit silent weakening of a required capability or assurance class.

A contradiction between normative passages is a specification defect to be
reconciled at the owning section. It is not permission to select whichever
passage makes an implementation easier to accept.

A declared recovery path establishes available modeled behavior. It does not
by itself establish that the environment will cause that path to execute or
that every execution terminates. Liveness claims retain their named premises.


** Correctness scopes

The system intentionally combines several correctness scopes.  No one scope
subsumes the others.

*** Domain correctness

Application models define domain meaning.

Examples include:

- whether a Request may be claimed;
- whether a Membership is active;
- whether an Organization permits an operation;
- what a "reconciled" claim outcome means;
- which facts must be protected atomically at commit time.

Gesso may check that a rule expression is well typed, that a declared operation
contract composes with its dependencies, and that the distributed execution
respects that contract.  Gesso does not infer whether the Organization chose
the right business policy.

*** Choreographic correctness

Choreo defines and checks distributed coordination around public semantic
operations.

It reasons about:

- participating roles;
- principal and authority requirements;
- knowledge;
- provenance;
- communication;
- authoritative observation;
- branch discriminators;
- provisional state;
- command and execution identity;
- settlement;
- resource ownership;
- convergence;
- failure and recovery;
- projection into role-local behavior.

*** Runtime correctness

Runtime code realizes the checked semantics.

It must preserve:

- semantic identities;
- execution-instance identity and declared resource-instance ownership;
- stale-work rejection;
- correlation;
- progression requirements;
- resource lifetimes;
- provisional-versus-authoritative distinctions;
- permitted machine transitions;
- transport and server realization.

*** Whole-application closure

Individually valid components can still form an impossible application.

The assembled application therefore has its own closure boundary.  For an authoritative browser command, a rendered
semantic affordance must have a coherent path through the applicable application
boundaries:

| Closure step | Required relationship |
|--------------+-----------------------|
| Affordance | Resolves to the declared semantic operation and valid arguments |
| Choreography | Supplies an admitted trajectory for that operation |
| Projection | Produces the required actor-local plan |
| Browser artifact | Realizes that plan under the admitted compatibility contract |
| Transport | Reaches the declared trusted server capability |
| Model binding | Invokes the public authoritative operation with bound inputs |
| Outcome handling | Preserves typed settlement and progression obligations |
| Acquisition | Obtains a permitted authoritative successor under current read authority |
| Presentation | Renders that successor through the admitted ownership and lifecycle rules |

This is the path for the stated browser-command case. A read-only operation,
subscription, background task, or workflow with no browser presentation has its
own declared effects, outcomes, and lifecycle; it need not manufacture a browser
plan, domain write, or card reacquisition. Closure checks follow the obligations
of the declared operation kind.

Later parts of this design specify that closure in detail. Its inclusion here
establishes an important foundational rule: local correctness does not imply
whole-application correctness.

*** Three distinct application assurance claims
:PROPERTIES:
:CUSTOM_ID: req-application-assurance-claims
:END:

Whole-application assurance separates three claims that are related but not
interchangeable.

| <18> | <41> | <41> |
| Claim | What it establishes | What it does not establish |
|-------+---------------------+----------------------------|
| Declared closure | Required relationships among the application elements within the declared assembly scope are checked | That every intended product capability was declared |
| Production enforcement | Actual supported execution passes through the boundaries that make the declared checks effective | That every possible host-language escape hatch is impossible |
| Behavioral completeness | Required user capabilities and authoritative outcomes are present and usable | That their internal assembly is structurally closed unless closure is checked separately |

A self-consistent assembly can omit intended functionality.  Conversely, a
behaviorally successful path can exist while bypassing a checker that the design
claims is mandatory.  The three claims therefore reinforce one another without
collapsing into one another.

Assembly closure is always relative to declared scope.  Gesso cannot infer an
application author's missing business intention merely because the remaining
graph is closed.  Required product behavior therefore needs an acceptance basis
independent of the assembly's own declaration set.  That acceptance basis should
state user capabilities and authoritative outcomes rather than duplicate route
strings, operation registries, projected-plan identities, or other realization
metadata already owned by the assembly.

Production enforcement is a separate obligation.  A checker that correctly
rejects an isolated malformed fixture provides no application guarantee when the
real application path can bypass that checker.  Strong claims about an assembled
application must therefore identify the production boundary that makes the
relevant check effective.

Inside trusted host-language code, deliberate escape hatches may remain possible.
For example, trusted application code that intentionally obtains a lower-level
transaction capability may bypass the model/Gesso path.  The ordinary assurance
goal inside that trusted boundary is misuse prevention: supported application
construction should make accidental semantic bypass difficult, explicit, and
diagnosable. A deliberate departure from that supported path requires an
explicit boundary
and assurance scope. A raw writer can invalidate dependent invariants for later
operations over the affected state, not just the assurance of its own request.
The dependency graph must represent that impact. Ordinary opaque computation
inside a managed contract is not itself such a departure.

These distinctions are foundational for later HumanHelp acceptance:

#+begin_example
assembly closed
    !=
production path demonstrably enforced
    !=
all required HumanHelp capabilities present
#+end_example


One Claim implementation can be used to see all three application-level claims
without inventing three unrelated examples.

The author supplies operation declarations and independent realization choices.
The following source is an excerpt of an application declaration; named view,
acquisition, recovery, and artifact providers must be supplied by the surrounding
application. Admission rejects unresolved providers.

#+begin_src clojure
(def humanhelp-application
  {:assembly/id :humanhelp/web
   :operations [claim-request]
   :views [:request/card]
   :realizations
   {:request/claim
    {:model-implementation #'request-model/claim!
     :transport {:kind :http/post :path "/requests/claim"}}}
   :providers
   {:request/card request-card-provider
    :request/reconcile-claim claim-outcome-provider
    :browser/runtime gesso-browser-artifact-provider}
   :assurance-policy :humanhelp/managed-application})

(def humanhelp-assembly
  (assembly/prepare humanhelp-application))
#+end_src

The operation supplies its semantic identity, input, settlement, and recovery
requirements. The realization supplies a concrete model implementation and a
transport choice. Framework-owned plan, route, and capability identities are
derived and resolved; the author does not reproduce them in several registries.
The policy reference resolves to the application's declared admission policy.

Inspection can expose the expanded graph without making that graph a second
source of truth:

#+begin_src clojure
(assembly/inspect humanhelp-assembly)
;; illustrative derived output, not an author-maintained input:
{:assembly/id :humanhelp/web
 :operation :request/claim
 :edges
 [[:request/card :claim :request/claim]
  [:request/claim :plan :plan/request-claim]
  [:plan/request-claim :artifact :artifact/gesso-live]
  [:request/claim :transport :transport/trusted-post]
  [:transport/trusted-post :route :route/request-claim]
  [:route/request-claim :capability :server/request-claim]
  [:server/request-claim :model-operation :request/claim]
  [:request/claim :settlement :request/claim-settlement]
  [:request/claim-settlement :acquisition :request/card]
  [:request/claim-settlement :recovery :request/reconcile-claim]]}
#+end_src

A closure checker establishes relationships over the resolved sources:

#+begin_src clojure
(assembly/check humanhelp-assembly)
;; =>
{:result :accepted
 :evidence :assembly-verified
 :closed-edges
 [[:request/card :claim :request/claim]
  [:request/claim :choreography :request/claim]
  [:request/claim :plan/request-claim]
  [:plan/request-claim :artifact/gesso-live]
  [:request/claim :transport/trusted-post]
  [:transport/trusted-post :route/request-claim]
  [:request/claim :route/request-claim]
  [:route/request-claim :server/request-claim]
  [:server/request-claim :request/claim]
  [:request/claim :request/claim-settlement]
  [:request/claim-settlement :request/card]
  [:request/claim-settlement :request/reconcile-claim]]}
#+end_src

The checker must collect these entries from the actual admitted choreography,
projected plan, artifact bytes, route table, server binding, model operation,
settlement, and acquisition/recovery declarations. Copying plausible entries
into a disconnected map would show only that the map agrees with itself. The
accepted report is illustrative of a checker that resolves every referenced
source and validates the recorded edges. In this example, =:result :accepted=
reports only that the closure judgment succeeded for its checked subject. It
is not an admission handle, evidence of current authorization, or proof that
a serving host installed the checked realization. The managed issuer and
actual host-adoption boundary have separate obligations. A copied inspection
result can satisfy neither.

That still does not establish production enforcement. The actual startup and
request path must make the admitted assembly unavoidable for the claimed
supported path. Conceptually, production wiring might look like:

#+begin_src clojure
(defn start-humanhelp!
  [ctx]
  (let [prepared (assembly/prepare humanhelp-application ctx)
        admitted (assembly/admit! prepared)
        handler (routes/build admitted)]
    ;; The Biff integration owns installation and the before-serving gate.
    ;; Returning a handler in an unused map is not installation evidence.
    (biff-host/start!
      ctx
      {:biff.ring/handler handler
       :before-serving
       (fn [installed-runtime]
         (assembly/require-installed! admitted installed-runtime))})))

(defn claim-handler
  [ctx request]
  (let [binding
        (assembly/require-route-binding!
          (:admitted-assembly ctx)
          :route/request-claim)]
    (server/invoke-bound-operation! ctx binding request)))
#+end_src

Now the relevant malformed production fixture is not merely passed to an
isolated checker. It is sent through the same startup boundary:

#+begin_src clojure
(deftest stale-artifact-prevents-startup
  (is
    (thrown-with-msg?
      clojure.lang.ExceptionInfo
      #"browser artifact does not realize admitted plan"
      (start-humanhelp!
        (assoc test-ctx
          :browser-artifact
          artifact-without-request-claim-plan)))))
#+end_src

The Biff-host calls are an illustrative integration contract, not additional
public Biff APIs. The integration must own the actual module lifecycle, final
handler installation, and ordering before requests are served. Checking a
detached route table or accepting an unused handler does not satisfy it.

The controlled defect supplies tested evidence for production enforcement of
this boundary. A corresponding valid startup and usable Claim path must also
succeed. Broader production enforcement requires the other applicable
boundaries to have their own evidence.

Behavioral completeness still needs an independent statement of what the user
must actually be able to do:

#+begin_src clojure
(def required-humanhelp-capabilities-excerpt
  [{:capability :request/create
    :eligible-scenario :authenticated-customer
    :required-outcome :request/created-and-visible-to-creator}

   {:capability :request/claim
    :eligible-scenario
    :authenticated-active-helper-sees-open-request
    :required-outcome
    :request/claimed-with-active-primary-assignment}

   {:capability :board/refresh
    :eligible-scenario
    :authenticated-viewer-clicks-refresh-with-no-advisory
    :required-outcome
    :authorized-current-board-observed-and-installed}

   {:capability :board/refresh
    :eligible-scenario
    :authenticated-viewer-clicks-refresh-with-pending-advisory
    :required-outcome
    :authorized-current-board-adopted-with-only-covered-debt-discharged}])
#+end_src

These entries are an excerpt for the Claim illustration, not HumanHelp's
complete required-capability basis. The two Refresh scenarios cover different
obligations. Explicit user permission can authorize a new scoped acquisition
without an advisory; a pending advisory does not itself authorize acquisition
and can be discharged only by sufficient, permitted, actually installed
observation. Mere response receipt does not satisfy either adoption outcome.

The Claim result means production Request claimed status *and* the appropriate
active primary RequestAssignment, not an invented helper field on Request.
The outcome keywords in these illustrative product-oracle entries are neither
new persisted status values nor implemented Gesso API names. The complete
independent acceptance basis and its operational milestone scope are specified
in [[#req-humanhelp-required-capabilities][Part VIII's required capabilities]].

If =:request/claim= is removed from both the view and the assembly, the remaining
assembly may still be perfectly closed. The independent capability list is what
prevents that self-consistent omission from being called complete.

Conversely, a hand-written =POST /claim= route may make a browser acceptance test
appear green while bypassing =assembly/admit!= and the declared Claim operation.
Behavior happened, but production enforcement of the claimed Gesso boundary was
not established.

The point of keeping all three claims separate is therefore practical rather
than terminological: each one catches a different way a plausible application
can "work" while failing the assurance statement the project intends to make.

*** Operational correctness

Formal semantics do not eliminate operational concerns.

Real-browser tests, fault injection, property tests, load tests, lifecycle
tests, and application acceptance remain necessary for:

- browser primitive assumptions;
- HTMX and EventSource/SSE behavior;
- compiler/runtime implementation correspondence;
- scheduler and timer behavior;
- memory and CPU characteristics;
- dependency outages and reconnect behavior;
- application-specific semantics;
- human-visible interaction behavior.

*** Required capabilities are independent of exposed capabilities

A milestone's behavioral acceptance must name the required user capabilities
and authoritative outcomes independently of the set currently exposed by the
implementation. Tests derived only from existing affordances cannot establish
that an intended affordance was not omitted.

For each required capability, acceptance must establish an eligible scenario in
which the intended interaction is usable and reaches its required outcome.
Relevant ineligible scenarios must establish the specified unavailability,
rejection, or recovery behavior. Marking every occurrence unavailable does not
satisfy a requirement to provide a usable capability.

An explicitly narrower milestone may defer a capability. Its scope must say so;
its completion must not be reported as completion of a broader milestone that
requires that capability. This specification distinguishes such deferral from
unavailability caused by current production model policy.

The independent acceptance basis owns user capabilities and outcomes. It must
not become a second registry of route strings, generated plan identities,
transport metadata, or model implementation already owned by the assembly.

#+LATEX: \newpage


** Assurance model
:PROPERTIES:
:CUSTOM_ID: req-assurance-classification
:END:

Gesso uses several kinds of evidence, and the design must not collapse them
under a single word such as =verified=, =safe=, or =proved=.

The governing question for every assurance claim is:

#+begin_quote
What proposition is being claimed, over what object, under what assumptions,
and what evidence justifies accepting it?
#+end_quote

Every claim has separately identifiable dimensions:

| Dimension | Required meaning |
|-----------+------------------|
| Proposition | The statement, variable bindings, quantifiers, and observation scope |
| Subject | The semantic interface and, where relevant, concrete implementation or artifact |
| Mechanism | Derivation checking, dedicated checking, runtime enforcement, testing, or an explicit assertion |
| Premises | Assumptions, dependency guarantees, and concrete premises required for application |
| Coverage | Supported language, bounds, abstractions, and correspondence relation |
| Applicability | Versions, configuration, validity conditions, and evidence that the claim still applies |
| Status | Established at the stated scope, accepted as a premise, open, contradicted, or inapplicable |

These dimensions need not appear as one literal map in every API, but they must
be recoverable in the assurance explanation. Conditionality and boundedness
qualify a claim; neither supplies an evidence mechanism. Several mechanisms can
support different parts of the same argument. There is no single total ranking
that turns all evidence into a universal confidence score.

A claim's *disposition*, its *evidence mechanism*, an individual check's
*result*, and the selected application's *admission or release decision* are
separate meanings. An established judgment states what its evidence actually
established within its quantification and observation scope. Its evidence may
be a proof, an exact finite check, or a completed test of expressly named
scenarios; sharing a claim disposition does not make those mechanisms equal.
A declared enforcement requirement is not evidence that the actual installed
host enforces it. A named trusted premise remains a premise even if policy
accepts it. Part XI's =:passed=, =:failed=, and other closed gate results
describe whether required checks completed at their scopes, not the semantic
strength of the propositions or the authority of their subjects.

The assurance model distinguishes:

1. properties established mechanically from explicit semantics or checked
   derivations;
2. premises enforced dynamically when a concrete execution meets the external
   world;
3. assumptions that remain outside the mechanically discharged core;
4. whole-application closure properties checked over assembled artifacts;
5. liveness claims whose validity depends on named environmental assumptions;
6. test evidence over trusted implementation boundaries and concrete systems.

These classifications are related, but they are not interchangeable.

For example:

#+begin_example
proved semantic property
!=
exact finite-state check
!=
closed application assembly
!=
runtime-enforced premise
!=
trusted assumption
!=
green integration test
#+end_example

A complete assurance argument may require several of them simultaneously.


A store checkout provides a useful worked example because one ordinary button
crosses nearly every assurance class without any one class subsuming the rest.

Suppose the semantic operation is declared approximately as:

#+begin_src clojure
(def place-order
  {:operation/id :checkout/place-order
   :actor :customer
   :input [:map [:cart/id uuid?]]
   :invocation
   {:requires [:authenticated-customer :admitted-command-binding]}
   :new-incorporation
   {:guard :cart/checkout-eligible?
    :requires [:bound-current-cart]
    :atomic-with :command/result-record}
   :repetition
   {:requires :command/result-disclosure-authority
    :result :permitted-recorded-outcome}
   :provisional
   {:view :checkout/submitting
    :owner :gesso/execution-id
    :correlate :gesso/command-id}
   :effect
   [:model/invoke :order/place
    {:cart-id [:cart/id :arguments]
     :customer :authenticated-customer
     :command-id :gesso/command-id}]
   :settlement
   {:accepted
    {:learns [:command/recorded-success :gesso/command-id]
     :reacquire [:order/by-command :gesso/command-id]}
    :rejected
    {:learns [:command/typed-rejection :gesso/command-id]
     :reacquire [:cart/current [:cart/id :arguments]]}
    :unknown
    {:recover [:order/reconcile-command :gesso/command-id]}}})
#+end_src

The command envelope supplies the stable command identity. Every presentation
execution and managed resource has its own applicable ownership identity.
Payment authorization, if required, is a separately declared external protocol;
a database transaction must not pretend to make a payment provider atomic with
an order write. The operation must define which provider outcome or durable
obligation permits order placement and how unknown external outcomes recover.

An assurance report during assembly may include both accepted claims and an
open progress obligation:

#+begin_src clojure
{:subject
 {:assembly :store/web
  :operation :checkout/place-order
  :plan :plan/checkout-place-order
  :artifact-digest "sha256:..."}

 :claims
 [{:id :checkout/rule-well-typed
   :proposition [:rule/well-typed :cart/checkout-eligible?]
   :status :established
   :evidence {:class :semantic-checked
              :mechanism :typed-rule-checker
              :result :check/cart-checkout-rule}}

  {:id :checkout/principal-required-at-runtime
   :proposition [:runtime/requires-current-principal
                 :checkout/place-order]
   :status :open-obligation
   :required-evidence
   {:class :runtime-enforced
    :boundary :server/authenticated-checkout-handler
    :obligation :actual-installed-boundary-correspondence}
   :premises #{:authentication/correct-principal-binding}}

  {:id :checkout/payment-provider-contract
   :proposition [:provider/validated-acceptance-means
                 :payment-authorized]
   :status :accepted-as-premise
   :evidence {:class :trusted
              :owner :external/payment-provider
              :assumption :payment/provider-contract-v4}}

  {:id :checkout/application-path-closed
   :proposition [:application/closed-path :checkout/place-order]
   :status :established
   :evidence {:class :assembly-verified
              :report :assembly/store-web-A12}}

  {:id :checkout/browser-realization-tested
   :proposition [:implementation-corresponds-in-scenarios
                 :checkout/place-order
                 #{:accepted :rejected :unknown}]
   :status :established
   :coverage {:scenarios #{:accepted :rejected :unknown}}
   :evidence {:class :tested
              :suite :chromium/checkout-lifecycle}}

  {:id :checkout/retry-eventually-recovers
   :proposition [:eventually [:checkout/settled-or-reconciled]]
   :status :open-obligation
   :environment-premises
   #{:eventual-provider-availability
     :eventual-authoritative-read
     :continued-participant-execution
     :fair-recovery-scheduling}
   :required-evidence :checked-progress-argument
   :evidence []}]}
#+end_src

Names in this report resolve to source-bound evidence or accepted premises;
they are not self-authenticating flags. In particular, the authentication row
is an *open physical enforcement obligation*. Naming a server boundary does
not establish that an actual running handler adopted it, and neither this
declaration nor a test of an isolated checker supplies a principal for a
future request. Actual adoption needs its own evidence under Part VII.

The browser row's =:established= disposition concerns only the expressly
listed scenarios and their completed, source-bound test evidence. Its
=:tested= evidence class does not prove universal browser correspondence,
and a suite name alone is not evidence that a current test ran or passed.
This row would remain open if the required run or artifact binding were
unavailable. The example's status labels illustrate these distinctions;
they do not introduce a rival schema for Part XI release-gate results.

The last row is deliberately open. Naming environmental premises is not a
progress proof. A release whose acceptance policy requires that progress
argument cannot claim completion from this report. If a suitable argument is
later checked, its mechanism and scope replace the open status while its
environmental premises remain attached.

The report is deliberately heterogeneous. Consider what happens if each claim is
misread as another:

#+begin_src clojure
;; Wrong: a type-check result does not authenticate this request.
(when (checking/accepted? :check/cart-checkout-rule)
  (treat-request-as-authenticated! request))

;; Wrong: a green Chromium test does not prove the provider contract.
(when (tests/green? :chromium/checkout-lifecycle)
  (assume-provider-cannot-lie!))

;; Wrong: assembly closure does not imply eventual provider availability.
(when (assembly/closed? :store/web)
  (claim-unconditional-termination!))

;; Wrong: the trusted provider premise does not prove the browser adapter.
(when (trusted? :payment/provider-contract-v4)
  (claim-browser-correspondence-proved!))
#+end_src

The correct composition keeps the propositions separate. A downstream release
claim may depend on all of them, but the resulting explanation should still be
able to say exactly which part is mechanically checked, which is dynamically
enforced, which remains trusted, which is assembly evidence, which is tested,
and which is conditional on future environmental behavior.

That is what the assurance vocabulary is for. It is not a taxonomy applied after
the fact; it prevents evidence from silently acquiring a stronger meaning as it
moves through the application.

The classification belongs to the *claim and its evidence*, not merely to the
source file, namespace, subsystem, or tool that produced it.  A single
component may therefore participate in several assurance classes.

For example, the browser adapter may have:

- machine-checked transition invariants;
- runtime-enforced event normalization and plan-identity checks;
- trusted assumptions about DOM/browser primitives;
- Chromium integration tests providing tested evidence of implementation
  correspondence;
- conditional liveness claims requiring eventual event delivery.

The root assurance report must preserve these distinctions rather than reducing
them to a single boolean such as =verified?=.

Nominal or otherwise admitted semantic categories participate in this model but
do not add a new assurance class by themselves.  For example, an admitted
=VerifiedChoreography= value may be the product emitted after verification, but
its assurance comes from the verifier/checker and its stated premises, not from
the runtime type name.  Likewise, an =AuthoritativeObservation= representation
is authoritative only when the trusted acquisition path establishes that
provenance.

This distinction prevents the implementation convenience of nominal typing from
being mistaken for proof:

| Boundary | What acceptance establishes |
|----------+-----------------------------|
| Representation validation | The value has the permitted shape |
| Semantic-category admission | Supported code may treat the value as category C at this boundary |
| Checked judgment or certificate | The stated proposition follows under the recorded premises and mechanism |

Those stages may be represented by different types, by checked constructors, or
by other existing mechanisms.  Their assurance meaning remains distinct even
if an implementation combines some of the physical representations.

*** Admission policy and unresolved proof obligations
:PROPERTIES:
:CUSTOM_ID: req-admission-assurance-policy
:END:

Admission is a decision under a declared policy, not a synonym for proving every
application function. The policy identifies mandatory structural checks,
required evidence for particular claims, and which explicitly owned contracts
may remain asserted. The normal policy supports full-language implementations
while retaining their assumption dependencies.

Construction derives the obligations relevant to its declared claims and runs
the supported automated checks under an explicit resource policy. Results must
identify unsupported reasoning and exhausted checking budgets rather than omit
the obligation. An accepted assumption must not hide an available failed check.

Mandatory identity, interface, authority-source, effect-binding, and required
recovery checks cannot be disabled by adding an assertion. A named opaque
functional contract may be an accepted premise where policy permits it. The
result remains conditional; the premise is not marked discharged.

The checker and assembly must distinguish these outcomes:

| Outcome | Meaning and consequence |
|---------+-------------------------|
| Established judgment | The stated proposition follows by the identified mechanism over its stated scope |
| Accepted assumption | A named premise is permitted by policy and remains in dependent explanations |
| Unsupported proof fragment | The reasoning mechanism lacks a rule or representation; this does not establish that the program is false |
| Inconclusive check | A limit, cancellation, or tool failure prevented a result; no success may be inferred |
| Counterexample | The checked model contains a violation; report its scope and whether concrete correspondence is established |
| Malformed declaration | Required semantic structure does not compose; reject construction |
| Failed runtime premise | A concrete execution cannot proceed on that premise; follow declared rejection or recovery |
| Inapplicable evidence | The subject, scope, dependency, or backend profile no longer matches; dependent acceptance requires re-establishment |

An unsupported or inconclusive proof obligation may be retained as an explicit
assumption only by a policy that permits that exact kind of premise and an
independently identified, scoped semantic or implementation contract whose
truth is being assumed. An exhausted proof budget, unavailable checker, or
unsupported expression is a checking outcome, not itself an assumption
asserting the original proposition. The policy must identify the original
obligation, selected weaker basis, affected dependent claims, and still-missing
evidence; a mandatory gate cannot be satisfied by renaming its failure.
The system must not silently convert a checker failure into trust. A known counterexample
cannot be erased by asserting the contradicted proposition under the same
claim. A correction to the specification, abstraction, implementation, or claim
scope must itself be explicit and checked as applicable.

The interface must make clear which obligations block admission and which
remain accepted premises. A component may be structurally admitted yet lack a
particular application theorem or release qualification. The root report must
not confuse these states.

*** Machine-checked semantic properties

A machine-checked semantic property is established mechanically from an
explicit semantic model, checked derivation, exhaustive semantic state space,
proof kernel, model checker, theorem prover, or another precisely identified
formal mechanism.

The important requirement is not the name of the tool.  The important
requirement is that the claimed proposition and the relationship between the
checked object and the production semantic object are explicit.

Candidate framework properties include:

- well-typed checked rule expressions;
- knowledge entailment;
- provenance entailment;
- authority derivation and non-escalation;
- message payload closure and knowledge-transfer constraints;
- behavior-sensitive branch knowledge;
- projection preservation for the supported language subset;
- declared resource invariants;
- progression algebra invariants;
- browser-adapter transition invariants;
- retired execution/resource isolation;
- semantic dependency compatibility;
- executable-plan provenance;
- certificate dependency consistency.

The individual phrases above name different judgments rather than one generic
notion of "verification":

- *Well-typed checked rule expressions.* The baseline Part IX checker admits
  only its closed, reader-based expression grammar. Referenced readers must be
  declared with compatible nominal types; operators require compatible operand
  types; enum values must belong to their declared domains; and optional or
  nullable values require the supported presence/non-nil refinements before
  operations that need them. Strict Boolean evaluation and short-circuit order
  are part of that grammar's semantics. An embedded arbitrary function call,
  relationship query, or case expression is not silently an operator in this
  baseline language.

  Richer semantic construction may use opaque calls, relational predicates,
  and closed case analysis through separately defined interfaces and checking
  judgments. Such a predicate must use valid endpoint types and a checked
  source-to-interface binding; closed case analysis must be exhaustive where
  required by its admitted language. Any elaboration into the closed rule
  language needs an explicitly checked translation. Otherwise the opaque
  implementation premises remain in every dependent claim. A named interface
  is not proof that its callable satisfies the declared policy or effect
  contract. These checks establish supported semantic well-formedness, not
  whether the product organization chose the intended rule. A coherent but
  undesirable policy remains representable.

- *Knowledge entailment.*  The checker asks whether a role is justified in
  knowing a semantic fact at the point where that fact is consumed.  Relevant
  sources include declared entry knowledge, communication, authoritative
  observation, checked deterministic derivation, and explicit trusted
  assertion.  Knowledge does not arise merely because a value happens to exist
  in a host-language map, another role knows the fact, the browser physically
  received related data, or an undeclared field survived serialization. A
  static knowledge judgment assumes its named entry/acquisition/communication
  premises; it does not prove that an actual browser message was authenticated
  or that an authoritative observation was acquired for this execution.

- *Provenance entailment.*  The checker asks whether the claimed source or
  epistemic strength of a fact follows from the path through which the fact was
  obtained.  A browser-supplied value is not an authoritative observation
  merely because it has the same shape or value.  A fact learned by
  communication does not automatically become an independent authoritative
  observation.  Any strengthening of provenance must be an explicit semantic
  rule rather than an inference from physical message origin.

- *Authority derivation and non-escalation.*  Every authority or capability
  consumed by a semantic step must arise from an explicit trusted/runtime
  premise or an allowed checked derivation.  Untrusted input, mere knowledge,
  provenance labels supplied by the browser, possession of a rendered
  affordance, possession of a URL, or successful schema validation cannot
  silently manufacture stronger authority.  Principal, resource, scope,
  operation, and authority identity remain part of the judgment, so authority
  over one resource cannot be reused for another merely because their
  representations have the same shape.

  The framework-level claim is not "Alice is currently authorized to claim
  Request R."  That concrete fact normally depends on runtime authentication
  and current model state.  The machine-checkable claim is closer to:

  #+begin_quote
  No admitted semantic execution may consume claim authority unless the
  required authority premise is present through a declared trusted/runtime
  source or permitted derivation, and no weaker or untrusted fact can silently
  manufacture stronger authority.
  #+end_quote

#+LATEX: \newpage

  The following inference is invalid:

  #+begin_quote
