  The browser says that its role is helper, therefore it has helper authority.
  #+end_quote

  A valid new-incorporation path instead establishes the relevant premises:

  | Establishing boundary | Required premise |
  |-----------------------+------------------|
  | Trusted authentication | This invocation represents principal P |
  | Bound authoritative state | The Membership belongs to P and the applicable Organization |
  | Atomic new-incorporation guard | Membership, Request, Organization policy, and their relationships permit this transition for P |
  | Authoritative operation | Incorporation is permitted only under those current guarded premises |

  Every establishing edge must have the appropriate declared evidence and
  current runtime enforcement. An observation from an earlier basis does not
  silently satisfy a transaction-current premise.

- *Message payload closure and knowledge-transfer constraints.*  A semantic
  message defines the information flow permitted by one choreography
  communication boundary.  By default its semantic payload is closed: only
  fields declared by the message contract participate in the semantic message.
  Physical transport metadata may accompany the message, but it does not
  silently become choreography knowledge.

  The checker should establish that every semantic payload field is declared,
  the sender has justified knowledge of every semantic fact it communicates,
  receipt introduces only the semantic facts declared by the message contract,
  provenance introduced by receipt follows the declared communication rule,
  and undeclared transport or implementation fields cannot become branch
  discriminators, authority premises, or arbitrary additions to choreography
  context.

  Conceptually:

  #+begin_example
  receiver knowledge after receive
      =
  receiver knowledge before receive
      +
  declared semantic consequences of message
  #+end_example

  rather than:

  #+begin_example
  receiver knowledge after receive
      =
  receiver context merged with arbitrary incoming map
  #+end_example

  An explicitly extensible payload may be supported where required, but the
  semantic status of extension data must remain explicit.  For example,
  extension data may be transported opaquely without automatically creating
  first-class choreography facts.  Payload closure is therefore distinct from
  ordinary Malli shape validation: Malli may establish that a value has the
  expected structure, while choreography checking establishes which
  information that communication is semantically allowed to transfer.

- *Behavior-sensitive branch knowledge.*  A role must know enough to
  distinguish branches before its observable behavior diverges between those
  branches.  If a role behaves identically in both alternatives, it need not
  learn a choice solely because the condition occurs in the global
  choreography.  If its behavior differs, the verifier must justify knowledge
  of the discriminator through an allowed path. The evidence must refer to
  the applicable subject, decision, scope, and continuation: observing a
  Request's current status does not by itself establish which historical
  command succeeded or which earlier branch was selected. This prevents both
  under-checking and needless communication introduced only to mirror global
  syntax.

- *Projection preservation.*  Projection relates the accepted global
  choreography to generated role-local machines.  Executions of those
  projected machines must remain within behavior admitted by the global
  choreography for the supported language subset.  Projection must not invent
  knowledge or authority, erase communication required for justified behavior,
  lose required resource constraints, admit forbidden branch behavior, change
  terminal/failure meaning, or introduce executions absent from the accepted
  global semantics. The preservation/refinement claim must state the
  supported language subset, direction of refinement, observable behavior,
  and treatment of internal steps. Safety refinement does not by itself
  establish liveness when internal divergence or unfair scheduling is
  possible; a progress claim has separate fairness and transfer obligations.
  Nor does correctness of generated local semantics prove that an adversarial
  browser or physical shell obeys those semantics.

- *Declared resource invariants.*  Where choreography semantics include
  resources, the checker may establish that a resource is used only after
  acquisition, exclusive ownership is not duplicated, transfers occur only
  through declared rules, release occurs according to the declared lifecycle,
  terminal paths do not retain resources that must be released, and stale or
  retired executions cannot retain semantic ownership.  Physical cleanup debt
  does not confer continuing semantic ownership.

- *Progression algebra invariants.*  Progression requirements form a semantic
  consistency algebra rather than an arbitrary collection of tokens.
  Canonicalization should be deterministic; composition must preserve every
  required authoritative constraint; weaker frontiers must not masquerade as
  satisfying stronger requirements; unrelated requirements must compose
  without destructive interference; contradictory or malformed requirements
  must be rejected; and normalization must not silently discard semantically
  relevant coordinates.  Concrete XTDB tokens remain runtime values even when
  the algebra governing their requirements is checked independently.

- *Browser-adapter transition invariants.*  The browser adapter is modeled as
  an explicit transition relation such as:

  #+begin_example
  AdapterStep
    (ExecutablePlan,
     AdapterState,
     NormalizedEvent)
        ->
    (AdapterState',
     AbstractEffects)
  #+end_example

  Candidate invariants include execution-instance isolation, resource-instance
  ownership, prevention of obsolete presentation being restored after justified
  authoritative supersession within the applicable observation scope,
  separation of provisional and authoritative state, immediate semantic
  retirement of obsolete work, scope-preserving acquisition requirements for
  queued refreshes, and terminal ownership/cleanup conditions.  The proof applies to the abstract
  transition semantics; separate implementation-correspondence evidence is
  required for the browser shell that normalizes concrete events and performs
  abstract effects.

- *Retired execution/resource isolation.* Once an execution instance or resource
  instance loses its relevant semantic ownership, a callback, timer, network
  result, settlement, continuation event, or delayed effect cannot use that
  retired ownership to resume execution or mutate a replacement owner's state.
  Admission identifies the event's declared owner and concrete resource instance;
  matching a reused logical target name is insufficient. Physical cleanup may
  occur later, and new logical ownership need not wait for every obsolete
  physical operation to disappear. Independently useful authoritative or
  command-outcome evidence may enter only through its separately declared
  admission path; it does not reactivate the retired owner.

- *Semantic dependency compatibility.*  A certified downstream artifact may
  depend only on upstream semantic interfaces whose guarantees satisfy the
  assumptions recorded when the downstream artifact was checked.  A
  same-shaped value, namespace, or source path is insufficient.  A relevant
  upstream semantic change must invalidate stale downstream certification
  rather than silently compose.

- *Executable-plan provenance.*  An accepted =ExecutablePlan= must remain
  traceable to the semantic inputs from which it was produced, including the
  accepted choreography, relevant semantic dependencies, projection target,
  and exact executable representation identity.  Executable identity is not
  itself a proof; it binds the executable object to the checking history and
  semantic inputs that produced it.

- *Certificate dependency consistency.*  A certificate may claim only
  guarantees justified by its checked derivation, certified dependencies,
  explicit assumptions/assertions, and the checker or proof-kernel rules applicable to
  its certificate class.  Certificates may not self-certify, depend on
  undeclared semantic inputs, silently accept stale dependencies, form
  unsupported circular justification, or claim stronger conclusions than
  their derivations establish.

"Machine checked" is deliberately broader than "formally proved."  Useful
result classifications include:

- *Kernel-checked or theorem-proved:* a proposition is accepted by a proof
  kernel or theorem prover from explicit premises and checked derivations.
  Acceptance of a particular derivation is relative to the admitted checker
  and proposition encoding. A universal soundness theorem for that checker
  is a separate claim unless independently established and related to the
  actual production checker. A finite per-derivation audit cannot silently
  stand in for that quantified theorem.

- *Exact finite-state checked:* a finite semantic state space is exhaustively
  explored and the property holds for every state/transition in that exact
  model.  This is stronger than sampled testing but is not automatically a
  theorem about an unbounded concrete system.

- *Abstraction-based machine proof:* an unbounded concrete claim may be
  justified through a finite or symbolic abstraction only when a stated
  abstraction/refinement argument shows that every semantically relevant
  concrete behavior is represented soundly by the abstraction.

- *Proof-producing elaboration:* a richer compiler or elaborator constructs
  derivations that are accepted by a smaller checker/kernel.  The elaborator
  does not become trusted merely because it emits proof-looking data; a buggy
  elaborator must be unable to convince the checker of an invalid conclusion.

Where the design calls a property *proved*, the proof claim must identify:

- the exact proposition;
- the formal or executable semantic model over which it is established;
- the assumptions/premises;
- the supported language subset;
- the observable/refinement relation where one is involved;
- any abstraction used to reduce an unbounded concrete domain;
- why that abstraction is sound for the claimed property;
- whether the result is bounded or unbounded;
- the checker, kernel, model checker, theorem prover, or proof mechanism;
- the identity/version of the checked semantic object where relevant;
- the relationship between the checked object and the production object;
- any implementation-correspondence assumption remaining outside the proof.

Passing generated examples is not by itself a proof.

Property-based testing is not by itself a proof.

Exhaustively checking a finite concrete truncation is not by itself an
unbounded proof.

A proof over an abstraction may support an unbounded claim only when the
abstraction/refinement argument justifies mapping all semantically relevant
concrete cases into that abstraction.

Bounding a count of requests, executions, or queue slots does not by itself
bound the information retained inside them or establish a finite semantic state
space. The claim must identify the state dimensions being bounded, the retained
data that remains unbounded if any, and the abstraction used for the property.

Conformance vectors generated from a formal model retain their actual evidence
class. Executing every generated vector is not proof that those vectors cover
all production inputs or derivations. Rule coverage alone is not a general
production/formal correspondence theorem. A stronger claim requires a stated
exhaustiveness or sound correspondence argument for its claimed domain.

The unqualified word =proved= must never be used merely to mean:

- unit tested;
- property tested;
- preflight accepted;
- schema valid;
- assembly closed;
- observed to work in Chromium.

Those may all be important evidence.  They are different evidence.

#+LATEX: \newpage

*** Runtime-enforced premises

Some semantic or proof premises can be discharged only when a particular
execution meets concrete external state.

Examples include:

- Malli value shape at external boundaries;
- authenticated principal binding;
- operation-registry lookup;
- route and capability correspondence;
- execution-instance identity and relevant resource-instance identity;
- command/correlation identity;
- projected-plan compatibility;
- browser-artifact identity;
- progression token/header decoding;
- current server-side authorization;
- authoritative basis interpretation;
- protected read/subscription authorization;
- concrete effect results;
- transaction outcomes;
- current model/entity existence;
- current membership or relationship state.

A runtime-enforced premise is best understood as:

#+begin_example
static semantic result:
    if premise P holds,
    transition T is admissible

concrete runtime:
    check P for this execution

if P succeeds:
    execute within proved/checked boundary

if P fails:
    reject or follow declared recovery semantics
#+end_example

Runtime enforcement connects the static result to a concrete execution only
when it establishes the required premise for the relevant subject, basis,
scope, and time. A pre-read followed by an unguarded write does not establish a
commit-time premise. A postcondition check after an irreversible effect cannot
be described as preventing that effect.

An instance check does not discharge a universally quantified implementation
contract. Validating one returned candidate does not prove that the callback
was pure, that it had no earlier hidden effect, or that it returns valid
candidates on every input. The enforcement mechanism and its correspondence to
the checked predicate are themselves part of the assurance argument.

For example, a static semantic result may establish:

#+begin_quote
A new incorporation of =:request/claim= requires an authenticated principal
and a transaction-current claim-authority premise. A replay requires the
compatible command binding and current disclosure authority instead.
#+end_quote

The runtime system must still establish which principal this HTTP request
actually represents and whether the model currently authorizes that principal
to perform the operation.

These are not second-class guarantees.  They are explicit dynamic boundaries
whose successful enforcement keeps concrete execution inside the premises of
the semantic result.

If a runtime premise fails, execution must reject, reacquire authority, restart
under a current plan, reauthorize, or follow another explicitly declared
semantic recovery path.  It must not silently weaken the operation.

In particular:

#+begin_quote
A required choreography premise fails, but the runtime performs an ordinary
weaker HTMX action anyway.
#+end_quote

is forbidden.

#+LATEX: \newpage


*** Trusted assumptions

Some propositions remain outside the currently mechanically discharged core.

Examples include:

- authentication middleware establishes the named principal correctly;
- the qualified XTDB backend profile supplies the specific guarded transaction,
  outcome, and consistency semantics on which the claim relies;
- an application model operation satisfies a semantic contract not yet
  discharged by a stronger model certificate;
- HTMX follows the documented lifecycle subset Gesso depends on;
- browser primitives implement the operations assumed by the browser effect
  shell;
- Clojure, ClojureScript, JavaScript, JVM, and compiler/runtime behavior
  preserve the implementation semantics assumed by the checker;
- cryptographic/hash primitives used for artifact identity or authenticated
  evidence satisfy their required engineering assumptions;
- operating-system/network primitives behave according to the explicitly
  assumed contract.

A trusted assumption is part of the trusted computing base for every
proposition that depends upon it.

An assumption is not a failure.

An invisible assumption is a failure of the assurance boundary.

Assumptions must therefore be named, classified, attached to the claims that
rely on them, visible in explanation/root assurance output, and narrowed or
discharged when stronger evidence becomes available.

Useful classifications include:

- =:authentication=;
- =:trusted-model-contract=;
- =:runtime-primitive=;
- =:external-library=;
- =:external-system=;
- =:compiler-runtime=;
- =:environment-liveness=.

*** Backend contracts and qualification
:PROPERTIES:
:CUSTOM_ID: req-backend-assumption-qualification
:END:

Gesso proves or checks its own semantic and realization properties relative to
explicit backend assumptions. A proof of XTDB's implementation is not required
to make such a conditional argument useful. The exact behavior relied upon must
nevertheless be stated and actively challenged by qualification evidence.

A backend profile records:

- backend product, exact version or build, and relevant configuration;
- Gesso adapter/lowering identity and supported transaction forms;
- value encodings, schema/storage mapping, and relevant time/basis semantics;
- the named assumptions on which each dependent claim relies;
- conformance cases, adversarial schedules, results, and their coverage limits;
- conditions requiring requalification or invalidating applicability.

The profile is derived from resolved dependencies and actual deployment
configuration. A manually entered version label or passing report for another
configuration does not qualify the deployment.

The contract must distinguish at least these obligations where a claim uses
them:

| Obligation | Required backend behavior and challenge |
|------------+-----------------------------------------|
| Atomic guarded transition | Relevant assertions and writes form the declared atomic operation; a failed assertion cannot leave a partial domain or ledger write |
| Current dependency protection | Point reads, cross-document relationships, absence, and predicate dependencies used for the decision receive the protection assumed by the proof |
| Write and frame semantics | Replacement, update, deletion, metadata, and missing-field behavior match the compiler's interpretation |
| Command incorporation | Domain effects and the compatible command-result record cannot be committed independently where the contract requires atomicity |
| Command exclusion and retention | Compatible concurrent attempts cannot incorporate twice; recorded binding, expiry, tombstones or other exclusion mechanisms have the declared lifetime and replay semantics, with result-disclosure retention distinguished from duplicate-prevention retention |
| Required publication intent | Where the operation promises durable advisory work, that intent is incorporated with the authoritative model effect and command record; provider atomicity does not itself prove dispatch or browser delivery |
| Outcome evidence | A reported committed or rejected result has the stated authoritative meaning; delivery failure remains distinguishable from rejection |
| Observation basis | Read tokens, visibility, valid/system time where relevant, and progression requirements have the stated scope and interpretation |

A generic claim of transactional support is insufficient. For example, two
blind writes and two guarded writes may have different conflict behavior. A
revision check protects a dependency only if all relevant changes advance the
revision under the accepted writer contract. A per-document check does not
automatically protect a predicate over a changing collection.

Qualification tests must be indexed by the assumption they challenge. Required
cases include conflicting guarded attempts, aborted writes, ledger/domain
agreement, missing and extra fields, concurrent changes to protected
relationships, incompatible or repeated command identities, result expiry
versus continued duplicate prevention, required outbox incorporation, outcome
loss, and basis-sensitive reads where applicable.
Independent expected results and deliberately weakened guards must demonstrate
that the suite can expose the relevant violation. Merely replaying the same
compiler logic as an oracle is insufficient independent evidence.

Finite testing cannot guarantee discovery of every possible backend violation.
Successful qualification supports an explicitly accepted backend premise; it
does not convert that premise into a theorem about all backend executions.
Part X specifies the required evidence scope and correspondence argument.

A relevant backend, adapter, configuration, encoding, or transaction-form change
requires requalification before the affected qualified claim is reused.
Contradictory evidence marks the premise violated; a mismatched or expired
applicability condition marks it unavailable. Both propagate to dependent
deployment claims. The system must identify the affected operations and apply
their declared admission or operational failure policy, rather than continue
advertising the old guarantee. Existing uncertain commands remain subject to
their outcome protocol; withdrawing qualification does not invent their result.

The conditional abstract theorem may remain valid when a backend violates a
premise. What becomes unavailable is its application to that realization.
Reports must distinguish theorem validity from deployment qualification.

An externally observable transaction-internal prestate is one possible evidence
mechanism, not a universal prerequisite. A valid realization argument may rely
on the specified atomic assertion/write semantics and a correct lowering under
the qualified contract. The proof obligation is semantic correspondence, not
possession of a particular internal snapshot token.

*** Application assertions

Application assertions remain distinct from framework/trusted implementation
assumptions.

An application may need to state semantic facts that Gesso cannot derive.  For
example:

#+begin_example
"this external identity provider is the authority for employee status"

"this role mapping is organizational policy"

"this third-party callback means payment has been accepted"
#+end_example

Such statements may be necessary premises.  They must not be represented as
though Gesso proved them.

An =:application-asserted= proposition remains an explicit premise until
evidence establishes that same proposition over the required scope. A runtime
check may discharge an invocation-specific premise; it must not be used to
silently discharge a universal implementation contract. If another accepted
assumption replaces a premise, the explanation retains that dependency rather
than reporting an assumption-free result.

This distinction is useful because:

#+begin_example
framework trusts browser primitive X
!=
application asserts business fact Y
#+end_example

Both are assumptions, but they have different owners and repair paths.

*** Assembly-verified properties

Some important propositions concern whether a finite collection of individually
valid artifacts forms one closed executable application.  These are naturally
checked as graph/assembly properties.

Examples include:

- every rendered semantic affordance names a declared semantic operation;
- every browser-managed semantic operation has its required projected plan;
- every browser plan has a corresponding compatible browser artifact;
- every operation requiring transport has a declared transport realization;
- every such transport resolves to its declared trusted boundary;
- every trusted capability resolves to the declared authoritative operation;
- required execution capabilities are supplied;
- settlement/progression obligations have declared realization paths;
- every managed fragment has initial authoritative content or an allowed
  acquisition path;
- every operation successor can be reacquired through an authorized
  authoritative path;
- no ordinary anonymous transport occupies a route reserved for a semantic
  operation;
- generated browser artifacts correspond exactly to the current assembly;
- the declared startup lifecycle orders required preflight before managed
  serving and names the actual installation boundary that must enforce it.

Assembly verification is mechanical, but it is useful to classify the result
separately from a semantic theorem. It establishes closure over a concrete
application graph. A closed graph and an internally consistent lifecycle
declaration do not prove that the running server installed that handler, that
its captured dispatch path cannot bypass the gate, or that all relevant
non-HTTP writers are covered. Those are distinct production-enforcement
obligations under Parts VII and X, and their unresolved status remains visible.

For example:

#+begin_example
choreography theorem:
    projected Claim respects knowledge requirements

assembly verification:
    this application's Claim button actually resolves to that plan,
    current browser artifact,
    route,
    server operation,
    settlement,
    and reacquisition path
#+end_example

Both can be true or false independently.

Assembly checks should therefore be classified with precise language such as:

- =:assembly-verified=;
- =:preflight-closed=;
- =:artifact-current=;

rather than being upgraded automatically to =proved=.

Where an assembly proposition is established by a formal proof mechanism, its
evidence may state that stronger result with the exact proposition and scope.
Ordinary graph checking does not acquire that classification by association.

#+LATEX: \newpage

*** Conditional liveness

Liveness is not an independent evidence mechanism.  It is a qualification on
propositions whose truth depends on future behavior of the environment.

A statement such as:

#+begin_quote
Every provisional claim eventually reaches a resolving outcome.
#+end_quote

is meaningful only relative to premises such as:

- required events are eventually delivered;
- authoritative dependencies remain reachable;
- required authoritative rereads eventually complete;
- participants continue executing;
- relevant clocks/timers eventually fire;
- retry policy continues where required;
- the application can recover from an incompatible stale projection;
- application-defined conflicts do not remain permanently unresolved;
- required external systems eventually respond where the claim depends upon
  them.

The claim should therefore have a form conceptually like:

#+begin_example
assuming:
    eventual event delivery
    eventual authoritative availability
    continued participant execution

prove/check:
    every admitted provisional state eventually reaches
    a resolving semantic state
#+end_example

The assumptions are part of the proposition. Removing them changes the
proposition.

For commands, recovery of an authoritative *current presentation* and
recovery of the *historical command disposition* are separate progress claims.
An authorized fresh Request/card read may repair provisional display without
identifying which command incorporated. Eventual attribution requires the
appropriate retained command evidence, compatible binding, continuing
disclosure permission, and an available reconciliation path; those premises
must not be smuggled into "eventual authoritative read." After expiry or lost
disclosure authority, the declared system may preserve an explicit unresolved
command status even when presentation converges. That is not evidence of
settlement to accepted or rejected. Likewise, when the product requires a
user-initiated Refresh, the user's eventual action is an environmental premise,
not something the scheduler can compel or derive from a pending advisory.

The design must distinguish:

- *reachability:* there exists a path to a terminal/resolving state;
- *deadlock freedom:* every reachable nonterminal state has an enabled modeled
  continuation; this does not by itself require that the continuation is taken;
- *fairness-dependent progress:* enabled progress eventually occurs under a
  fairness assumption;
- *environment-dependent convergence:* the system converges if specified
  external events eventually occur;
- *unconditional termination:* every execution terminates without such
  assumptions.

These are materially different claims.

The design must not call "there exists a path to terminal state" an
unconditional termination proof, nor hide network recovery, browser resumption,
user action, or external-system availability inside the word =eventually=.

*** Tested evidence

Tests remain a required assurance layer even where stronger semantic checking
exists.

Testing is particularly important for:

- implementation correspondence between semantic core and runtime shell;
- real JVM/Node/Chromium execution;
- HTMX/SSE lifecycle behavior;
- XTDB integration;
- browser primitive assumptions;
- HTTP/session/authentication integration;
- generated-artifact loading;
- fault injection;
- race schedules;
- reconnect behavior;
- load/resource behavior;
- multi-client HumanHelp behavior;
- multi-node realization once it exists.

Useful test classes include unit tests, property/generated tests, differential
tests, mutation tests, integration tests, adversarial tests, browser acceptance
tests, and load/fault tests.

Tests may provide very strong practical evidence.  They must nevertheless
remain classified as =tested= unless the particular procedure genuinely
exhausts the explicitly claimed semantic domain and is classified more
precisely, for example =exact-finite-checked=.

Thus:

#+begin_example
100,000 generated executions passed
#+end_example

does not mean:

#+begin_example
all executions satisfy the theorem
#+end_example

unless a separate argument establishes that the tested set is exhaustive for
the claimed semantic domain.

#+LATEX: \newpage

*** Composition of assurance claims

The most important property of the assurance model is that evidence composes
without losing its classification.

A downstream artifact should be able to say conceptually:

| Claim-plan dependency | Evidence and retained premises |
|-----------------------+--------------------------------|
| Rule well typed | Dedicated typed semantic check |
| Helper knows the Request identity | Checked knowledge derivation |
| New-incorporation authority | Checked semantic requirement and concrete atomic runtime enforcement |
| Model implementation contract | Proof where supplied; otherwise an explicitly accepted implementation premise |
| Projection preservation | Appropriate checked argument; a finite abstraction requires a sound refinement argument for an unbounded concrete claim |
| Browser realization closure | Assembly verification against actual admitted sources and artifacts |
| Browser shell correspondence | Stated implementation argument, trusted primitive contracts, and independently classified browser tests |

The resulting assurance claim must not erase those differences and simply say
"Claim is verified."

A stronger downstream result cannot silently upgrade a weaker premise.

For example:

#+begin_example
trusted model contract
    +
proved choreography rule
#+end_example

does not become:

#+begin_example
proved model implementation
#+end_example

The conclusion remains conditional on the trusted model contract.

Likewise:

#+begin_example
assembly verified
    +
browser test green
#+end_example

does not establish a projection theorem.

Each evidence class retains its identity through composition.

The root report should therefore expose what was proved, kernel-checked,
exact-finite checked, assembly-verified, runtime-enforced, trusted,
application-asserted, conditional on liveness assumptions, and supported by
testing.

#+LATEX: \newpage

*** Failure and repair interpretation

The assurance classification should tell the developer where repair belongs.

Typical relationships include:

| Failure | Owner of repair or interpretation |
|---------+-----------------------------------|
| Rule typing | Rule or domain declaration |
| Knowledge entailment | Justified information path or the consuming behavior |
| Authority derivation | Authority premise, binding, or policy boundary |
| Message payload closure | Message contract or undeclared information transfer |
| Projection preservation | Choreography, projector, or semantic definitions |
| Assembly closure | Application construction and bindings |
| Runtime authorization | The attempted concrete operation is not presently admissible |
| Contradicted assumption | The trusted boundary or applicability of the assumption |
| Browser failure despite a valid abstract theorem | Runtime correspondence or an assumed primitive |
| Missing liveness premise | The dependent progress conclusion is unavailable |

This is why precise assurance terminology is not cosmetic.  It makes a failed
claim point toward the layer that owns the repair.

*** Assurance-model invariant

The governing invariant is:

#+begin_quote
Every meaningful Gesso guarantee identifies the proposition being claimed, the
evidence supporting it, the premises on which it depends, and the boundary
between mechanically discharged facts and facts that remain runtime-enforced,
trusted, asserted, conditional, or tested.

No stronger assurance classification may be inferred merely because several
weaker forms of evidence happen to agree.
#+end_quote

The intended result is not that every statement becomes a formal theorem.

The intended result is that Gesso can state, mechanically and honestly, *why*
each accepted artifact or application is believed to be valid, what remains
outside that claim, and exactly where construction or execution must stop when
one of its premises fails.

#+LATEX: \newpage

** Semantic evidence vocabulary

The following vocabulary is shared by the later compositional hardening and
whole-application proof architecture.

It is defined here so later layers do not need to redefine what their evidence
means.

*** Identity and instance terminology

An identity names a particular semantic object or concrete instance. Its meaning
must be explicit wherever admission, ownership, compatibility, or evidence
binding depends on it. The canonical distinctions include:

- *Command identity:* the logical intent, which may survive multiple attempts.
- *Execution identity:* one concrete semantic execution of a choreography or
  operation; its relation to a command is explicitly declared.
- *Resource-instance identity:* one concrete timer, subscription, transport
  request, continuity capture, or other managed resource, distinct from its
  reusable logical resource/target name.
- *Transport-request identity:* one transport attempt, distinct from the domain
  object being acted upon and from the command it may carry.
- *Submission-attempt identity:* one attempt to incorporate a command at an
  authoritative boundary; one transport request need not imply exactly one
  backend attempt.
- *Capability-instance identity:* a concrete grant to perform a scoped action
  under its lifetime and usage contract; it is not the command identifier.
- *Admitted assembly generation:* the immutable application realization admitted
  together, including its routes, providers, prepared operations, and artifacts.
- *Compatibility identity/version:* the declared protocol or plan compatibility
  class, distinct from exact executable-artifact identity and from deployment.

A deployment may host multiple admitted assembly generations during a supported
transition. A deployment identifier, assembly generation, execution identity,
and resource-instance identity are not interchangeable coordinates.

Use =generation= only when its owning subject and purpose are explicit, such as
=assembly generation= or a declared =resource-instance generation counter=.
A counter is one possible representation; opaque identity is sufficient where
only equality and non-aliasing are needed. Do not imply an ordering, universal
counter, or shared lifetime merely by calling a value a generation. A later
reference may abbreviate a locally established subject only when it remains
unambiguous.

For browser transport examples, =:transport-request-id= names the transport
attempt. Domain Request arguments such as HumanHelp's =:request-id= retain their
domain meaning. Different transport attempts must not be conflated because they
carry the same command or concern the same domain Request.

Operation identity is *preserved* through realization: it cannot be silently
erased or substituted. Reserve *monotonic* for a stated ordering or information-
growth relation. In particular, preventing retired work from restoring obsolete
presentation does not imply that all observations form one totally ordered
history or that every valid domain transition increases a numeric value.

*** Executable semantic core, proof kernel, and dedicated checkers

The *executable semantic core* defines the production transition meaning for its
supported semantic subset. It consumes the applicable executable rules, admitted
state, and inputs/events, and yields semantic state and declared effects. A
portable machine step or browser adapter transition function is an executable
semantic core within its stated scope. There need not be one universal step
function for all layers.

The *proof kernel* checks derivations against explicit inference rules and
premises. It accepts or rejects the claimed judgment; it does not perform the
application's runtime transitions or supply runtime authorization. It is
separate from the richer elaborator that proposes terms and evidence. It must
not trust the elaborator's conclusion merely because the elaborator supplied it.

A *dedicated semantic checker* establishes a particular judgment or property,
such as exact finite-state exploration or structural application closure,
through its declared checking mechanism. It need not be implemented as part of
the proof kernel. Its result retains the evidence class and trust premises of
that mechanism.

These components may share canonical semantic definitions. Sharing definitions
neither merges their responsibilities nor establishes implementation soundness.
The relationship between the checked subject and the production object remains
an explicit correspondence obligation. Canonical terminology calls the runtime
component the executable semantic core, reserving =proof kernel= for derivation
checking; external proof-assistant kernels must be identified as external.

The trust base of a claim includes every component that establishes a judgment
without supplying evidence checked by another identified mechanism. Depending
on the claim, this includes parsing, typing, normalization, substitution,
transition interpretation, frame rules, initiality, invariant preservation,
induction, certificate admission, and source-to-artifact binding.

A small propositional kernel does not make the whole assurance system equally
small if other modules directly establish additional semantic judgments. Those
modules must either produce evidence accepted by the appropriate checker or
remain explicit parts of the trusted checker implementation. Part IX owns their
rules; Part X owns the corresponding soundness and implementation arguments.

The architecture separates semantic definitions, elaboration, derivation
checking, runtime realization, and observations/reports. Checking a derivation
does not submit a database transaction. An integration runner may perform real
effects to collect evidence, but it is then an effectful realization boundary,
not part of the pure proof kernel. The runtime consumes admitted semantics and
current premises, not a diagnostic report standing in for either.

These definitions fix responsibilities without requiring one monolithic
namespace. Shared definitions reduce drift; independent correspondence checks
and soundness arguments address mistakes shared by execution and checking.

*** Raw declaration

A *raw declaration* is user, application, or framework data that has not yet
crossed the semantic checker appropriate to its role.

Examples include:

- a raw Malli or domain schema;
- a raw business-rule expression;
- a raw operation contract;
- a raw choreography;
- a raw authority declaration;
- a raw derivation;
- a raw dependency reference;
- a raw application assembly declaration.

Raw data is permitted at construction boundaries.

Raw data must not masquerade as a certified semantic artifact merely because it
has the same map shape as one.

*** Admitted semantic value

An *admitted semantic value* is a value that has crossed the construction,
verification, authoritative-acquisition, or other checking boundary required
for the semantic category in which downstream code will consume it.

Admission answers a question such as:

#+begin_quote
May this value be treated by the supported program as an instance of semantic
category C at this boundary?
#+end_quote

Admission does not automatically answer every stronger question about the
value.  In particular:

- admission into a nominal category is not automatically a proof of every
  proposition named by that category;
- admission does not create current authorization unless authorization is the
  proposition established by the trusted runtime boundary;
- admission does not make a client-carried value authoritative merely because
  it was once authoritative before serialization;
- an admitted artifact identity binds the relevant object to its construction
  history but does not establish semantic truth by identity alone.

A nominal type, opaque wrapper, private constructor, checked constructor, or
registry-resolved object may help represent admission.  The requirement is that
unsupported construction or same-shaped raw data cannot silently receive the
stronger semantic treatment through the normal API.

*** Semantic interface

A *semantic interface* is the normalized meaning exported by one checked
component to its dependents.

It contains only propositions downstream reasoning is permitted to rely on.

Depending on the component, this may include:

- declared value types;
- variants;
- cardinality;
- optionality/refinement rules;
- relationships;
- operation input/output facts;
- preconditions;
- postconditions;
- authority requirements;
- provenance requirements;
- effects and resources;
- named assumptions;
- named guarantees;
- compatibility constraints.

An exported interface distinguishes guarantees from the assumptions under
which those guarantees hold. Listing a proposition as a required premise does
not export that proposition as already established. A dependent component must
either inherit the exact applicable premise, discharge it using a checked
justification, or decline the stronger claim. The interface's named obligations
and dependencies must be resolved to their source-owned subjects; a convenient
summary is not an independent source of semantic truth.

Implementation details irrelevant to downstream reasoning should not become
semantic commitments merely because they are convenient to serialize.

*** Assumption

An *assumption* is a proposition accepted from outside the proof currently
being established. It is identified by its proposition *and applicability*:
subject, parameters and bindings, semantic or authority context, scope, origin,
and the implementation/runtime boundary where relevant. Its human-readable
name alone is not sufficient identity. Two claims about current Membership for
different principals, Organizations, Requests, or invocations do not share one
premise merely because both are called =:current-membership=.

Assumptions are explicit leaves in the selected proof justification or
explanation graph. Acceptance under an admission policy keeps the dependent
claim conditional; it does not discharge the assumption. Discharge requires a
separately checked, scope-compatible justification that inherits its own
premises, as specified in Part IX.

They are not inferred from trust in a namespace name, source location, familiar
implementation, passing test, or matching hash.

*** Guarantee

A *guarantee* is a proposition established by the current checked component
relative to its certified dependencies and named assumptions.

*** Obligation

An *obligation* is a proposition required for a particular judgment, admission,
or assurance claim. A mandatory check must be established before its result is
issued. Where admission policy permits an unproved contract as a premise, the
resulting certificate states the dependent conditional judgment; it does not
claim that the original contract obligation was discharged.

An unresolved obligation must remain visible.

It must not be replaced by a default success value or silently omitted from the
result.

*** Derivation

A *derivation* is machine-readable proposed evidence describing how a guarantee
follows from specified premises and inference rules. A raw derivation is not
self-validating. Only a successful check under the applicable calculus and
subject/premise bindings can establish the judgment it proposes; the
interpretation and soundness of that checking mechanism remain separately
classified claims.

Derivations are useful for:

- mechanical checking;
- diagnostics;
- explanation;
- repair;
- trusted-computing-base reduction through independently checked evidence.

A derivation is evidence, not runtime authority.

*** Certificate

A *certificate* is a closed evidence artifact stating enough information for an
appropriate checker to decide the claims it represents. Closed means that its
required references and dependencies are accounted for, including named
assumption leaves. It does not mean that those assumptions have been proved or
that future runtime premises already hold.

A certificate may include:

- the semantic object checked;
- its semantic identity;
- certified dependency identities;
- assumptions;
- guarantees;
- proof obligations;
- derivations or checked references to derivations;
- applicable semantic-checker or proof-kernel version;
- result classification.

A certificate is not a boolean.

A certificate is not accepted because an ordinary Clojure map contains a key
such as =:verified? true=. A submitted certificate-shaped value remains raw
evidence until its required checking/re-admission boundary succeeds.

A certificate is accepted only through the checker and issuer boundaries
appropriate to that certificate class. Admission binds the checked subject,
claims, required source-derived obligations, dependency closure, permitted
premises, and applicability. A copied successful report or a matching digest
does not supply that issuer binding. A partial explanation of failed admission
is useful diagnostic material, not a certificate satisfying the missing claim.

*** Semantic identity

A *semantic identity* is a deterministic identity of the semantic material
normalized under a declared encoding and normalization contract. It identifies
that material; it is not a decision procedure for equivalence of arbitrary
Clojure programs.

It is deliberately distinct from:

- source-file checksum;
- file path;
- namespace name;
- build timestamp;
- runtime locator;
- physical artifact location.

Whitespace, comments, local helper names, and implementation details outside
the exported contract need not alter its semantic identity. A claim about the
concrete implementation may nevertheless need a new implementation binding or
new correspondence evidence after such a change.

Changes to relied-upon semantic commitments must invalidate dependent evidence
unless a checked compatibility or implication argument justifies reuse. A
matching contract identity alone does not authorize evidence reuse across
different implementations.

Examples include changes to:

- value types;
- rule contracts;
- authority contracts;
- operation postconditions;
- provenance requirements;
- compatibility rules;
- resource semantics.

Semantic identity identifies normalized semantic material under the declared
normalization and identity contract. A matching untrusted identifier is not
self-authenticating evidence that the corresponding material was checked.

Semantic identity by itself does not prove the truth of that material. Evidence
about a particular generated artifact or implementation must also remain bound
to the concrete object to which that evidence applies. Equality of normalized
contract material does not automatically transfer test
results or physical artifact correspondence from an earlier build to a different
one. For opaque functions, the exported contract, admitted implementation
binding, and evidence applicability are separate identities. Gesso does not
require deciding extensional equivalence of those functions.

*** Proof DAG

A *proof DAG* is the dependency graph from a root checked artifact through all
certified semantic dependencies and named assumptions.

A root may depend on the following semantic layers; actual dependencies form
a DAG, not necessarily one linear chain:

| Semantic layer | Typical exported evidence |
|----------------+----------------------------|
| Schemas, domains, and relationships | Typed interfaces and relationship constraints |
| Business rules | Well-formedness, proved properties, and explicit opaque contracts |
| Model operations | Transition obligations, invariants, and realization premises |
| Choreography | Knowledge, authority, coordination, and resource judgments |
| Projection | The stated global-to-local behavior relation |
| Executable plans | Semantic and artifact identity bindings |
| Whole application | Closure, production enforcement, and independent acceptance evidence |

The proof DAG records the justifications and inherited premises for the
particular claims being established. Its acyclicity and internal completeness
are necessary, but do not establish that all *required* application obligations
were included. The constructor separately derives the mandatory obligation
ledger and required dependency edges from the original source, actual semantic
subject, and selected profile. It must check that the selected proof DAG
accounts for those obligations as established, explicitly accepted premises
where policy permits, or unresolved blockers. A caller-supplied graph with a
conveniently omitted guard, operation, authority check, writer, or correspondence
edge cannot certify the reduced subject as the complete application.

Alternative sound justifications may have different dependencies; only the
selected justification's actual premises are inherited by its dependent
claim. No premise can be discarded merely because another claim in a shared
artifact is assumption-free. Required obligation coverage and per-claim
dependency closure are separate checks, not a second author-maintained proof
registry. Part IX owns their normative checking and issuance rules.

A later stage may rely only on propositions actually exported by its certified
dependencies or named as assumptions.

No stage receives credit for a predecessor's intended meaning when that meaning
was never certified.

The certificate dependency DAG must be acyclic. Recursive or fixed-point
semantics may be supported only through a deliberately formalized rule with
checked premises; introducing a dependency cycle does not supply that
justification.

This requirement is distinct from ordinary recursive computation. In
particular, a cycle among Clojure namespace dependencies is a load-time
dependency error, not a mechanism for expressing logical recursion. Any
recursive reasoning admitted by the certification system must therefore be
represented explicitly in its semantics rather than encoded as a cyclic
namespace or certificate dependency.

#+LATEX: \newpage

** Construction principles

The following principles apply throughout the design.

They are not implementation-history advice.  They are properties of the
intended finished system.

*** Canonical semantic construction and controlled effects
:PROPERTIES:
:CUSTOM_ID: req-canonical-transition-construction
:END:

The operation's canonical semantic source determines the obligations of its
realization. For an authoritative state-changing operation, that source contains
or references:

1. The typed state projection and input contract, including optionality, nominal
   distinctions, identity bindings, and supported value representations.
2. Its invocation, repetition, and new-incorporation protocols.
3. Its guard and declared dependencies on authoritative state or external facts.
4. Its permitted transition relation, writes, preserved fields, and other
   declared effects.
5. Its result meanings, command outcome protocol, and required acquisition or
   recovery successors.
6. Its opaque implementation contracts, assumptions, and evidence requirements.

State semantics distinguish absence, present nil where permitted, and false.
An accessor, serializer, predicate, or physical database mapping must not erase
that distinction when the declared semantics uses it. Numeric ranges, overflow,
comparison, nominal enums, and time representations are equally explicit; host
runtime defaults do not define portable semantics by accident.

For a guarded assignment, all right-hand sides refer to the same prestate and
admitted inputs unless the operation explicitly declares sequential intermediate
steps. Its frame identifies state required to preserve both presence and value.
For supported expressions and assignments, construction derives the direct
read and write footprints and the default unchanged-field frame relative to
the declared state projection. This syntactic footprint is not automatically
the complete *protected semantic dependency set*: relational predicates,
absence/uniqueness conditions, opaque policy calls, and cross-model
authorization may depend on state not named by a direct field read. Those
dependencies are exported through their owning semantic interfaces and
incorporated into the source-derived obligation set. Where Gesso can check
their coverage and physical protection, it does; otherwise the precise
unestablished relation remains an explicit premise or an admission blocker
under policy. A caller-supplied footprint may provide a declared dependency
contract but cannot override derived evidence, hide dependencies, or grant
authorization by assertion.

An abstract frame over three declared fields does not prove that every other
physical database field is preserved. The storage mapping must account for
domain fields, framework revision/time metadata, replacement versus patch
semantics, and any fields outside the projection. Mapped identities must not
collide through key normalization or encoding. Part IV specifies that mapping
and its authoritative effect contract.

An opaque computation may supply a candidate result or change plan. Admission
can check its typed result, target binding, supported guard/assignment/frame
relation, and effect footprint before those effects are submitted. Such a check
can establish those instance properties without proving the computation for
all inputs. It does not prove that the computation had no earlier hidden effect;
effect containment still needs its own enforcement or retained assumption.

*** From an admitted candidate to an authoritative outcome

A candidate is neither a committed transition nor a receipt. The controlled
realization has these distinct responsibilities:

| Boundary | Required responsibility |
|----------+-------------------------|
| Preparation | Obtain appropriately bound inputs and observations; construct the candidate using admitted semantic sources |
| Candidate admission | Check the actual proposed targets, changes, frame, declared effects, and command binding rather than a caller-supplied success report |
| Lowering | Translate the admitted semantic operation to a physical transaction/effect plan under the applicable storage and backend contract |
| Submission | Submit that admitted plan through the scoped capability; reject unnoticed substitution or additional effects |
| Incorporation | Enforce current dependencies atomically with the required domain and command-record changes |
| Outcome admission | Interpret authoritative result evidence at its actual scope; preserve unknown status where evidence is insufficient |
| Delivery and recovery | Resolve participant knowledge and declared propagation obligations without inventing a commit outcome |

The boundaries may be combined in an implementation, but their obligations
cannot disappear. A candidate validated against an earlier observation needs
commit-time guards or an equivalent atomic realization. Independently writing
the ledger after the domain change does not implement an atomic command
protocol. Postcommit invalidation or external delivery requires its own durable
or otherwise justified recovery contract; a successful domain write does not
prove that an interested browser learned about it.

The physical transaction may involve several resources. HumanHelp self-Claim
can depend on the current Request, Membership, Organization and relevant
RequestAssignment facts, including absence of a conflicting active primary
assignment. The admitted incorporation changes the Request and its production
assignment relationship, and atomically records the command result and
required durable publication intent under the operation's declared policy.
Protecting only Request status or constructing a toy =:request/helper= field
does not establish this composition. The model's own public contract determines
which relationships, guards, and assignment writes are actually necessary;
this example does not invent their physical schema. A supported backend
profile may impose explicit limits, but prototype restrictions such as
one document, literal-only assignments, or disabled notifications are not the
general semantic model.

*** Invariant obligations and coverage

For a stated invariant =I=, a closed operation catalog supports induction only
when the relevant obligations are established:

- every admitted initial state satisfies =I=;
- each admitted transition preserves =I= from a state satisfying =I=;
- all state-changing behavior relevant to the claim is represented by those
  transitions or by explicit environment assumptions;
- the concrete realization corresponds to the stated transition semantics under
  its retained premises.

Conceptually, the base and step obligations are:

#+begin_example
For every s:
    Init(s) implies I(s)

For every admitted operation o and every s, x, s':
    I(s) and T_o(s, x, s') imply I(s')
#+end_example

=T_o= includes that operation's permitted guards, assignments, and effects at
the stated abstraction. The proof scope names the state projection and operation
catalog; it does not silently include every possible database writer. Feasible
initialization and usable required operations need separate positive evidence,
so an impossible initial condition or a guard rejecting every invocation cannot
be used to satisfy product completeness.

Initializers, migrations, imports, administrative operations, scheduled work,
and external writers must have an explicit place in the coverage argument.
Their absence from a developer-maintained list is not evidence that they do not
exist. A proof about the supported catalog remains a conditional catalog proof
until production writer coverage and correspondence justify its application.

*** Managed capabilities and admitted realizations

The ordinary application assembly supplies the capabilities needed to realize
declared effects. Code receives the scoped capabilities required by its role;
it should not ordinarily obtain raw database submission authority merely to
construct a candidate. Read-only and static routes do not need writer
capabilities. Background and asynchronous work receive explicit lifetime and
transfer rules rather than borrowing an HTTP request's identity indefinitely.

A one-use capability bounds one grant's use. It does not make a logical command
idempotent across new grants or retries. That requires the authoritative command
binding and record protocol. Conversely, a command record does not prove that
every write occurred through the intended scoped capability.

An admitted assembly generation binds the semantic sources, implementations,
providers, routes, artifact identities, qualification profiles, and policy used
by its realization. A relevant replacement requires re-admission or a checked
compatibility transition. Supported development reload and deployment overlap
must make that transition explicit; repeatedly checking mutable Var identities
is not a substitute for a declared lifecycle and dependency contract.

Managed capability construction prevents accidental bypass in trusted
application code. It is not a sandbox against hostile code sharing the JVM.
Any additional containment claim must identify the actual isolation mechanism
and its assumptions. Neither opaque Clojure nor explicit assertions excuse
undeclared interference with protected state.

*** State semantic intent once

The ordinary coherent formulation should state each semantic fact at its
owning source, then derive or verify its uses. "One canonical place" means
one authoritative owner *per fact*, not one monolithic declaration for every
domain rule, choreography, view, route, acquisition, and runtime adapter.
The public model owns business/transition meaning; choreography owns declared
coordination; views select operations and bind actual arguments; ingress and
providers own genuine physical choices. The application constructor joins
those exports and checks required correspondences. No layer gains authority
to replace another owner's contract merely by generating plausible metadata.

If Gesso already knows:

- operation identity;
- participating role;
- projected browser plan;
- command schema;
- transport requirement;
- expected settlement;
- progression requirement;

then views, routes, browser registries, and server handlers should not all
independently restate those facts unless an independent physical choice
genuinely exists.

Prefer:

One semantic declaration supplies derived browser metadata, derived or checked
transport bindings, diagnostics, and application closure edges.

over:

An operation, button, plan name, transport, route string, and bootstrap entry
are independently maintained as if they were unrelated declarations.

When independently authored values must agree, correspondence must be checked
explicitly.


A Claim card reuses the =claim-request= operation already defined. It does not
introduce a second version of Claim's authority, replay, or recovery semantics.
The view supplies only the operation reference, domain arguments, and local
presentation choices:

#+begin_src clojure
(defn request-card
  [{:request/keys [id status title]}]
  [:article.request
   [:h3 title]
   [:p (name status)]
   (when (= status :open)
     (gesso/action
       {:operation :request/claim
        :args {:request/id id}}
       "Claim"))])
#+end_src

The example's status-only =when= is a presentation filter, not a complete
Claim-eligibility rule. Actual HumanHelp availability may additionally depend
on the selected actor, effective Membership, Organization policy, current
assignment, and permitted view projection. Those policies remain model-owned;
a view can consume a prepared permitted affordance without rewriting the
authoritative predicate. An eligible positive path must still exist and be
tested under the independent product acceptance contract.

Visibility is not authorization. The action constructor resolves the admitted
operation, validates the exposed arguments under its construction contract,
and obtains the command/execution protocol from that operation. A rendered
action and browser-carried command ID do not establish the current principal,
commit-time eligibility, or command incorporation. Those remain trusted
invocation and authoritative-operation responsibilities. The author does not
manually create an authority token or a command-outcome query.

From those semantic declarations, Gesso may derive or validate lower-level
realization data:

#+begin_src clojure
(project :request/claim)
;; =>
{:plan/id :plan/request-claim
 :operation :request/claim
 :role :helper
 :argument-schema ClaimInput
 :command-envelope-schema
 [:map
  [:arguments ClaimInput]
  [:gesso/command-id uuid?]]
 :presentation-owner :gesso/execution-id
 :command-correlation :gesso/command-id
 :transport-requirement :trusted-semantic-post
 :settlement
 {:accepted :request/card
  :rejected :request/card
  :unknown :request/reconcile-claim}}

(realize humanhelp-assembly
  :request/claim)
;; =>
{:browser/binding
 {:operation :request/claim
  :plan :plan/request-claim}

 :transport/binding
 {:kind :trusted-semantic-post
  :route :route/request-claim}

 :server/binding
 {:capability :server/request-claim
  :model-op :request/claim}}
#+end_src

The exact projection and realization representations are open design choices.
What matters is that the view author did not separately type:

#+begin_src clojure
;; This is the kind of manually synchronized authoring Gesso should avoid.

[:button
 {:hx-post "/requests/claim"
  :data-operation "claim-request"
  :data-plan "humanhelp-claim-plan-v7"
  :data-command-param "__gesso_live_optimistic_command"
  :data-server-handler "claim-handler"
  :data-model-op "request/claim"}
 "Claim"]
#+end_src

That second version contains several strings that all purport to describe one
semantic intent. Each value can be locally plausible while the collection is
globally contradictory. A typo can easily produce a path that appears to render
correctly and even sends an HTTP request while no longer corresponding to the
declared choreography.

The desirable API therefore pushes complexity inward. Application code states
the semantic operation and domain arguments; Gesso derives what it owns and
checks correspondence where an independent physical choice genuinely remains.
The illustrative =gesso/action= form is not an API commitment. It is a usability
constraint on the supported public API.

*** Derive rather than synchronize

Duplication creates programs whose pieces are individually plausible but
mutually contradictory.

Whenever a fact can be derived safely from a stronger semantic source, derive
it.

Do not create a second source of truth merely to make one layer easier to
implement.
#+LATEX: \newpage
*** Fail at the earliest legitimate boundary

A contradiction should fail at the earliest layer that possesses enough
information to establish it.

Examples of definition/construction-time failures include:

- malformed choreography;
- unknown role;
- impossible local transition;
- invalid message declaration;
- inconsistent operation metadata;
- invalid certified dependency reference.

Examples of build/application-preflight failures include:

- declared semantic affordance with no projected executable plan;
- stale generated artifact;
- missing transport;
- missing trusted route/capability;
- missing server execution capability;
- managed fragment with no permitted initial acquisition;
- authoritative successor with no permitted reacquisition path.

An affordance introduced only while constructing a concrete view is checked
before that rendered surface is serialized or exposed through the managed
renderer. The checked subject is the *effective* action in its admitted render
context, including relevant ancestor form/HTMX inheritance, target and selector
interpretation, operation binding, and current assembly compatibility. A
fragment checked alone cannot certify inherited behavior that depends on an
unknown outer context. That context must be supplied and checked, or the
corresponding managed-output claim remains unsupported and the required
boundary rejects the output.

Arbitrary Hiccup or raw HTML that bypasses this boundary does not inherit the
rendered-surface assurance claim; supported semantic action construction must
make the distinction explicit. Deferred, streamed, cached, and transformed
responses require the declared checking boundary before their effective
managed output is exposed. Static assembly preflight checks only affordances
and operation bindings knowable from its declarations; it cannot claim to
have inspected future arbitrary view data.


The same HumanHelp Claim slice can fail legitimately at three different times,
depending on when enough information exists.

A static construction defect can be rejected before the application starts:

#+begin_src clojure
(def broken-assembly
  {:operations
   {:request/claim
    {:plan :plan/request-claim
     :route :route/request-claim}}

   ;; Accidentally generated from an older application assembly.
   :artifact
   {:plans #{:plan/request-create
             :plan/request-refresh}}})

(assembly/admit! broken-assembly)
;; throws:
{:error/type :assembly/missing-browser-plan
 :operation :request/claim
 :required-plan :plan/request-claim
 :artifact-plans #{:plan/request-create
                   :plan/request-refresh}}
#+end_src

Nothing about a concrete Request or principal is needed to establish that
contradiction, so runtime is too late. This deliberately abbreviated
=broken-assembly= is a controlled negative fixture, not the recommended public
application-definition shape. Real construction derives its required edges
from source-owned operations and actual realization bindings, and checks the
real build artifact rather than accepting a caller-supplied =:artifact/plans=
report as proof of compiled content. A passing detached fixture is not
evidence that the installed server uses this admission gate.

A rendered-surface defect may depend on concrete view construction. Suppose a
generic Request-card renderer allows applications to choose actions, but one
particular rendering asks for =:request/reassign= without supplying the required
target relationship:

#+begin_src clojure
(render
  configurable-request-card
  {:request request
   :actions
   [{:operation :request/reassign
     :args
     {:request/id (:request/id request)}
     ;; required :helper/id is absent
     }]})

;; render preflight rejects before serialization:
{:error/type :view/operation-arguments-incomplete
 :view :request/configurable-card
 :operation :request/reassign
 :missing #{:helper/id}
 :available #{:request/id}}
#+end_src

The assembly may contain a perfectly valid Reassign operation. The defect exists
only in this attempted concrete rendering, so render-time preflight is the
earliest legitimate boundary.

Finally, current authorization may change after a completely valid render:

#+begin_src clojure
;; T1: Alice is currently an active helper.
(html
  (request-card
    {:request/id R
     :request/status :open}))
;; => contains a valid bound :request/claim affordance

;; T2: Alice's Membership is withdrawn.

;; T3: Alice submits a new command C42 from the still-visible affordance.
;; The authoritative operation establishes this rejection and its reason.
(invoke-claim!
  current-server-context
  {:request/id R :gesso/command-id C42})
;; => {:outcome :rejected :reason :membership-inactive}
#+end_src

Static preflight should not have rejected the application merely because a
helper can later lose authorization, and rendering should not claim that the
authorization can never change. The runtime boundary owns that dynamic fact and
must reject the concrete invocation using current authority.

The three failures therefore form one continuous construction story:

| Information becomes available | Earliest legitimate rejection boundary |
|-------------------------------+----------------------------------------|
| From declarations | Construction or assembly admission |
| From a concrete rendered surface | Before serialization and exposure |
| From current external or model state | The trusted runtime boundary with the required current-state protection |

"Fail early" means the earliest *legitimate* boundary, not the earliest point at
which the framework could guess. An established contradiction rejects at its
owning boundary. An unsupported analysis, unavailable source, or exhausted
checking budget is *not* an established contradiction or an acceptance result:
the selected admission policy must either require more evidence or explicitly
retain a permitted premise and its enforcing boundary. A mandatory check cannot
be silently skipped or converted into a green result because the earlier
checker lacked enough information.

A negative conformance case identifies the first expected enforcing boundary
and the prohibited action or exposure. Its paired valid case must succeed
through the supported path; universal rejection is not a usable admission
policy. In particular, a late response/render failure cannot undo an earlier
valid authoritative incorporation or be reported as a command rejection.
Command outcome, response admission, and browser installation retain their
separate evidence and recovery paths.

*** Runtime-only conditions and required recovery

Some facts relevant to an execution can be established only at runtime. Examples
include:

- the current authenticated principal is not authorized for a concrete Request;
- the Request changed after it was rendered;
- a transaction guard fails;
- an external provider is unavailable;
- a browser or another required participant disconnects;
- an expected environment event has not occurred within an application-relevant
  lease, deadline, or interval.

Do not attempt to statically prove genuinely dynamic domain facts merely to
increase preflight coverage.

Runtime-only establishment does not place these conditions outside the
application's correctness model. The distinction is between knowing before
execution whether a condition will occur and knowing before execution that the
application has a coherent response if it does occur.

Where a declared operation or workflow can encounter a runtime condition that
invalidates its premises, removes a participant required for progress, or would
otherwise strand the workflow, the application must define a permitted path
forward. Depending on the application, that path may involve rejection,
authoritative reacquisition, retry, compensation, timeout, retirement,
reassignment, cancellation, explicit degradation, or another declared successor
state.

Static checking may therefore establish a conditional property such as:

#+begin_example
if runtime condition F is established,
the admitted application has a declared path
from F to a valid recovery, successor,
or terminal state
#+end_example

without claiming to establish statically whether F will occur in a particular
execution.

A Request changing after rendering is one example. Gesso cannot establish
beforehand that the Request will remain unchanged until the user acts. It can
require that an operation whose rendered premises have become stale is checked
against current authority and model state and that failure of those premises
leads through declared rejection, reacquisition, or recovery semantics rather
than allowing execution to proceed from obsolete state.


A seat-reservation operation shows what that requirement can look like as a
small executable contract rather than a prose-only promise.

#+begin_src clojure
(defoperation reserve-seat
  {:operation/id :flight/reserve-seat

   :actor :traveler

   :input
   [:map
    [:flight/id uuid?]
    [:seat/id uuid?]]

   ;; This observation justifies what the traveler saw. It does not reserve the
   ;; seat or guarantee that the observation remains current until invocation.
   :entry
   [[:authoritative-observation
     :seat/availability
     {:scope [:flight/id :seat/id]}]]

   :invocation
   {:requires [:authenticated-traveler :admitted-command-binding]}

   :new-incorporation
   {:requires [:current-seat-state :current-traveler-eligibility]
    :atomic-with :command/result-record}

   :repetition
   {:requires :command/result-disclosure-authority
    :result :permitted-recorded-outcome}

   :effect
   [:model/invoke :seat/reserve
    {:flight-id :flight/id
     :seat-id :seat/id
     :traveler :authenticated-traveler
     :command-id :gesso/command-id}]

   :settlement
   {:accepted
    {:learns [:command/reservation-recorded :gesso/command-id]
     :reacquire [:flight/seat-map :flight/id]}

    :rejected
    {:reason-set #{:seat/already-reserved
                   :seat/no-longer-offered
                   :traveler/not-eligible
                   :reservation/precondition-changed}
     :reacquire [:flight/seat-map :flight/id]}

    :unknown
    {:recover
     [:seat/reconcile-reservation
      {:flight-id :flight/id
       :seat-id :seat/id
       :command-id :gesso/command-id}]}}})
#+end_src

The admitted command boundary allocates =:gesso/command-id= once, before the
first possible submission, and the authoritative boundary establishes or
validates its trusted binding as described for Claim. The model guards
eligibility, the flight/seat association, and availability under the same atomic
contract that records the reservation and command result. A pre-read may aid
presentation or preparation but cannot replace that guard or authoritative
command reconciliation:

#+begin_src clojure
(defn reserve-seat!
  [{:keys [db principal now]} {:keys [flight-id seat-id command-id]}]

  (seat-model/transact-reservation!
    {:db db :now now}
    {:flight-id flight-id
     :seat-id seat-id
     :traveler-id (:user/id principal)
     :command-id command-id

     ;; New incorporation protects these transaction-current predicates.
     ;; A compatible replay is handled before applying new-command guards.
     :commit-guards
     [[:traveler/eligible? (:user/id principal) flight-id]
      [:seat/belongs-to-flight? flight-id seat-id]
      [:seat/offered? flight-id seat-id]
      [:seat/unreserved? flight-id seat-id]]

     ;; The scoped identity binds principal, operation, flight, and seat.
     ;; A compatible repeat returns the permitted recorded outcome,
     ;; subject to current disclosure authority, without another reservation.
     :deduplicate-by
     [:flight/reserve-seat (:user/id principal) command-id]
     :bind-arguments
     {:flight-id flight-id :seat-id seat-id}}))
#+end_src

The transaction API is schematic. Its realization must establish the stated
guard, relationship, frame, and atomic command-record properties under the
qualified backend contract. If ordinary Clojure computes eligibility outside
the transaction, all facts on which it depends must receive equivalent
commit-time protection; pre-read correctness alone is insufficient.

An aggregate transaction-guard failure may not identify which predicate failed.
The model can return =:reservation/precondition-changed= when that is the
strongest supported reason. A more specific reason requires authoritative
evidence of the stated scope. A later reread can describe current availability
but must not be presented as proof of the historical cause of an earlier
transaction failure.

Before interpreting a failed attempt as command rejection, the outcome protocol
must account for a compatible command incorporated by a concurrent attempt.
When incorporation or delivery cannot be established, the participant retains
=:unknown= and reconciles by the bound command identity. A timeout, a missing
record at an insufficient read basis, or an unavailable dependency is not
authoritative rejection.

A valid browser interaction may therefore begin from an authoritative observation
at =T1= and still receive a typed rejection because Bob reserved the seat at
=T2=. That rejection does not mean the earlier observation was fraudulent; it
means the dynamic premise changed before the authoritative operation committed.

Preflight can check that =:rejected= is represented and that its reacquisition
path exists. It must also distinguish the declared =:unknown= reconciliation
