| Trusted executor | Installed callable implements the model-owned command and recovery contract; an entry naming a different function does not establish execution correspondence. |
| Providers | The actual clock and principal have the value shapes required by the executor, including =:biff.fx/now= when that concrete model FX integration is selected; simply listing =:clock= is insufficient. |
| Browser and Live | The loaded generated plan/physical handlers, authorized reread, progression and subscription/Refresh policy join the same admitted operation; a build-only manifest or missing acquisition does not close the path. |

One command identity persists through permitted delivery uncertainty and retry;
a later current card observation is not by itself historical incorporation
evidence. Current authorization, atomic execution and actual DOM installation
require their own runtime evidence. The Claim illustration cannot stand in
for separately required Create, Unclaim, Cancel or manager Reassign paths.

*** Checked construction supports opaque application code

An ordinary Clojure function can implement a rule, renderer, projection, candidate
builder, or input conversion behind a declared interface. Construction establishes
what can be checked and retains a named premise for the rest, under
[[#req-admission-assurance-policy][the admission policy]].

For a candidate builder, the actual returned targets, assignments, frame,
command binding, and supported effect footprint can be checked before submission.
That instance check does not prove that the builder had no hidden earlier effect
or that it produces valid candidates for every input. Effect containment and
functional conformance remain separate enforcement or assumption obligations.

Normalization must not silently execute arbitrary application work to discover
its meaning. Functions invoked during construction have an explicit purity,
determinism, totality/failure, and resource contract. Compilation, dependency
resolution, and model exploration use their declared budgets. An effectful
builder cannot be called repeatedly by inspection or diagnostics as though it
were inert data.

 
The boundary between a checked *instance* and a function's general behavior
is retained in the report. A pure bounded export may be evaluated under its
admitted inputs; an uncontained effectful callback cannot be probed for
inspection as though it were data. Exception, timeout, unknown dependency,
nondeterminism or undeclared side effects produce explicit dispositions rather
than an empty declaration. Agreement between a callback's own generated
assumptions and its reported result is not independent evidence.

A canonical admitted construction should derive execution and checking products
from the same semantic subject wherever possible. An independently supplied
reference model remains useful, but its relation to the production operation is
an explicit obligation. Agreement between two copies of the same mistaken policy
is not evidence that the intended business rule was correct.

*** Closed registries and explicit extension boundaries

Registries declared closed reject unknown, duplicate, ambiguous, or incompatible
members before use. Extension points identify how new modules, routes, operations,
or providers become a newly admitted construction. Dynamically loading a plugin
must not mutate an admitted registry while retaining old closure evidence.

 
Closure is scoped by registration source, deployment profile, effect family and
inventory boundary. A closed declared route table does not imply an exhaustive
inventory of background writers. A validated collection of rendered Hiccup
snapshots does not prove all future conditional responses. Where a stronger
claim needs that coverage, the system needs independent inventory evidence,
a real producer/effect-boundary guard, or a truthful weaker disposition.

Adding or replacing a plugin creates a candidate new generation with new
admission and compatibility decisions. During rolling installation, older
requests and workers retain their previously admitted generation; loading new
code cannot silently grant them the new generation's rights.

Unused declarations can be available for composition without being exposed or
active. They are labeled accordingly. A generated executable or installed writer
that claims a role in the active application must have a corresponding source
and coverage classification; it cannot disappear from the graph as unused merely
because no UI currently invokes it.

*** Construction phases and admitted assembly identity
:PROPERTIES:
:CUSTOM_ID: req-assembly-construction-phases
:END:

Construction has an acyclic dependency order. It may expose several internal
products without asking application authors to maintain several definitions.

| Phase | Product and admission responsibility |
|-------+--------------------------------------|
| Normalize | Resolve source-owned semantic declarations, physical choices, configuration, and explicit opaque contracts. |
| Derive | Produce required role plans, interfaces, closure graph, proof obligations, and the browser build manifest. |
| Build/check | Generate assets and correspondence products; run applicable semantic, closure, qualification, and assurance checks. |
| Admit candidate | Bind accepted evidence and retained premises to an immutable candidate realization under the selected policy. |
| Install | Construct actual router, wrapped handler, providers, worker entrypoints, and asset serving from that candidate. |
| Activate | Verify the required installation relationships and permit external application service. |
| Retire | Revoke or transfer owned rights/work, drain permitted users, and release resources under the lifetime contract. |

Some installation facts cannot exist before installation. The lifecycle therefore
allows private preparation and a final activation gate, while preventing unchecked
application operations from becoming externally available. A report saying a
candidate is structurally closed is not a report that its server was activated.

 
The activation gate verifies what was actually installed or bound for serving:
the dispatcher and checked handler, executable and served assets, provider
and worker registrations, required acquisition paths, and the selected
deployment's physical applicability premises. A constructed router value alone
does not establish that the serving host adopted it. An unsuccessful build,
partial installation or rejected activation must not expose unchecked operations;
already acquired resources retain identified cleanup, cancellation and
surviving physical-remnant obligations. Repeated startup must not silently
duplicate workers or reuse another generation's installation receipt.

The identities used in these phases identify different objects:

- normalized semantic/realization input identity;
- concrete implementation closure and qualification-profile identity;
- exact executable plan identity;
- browser manifest identity;
- emitted asset content identity;
- checker result/evidence identity with its applicability;
- admitted assembly instance, optionally described as an assembly generation;
- deployment instance/placement identity.

An assembly generation is a scoped application-construction lifetime. It is not
a universal freshness number, browser execution ID, resource incarnation, command
ID, or database progression token. Examples use =:assembly-instance/id= when
referring to that admitted lifetime.

A digest recipe specifies the object, canonical encoding, schema, relevant
compiler/provider dependencies, excluded self-identifying fields, and collision
premise. Formatting-only source changes need not alter semantic identity, but a
changed opaque implementation can invalidate implementation evidence even when
its public contract is unchanged. Part V's exact plan and asset distinctions
apply here.

 
Identity comparisons are typed relations. Equal semantic identities may
coexist with different handler implementations; equal artifact bytes can be
installed under different execution permissions; distinct deployment instances
can use one generation. Evidence is reusable only when its *complete*
dependencies, mechanism and applicability premises remain valid. A digest
cannot issue a trusted executor, prove artifact provenance, or establish
physical serving. The normalization contract must detect omitted dependency
fields and ambiguous encodings, not merely select a digest algorithm.

The final asset digest cannot be an input to the same bytes containing that
digest without an explicit cycle-breaking construction. Detached receipts and
content-addressed asset locations provide a straightforward solution.

*** Immutable admitted bindings and scoped revalidation

An admitted assembly binds the actual implementations, providers, policy,
qualification profiles, route semantics, rendering contract, and artifact set
on which its claims depend. A request captures that assembly instance at entry.
Its later callbacks, rendering, and response completion preserve that reference.

 
Capturing a generation never freezes changing principal authority, live
RequestAssignment state, transaction progression or physical target/resource
ownership. Those are re-established at the relevant current effects. An
incompatible deployment may permit an old request to finish only under its
explicit retirement policy; otherwise its obsolete physical actuation rights
must be revoked and any surviving durable command resolved through compatible
recovery. A callback must not splice a new route, plan or provider into an old
continuation merely because names still match. Subscriptions and background
workers require corresponding generation and resource lifetimes.

An immutable map containing mutable Vars or registries is not automatically an
immutable realization. The supported construction captures applicable callable
bindings, uses assembly-owned registries, or detects and re-admits relevant
replacement before dependent use. An ordinary reload is a declared construction
transition, not an arbitrary mutation excused by development mode.

Construction evidence may be cached by its complete dependency identity and
applicability conditions. There is no requirement to recompile plans, explore a
finite model, or hash every asset on every response. The runtime must preserve
or re-establish the relevant binding at the boundary where it is used. A mutable
asset path or live registry needs a concrete stability/invalidation mechanism;
a cached green report cannot supply one.

Admission handles can be opaque process-local values; explanatory reports remain
copyable data. A private issuance registry can prevent accidental substitution of
a copied map for an issued executor. Object identity alone is not durable proof,
remote attestation, or a sandbox against hostile code sharing the JVM. Process
restart reconstructs local admissions from their actual sources and any
independently checkable durable evidence.

 
*** Positive and adversarial construction histories

| History | Expected disposition |
|---------+----------------------|
| An eligible Claim has source-owned model, control, POST, issued executor, correct clock, built-and-served browser asset and authorized card acquisition. | Admit the candidate; require separate real installation, execution and product acceptance evidence for stronger claims. |
| A route and command use the same operation name but select different Request IDs. | Reject the route/command correspondence before a protected effect. |
| A provider is named =:clock= but the executor never receives the required =:biff.fx/now= value. | Reject the provider binding or block actual execution at the capability gate. |
| Sampled Hiccup cards are valid, but a conditional render emits an unannotated POST to a protected command route. | A static snapshot is insufficient; the installed response guard must reject the actual rendered request or the stronger claim remains open. |
| An unlisted background writer can mutate protected RequestAssignment state. | Treat writer coverage as incomplete; do not certify a complete protection argument from a declared subset. |
| A plugin adds a route or a mutable Var points to a new handler after admission. | Invalidate affected evidence and re-admit a new generation before dependent use. |
| A delayed callback belongs to a retired generation or superseded browser target. | Prevent stale actuation; retain only separately owned command/recovery obligations. |
| A fixture constructor passes with test providers but production uses another actual handler. | Preserve fixture-scoped evidence and leave production correspondence open. |
| A candidate is checked but the serving router never adopts its guarded handler. | Report candidate closure, not deployed enforcement or demonstrated user behavior. |
| A finite checker exhausts its budget or cannot express the selected obligation. | Report inconclusive/unsupported and apply the admission policy; neither success nor counterexample may be fabricated. |

These are scoped construction requirements, not a demand to prove every
ordinary Clojure function. Plain Clojure and explicit ordinary HTMX remain
legitimate while their real effects must respect any application-wide safety
property being claimed. Later sections define the detailed closure edges,
serving enforcement, diagnostics and positive acceptance criteria.

** Whole-application closure graph and evidence

The graph represents semantic interfaces and actual realization relationships.
It must expose enough structure to locate a failure without forcing a reviewer
to reverse-engineer many namespaces. The runtime need not carry the entire graph
on every request; it uses admitted bindings derived from it.

 
The graph has *typed nodes* for semantic sources and obligations, selected
application realizations, installed physical bindings, and the propositions
whose evidence can support admission. These are not interchangeable merely
because all happen to be represented by Clojure maps. Each node identifies its
source owner, semantic category, scoped identity, admitted generation where
applicable, and the implementation or deployment profile against which it is
being checked. A generated browser plan and the bytes that were actually
served are distinct nodes with a correspondence edge between them.

Edges identify a *relation and its justification*, not only the existence of
two endpoints. Construction derives required edges from each admitted
operation's interface, the independently specified application capabilities,
and the selected assurance/deployment policy. An explicit source declaration
and an observed physical binding can disagree; neither may silently rewrite
the other to make the graph close.

The realization graph may contain legitimate feedback paths such as command
settlement, Live advisory and authoritative reacquisition. Its *evidence
dependency argument*, however, must be well-founded: a report cannot certify
its own source binding, and two success summaries cannot mutually establish
one another without an independently admitted base. The proof-DAG layer of
Parts IX–X records these dependencies; Part VII requires their ownership and
non-circular applicability already at assembly time.

*** Operation-specific edges

| Edge or obligation | Required correspondence |
|--------------------+-------------------------|
| Affordance to operation | Concrete arguments, observations, selected realization, and availability implement the named operation. |
| Operation to choreography/projection | Required role-local behavior follows the admitted coordination and knowledge contract. |
| Plan to executable artifact | The generated runtime contains the intended admitted plans and bound implementation/profile dependencies. |
| Executable plan to physical handlers | Every reachable required effect has a compatible handler and completion/failure protocol. |
| Transport to ingress | Method, route semantics, encoding, selectors, correlation, and protocol agree. |
| Installed ingress to executor | Actual dispatch invokes the selected issued/admitted callable, not a metadata-equivalent substitute. |
| Executor to public model operation | The trusted operation binding implements the declared model interface and preserves its command/authority obligations. |
| Operation to providers | Required typed resources resolve to compatible providers with the right origin and lifetime. |
| Candidate to authoritative realization | Checked targets, guards, assignments, frame, and effects reach the admitted lowering/submission boundary. |
| Model outcome to participant settlement | Each supported outcome maps explicitly without collapsing incorporation, rejection, repetition, and uncertainty. |
| Required propagation to recovery | Publication/durable work, progress requirements, and missed-delivery recovery have actual owners and paths. |
| Observation to presentation | Scope, progression, authorization, representation, target ownership, and physical completion support the claimed adoption. |
| Application policy to enforcement | Mandatory checks are invoked at the actual construction, installation, request, effect, and output boundaries. |
| Product capability to acceptance | Independent promised behavior is exercised through the admitted application; closure alone does not establish it. |

Not every operation needs every edge. The operation's admitted interface derives
its obligations. A read cannot require a fictional mutation just to fit a universal
pipeline, and a mutation cannot omit recovery because it looks like an ordinary
POST.

 
*** Graph coverage, orphan nodes and independent capabilities

The assembly checks *both directions*: every required semantic effect has the
appropriate realization, and every installed realization that claims a
semantic/effect role is connected to an admitted contract and classified
coverage. A generated plan with no source operation, a semantic route with no
registered executor, a Live acquisition without its managed projection, or an
installed state writer outside the admitted effect inventory cannot be hidden
by reporting only successful edges. A declared but unused component may be
classified =available-not-active=; an installed writer that changes protected
state cannot use that classification to escape global invariant obligations.

A useful closure explanation distinguishes at least:

| Subject | Required graph disposition |
|---------+----------------------------|
| Exposed managed operation | All reachable semantic, physical, settlement and recovery edges required by its interface are checked or explicitly qualified under policy. |
| Ordinary read-only HTMX route | Its real transport, authorization, data/projection and response contract are accounted for; no fictional command mutation is added. |
| Ordinary state-changing route or non-HTTP writer | Its physical effects are classified and checked for interaction with protected state and invariants, even without a Choreo browser plan. |
| Installed worker, provider, browser asset or subscription | Its source ownership, effect scope, lifecycle and actual deployment binding are represented with applicable evidence. |
| Available but inactive declaration | Not counted as a deployed behavior or as positive product acceptance. |
| Unknown source, unclassified writer or incomplete host inventory | Remains an explicitly scoped coverage gap; silence or an empty supplied list cannot close it. |

Closure is always relative to a stated inventory, effect footprint,
deployment generation and policy. An operation whose *required* edge is
missing fails the corresponding admission gate; where the environment cannot
establish exhaustive physical inventory, the stronger all-writer or
production-enforcement claim remains open rather than being inferred from
the discovered subset. Section 07.04 owns the complete application assurance
policy and its writer-coverage obligations.

*** Evidence is attached to a proposition, not a prestige label

A checked edge records its subject, expected relation, actual binding, source
ownership, mechanism, premises, coverage, applicability, and result. These are the
[[#req-assurance-classification][assurance dimensions]] from Part I.

An illustrative inspection row is:

#+begin_src clojure
{:obligation/id :claim/installed-route-to-executor
 :subject {:assembly-instance/id assembly-id
           :route/id :route/request-claim
           :operation/id :request/claim}
 :expected {:executor/ref admitted-claim-executor-ref}
 :observed {:installation/ref route-installation-ref}
 :mechanism :issued-dispatch-construction-check
 :evidence/ref checked-binding-evidence-ref
 :status :established
 :scope :this-installed-dispatcher
 :premises [server-adopts-dispatcher-premise
            implementation-closure-premise]}
#+end_src

The checker derives this result from the relevant construction/installation.
Writing =:status :established= into a map does not satisfy the obligation. A
handler's operation name proves neither its body nor adoption by the real server.

 
The illustrative row is a *diagnostic view* of a checked proposition, not a
public constructor for trusted evidence. The original sources, selected
implementations, independent observations and actual checker mechanism remain
separately identifiable. For example, a route-to-executor report can establish
that the issued dispatcher closes over a particular callable in the current
construction; it cannot also assert that the deployed web server uses that
dispatcher, that the handler has no additional side effects, or that the
current caller is authorized. Those require separate evidence or named
premises at their actual boundaries.

For each edge the report records whether the relation was required,
how its expected and observed values were obtained, the exact identity and
lifetime of each physical participant where relevant, the evidence's
validation mechanism, the checker and input versions, and the original
source/dependency subject. A copied success report or forged discriminator
does not reproduce a live issued binding. A source-derived explanation can be
retained after admission without conferring the permissions of the admitted
executor or current physical target.

A report distinguishes unresolved structural edges from retained runtime or
external premises. Structurally arranging a trusted principal provider can close
an edge; the actual principal's current authorization remains a runtime/model
condition. The report must not list every future authorization decision as an
unfinished build task.

 
The same temporal discipline applies to command outcomes and presentation:
an issued command, a submitted XTDB transaction, a pinned historical readback,
a current authorized Request-card observation, and completed physical DOM
adoption answer *different propositions*. A branch receipt, callback label,
HTTP 200 or current-looking card cannot certify all five. Application closure
requires a lawful path to obtain each required fact; the actual fact remains
scoped to its source, time, authorization and physical observation.

*** Checked, unsupported, inconclusive, and contradicted are distinct

The admission policy identifies which obligations are mandatory, which require a
particular evidence mechanism, and which may remain named assertions. A missing
route, mismatched executor, invalid schema, wrong authority source, or missing
required recovery cannot be excused by adding a trusted flag.

Unsupported proof fragments and exhausted checking budgets do not establish
falsehood or success. They receive explicit dispositions under the policy. A
known counterexample to the same scoped claim cannot be relabeled an accepted
assumption to make admission green. Correcting an abstraction, narrowing a claim,
or fixing implementation requires a new explicit check of the changed subject.

Claims such as assembly-verified, runtime-enforced, exact-finite-checked, and
proof-kernel-checked describe different evidence at different scopes. They do
not combine into an unexplained percentage or one universal verified Boolean.
The permanent executable semantic core remains distinct from the proof kernel
and from dedicated correspondence/conformance checkers.

 
*** Evidence dispositions and safe composition

For a proposition and its exact scope, the evaluator distinguishes:
=established= with retained assumptions and mechanism, =open= when
required evidence has not been obtained, =unsupported= when the selected
checker cannot express the obligation, =inconclusive= when an attempted
check did not finish or exhausted its declared budget, and =contradicted=
when grounded evidence establishes a counterexample to the proposition.
The vocabulary in a concrete report may be more specific, but it must
preserve these semantic distinctions. An unsupported theorem cannot be
made established by an application-side label; an explored counterexample
cannot be discarded merely by lowering the assurance policy silently.

Evidence dispositions, assembly-admission results, Part IV model
command outcomes, browser participant settlements and HTTP statuses
are distinct type domains. An evidence =contradicted= or
assembly =rejected= is not an authoritative =:rejected= Claim.
A correctly rejected Claim may instead demonstrate a working
runtime authorization guard. Browser =:accepted=, =:rejected=
and =:unknown= remain participant-relative presentations under
07.08's explicit evidence/disclosure mapping.

Evidence composition uses *matching subjects and applicability*, not just
matching successful statuses. A finite model pass supports its bounded
state/transition proposition; conditional induction supports the exact
declared abstract catalog and retained premises; an in-process handle
supports its specified source/issuance identity; and observed XTDB or
browser behavior supports only the checked physical occurrence and
profile. The composite claim records every essential dependency, the
unproved bridge between independently authored model and implementation,
and any unknown writer, deployment adoption or host-trust assumption.
There is no transitive promotion from structural closure to universal
runtime correctness.

A sound failure report points to the minimal broken relation and its
owning source without presenting an inferred repair as a completed one.
A missing plan is not repaired by changing a server-side operation name.
A wrong HTTP target cannot be repaired by adding a browser success marker.
A model execution with an unknown outcome cannot be relabeled rejected
because the current card no longer shows the assignment.

*** A Claim realization closes more than its happy path

For HumanHelp Claim, the source-owned model operation protects current Request
state, helper Membership, Organization policy, and their association under the
Part IV command protocol. Assembly must connect that operation to all required
browser and trusted-server paths.

| Concrete requirement | Failure it prevents |
|----------------------+---------------------|
| Generated Claim binding includes typed Request arguments and the admitted observation context. | A visually enabled control lacks the input/basis its realization requires. |
| The actual browser asset loads the matching plan and physical handlers. | Startup succeeds but clicking the button cannot execute the plan. |
| The real request carries the selected command envelope and stable =:gesso/command-id=. | A working =hx-post= reaches the route without the required command. |
| Path Request selector and decoded command argument are checked for agreement. | The URL selects one Request while the command targets another. |
| Installed route invokes the bound public operation through its admitted executor. | A similarly named handler performs a different transition or bypasses command records. |
| Provider binding supplies sampled time in the representation the executor consumes. | A declared clock exists but the required context value is absent. |
| Model outcomes have explicit participant mappings and disclosure checks. | Repetition after a successful commit is mistaken for a fresh failed Claim. |
| Unknown has a current reconciliation owner and compatible resolver path. | Lost response strands the command or provokes a duplicate new command. |
| Scoped acquisition and physical installation close the presentation path. | HTTP 200 is counted as a current card despite no successful swap. |
| Required Live propagation and reconnect recovery close remote participant behavior. | The initiating user succeeds while other interested boards can never recover. |

The explanation derives these rows from the admitted construction and its evidence.
A shorter example that omits the resolver, physical completion, or publication
recovery must identify its narrower scope instead of being labeled a complete
application proof.

 
*** Required positive and adversarial graph histories

Each case is evaluated against the same source-owned assembly, not a manually
constructed substitute graph. The evidence mechanism and negative case are
independently identified; supplying a prefilled report is not a test.

| Observed history or construction | Required disposition |
|----------------------------------+----------------------|
| An eligible helper can render and execute Claim through the actual admitted browser plan, trusted request, guarded transaction, authorized reread and installed card. | Every applicable edge is discharged at its own scope; separately tested user behavior establishes positive acceptance, not automatically a theorem. |
| The generated artifact lacks the selected Claim plan, despite a valid choreography. | Fail the plan-to-actual-artifact edge; a green model proof cannot close it. |
| The POST route exists but selects Request R2 while the command and card select R1. | Reject transport/selector correspondence before a protected write; a matching operation name is insufficient. |
| A server realization advertises =:clock= but never supplies the required =:biff.fx/now= value. | Reject its typed provider edge or block at actual execution admission; not a successful Claim. |
| The model commits Claim, but no authorized Request-card acquisition or compatible unknown-command resolver is installed. | Leave settlement/recovery/acquisition edges open or reject the selected mandatory profile; HTTP success alone does not discharge them. |
| A Live advisory arrives but the remote user's one-Refresh grant has already been consumed. | Keep advisory/Refresh debt; do not invent another authorized physical read from a successful publication edge. |
| The current card no longer displays the helper after a later Reassign, while an earlier Claim remains historically incorporated. | Keep current-state and historical-command propositions separate; do not report the earlier command as rejected. |
| An apparently unused generated plan or installed write route has no admitted semantic owner, or a scheduled writer is missing from the declared catalog. | Report its orphan/unclassified scope and the resulting coverage gap; no false full-writer closure. |
| A static render sample passes, but a conditional response later emits a protected unannotated HTMX action. | Require actual response-boundary rejection or retain the production-enforcement gap; static Hiccup coverage is insufficient. |
| A finite checker times out, or a known source-bound counterexample contradicts a claimed invariant. | Return inconclusive or contradicted respectively; never substitute a successful assembly-edge status for proof. |
| A production server replaces the checked handler after preflight or serves an older JavaScript artifact. | Separate candidate graph closure from current deployed correspondence; invalidate or refuse the affected claim. |
| An ordinary authorized read or a server-only workflow has no browser command plan. | Admit the *applicable* read/server edges without requiring fictitious optimistic or command nodes. |

These histories preserve the R4 requirement that the same Claim can fail at
different edges for different reasons. They also prevent an error-free but
incomplete graph, a reject-all construction, or a certificate-shaped report
from being mistaken for a useful and fully realized application. The formal
policy and physical enforcement of these edges are developed in 07.04–07.15.

** Application assurance policy and operation coverage

The application definition contains one explicit assurance policy used by
construction, installation, and activation. Stronger finite, inductive, or
correspondence checks may be optional under one policy and mandatory under
another. Their selection is visible in the admitted subject and explanation.

A low-level compatibility API may preserve an unassured legacy path, but that
path cannot inherit the managed application's enforcement or theorem claims.
The ordinary managed startup path does not silently treat an omitted policy as
permission to skip required checks. It applies the declared default policy or
rejects a missing required selection.

 
*** Policy decisions are bound to subjects and effect boundaries

The policy is a source-owned selection of required *propositions*, evidence
mechanisms, qualification profiles, and failure dispositions. It is not an
unstructured =:strict?= boolean or a list of checker names that might run.
Each mandatory proposition identifies the assembly generation, operation and
effect scope, relevant implementation/source identity, proof assumptions,
and the lifecycle boundary where its evidence must be current.

| Boundary | Policy responsibility |
|----------+-----------------------|
| Source/assembly admission | Reject unavailable mandatory semantics, missing declared owners or an incomplete required catalog; retain explicit external premises where permitted. |
| Model checking | Require the selected finite, inductive or other proof obligations with stated bounds, soundness premises, rule/operation exercise and original semantic sources. |
| Installation and activation | Verify that the required checked dispatcher, assets, handlers, providers and writer restrictions are actually bound before exposing protected operations. |
| Invocation and protected effect | Revalidate dynamic authority, current provider/command binding, relevant physical target and commit-time guard through the trusted capability boundary. |
| Post-execution observation | Attribute results, record physical/model correspondence or contradiction, and trigger declared repair without pretending to veto completed effects. |
| Positive application acceptance | Verify independently required real capabilities and recovery histories; a closed reject-all application does not satisfy them. |

A selected strict profile cannot request a guarantee for which its implementation
has no supporting mechanism and then quietly lower that requirement. It
rejects admission or makes the limitation explicit under a separately selected
weaker profile. Unsupported, inconclusive and contradicted mandatory obligations
remain distinct. A compatibility/unmanaged path may be explicitly supported,
but must advertise its narrower assurance and must not inherit managed operation
credentials, protected effects or certification labels by resemblance.

*** One construction owns the semantic catalog and its checking products

A useful construction binds:

- the admitted application assembly;
- the exact relevant operation catalog and semantic definitions;
- rule/invariant declarations with their source ownership;
- actual executor/handler implementations;
- finite model families or inductive evidence where requested;
- the comparator and observation contracts used for implementation evidence;
- required exercise/coverage gates and their budgets;
- the installation and startup path consuming that construction.

Later comparison cannot accept replacement model callbacks or an unrelated
catalog while retaining the old admission handle. Diagnostic inspection reports
the already checked subject and results; it does not rerun user callbacks to
invent a fresh explanation.

This unified construction is an ownership discipline, not a requirement for one
large function or public record type. Layered internal constructors can provide
separate products while preserving their common sources and dependency bindings.

 
The admitted catalog is an *identified closed subject*, not whatever a test
chooses to enumerate. Each rule records its domain and source owner; every
operation's abstract meaning and required authoritative writer correspondence
are distinct from the executable handler body and its physical write capability.
An independent reference model can check a mistake in the production rule, but
a pair of identically wrong rules does not establish the intended business
policy. Unproved equivalence between a modeled callback and an issued executor
is retained as an obligation, not silently inferred from matching IDs.

Construction retains a dependency argument joining admitted initializers,
operations, effects, authorizations, rule/invariant subjects, checker
implementation and deployment qualifications. Later tests use that subject.
Substituting different families, predicates or host registrations after a
certificate/report has been produced cannot reuse its admission. Reports
are not capability-bearing replacements for the checked construction.

*** Finite operation families and non-vacuous coverage

A finite exploration may expand registered operations over declared principals,
arguments, states, and choices. The expansion must preserve the mapping from
each modeled occurrence to its actual operation contract. Synthetic model IDs
are diagnostic coordinates, not production command or execution identities.

The report records the declared bounds, resource budget, visited states or state
occurrences as appropriate, attempted transitions, remaining frontier, and whether
the requested exploration completed. A depth bound can define the intended finite
problem; exhausting a computation budget before exploring that problem is
inconclusive. Completing a depth-limited exploration does not establish unbounded
invariant preservation.

Coverage dimensions remain separate:

| Coverage question | What satisfying it establishes |
|-------------------+---------------------------------|
| Every relevant registered operation has a family. | No catalog member was omitted from that family mapping. |
| A rule matches a source in an explored state. | The rule's modeled domain was exercised at least there. |
| An operation has an enabled attempt. | The model's enablement relation selected an attempt; its incorporation guard may still reject it. |
| A required committed/rejected branch occurs. | That modeled outcome was exercised within the declared exploration. |
| A modeled path preserves an invariant. | The checked path/model satisfies the stated proposition at its scope. |
| A real observed invocation matches a modeled step. | The admitted comparison establishes its stated local correspondence, with retained premises. |

A policy can require particular rules, operations, and outcomes to be exercised.
These gates prevent vacuous green reports, but do not establish product usability,
all predicate branches, representative domain completeness, or production
execution. A rule with no matching modeled source is reported as unexercised;
it cannot be counted as a substantively tested business policy.

 
Nonvacuity is a vector of independent checks, not one coverage percentage.
For every named operation, the explanation can retain counts of disablement,
enabled attempts and committed/rejected modeled outcomes, with each observation
joined to the *original* registered operation and its finite principal/argument
choice. A disabled action is not a rejected transaction. A rejected attempt is
an attempted operation, but not a committed transition. A finite model that
visits only the empty initial state may be exhaustively explored within its
stated bound and still fail required Claim-positive exercise.

The complete report also identifies which chosen principals, arguments, guards,
branches and initialized states were *not* covered, when that is knowable. It
must never infer that the chosen fixture domain represents all possible
users, Requests, Organizations or membership races. A bounded model tree is
not an observed production execution trace, even where its terminal state
resembles a physical document. If an exercise gate is required and its
operation or outcome was not reached, an independent successful invariant
check cannot waive the failed gate.

Application authors should not write separate theorem-prover programs simply to
use these checks. Gesso derives supported model/checking inputs from its semantic
construction. Explicit reference callbacks or external models remain possible,
with their translation and correspondence premises visible.

*** Induction is scoped to a catalog and its realization

A conditional application invariant requires an admitted initial-state argument
and preservation by every relevant transition in the scoped catalog. Adding a
new operation or writer can change that obligation even if no existing operation
body changed. The evidence dependency graph records the actual catalog, rule,
backend, and implementation subjects.

An abstract catalog proof is not automatically a physical database proof. Applying
it to production also requires the stated initialization, writer coverage,
input/state mapping, atomicity, frame, and transition-correspondence premises.
Part IV defines the authoritative realization obligations; Parts IX and X define
how stronger evidence composes.

 
The target inductive safety argument has the form: every admitted initial
state satisfies =I=, and for each relevant operation, =I(s)= together with
its admitted transition premises implies =I(s')=. Its quantification is
over the *complete claimed transition catalog*, not over only the operations
that happened to be enabled in one finite exploration. A guard that is
always false makes preservation vacuously true; such a result does not establish
the positive behavior required by HumanHelp. Fairness, liveness, progress,
resource boundedness and eventual user Refresh/adoption require separate
named assumptions and arguments.

Applying the abstract invariant to actual XTDB state demands a justified
mapping for initial state, principal/arguments, transaction-internal
prestate, guarded commit, all relevant physical writers and observed
poststate. Concurrent transactions and multi-step external effects do
not become one serial transition merely because an abstract step is atomic.
A counterexample, unclassified operation or invalidated catalog requires
repair or a separately justified narrower claim, not deletion from the
proof subject to recover a green report.

A selected strict assurance policy must be invoked at the real candidate admission
and installation boundaries. Calling a checker in a test or exposing an optional
function named require-policy does not enforce that policy in production. The
installation result identifies which gates actually ran and which checks remain
required at invocation time.

*** Evidence must retain original subjects and provenance

An issued executor can be bound to a checked semantic source and its actual
implementation. An issued handler can then be constructed to call exactly that
executor after trusted request conversion. This provides stronger structural
correspondence than attaching an operation name to an arbitrary function.

The binding does not prove the correctness of opaque request conversion, output
rendering, backend behavior, or arbitrary extra effects. Those contracts remain
explicit. A wrapper around an issued executor does not automatically inherit its
issuance identity or all its guarantees; supported composition records the new
wrapper's role and effects.

A report copied from a genuine check is still a report. Admission consumes the
required original source/issued product or independently verifies a durable
certificate under its declared checker. It does not accept a caller's success
map as a substitute. Evidence about one callable cannot be transferred to another
because their names or displayed metadata agree.

*** Writer coverage includes routes and non-route work

The coverage graph joins the semantic catalog, admitted executors, installed
ingress, and actual effect providers. It distinguishes at least:

1. declared operations and their permitted effects;
2. registered/issued executor implementations;
3. installed HTTP and non-HTTP entrypoints;
4. observed invocation paths at the stated scope;
5. physical submission capabilities and any independent writers.

Matching operation ID sets is useful but does not prove semantic equivalence.
A host-provided inventory is evidence about what it enumerated, not proof that
it omitted nothing. Independent observations and effect containment can strengthen
coverage; the remaining exhaustiveness premise stays explicit.

The graph must not require every writer to be used by an HTTP route. Queue
consumers, scheduled jobs, migrations, and initializers have legitimate entrypoints
and different lifetimes. Each relevant writer has an admitted owner/path or an
explicitly classified external role. Conversely, a route can invoke several
admitted operations if its choreography/effect contract permits that composition.
The operation graph is not a universal one-route/one-writer bijection.

An unclassified writer blocks a claim requiring closed writer coverage. Under a
policy that permits a limited claim with external writers, their permitted
interference and its effect on dependent invariants are named premises. A generic
label saying external must not conceal a known contradictory mutation.

 
*** Protected-state closure covers physical write capability

The protected write domain is expressed in terms of the actual entities,
tables, fields and invariants the application claims to preserve. An accurate
operation-ID registry is still insufficient if a Biff handler, queue worker,
migration, initializer, raw XTDB call, external service or retry can reach the
same protected state through a different writer. An installed capability
inventory describes which paths can *potentially* mutate protected targets,
including broad full-document replacement, erasure or SQL effects; a claimed
write footprint does not itself enforce a restriction on the physical sink.

For a stronger all-writer claim, the system must either restrict the real
write capability at a boundary that every relevant path actually uses,
or establish correspondingly strong independent evidence of exhaustive
writer inventory and permitted interference. An instrumentation callback
that observes only the operations developers registered cannot certify
absence of an unregistered writer. Source-relative host enumeration,
path/handler identity, target-scope declarations and operation-ID equality
are useful intermediate evidence, but their scope and all unverified
completeness premises remain visible.

A selected invariant can survive *some* additional writers if their actual
effects are shown to preserve it under the declared interference model.
Neither a global raw-writer prohibition nor an assumption that every route
is managed is universal. The application instead declares its supported
writer policy and refuses to attribute the stronger invariant to effects
outside that policy. No trusted report map can grant itself physical
submission rights or prove a real XTDB gateway has excluded bypasses.

*** Request-scoped and work-scoped submission

The normal managed path gives candidate code the resources needed for preparation
and gives the admitted submission boundary the scoped effect capability. A raw
XTDB client need not be available to every handler merely because the application
uses XTDB.

A request has its own invocation identity, current principal binding, selected
assembly instance, issued effect resources, and completion/retirement protocol.
Fresh grants are issued for subsequent requests. A one-use observation or writer
handle must not become a production route that works once and then rejects every
later valid invocation.

A process-wide mutable slot that installs one request's callback and rejects
unrelated concurrent requests is not the general concurrency architecture. The
normal design uses request/work-local contexts or an equivalent isolated registry
with explicit ownership. A qualified serial controller can remain a supported
limited profile where the limitation is intentional and visible.

 
Two simultaneous valid Claim attempts must be allowed to reach independently
owned admitted request contexts without stealing each other's callable,
principal, source observation or one-use writer right. Their eventual guarded
transaction results may differ because only one can incorporate a conflicting
assignment; that is model concurrency, not a reason for the second request to
fail with an unrelated stale global-resource error. An application policy may
choose an explicit serialized deployment but may not present it as unrestricted
parallel progress.

An effect capability is issued to the correct owner and checked at its
actual use, not as a process-wide permanent flag. Reentrant callbacks,
cross-thread continuation, provider retries and cancellation must not
amplify that capability. The source of time, current principal, guarded
prestate and command attribution remain separately bound; completion of an
HTTP response does not by itself mean a durable submitted command has
committed or failed.

Asynchronous handlers, worker tasks, and durable workflows need explicit context
propagation or ownership transfer. Merely retaining a thread-local binding does
not establish their lifetime. Work that survives an HTTP response acquires its
own admitted owner; it cannot borrow the retired request's capability indefinitely.

Cancellation and cleanup first revoke further local use. They do not undo a
transaction already submitted or prove its rejection. Cleanup must not overwrite
an intervening registry change, and failure after dispatch retains command/effect
uncertainty and the required recovery owner.

One-use physical grants and semantic command deduplication remain separate.
Compatible retries preserve =:gesso/command-id= and its binding while receiving
new invocation/transport resources. Backend retries or repeated transaction
function evaluation obey the provider's declared contract and cannot silently
multiply external effects.

*** Observation after execution is not a pre-effect guard

A correspondence observer can detect that an installed route invoked the wrong
writer or that an actual result differs from its model. If that check runs after
dispatch, it is evidence and diagnosis; throwing from it cannot prevent or undo
writes that already happened.

Mandatory safety checks run before the protected effect, with commit-time
conditions enforced by the authoritative boundary. Post-execution observation
may add evidence, flag a broken premise, or trigger containment and recovery.
The explanation states which role each check plays.

A sequence of observed results matching a model path does not by itself establish
physical chronology or uninterrupted state continuity. Occurrence identities,
ordering evidence, captured state scope, and unobserved interference remain part
of the correspondence argument. Equal before/after documents do not prove that
no intervening writer ran.

 
A protected operation therefore has two deliberately separate questions:
*may this effect occur now?* and *what can later be concluded from observing
its execution?* A post-commit comparator cannot be offered as the former.
An observed mismatch may invalidate subsequent admission, demand
operator intervention or create a recovery obligation. It may not
retroactively convert a committed Claim into a rejected command, erase
an already visible physical mutation, or authorize a compensating write
without a separately admitted operation.

*** Policy acceptance and mutation histories

A compliant completed application must demonstrate both meaningful positive
execution and targeted rejection/failure, under the *same real selected
assembly* and evidence profile. The following histories are independent
acceptance requirements, not prefilled mock reports:

| History | Required disposition and evidence boundary |
|---------+--------------------------------------------|
| A current eligible helper clicks actual Claim and the issued command incorporates, then authoritative acquisition and installation complete. | The operation, guarded physical transaction, command attribution and physical presentation have separate positive evidence; a finite checker pass alone is insufficient. |
| Two eligible helpers concurrently attempt Claim on one open Request. | Independent request-local capabilities reach atomic guard evaluation; at most the admitted winner incorporates, and the other has a truthful rejection or recoverable unknown under its contract. |
| A finite model reaches a Claim guard but every configured outcome is rejected. | Report attempts but no committed-branch exercise; fail a policy requiring a positive Claim outcome. |
| Every abstract operation preserves =I=, but the finite model never enables required manager Reassign. | Keep conditional safety distinct; fail Reassign nonvacuity and independent product capability acceptance. |
| A registered operation has no matching finite family or its family uses a different abstract preparation callback than the physical executor. | Reject missing catalog coverage, or retain the source-to-executor correspondence obligation; equal IDs do not prove callback equivalence. |
| A rule exists and has been checked over some states, but no explored state matches its declared source predicate. | Record unexercised rule and reject a required exercise gate; do not count the rule as tested. |
| A scheduler or migration can write protected RequestAssignment through an undeclared XTDB path. | Leave all-writer coverage open or block the policy; a matching route/operation ID set is not complete physical enforcement. |
| A writer declares a narrow field footprint but can physically replace or erase the complete RequestAssignment document. | Use the real possible physical effect in interference/coverage obligations; declaration alone cannot narrow the sink. |
| A copied green assurance report is supplied at startup instead of a live checked construction and bound installation. | Refuse to promote a report to admission or transaction capability; recompute/check original admitted sources. |
| Two parallel requests share one one-use process slot and the second is rejected before its own valid execution. | Fail the normal concurrency contract; a deliberately serialized profile must disclose that limitation. |
| An unauthorized Claim is detected only by a comparator after the write has already committed. | The observation cannot discharge a pre-effect guard; require trusted invocation and atomic model guards, then record the contradiction and recovery. |
| An HTTP response is lost after submission and the client retries with the original command identity. | Permit compatible new invocation/transport resources while retaining command identity and uncertain outcome; no fabricated fresh logical command. |
| A check exhausts its time/memory budget or a required theorem lies outside the supported checker language. | Classify inconclusive or unsupported, applying the selected strict policy rather than silently accepting the obligation. |
| A strict policy requires complete physical writer coverage but the selected installation can only enumerate host-supplied registrations. | Refuse the strong guarantee; retain an explicitly weaker profile only when separately chosen and truthfully explained. |

The expected diagnostics identify original declaration, physical source,
required proposition, applicable policy, checker/host boundary, remaining
premises and missing or contradictory evidence. A negative-only test fixture
cannot establish the product's real positive capabilities. Nor does a
successful modeled or observed transition establish checker soundness,
deployed correspondence or future execution. Sections 07.05–07.15 own the
specific route, physical asset, acquisition, startup, output and acceptance
enforcement that makes these requirements operational.

** Transport, installed routes, and trusted execution

*** Preserve operation identity through physical realization

Once an action is declared to mean a semantic operation, later bindings preserve
that identity. Missing observation basis, plan, transport, or handler causes a
construction/rendering rejection or an explicitly unavailable action under its
UI contract. The system cannot erase the semantic tag and emit an ordinary POST
to keep the control clickable.

Alternate realizations are legal when each is independently declared and checked
for the same operation, and the selection rule is explicit. An optimistic path,
a non-optimistic command path, and a server-only path may have different
requirements. Choosing one is not permission to invent a weaker interpretation
at runtime.

An unavailable rendering preserves the operation and reason while suppressing
its effective executable paths, including form-level and inherited actions.
Styling alone does not disable a transport. A permanently unavailable required
capability still fails independent product acceptance.

 
*** Ordinary HTMX and rendered semantic-route collisions

A plain HTMX request remains a legitimate route realization when its effect
and authorization contract are ordinary. Introducing Choreo must not make
read-only filters, search, navigation, or independently declared ordinary
server actions illegal. The inverse rule is equally important: an action
targeting an assembled semantic-operation route may not become an anonymous
ordinary request merely by losing its =:choreo/op= binding, including when a
component or inherited form supplies the method and URL.

The rendered checker evaluates the *effective* supported action. This includes
native form =action=/=method=, form-level =hx-post=, relevant inherited
attributes, a submitter's =formaction=/=formmethod= overrides and conflicting
HTMX request attributes. A disabled-looking child still has an executable
form or submitter unless all supported physical activation routes are actually
suppressed. Semantic-route collision is evaluated using the method and concrete
selector under the *same* routing semantics that dispatch will use. A GET
and POST sharing a path are not automatically the same endpoint.

The full client DOM may change after checked server serialization. A rendered
surface checker cannot establish that arbitrary JavaScript will never forge
or mutate a request. Trusted ingress must independently reject malformed,
ambiguous and unauthorized operation envelopes, including direct HTTP
clients that never used an admitted browser control. Section 07.07 specifies
the complete dynamic-render enforcement and its raw-HTML escape boundaries.

*** Dispatch and checking share route semantics

The route constructor supplies both the installed dispatcher and the checker
projection, or establishes their correspondence through a qualified integration.
The checker must use the actual method/path interpretation, parameter decoding,
base path, route precedence, and discriminator rules that select the handler.
A guessed regular expression over a URL is insufficient if it disagrees with
real dispatch.

A supported routing profile declares its analyzable subset. Literal paths and
simple segment parameters are a useful initial subset. Unsupported patterns,
rewrites, wildcard dispatch, or content-based selection are explicitly rejected
for that profile or admitted through another qualified contract. Prototype
restrictions do not define the whole framework's eventual route language.

Overlapping routes are either rejected or have a deterministic precedence relation
that both checking and dispatch use. Merely forbidding every overlap is one
possible narrow profile, not a universal requirement. Routes serving several
operations use an admitted discriminator and closed registry; they do not execute
browser-supplied machine state or select by fuzzy names.

Method/path matching uses the effective request after the declared trusted
normalization chain. Proxy rewriting, host/base-URL rules, query selectors,
method overrides, and content negotiation are included where relevant. Unknown
or conflicting selectors fail explicitly rather than allowing one layer to
silently override another.

 
For example, a rendered =POST /app/requests/R1/claim= is not resolved by
comparing text with the route template =/app/requests/:request-id/claim=.
The same route matcher and codec that dispatches the request must establish
the match and decode R1. If the envelope separately names Request R2, neither
the path nor envelope can silently win: the trusted ingress rejects the
contradiction before invoking Claim. This remains true if the request came
directly from curl rather than the checked page.

The checked source is the installed router, or a constructor from which both
the actual router and its checking projection are derived. A supplied snapshot
of declared route metadata is weaker than independently checking the actual
installed method/template/callable and the deployed request path. Host
rewrites, middleware and multiple route alternatives belong to the
selected route profile. If an integration cannot inspect a custom router,
it requires a named adaptation/qualification premise rather than silently
claiming that a simplistic matcher covers all deployments.

A multi-operation endpoint needs a verified discriminator and a trusted
operation-to-executor mapping. Ambiguity, duplicate matches, a missing
discriminator, or a discriminator supplied only by untrusted metadata
cannot establish semantic dispatch correspondence.

*** The installed callable is the checked callable

The construction should issue or compose the actual route handlers and dispatcher,
then install those products. A separate map claiming that route R uses executor E
is weaker evidence than constructing R to invoke E and checking the actual
installation's binding.

The installation check distinguishes:

- a declaration naming a handler;
- a constructed dispatcher bound to that callable;
- a system map holding the wrapped dispatcher;
- the actual server instance accepting requests through that wrapped dispatcher.

Each is a different evidence boundary. Inspecting a caller-selected system map
does not prove what a running server captured earlier. The supported server
constructor must consume the admitted handler directly or establish its actual
adoption through an equivalent qualified mechanism.

Ordinary middleware remains possible. Its composition preserves the required
routing, principal, request, response, and effect contracts. A middleware stage
that rewrites an operation selector or replaces the handler changes the relevant
binding and cannot inherit the previous report without checking.

 
*** Actual host adoption and invocation lifetime

The source-issued route/executor, the installed Biff handler slot, the
network-facing server's captured handler and the physical effect invocation
are distinct evidence subjects. An opaque local handle or a fresh comparison
against a Biff system map can support the first two without proving the
server actually serves that map. A later module, hot reload, retained old
dispatcher, independent raw XTDB client or alternate HTTP entrypoint can
break the claimed relation after a report was issued.

The supported managed application constructor must either enforce the
admitted handler selection at the serving boundary, or carry explicit
deployment-adoption and bypass premises consistent with its stated
assurance profile. A protected route must not preserve the strong
production-enforcement label when its actual installation is unknown.

Each accepted HTTP invocation obtains a current request-owned context,
correct generation and appropriate scoped write capability; it is not
authorized by an old request's one-use handle or a copied result map.
Asynchronous completion, callbacks and durable work have separately
declared owners and retirement rules. A bounded-serial execution profile
may be qualified as such, but does not claim unrestricted parallel
request admission or execution.

*** Trusted command admission

The transport contract defines the real wire field/encoding, supported protocol,
operation/interface identity, command binding, argument codecs, and outcome
channel. The browser transports the stable command ID before any possible send.
=:transport-request-id= identifies an attempt and is not the domain Request ID.

At the trusted ingress boundary:

1. decode and validate the actual supported envelope and typed arguments;
2. resolve the operation through the admitted server registry;
3. require agreement between operation and subject selectors in the route,
   envelope, query, and trusted dispatch context where the contract duplicates them;
4. obtain principal/tenant context from its trusted provider;
5. bind the current invocation to the admitted public model operation;
6. enforce command repetition, disclosure, and atomic current-state guards as
   specified in Part IV;
7. encode only the permitted result and observation evidence.

 
The admitted server registry selects and invokes the actual issued executable
delegation to the *public model operation*. The route owns protocol decoding,
trusted subject selection, principal binding and outcome encoding; it must not
reimplement Request/RequestAssignment business policy in a second handler.
A route's successful response is not evidence that its declared operation
executed: the claimed outcome must be causally joined to the exact issued
invocation and its authoritative transaction or typed rejection.

The wire contract states where =:gesso/command-id=, the semantic operation,
argument schema, supported protocol revision and applicable observation
context actually appear in an HTMX/form/request transport. Unrecognized
versions and inconsistent duplicate fields fail before protected effect
submission. =:http-request-id= and =:transport-request-id=, where used,
identify request/attempt scopes rather than the durable domain command,
physical Request entity or browser execution. Compatible retries may use a
new transport attempt while preserving the original command binding; they
must not manufacture a second logical Claim merely because the first
response disappeared. An existing command result and a current entity read
answer different questions.

For a protected mutation, trusted request conversion and domain-model
validation are independently specified. The route must not accept
browser-owned principal, tenant, role, plan digest, or purported admission
certificate as proof of current authority. Trusted authorization and
transaction guards evaluate the appropriate *current* authoritative frame,
including current membership and Request state; a previously displayed
allowed affordance remains only a view of older knowledge.

Browser-supplied principal IDs, role labels, basis tokens, plan references,
certificates, or assembly IDs do not grant current authority. A basis carried by
a browser is protocol context unless its particular provenance/use contract
establishes more. Part II's observation-evidence distinction applies.

Where cookie-based or comparable ambient credentials make cross-site invocation
relevant, the selected transport/authentication profile includes the required
origin/request-integrity defenses. Structural route closure and typed decoding
do not substitute for that security contract.

 
The selected transport must also preserve disclosure and correlation policy:
a response for command C1 must not be accepted as C2 or reveal another
principal's protected result. HTTP acceptance, server-side settlement,
historical incorporation, authorized readback and physical client adoption
remain different evidence propositions. Their distinction survives
network retry, duplicate transport delivery, redirect, and loss after commit.

*** Required execution providers are typed bindings

A requirement is more precise than a member of a set such as =#{:clock :db}=.
It identifies the input/output contract, origin, invocation scope, lifetime,
ordering/dependency constraints, and supported failure outcomes of the provider.

For example, a Claim executor may consume a sampled instant under
=:biff.fx/now=. A zero-argument clock function under another key does not satisfy
that requirement until a declared adapter samples and binds it at the intended
boundary.

#+begin_src clojure
{:requirement/id :claim/commit-time-input
 :consumer {:operation/id :request/claim
            :input-path [:execution-context :biff.fx/now]}
 :value-contract :time/instant
 :provider/ref trusted-clock-provider-ref
 :binding-adapter/ref sampled-invocation-time-ref
 :lifetime :invocation
 :failure-continuation/ref time-unavailable-ref}
#+end_src

The example is a construction binding, not proof that a clock is accurate or
that the value is transaction time. The operation names the temporal meaning it
requires. Retry semantics state whether a sampled value is preserved or replaced
and how that affects command binding and guards.

 
If Request Claim requires =:biff.fx/now= as a sampled =Instant= at
the guarded model boundary, an application supplying only a function under
=:clock= has not closed that edge. The admitted adapter must actually sample
and place the value at the consumer's expected input path. Validation of
type, source, temporal meaning, and lifetime is separate from verifying
clock accuracy. On retry, the contract must distinguish an original
command-bound timestamp from a newly sampled invocation time; changing a
timestamp must not silently change the logical command's meaning.

When an execution provider becomes unavailable after structural admission,
the operation follows its declared typed failure, uncertainty or recovery
path. In particular, an external side effect or XTDB submission that
might have occurred is not rejected merely because its return path or
subsequent publication failed. A fallback clock, database or publication
provider is permitted only if its semantic and trust correspondence has
been explicitly admitted.

Providers include authentication, transaction execution, authoritative reads,
progression comparison, clocks, identity generation, publication, and external
services as needed. Missing, ambiguous, incompatible, or wrongly sourced supply
is rejected where statically knowable. Runtime unavailability follows its
required declared handling path. Having a transaction capability does not
authorize the transaction's business operation.

 
*** Positive and adversarial transport histories

The application must make real eligible operations usable and reject
individual invalid realizations at their earliest legitimate boundaries.
A schematic status map is not a test of the actual installed request path.

| History | Required disposition |
|---------+----------------------|
| An eligible helper uses the real annotated Claim control; its decoded Request selector, authenticated identity, command and trusted executor agree, and the guarded mutation commits. | Admit the route, execute the original public model operation, and preserve distinct transaction, outcome, acquisition and physical adoption evidence. |
| A parameterized Claim POST omits Choreo identity after a component strips its metadata, though its physical URL still resolves to a semantic route. | Reject the malformed managed affordance at the checked rendering boundary; direct server requests still require trusted protocol validation. |
| A form posts to a protected Claim route after the child button was visually disabled, or a submitter overrides its target. | Detect the effective action or suppress every active path in the unavailable rendering; CSS alone is insufficient. |
| POST and GET use the same URL, but only POST is a semantic Claim route. | Preserve method-sensitive dispatch; do not forbid the legitimate ordinary GET by path text alone. |
| A browser sends operation Claim for Request R1 while the decoded URL selects R2. | Reject contradictory selectors before the protected effect, even for a client that bypassed the browser. |
| Two routes overlap and checking chooses route A while the running router chooses B. | Reject the incompatible route profile or establish common deterministic precedence; no claimed closure based on the wrong matcher. |
| A current issued Claim handler is checked, but Biff or the deployed server instead installs another callable under the same route ID. | Fail or invalidate actual installation correspondence; in-process names or stale host snapshots are insufficient. |
| The same physical endpoint admits Claim and Cancel, but no validated discriminator binds the selected operation to its issued executor. | Reject ambiguous dispatch rather than guessing from request shape, route name or button text. |
| The incoming command claims its own principal or organization role, which conflicts with trusted session/tenant context. | Rebind authority exclusively from trusted sources; reject unsupported mismatches under the selected security contract. |
| Claim needs a sampled =:biff.fx/now= Instant, but the provider exposes only a differently shaped unsampled clock. | Reject the static provider mismatch or block invocation at its actual capability gate. |
| A Claim commits, its HTTP response is lost, and the browser retries. | Retain the original command ID and binding with fresh compatible transport attempt; do not duplicate the logical mutation or invent rejection. |
| An asynchronous handler or worker continues after the invocation or assembly generation is retired. | Use its own admitted lifetime or revoke obsolete effect rights; command recovery remains separately owned. |
| A post-commit observer reports a wrong handler while the domain write is already durable. | Record contradiction and repair obligations; do not claim the observation was a pre-effect guard or undo committed state. |
| A normal read-only HTMX search uses a route without any semantic-operation annotation. | Permit the ordinary route under its own effect/authorization contract; Choreo does not impose imaginary command semantics. |

These histories require source-derived routing, provider and executor identities,
real physical installation and appropriately qualified runtime evidence.
The next sections separately close browser artifact, generated HTML,
acquisition and installation joins. No transport checker, HTTP 200 or
copied certificate grants current model authority.

** Browser assembly manifest and physical artifacts
:PROPERTIES:
:CUSTOM_ID: req-browser-assembly-manifest
:END:

The browser build consumes the admitted semantic/build inputs of the same
application definition. Its manifest identifies the exact admitted plan set,
operation-to-plan correspondence, executable identities, interpretation/profile
contracts, required physical handlers, and relevant implementation/toolchain
inputs. It does not contain a digest of bytes that do not yet exist.

The admitted plan inventory must cover every required operation realization and
identify any deliberately included shared or currently unused plans. Missing,
duplicate, incompatible, or undeclared executable entries fail the applicable
inventory contract. Bundling an explicitly admitted extra plan is not intrinsically
wrong; letting an unexamined executable enter the claimed closed registry is.

 
*** Source-derived inventory and independent build choices

The required manifest is derived from the same admitted operation and role
sources as rendered actions, server transport and application preflight. It
names each executable plan's exact semantic digest and supported role,
features, protocol, source/projection version and compatible host runtime.
Derivation cannot start from a second manually maintained browser registry
whose members happen to agree today. A newly required Claim/Reassign plan
therefore changes the admitted build input even before any JavaScript exists.

| Inventory class | Required treatment |
|-----------------+--------------------|
| Required executable plans | Exactly matched to the admitted operation/role projection, with no missing, duplicate or mismatched entries. |
| Shared or deliberately inactive plans | Explicitly classified; they cannot be treated as active product capabilities or silently escape the effective executable/handler inventory. |
| Runtime/host effects | Enumerate physical handlers, event sources, transports, acquisition and supported completion/failure protocols for every reachable admitted effect. |
| Compiler, runtime and physical realization | Bind the implementations and options capable of changing emitted behavior, not merely friendly version labels. |
| Dynamically imported code and workers | Account for the transitive loaded resource set and the declared runtime loading/qualification contract. |

Source-owned semantic identity, exact projected payload identity, build
environment identity and emitted asset bytes identify distinct objects.
The manifest must not infer trusted source provenance from a filename or
self-advertised digest, and its graph must remain acyclic: the digest of an
output cannot be included in the very same unqualified bytes it digests.

*** A concrete generated-entrypoint construction

The normal build uses a Gesso-owned generated bootstrap source. It embeds or
imports the exact admitted manifest/plan payloads and invokes the canonical
runtime bootstrap. Application code supplies typed physical realization options;
it cannot replace the manifest-owned operation registry or plan resolver through
those options.

A concrete build sequence is:

1. Resolve the application definition once into the candidate semantic inputs and
   selected browser realization.
2. Derive the manifest and exact executable payloads from that construction.
3. Generate the bootstrap entrypoint and explicit imports for the admitted
   physical realization implementations.
4. Compile with the declared toolchain, dependency versions, options, and inputs.
5. Record the generated-input correspondence and digest the actual emitted assets.
6. Verify the staged manifest/receipt/asset set before publication.
7. Admit an immutable asset location set and bind it to the candidate assembly.

A low-level emitter accepting arbitrary JavaScript plus a copied manifest is not
equivalent to this construction. It may remain a testing or integration API with
a narrower guarantee.

 
The default builder must actually generate the entrypoint from the admitted
manifest and resolve its physical realization options through a constrained,
typed interface. A physical options value may select concrete DOM/HTMX
adapters and integration callbacks, but may not inject a second plan resolver,
rewrite admitted operation IDs, replace semantic transitions or bypass required
effect handlers. The options Var's identity, its resolved implementation,
compiler classpath and deployment profile participate in evidence invalidation.

The exact build result is tied to the *source-generated input* and the
compiler/toolchain actually invoked. A successfully staged JavaScript file
does not prove that the compiler preserved Gesso's intended semantics; that
