remains a named fidelity/correspondence premise until stronger checking exists.
Likewise the existence of a generated entrypoint in source does not prove
the intended runtime bundle was emitted or later loaded.

There is no requirement for a magical parser that extracts all semantic plans
from arbitrary optimized JavaScript. Source-generation correspondence, compiler
fidelity under a named premise, and exact emitted-byte binding provide a concrete
argument. Stronger independently checked compiler/artifact correspondence can
replace the relevant premise when available. A runtime registry probe can add
conformance evidence, but a self-reported registry is not independent proof of
all code executed by the bundle.

 
A supported producer may expose an independently checked emitted-plan
inventory, but the method of obtaining it must be declared. It cannot be
satisfied by merely copying the expected plan digests into a receipt beside
unrelated bytes. If the compiler does not support a trustworthy registry
extraction, the build can instead retain its exact source-generation
witness and a scoped compiler-fidelity premise, with real-browser
startup/plan execution supplying additional behavioral evidence. Neither
method licenses a claim of universal equivalence for arbitrary optimized
JavaScript, third-party scripts or dynamically loaded unknown chunks.

*** Receipts bind provenance and bytes separately

A detached build receipt records the manifest identity, generated input/plan
identities, compiler/runtime/implementation closure, relevant build options, and
the exact digest/size/location of each emitted asset. Its evidentiary value depends
on provenance from the admitted build/checking boundary, not on the receipt's
own claims. It conveys no permission to perform a domain operation.

Verifying a digest establishes equality with recorded bytes under the digest
premise. It does not establish that those bytes implement the intended semantics.
Conversely, trusted compilation from the correct source does not establish that
the server later serves those same bytes. Both relationships belong in closure.

 
The receipt and build manifest have *different provenance*. A copied receipt
with matching expected labels cannot authenticate either the emitting
compiler or the served file. The receipt issuer must be the admitted
build/checking boundary or another independently qualified source, and the
checker must read the actual bytes being admitted at the relevant storage
boundary. Exact byte digest matching is a content-identity assertion under
the collision premise, not a proof of inclusion, runtime behavior or
permission to execute a protected domain operation.

If the selected output is more than one file, each member's digest, relative
location, dependency edge, load policy and serving identity contribute to
the retained asset-set evidence. Content/security headers, cross-origin
loads, service-worker caches and import maps can alter which code executes
even when the entrypoint file itself is correct; the selected physical
profile accounts for these paths or leaves their implications explicitly
unestablished.

The asset set includes dynamic chunks, workers, imported runtime libraries, and
other resources whose behavior affects the claim. Relevant CSS or configuration
that can suppress or redirect an affordance also has a declared dependency or
qualification role. Diagnostic-only sidecars retain their separate noninterference
contract from Part V; they do not become executable semantic inputs.

Build inputs include opaque physical implementation changes where their behavior
matters. Reusing the same named =current= toolchain/runtime label across changed
implementations cannot preserve evidence applicability. Deterministic compilation
is useful but not a prerequisite for naming actual emitted bytes: a receipt can
bind one actual output even when another valid build yields different bytes.

*** Publication and serving preserve the checked binding

Candidate builds use isolated staging locations. A failed build or rejected
candidate cannot overwrite assets still served by an admitted assembly. Atomic
replacement of one file is insufficient if readers can observe a new bundle with
an old receipt or a mixture of old and new chunks. Publish a verified immutable
asset set, then switch the admitted serving reference.

The concrete serving strategy must prevent or detect substitution between check
and use. Content-addressed/versioned immutable assets are a useful default. An
open immutable resource handle, qualified store, or equivalent serving contract
can also work. Reading a mutable file once at startup and trusting its path
forever is not exact serving correspondence.

A page generated under assembly A must reference assets bound to A even if
assembly B activates before the browser requests them. A mutable logical URL that
now serves B can break that relationship. Versioned URLs or a qualified
assembly-specific asset selection protocol close it. Cache, CDN, service-worker,
and old-client behavior follow the selected deployment/profile contract.

 
*** Atomic set activation and failure recovery

Staging one JavaScript file and separately writing its receipt with atomic
per-file renames is *not* atomic publication of the pair, much less of a
multi-file bundle. If the artifact is replaced but receipt publication then
fails, the failed candidate cannot be considered admitted even when a
subsequent reader notices the mismatch. More importantly, changing a mutable
live asset path may already have disturbed the previously served generation.
A valid end-state design stages a complete candidate set in isolation,
verifies it, and activates an immutable set reference atomically with the
serving-generation selection or provides an equivalently qualified mechanism.

The previous admitted generation must remain serveable until its references
and permitted old-client lifetimes have been retired. Candidate failure,
cancelled compilation or a partial publish does not overwrite or delete its
live assets. A publish pointer switch may be rolled back only under an
explicitly safe deployment/compatibility policy; restoring asset bytes after
clients have fetched the new set does not undo those clients' execution.

A successful build receipt establishes only the candidate artifact relation.
Activation additionally needs actual route/static-handler adoption and the
asset set available at the URLs generated for that assembly. A page rendered
under A is bound to A's immutable asset coordinates even if B becomes current
before the browser fetches them. The storage, CDN and cache policy must
either preserve that binding or detect a mismatched response before
accepting it. Same-name shared URLs are safe only with a qualified
generation-aware selection or compatibility contract.

The currentness check asks whether the assets intended for this admitted assembly
match its required build. It does not demand that every sleeping browser already
runs the newest deployment. Older continuations follow Part VI's compatibility
and recovery rules, including retained command resolution.

 
Browser plan compatibility is weaker than build/serve exact currentness:
an older client may legitimately continue or recover under Part VI even
while a new deployment must reject its stale build receipt. Conversely,
byte-equal current assets do not automatically make a retired execution
legal, confer principal authority, preserve a stale physical target or
resolve a submitted command. Both generation/host identity and exact
resource/command lifetimes remain necessary.

A build that adds a required manager Reassign control and plan to assembly
B cannot reuse A's browser bundle merely because the old Claim plan is
still present or both bundles advertise a compatible transport version.
An application that starts with B's semantic registry but serves A's
runtime has not closed its protected operations. It must refuse
activation or explicitly choose and admit a compatible, honestly
described lesser realization that still meets independent product
requirements.

Tests of startup/currentness use the same verification mechanism and actual
artifact path as production. Synthetic stamped files can test a narrow checker,
but cannot stand in for the real generated runtime in application acceptance.

 
*** Positive and adversarial artifact histories

Tests and deployment qualifications must connect the *real* source-generated
browser bundle to the admitted application. A unit test with arbitrary
JavaScript and a copied stamp has a narrower subject.

| History | Required disposition |
|---------+----------------------|
| The canonical application constructor derives Claim and Reassign plans, builds the generated CLJS bootstrap, verifies actual staged bytes and receipt, activates an immutable set, and a real browser loads it. | Distinct semantic-plan, builder, byte-identity, served-set and runtime adoption evidence are established at their respective boundaries. |
| R5.1 application B requires Reassign but the browser artifact and receipt still belong to A. | Reject B's startup/activation as stale even if the old Claim plan would have remained protocol-compatible. |
| An extra unregistered executable plan appears in a supposedly closed runtime bundle. | Reject or classify the extra entry under the declared inactive/shared contract; do not infer that untracked code is authorized. |
| A caller supplies arbitrary JavaScript and manually stamps it with the correct plan digests. | The low-level byte/receipt relation may be checkable, but the ordinary source-generated implementation claim remains unestablished. |
| A build updates the exact JavaScript bytes but leaves the previous receipt or tampers with its digest. | Fail byte/receipt currentness; a matching filename or nominal version is insufficient. |
| A generated entrypoint embeds the right plans while its declared physical realization Var points to a changed implementation. | Invalidate the affected build correspondence and rebuild/requalify the executable implementation dependencies. |
| The JavaScript entrypoint is current, but an old dynamically imported chunk or service-worker cache provides incompatible runtime behavior. | The qualified transitive resource/serving relation is unsatisfied; entrypoint digest equality cannot close it alone. |
| Candidate B's compilation fails before publication, while A is still serving. | Keep A's admitted asset set intact and available; reject B without damaging live A. |
| Candidate B replaces the shared JavaScript filename, then receipt publication fails. | Fail B; report the old generation's serving risk and repair it rather than claiming two atomic file moves made an atomic set. |
| A is rendered before B activates, and the browser fetches an unversioned URL that now serves B's incompatible bundle. | Prevent the cross-generation substitution through immutable coordinates or qualified generation-aware serving. |
| A current asset receipt matches locally, but the network server or CDN sends different bytes. | The local candidate check is not deployed serving evidence; reject or explicitly leave the stronger serving claim open. |
| The new B bundle is exact, but a sleeping A browser still owns a durable unknown Claim. | Apply the old-plan continuity/command resolver policy; do not relabel the historical command or force unsafe migration merely because B is current. |
| A unit checker passes on a fake stamped bundle, but the actual shipped browser cannot register or execute Claim. | The unit test remains valid for its narrow relation; real-browser positive acceptance and source-generation conformance fail. |
| A build's compiler or physical handler is outside a declared proof/qualification profile. | Record unsupported or open premises and refuse an unearned strong certificate; do not invent a compiler proof. |

These cases do not require every build to be bitwise reproducible. They
require that *the actual admitted bytes* and their required dependencies
are identified and correctly served with provenance sufficient for the
selected profile. The source-generated pathway, exact content check,
physical activation and real-browser behavior are complementary claims,
not substitute green flags.

** Rendered affordances and concrete response closure

*** Minimal semantic intent in views

The view selects an admitted operation, supplies concrete arguments and required
observations, and chooses presentation/availability. Prepared bindings from Part
V derive the plan, transport, encoding, and other realization details from the
assembly. A view should not manually copy browser registries, authority roles,
command envelope formats, or artifact digests.

A prepared action is not current authorization. The trusted model boundary still
checks the principal, Request, Membership, Organization policy, and other
commit-time dependencies. Rendering an action establishes neither a permanent
permission nor a promise that a later attempt will succeed.

An action can be deliberately unavailable under its UI contract. Its semantic
identity and reason remain inspectable, and no effective transport survives that
unavailability. A missing required basis cannot be repaired by discarding semantic
metadata or forging a browser observation record.

 
The authored view may be a Request card rendered for an eligible helper, a
manager with an admitted Reassign target, or a participant who lacks the
required authoritative basis. Those produce different concrete controls,
but the underlying semantic operation does not change to satisfy a template.
A rendered enabled Claim/Reassign action is *structurally usable* only if its
selected operation, typed arguments, basis/observation obligation, actual
browser plan, required physical transport and return path close together.
That observation need not promise current authorization: a competing Claim
or Organization policy change can invalidate the action before commit.

Positive product acceptance remains independent: a perfectly well-formed
permanently disabled Reassign button does not demonstrate that a manager
can reassign an eligible Request. A rendered affordance is also not an
authorization token; client-supplied metadata cannot substitute for the
trusted principal and current guarded model operation.

*** Check the effective action, not one attribute

The render profile defines the HTML/HTMX subset whose effective behavior can be
checked. It accounts for all supported request sources and their composition,
including:

- generated semantic bindings and ordinary explicit request attributes;
- form action/method and submitter overrides;
- form association, including detached controls;
- applicable inherited attributes and explicit inheritance controls;
- relevant defaults, relative URLs, document/base context, and current path;
- supported boosting, extensions, response triggers, and navigation behavior;
- string/keyword or other attribute spellings that the serializer treats alike;
- conflicts between authored and generated transport, target, and protocol fields.

The profile must follow the actual selected browser/library behavior. It cannot
assume every attribute inherits, ignore a supported default action, or accept
silent last-write-wins merging where effective dispatch becomes ambiguous.
Duplicate IDs, invalid nested forms, conflicting attribute spellings, and browser
repair of malformed markup are rejected or explicitly handled where they affect
the claim.

 
*** Derive the effective request under the selected HTML/HTMX profile

The checker and actual browser must agree on the action of the *activated
control*, not merely on attribute names present in one Hiccup vector.
A detached submitter's =form= owner may be elsewhere in the document; a
button may default to submit; its =formaction= and =formmethod= can override
the parent form; an ordinary form may default to GET. Explicit
=:hx-post= and a native submit path can coexist and may have different
effective actions. Duplicate keyword/string spellings can serialize as
two physical attributes, so deterministic selection of one Hiccup map key
does not establish unambiguous HTML behavior.

A checker for the current selected profile must enumerate *all*
supported actions that can cause relevant semantic transport, including
the activation path of each submitter, not just the primary button or one
handpicked =hx-*= attribute. If the same DOM node offers a valid managed
Claim =hx-post= *and* an additional unadmitted protected native form
submission, the valid action cannot exempt the second one.
Conflicting transport, argument, target and observation selectors reject
unless the profile supplies an explicit, independently checked resolution.

The physical route match uses the same supported method, path decoding,
base URI, precedence and normalization as actual installed dispatch, or
a qualified correspondence to it. A plain GET search that happens to share
the path text of a semantic POST is not silently transformed into Claim.
Conversely a concrete =/requests/R/claim= POST does not become ordinary
because its metadata disappeared. Rewriting and inheritance outside the
supported profile must be classified as unsupported or explicitly constrained;
they cannot be counted as checked merely because the scanner did not find them.

A fragment can depend on a form or inherited context outside the returned tree.
Its assembly/rendering contract supplies the necessary host context or constrains
it to a self-contained composition. If required context is unknown, the checker
reports unsupported/unestablished behavior; it does not declare the fragment
complete because the missing ancestor was outside its scan.

 
The target's scoped identity and composition environment are first-class
inputs where needed: document/base URL, HTMX inheritance rules, owning
form, submitter, current route coordinates and authorized target/fragment
ownership. A standalone fragment can be preflight-closed *relative to its
declared self-contained host contract* without claiming that a future
uncontrolled parent element will preserve that contract. If an out-of-band
replacement, boosted navigation or cache insertion can change those
coordinates, the selected output/installation integration must check the
changed effective context or retain the corresponding external premise.

An ordinary effective action targeting an assembled semantic route must carry
that route's required semantic realization. Moving the action to an ancestor or
substituting concrete path parameters does not make an anonymous semantic request
legal. Conversely, an ordinary read/search route remains ordinary when it meets
its declared acquisition and effect contracts without a command choreography.

Arbitrary client JavaScript can alter the DOM or send requests directly. Render
checking establishes the trusted output's supported realization, not honesty of
a hostile browser. Server admission remains independent. Effects of ordinary
scripts within protected browser footprints follow Part VI's ownership and
noninterference contract.

*** The final structured value is the checked value

Dynamic rendering is checked after the application has produced the concrete
structured output and before prohibited output is delivered. Checking a prepared
view model and then running an unchecked renderer is insufficient: the renderer
can introduce a malformed control after the check.

The normal response path is:

1. retain the request's admitted assembly and response-context binding;
2. perform view preparation and component expansion under their declared contracts;
3. materialize the concrete structured tree and effective-action context;
4. validate semantic bindings and all supported effective actions against that
   assembly;
5. serialize that same checked value through the admitted serializer;
6. apply only response transformations whose correspondence contract preserves
   the checked properties, or recheck after a relevant transformation;
7. release the response through the admitted delivery boundary.

Lazy values, component callbacks, mutable references, and serializer-time code
must not be evaluated once during checking and again with different results during
serialization. A supported implementation can materialize a bounded immutable
tree first, or use a serializer with an equivalent checked occurrence protocol.
It must state the actual mechanism and resource/failure limits.

 
A pre-serialization guard that receives the *same top-level Hiccup reference*
does not by that fact ensure that lazy descendants, custom components or
a mutable reference produce the same expanded HTML twice. The supported
render profile must identify which values are inert, which must be fully
realized before checking, how custom renderer callbacks are constrained,
and whether serializer-time transformation invalidates the check. A
materialized exact occurrence is preferable when feasible; where a
paired inspect/emit protocol is used, its semantics, effect containment,
failure behavior and implementation assumptions are explicit. A
counterexample discovered after some output is already streamed can
block further delivery and demand repair, but cannot retract sent bytes.

When validation fails, the response producer must not silently invoke
a different unchecked serializer, return a pre-rendered copy, or use
a privileged raw HTML fallback to keep serving the control. The
fallback is itself within a qualified minimal-output protocol, which
must fail safely without unbounded recursion or accidental disclosure.

This is structural/effective-action checking, not automatic HTML sanitization or
proof of arbitrary renderer purity. Content safety and active-content policy are
separate contracts, as in Part VI. A renderer that has already performed an
external side effect cannot have that effect undone by rejecting its output.

*** Systemic enforcement covers deferred and alternate responses

The canonical application handler installs the guard once for all supported
structured responses. Nested guards compose without disabling the outer guard.
Application authors need not remember a manual validation call at every render.

A dynamically scoped guard can implement the synchronous path, but an asynchronous
response may be completed after that dynamic scope has ended or on another
thread. The response completion carries an explicit assembly/guard context or
uses another qualified propagation mechanism. Absence of the required guard at
a managed serialization boundary is a failure, not a silent return to legacy
unchecked behavior.

 
The ordinary Gesso/Biff synchronous handler integration can use a
dynamically bound guard around =gesso.http/html-response=. That mechanism
does not automatically cover a response serialized after the handler returns,
a future completed on another thread, a raw pre-serialized Ring body,
a server module replacing the checked handler, or a server that never
uses the wrapped =:biff.ring/handler=. Such a path is not magically
checked by the existence of a valid ApplicationAssembly or by an earlier
test of =check-rendered-surface=.

The finished managed application contract identifies how the guard reaches
each admitted producer and final response emission: captured generation
and currentness validation, explicit propagation to deferred continuations,
and a startup/installation gate that actually adopts the protected
serialization boundary. The policy may explicitly exclude an ordinary
unmanaged response whose effects are disjoint from its managed claims,
but it must refuse a whole-managed-surface guarantee if the omitted
response can emit protected operations. An opt-in unit checker cannot
prove the checked production path was used.

The supported response profile covers or explicitly classifies:

| Response path | Required treatment |
|---------------+--------------------|
| Ordinary structured page/fragment | Check the actual final structured occurrence before serialization/delivery. |
| Deferred/asynchronous response | Preserve the admitted assembly and guard through completion, timeout, cancellation, and error handling. |
| Streaming output | Check each delivered managed portion under a compositional context or buffer the required scope; acknowledge that already-sent bytes cannot be withdrawn. |
| Cached structured fragment | Preserve semantic binding and applicability; check the concrete occurrence in its current context where needed. |
| Cached/pre-serialized HTML | Establish a separate admitted output correspondence and context/authority policy; a previous check does not authorize disclosure to another principal. |
| Error response after handler failure | Use the same supported output boundary or an explicitly admitted minimal error protocol. |
| Redirect/navigation/secondary-target response | Check its declared effect and target/protocol behavior, not only the main HTML body. |
| Raw HTML/custom renderer | Admit a separate realization contract or exclude it from the specific structured-output claim. |

Naming an escape hatch does not satisfy a requirement that all application
managed surfaces are covered. A policy requiring that coverage rejects an
uncovered managed path. Static assets or truly unmanaged output can be explicitly
outside that claim, provided their effects do not invalidate its premises.

A response cache key is not just a URL when its contents depend on tenant,
authorization, query, semantic contract, or assembly instance. The cache contract
states the partition, freshness, revocation, and revalidation behavior needed for
its claims. Returning a cached checked card to an unauthorized user is still a
disclosure failure.

 
Cached output has at least two independent questions: *was the stored
structured occurrence checked against the generation that produced it?*,
and *is disclosing and executing it valid for this recipient, context and
current generation?* Cached HTML cannot inherit indefinite permission
from an earlier checked render. Invalidation and reacquisition are
separate from permission to disclose a cached body; an old card can be
structurally coherent yet expose an operation no longer available to
the current principal. A cache hit that bypasses the admitted checking
or authorization boundary must be classified as such.

*** Worked example: a render-time defect after a valid Claim

Startup admits the Claim operation and its return path. For a particular request,
the trusted model incorporates command C42 successfully. While preparing the
resulting card, a bug creates a Cancel affordance without its required Request
argument.

The output guard rejects that concrete card before delivery. It does not change
the authoritative Claim outcome to rejected. The trusted request boundary retains
its known result and follows the admitted response-failure protocol.

| Evidence available to the participant | Required treatment |
|---------------------------------------+--------------------|
| A permitted, correlated committed outcome is delivered through the supported error/settlement channel. | Preserve known incorporation; present response/installation failure separately and offer the authorized recovery path. |
| The server knows incorporation, but its response is lost or the browser cannot admit the payload. | The browser remains unknown until its resolver supplies admissible evidence. |
| A later card read shows the current claimant without command attribution. | It can establish current state at its scope; it does not by itself resolve C42. |
| The malformed response concerns an operation rejected before submission. | Preserve that actual disposition; do not route all response failures through a committed-only handler. |

The error protocol defines the actual HTTP/transport representation and the
browser hook that can decode it, including non-success status handling where
used. A map containing settlement metadata is not enough if the selected HTMX
profile never exposes that metadata to the runtime.

The fallback response itself must be valid and bounded. It must not recursively
invoke the same failing renderer forever or expose privileged diagnostics. A
minimal typed response or a later authenticated resolver may be more reliable
than trying to render the full card again inside the error handler.

 
The error path must preserve the distinction between the *server's known
authoritative result* and *the browser's participant-relative knowledge*.
For example, the server may know that Claim C42 committed and that the
Cancel action in its response is malformed. If a correlated, authorized
settlement is actually delivered and admitted by the selected browser
HTTP/HTMX error protocol, the client may learn the incorporation and
separately report presentation failure. If the error response is lost,
the client retains =:unknown= until the durable command resolver supplies
admissible attribution. A current Request card is insufficient proof of
which earlier Claim command won.

A bad result renderer may also have run *after* the protected transaction,
and its failure cannot retroactively veto that transaction. Conversely,
a rejected pre-effect command remains rejected when rendering its error
body fails. The fallback must not opportunistically invent another
domain write or refresh authorization under the pretext of recovery.
The next section owns the complete authoritative outcome, acquisition and
propagation mappings.

Tests distinguish no malformed output was delivered from no protected mutation
occurred. The former is the render guard's responsibility; the latter requires
an earlier command/model gate. Both need a positive control showing that valid
requests remain usable.

 
*** Positive and adversarial rendered-response histories

Each test uses the selected source-owned assembly, *actual* relevant
production response boundary, and where applicable the real browser
control. Supplying an already successful report or constructing a
valid protocol command in place of a broken control is insufficient.

| History | Required disposition and evidence scope |
|---------+-----------------------------------------|
| An eligible helper renders a well-formed Claim button, activates it, and an admitted plan submits the command to the protected route. | The concrete enabled control and its supported effective request close against the assembly; model execution and actual browser completion need separate evidence. |
| A manager sees an eligible Reassign affordance with typed Request and target Helper IDs. | Preserve its semantic identity, complete arguments and original required observation; do not claim that rendering grants lasting authority. |
| The Reassign renderer omits =:helper/id= on one conditional card while startup's registry is correct. | Reject that concrete enabled affordance before checked output serialization; a static route/plan success cannot excuse it. |
| A Claim button lacks basis and is marked visually disabled, but its enclosing form retains an active semantic POST. | Reject the effective request or suppress every active transport while preserving the unavailable semantic identity. |
| A marked Claim button emits the certified =hx-post= and an additional unadmitted protected =hx-put=. | Reject the extra executable action; valid metadata for one route does not authorize a second route. |
| A detached submit button overrides a search form to the Claim POST route. | Resolve its real =form= owner and =formaction=/=formmethod=; reject anonymous protected transport while allowing unrelated ordinary search. |
| A keyword and string Hiccup key both serialize a relevant physical request attribute. | Reject ambiguity instead of relying on one key chosen by a scanner. |
| A form uses the browser's implicit action/current document URL, which the selected analyzer cannot reconstruct. | Demand a qualified host/default context or report the behavior outside proven coverage; do not accept on absence of explicit =action=. |
| A fragment is valid in isolation but gains a protected inherited action after installation in another parent. | Check the host composition or retain a named compatibility premise; standalone fragment evidence is not parent-independent. |
| A lazy child renders safely when inspected but emits a different protected action on the serializer's second evaluation. | Reject the unsupported nonrepeatable producer or use a qualified single-materialization/check-and-emit protocol. |
| An asynchronous task serializes Hiccup after the dynamically scoped handler guard has ended. | Require captured, generation-bound response enforcement or reject managed output; synchronous guard installation alone is insufficient. |
| A cache serves a previously valid Request card to a different principal or retired generation. | Enforce recipient disclosure, freshness and generation context; a prior artifact/render success cannot authorize this cache hit. |
| A valid Claim C42 commits, but a malformed Cancel affordance is discovered while building its response. | Block malformed HTML, retain the known committed result at the server, and provide a declared correlated settlement/recovery path without fabricating command rejection. |
| C42 commits but its render-failure settlement is lost or ignored by the selected HTMX error lifecycle. | Preserve client-side unknown command knowledge and resolve it through the admitted command resolver; current card alone is not command attribution. |
| A renderer fails before a prohibited protected write would be initiated, and the guard catches the malformed page. | The malformed output is blocked; whether a write was prevented must be established from the actual pre-effect gate rather than inferred from a rendering exception. |
| A handler returns raw pre-serialized HTML while the canonical Hiccup wrapper would otherwise be installed. | Declare an alternate independently qualified output path or explicitly exclude it; no whole-managed-render claim arises from a guard that never sees the body. |
| A real valid ordinary HTMX search form uses a nonsemantic GET route. | Admit its own read/acquisition contract without fabricating a Choreo operation or treating shared path text as a protected POST. |

Controlled-defect tests distinguish source mismatch, effective physical
request, response producer, delivery and postcommit recovery. An application
that disables every action or turns every server result into HTTP 500
does not satisfy independent positive HumanHelp product acceptance.
The fact that Gesso can check one current Hiccup occurrence is not
by itself a claim that the deployed server checks *every* possible
rendering path or that the browser interprets it correctly.

** Authoritative outcome, acquisition, and propagation closure

*** Model outcomes and presentation settlements are explicit mappings

The authoritative command protocol uses Part IV's =:committed=, =:rejected=,
=:already-incorporated=, and =:commit-unknown=. Domain result payloads and browser
presentation settlements are separate types.

A Claim presentation may use =:accepted=, =:rejected=, and =:unknown=. Assembly
checks the explicit mapping, including a permitted recorded success from
=:already-incorporated=, incompatible command reuse, nondisclosable prior results,
and unresolved evidence. It does not substitute an assortment of transport
labels such as confirmed or superseded for the model outcome contract.

The trusted boundary checks permission to disclose a prior outcome. A successful
replay lookup does not confer disclosure authority on the caller. A local timeout,
HTTP 500, missing command row under an insufficient lookup, or present-state card
cannot be wired as unconditional proof of command rejection.

A direct response, durable resolver, and current-state acquisition have different
claims. Assembly closes the paths required by the operation rather than assuming
one route serves all three purposes.

 
*** Historical command truth, presentation, and disclosure

The four authoritative outcomes are not four interchangeable HTTP statuses.
The supported command protocol has an explicit, provenance-aware mapping to
participant-facing settlement and to the particular observation/recovery path
needed after ambiguous transport delivery.

| Authoritative outcome or evidence | Permitted participant interpretation |
|-----------------------------------+--------------------------------------|
| =:committed= with admissible command binding and disclosure | =:accepted= for that command, with the required progression/acquisition contract; not proof that its card was installed. |
| =:already-incorporated= with exact recorded binding and authorized disclosure | A permitted replay of recorded incorporation without another domain write; incompatible reuse or undisclosable result has a separate guarded disposition. |
| =:rejected= from the authoritative operation for this command | =:rejected= with only the disclosed reason; not an inference from HTTP failure, current state, or a missing record. |
| =:commit-unknown= or uncorrelated/lost outcome | =:unknown= with a retained command-resolution owner; neither automatic repetition as a new command nor fabricated rejection. |
| A current authorized Request-card acquisition | Current projection at a stated scope and basis, which may differ from the historical effect of this particular command. |

A transient retry and a durable command are separately identified. Retries
preserve the original =:gesso/command-id=, principal/operation/argument binding
and the versioned protocol required to interpret it, while a new HTTP or
transport attempt may have its own correlation identity. A command ID is not
authority or permission to disclose another user's recorded outcome.
Reconciliation must validate the current disclosure predicate and the
*original* binding before revealing replay or enabling any further action.
An absent record in one read, even a pinned read, is not evidence of
nonincorporation unless the selected storage/consistency model establishes
the stronger negative proposition.

When a domain update and durable command record are claimed to be atomic,
the qualified physical transaction must actually write both in the same
guarded commit. An unrelated single-update writer plus a later diagnostic
lookup cannot establish that stronger command-record claim. The
source-owned assembly must retain the distinction in its assurance report.

*** Recovery includes an owner, trigger, and retained binding

A declaration that names a resolver endpoint is incomplete if nothing can invoke
it or the command binding is lost when the local execution retires. Required
recovery states identify:

- the work/command and sufficient retained binding or protected recovery reference;
- the current owner and lifetime, including transfer on retirement;
- the evidence needed to resolve the condition;
- current authorization and disclosure requirements;
- the actual trigger and permission for the next action;
- bounded automatic retry/backoff where permitted;
- behavior when plans, contracts, providers, or retained records are unavailable;
- the explicit terminal, blocked, deferred, or manual-reconciliation state.

Part VI's cross-deployment command recovery applies. A new plan cannot reinterpret
old arguments under changed operation semantics while keeping the old command ID.
The assembly identifies retained resolver/compatibility support independently of
new invocation support.

 
A recovery endpoint's mere existence is not a recovery *behavior*.
For a possibly submitted Claim, the resolver must preserve typed uncertainty
until it obtains admissible command-specific evidence or reaches a separately
defined blocked/manual state. Its invocation permission, authorized principal,
record retention, operation-version decoder and outcome-disclosure policy are
independently checked. A response renderer failure, timeout, disconnected
tab, browser refresh, retired generation or process restart must not
silently discard ownership of the outstanding resolution obligation.

Where a retry is admitted after uncertainty, the system establishes the
original operation/argument binding and declared deduplication guarantee
rather than treating an unobserved outcome as a fresh operation. A
read-only command-record lookup is not a retry permit or an
implementation of the authoritative operation. Loss of command
retention or an incompatible replacement plan produces an explicit
defer, block, transfer or manual reconciliation condition, never a
made-up successful or rejected settlement.

*** Progression remains scoped through the return path

The mutation, command record, publication/durable intent, acquisition, renderer,
and browser coordinator must agree on the meaning of their progression and
coverage requirements. Generic assembly code validates compatible provider
contracts; it does not calculate a universal maximum over unrelated tokens.

Acquisition requests carry the required scope and lower bound under the provider's
semantics. Returned evidence reports the actual established observation. An
installation uses that observation and the browser's current target/owner rights.
Adoption and debt discharge require the applicable physical completion, as in
Part IV and Part VI. HTTP completion is not a substitute.

 
The progression contract is typed by its provider and queried subject.
An XTDB transaction key, snapshot token, read-consistency requirement,
fragment advisory and physical DOM installation receipt may all contain
opaque values without sharing an order. Requirements compose only under
the declared scope and combination relation; generic maximum, string
comparison or receipt equality must not fabricate an advancement
witness. Where a mutation's returned basis is needed for a later
projection, the selected acquisition route must establish the required
lower bound and expose its *actual* satisfied observation, not simply
echo the requested token.

The browser may mark an observation adopted only after authorized
projection acceptance and the applicable physical installation/target
completion, under the selected progression and owner-generation policy.
A 200 response, swap attempt or Live advisory is insufficient. If
continuity restoration fails after a successful authoritative DOM
installation, that local failure must be represented separately; it
does not roll back the installed observation or the server's transaction.

A query membership obligation may require different evidence from a card-content
obligation. Initial server-rendered content is also an acquisition path with
provenance and coverage. An empty managed fragment needs a permitted acquisition
path and a truthful loading/unavailable state; absence of both initial knowledge
and acquisition is a structural defect.

 
*** Subscription establishment cannot open a silent knowledge gap

An initial server-rendered card and the subsequently active interest
subscription have a *relative* consistency problem: a relevant commit may
occur after the initial read but before the subscription is registered.
Likewise a subscription may become active first and then a later read
may cover already published changes. The selected strategy identifies
the baseline observation, interest-registration fence/receipt, replay or
buffering horizon, and the provider's consistency comparison by which
one phase covers the other. It may use re-acquisition instead of
replaying every invalidation, because an invalidation requests
fresh authority rather than carrying authoritative domain content.

A Live assembly that validates only a configured SSE route and GET
endpoint has not thereby established the no-gap property. Startup,
new subscription, reconnect, host change, authorization-context change,
interest evolution and router failover must each have a qualified
continuity/reconciliation path. The registration and baseline need
not be performed in one atomic database transaction if a suitable
fence and recovery argument closes the interval. Without one, the
application retains advisory/acquisition debt rather than claiming
an interest was up-to-date merely because no advisory arrived.

*** Required publication and durable work have recovery semantics

When operation semantics or product convergence requires publication, it belongs
in application closure. Naming a publisher function does not establish that it
runs after commit or survives a crash between commit and publication.

The assembly binds the chosen Part IV recovery strategy: durable publication/work
intent with a worker, a qualified replay stream, periodic reacquisition, explicit
Refresh under its conditions, or another declared mechanism. It identifies the
failure domain and liveness premises. There is no universal promise of event
delivery merely because an SSE connection exists.

A lost settlement or publication leaves incorporation intact and creates or
preserves the relevant delivery/recovery debt. Worker acknowledgment and retries
must agree with the durable work contract. External effects such as payment or
notification are not undone by browser retirement or response failure.

 
The commit-to-publication failure interval is a real failure boundary.
A completed XTDB mutation followed by process failure before an
in-memory SSE dispatch is not repaired by adding another function
named =publish!= to the assembly. An application requiring durable
convergence chooses an actual mechanism: e.g. transactionally bound
outbox/change intent, replayable write log with stated ordering and
retention, or a qualified independent periodic/permitted authoritative
reread. These strategies differ in latency, permissions and liveness,
and the assembly records which one closes the selected product promise.

A durable work processor acknowledges only after the relevant delivery,
handoff or recovery contract is satisfied; retry after crash must be
idempotent or have an admitted duplicate-safe effect protocol. A
publication may be redelivered because its meaning is advisory, but
repeated delivery must not issue repeated one-use Refresh grants,
new command IDs or unbounded acquisitions. Delivery loss, worker
failure and compaction/retention expiry lead to honest recovery debt
or an explicitly bounded unavailability, not an assertion that
the original guarded mutation was rolled back.

*** Live closure includes subscription continuity and adoption policy

The Live declaration binds the authoritative query/projection, relevant interests,
initial observation, subscription owner, progression provider, acquisition route,
and coordinator policy. The stable logical owner and replaceable physical target
have distinct identities and reconstruction rules.

The application closes the baseline/subscription gap and reconnect gaps using a
qualified fence, replay, buffering, polling, or reacquisition strategy. A process
that publishes changes only for interests known locally must justify how remote
or newly registered interests avoid missed updates. Absence of a locally known
interest is not proof that no other participant needs the change.

Shared subscriptions retain per-interest ownership and authorization. Connection
replacement, authorization-context changes, and lost continuity produce the
required recovery work even when no new advisory arrives. Coarse routing/filtering
can optimize delivery only under a contract that preserves the required coverage
or has a compensating recovery path.

 
The semantic interest is owned by its logical participant/fragment
scope, not by the accidentally selected SSE connection or router node.
One physical stream may carry multiple authorized interests, and a
router may hold coarse or hierarchical filters as a performance
optimization. Neither the absence of an interest in one process's
memory nor failure of a particular router establishes that no
remote participant needs a relevant refresh.

For distributed deployment, the same single-node semantic rule holds:
a change relevant to a registered or newly established interest must
eventually become recoverable by a permitted authoritative acquisition
under the declared fairness/availability assumptions. Interest
advertisement, invalidation routing, router replacement, replay
horizon, duplicate-safe redelivery and authorization are separate
contracts. A router that learns an interest after an invalidation
was forwarded requires a fence/replay/reacquisition argument; copying
a coarse filter to another node does not prove that the intervening
change was preserved. A failed router can be handled by conservative
re-delivery of a qualifying range when the protocol is idempotent
and bounded, but the availability of such a replay source is an
actual premise, not an implied fact about SSE.

The design does not require storing every successfully delivered
advisory for each client. It requires sufficient provenance,
retention, scope and failure detection to repair possible loss
without assuming exactly-once messaging. A single-node
implementation and a multi-node implementation realize the same
interest/progression/acquisition obligations; extra routers
introduce deployment evidence, not a different semantic model.

Advisory debt, acquisition permission, and adoption permission remain distinct.
HumanHelp may announce remote changes and wait for explicit Refresh. A newly
arriving advisory does not silently inherit an expired one-read grant. Closure
checks that the declared policy has a real trigger, retained debt, and a viable
path to the promised scoped adoption.

 
*** Positive and adversarial end-to-end settlement histories

The following cases must be exercised against the selected source-owned
application, qualified transport and relevant browser/Live boundaries.
A model trace or a synthetic SSE frame does not establish real
production-path acceptance by itself.

| History | Required result and evidence |
|---------+------------------------------|
| An eligible helper Claims an open Request; the guarded command incorporates and the initiating card is authoritatively reread and physically installed. | Preserve command-specific accepted settlement, scoped progression and a separate successful DOM adoption receipt. |
| Another helper receives an advisory about that Request, but HumanHelp policy requires explicit Refresh. | Retain advisory debt and show the prompt; do not silently fetch or install without a valid grant. |
| The remote user exercises one permitted Refresh, then a second advisory arrives after that grant is consumed. | The first authorized acquisition may adopt its observation; the new debt needs a newly permitted action and must not reuse the consumed grant. |
| A Claim commits, but its HTTP response disappears. | Server incorporation remains; the participant is unknown until admissible command-specific evidence resolves it. |
| A compatible retry locates the same disclosed durable command record. | Replay the recorded outcome without a new domain mutation, while retaining original binding and disclosure checks. |
| A pinned command-record read returns no row, or prior disclosure is not permitted. | Report unresolved or nondisclosable as appropriate; do not infer rejection, absence of a write or a retry permit. |
| A source-observed domain update exists but the selected physical writer did not atomically create the canonical command record. | Do not certify durable command incorporation or causal attribution from current state and a later lookup. |
| A later manager Reassigns a Request after a helper's earlier Claim incorporated. | The current card may show a new assignee while the earlier Claim remains historically incorporated; neither observation rewrites the other. |
| The acquisition route returns a card whose snapshot is older than the required mutation progression. | Retain unmet scope/debt and retry/defer under policy; HTTP 200 cannot establish advancement. |
| The authoritative HTML is installed, but browser continuity restoration then fails. | Preserve the adopted observation and classify continuity failure separately, without undoing the XTDB commit or fabricating rollback. |
| A fragment has neither initial authoritative content nor an admissible acquisition path. | Reject structural Live closure or mark the required capability unavailable; absence of advisories is not initial knowledge. |
| A change occurs between initial page observation and SSE interest registration. | Fence/replay/buffer/reread closes the gap or the no-gap claim remains open; loss is not disproved by silent stream startup. |
| The transaction commits and the server crashes before it sends the declared invalidation. | Recover from the selected durable intent/replay/reacquisition path, or disclose the unmet convergence obligation; no false transaction rejection. |
| One advisory is duplicated during failover or replay. | Preserve idempotent debt handling and grant accounting; do not create a second logical command or unrestricted acquisition. |
| Router A loses state while Router B learns an interest after the relevant invalidation. | Establish a valid replay/fence/reacquisition interval or retain a coverage gap; a coarse filter alone is not a delivery proof. |
| A Live stream reconnects with a changed principal or lost authorization. | Revalidate each interest and acquisition/disclosure permission, retire obsolete subscriptions, and recover knowledge without leaking protected projections. |
| A publication topic is declared but the actual model executor never emits it. | Structural application-summary closure may pass, but production publication/convergence remains unestablished and positive integration must fail. |
| The browser receives an advisory but its target was replaced before the response completes. | Enforce logical owner and current physical generation/target rights; do not adopt stale DOM or discharge debt without admissible completion. |

Successful acceptance requires usable Create/Claim/Unclaim/Reassign
histories where promised, including the remote advisory and user
Refresh policy, not just a structurally valid but inert graph.
No green assembly report establishes eventual progress without
named fairness, network, replay-retention, provider and user-action
premises. Parts VIII–X define stronger product, compositional and
physical correspondence evidence separately.

** Static preflight and required dynamic handling

Static preflight is mandatory construction/startup work for the managed application.
It consumes the actual canonical construction and artifact products, rather than
a manually reconstructed preflight-only registry. It runs at the earliest stage
with enough information and produces structured obligations/results.

 
The supported managed constructor owns the admission sequence. Application
authors must not remember to invoke a separate optional checker before
starting an otherwise unchecked server. A narrower low-level or legacy
startup path may exist, but it does not inherit the checked-managed policy,
its issued executor rights, or production enforcement claims.

A successful *structural* preflight records the exact application generation,
source-owned operation and failure catalog, selected evidence policy,
constructed executable/asset products, and still-unmet installation,
invocation, runtime and external premises. It cannot claim that the
network listener adopted the guarded handler merely because a candidate
assembly was checked. Installation, activation and serving adoption are
distinct mandatory gates where the policy requires them.

The preflight checker rejects *known missing* mandatory edges, while
preserving separate classifications for unsupported, inconclusive and
externally assumed obligations. An opaque =:recovery-exists? true= field,
copied success report or abstract terminal state is not a checked
continuation. A proof checker that cannot model a required recovery
transition must not relabel its inability as structural success.

*** Failure belongs at the earliest legitimate boundary

| Boundary | Representative checks |
|----------+-----------------------|
| Semantic construction | Malformed interfaces, contradictory roles/knowledge, invalid transition terms, unsupported declaration structure. |
| Assembly/build | Missing operation realization, incompatible provider, wrong plan/route binding, incomplete required recovery, stale asset set. |
| Installation/activation | Wrong actual handler/executor, missing policy gate, unsupported lifecycle ordering, incorrect server/asset adoption. |
| Concrete rendering | Missing bound argument, anonymous semantic route, unavailable action retaining transport, unsupported effective-action context. |
| Request/effect admission | Malformed envelope, contradictory selectors, stale assembly/resource binding, invalid actual candidate or effect target. |
| Authoritative incorporation | Current permissions and dependencies, atomic guard failure, command binding/replay/disclosure rules. |
| Completion/recovery | Actual outcome, acquisition/installation evidence, unresolved delivery, partial effects, cleanup and retry conditions. |

A valid assembly can receive a rejected Claim because Membership changed after
render. That is not assembly corruption. Conversely, a known missing clock
binding should not be deferred until the first Claim throws a missing-input
exception.

 
A different failure layer can become relevant *after* the previous layer
succeeded. For example, a Claim route and its required sampled
=:biff.fx/now= provider can be structurally closed at admission,
yet the trusted principal may lose Membership before incorporation.
The earlier check remains valid for its actual proposition; the runtime
must still reject the now-unauthorized command under the model's
current-state guard and preserve its real typed outcome.

A malformed Claim command envelope can be rejected at trusted request
admission even if its rendered control previously passed Hiccup checks.
An actual DOM target can retire during acquisition even if the response
was correct. A post-commit response-render failure blocks the invalid
output but never proves the earlier authoritative write failed. The
diagnostic identifies the earliest *legitimate* boundary with the needed
information without confusing a later detection with prevention at
an earlier boundary.

*** Required handling coverage
:PROPERTIES:
:CUSTOM_ID: req-preflight-dynamic-handling-coverage
:END:

Preflight need not predict dynamic facts. It must check declared handling/recovery
paths for supported dynamic conditions that could strand an operation. A happy-path
provider or reachable terminal node is insufficient.

The obligation identifies the condition, source contract, continuation input,
owner, required resources/evidence, trigger, and permitted outcome. Construction
checks the corresponding graph edges and type/binding compatibility. An opaque
statement saying recovery exists cannot replace an available structural check.

 
*** Derive recovery obligations from the operation, not a second catalog

The source owner declares the selected operation's failure/outcome classes,
delivery and recovery expectations, and admissible continuation semantics.
Application construction derives a *coverage relation* for those classes
through its installed route, physical providers, browser projection, Live
and acquisition sources. A separate hand-authored recovery registry
that repeats operation names is not independent coverage evidence.

Each required continuation is inspectable as a typed edge with:

| Evidence dimension | Required content |
|--------------------+------------------|
| Original condition | Which operation phase/failure/outcome class creates the obligation, and its source/version. |
| Trigger and permission | The real event, timer, explicit user action or retained work that may initiate continuation, including whether it has an unspent grant. |
| Current owner | Command/work identity, assembly generation, principal or authorization scope, resource lifetime and transfer/retirement rule. |
| Inputs and evidence | Typed prior result, original command binding, current authorized observation, progression lower bound or error/unknown discriminator actually available at that point. |
| Physical realization | An actually constructed and installed resolver, route, worker, provider, browser effect or explicitly qualified external mechanism. |
| Continuation contract | Which outcomes may be reported, what can be retried, what remains unknown, which effects or targets are forbidden and whether partial completion survives. |
| Applicability and failure | The preflight evidence mechanism, required premises, unsupported opaque behavior, boundedness and fallback disposition when continuation is unavailable. |

An edge is not covered merely because a function with a matching name
exists. The expected result type must match the actual continuation input,
and its owner must be able to invoke that continuation through a
permitted live path. A required =:commit-unknown= resolver that
can never retain the original command ID has no usable input; a
valid GET acquisition endpoint without an authorized trigger cannot
satisfy a user-mediated one-Refresh contract.

For opaque Clojure callbacks, a checked interface can establish the
declared input/output and provenance relation only to the extent of
the actual mechanism. It does not prove every callback return value,
side effect or eventual completion. Required stronger properties need
their own contract checks or named assumptions. A declaration whose
supported checker cannot establish a mandatory relation remains
unsupported/open under the selected policy, rather than green by
unchecked assertion.

| Condition | Required declaration and realization |
|-----------+--------------------------------------|
| Provider fails before submission | A typed local failure/retry path that does not claim authoritative incorporation or rejection without evidence. |
| Delivery is lost after possible submission | Unknown command disposition, retained binding, and a valid reconciliation owner/path. |
| Prior result cannot be disclosed | A permitted nondisclosing continuation without false rejection or information leakage. |
| Acquisition cannot establish required scope/progression | Retained debt and a declared stronger read, retry, defer, or blocked state. |
| DOM installation is partial or completion is lost | Repair/reconciliation without premature adoption. |
| Continuity restore fails after adoption | Local continuity failure without undoing authoritative installation. |
| Subscription misses changes | Gap recovery independent of receiving a fresh advisory. |
| Plan/operation version becomes incompatible | Retirement/transfer and retained command resolution under a compatible contract. |
| Recovery budget or retention expires | Truthful deferred/blocked/manual handling with no fabricated authoritative disposition. |

These checks cover the declared supported conditions. They do not prove that
arbitrary external software has no additional failure modes or that recovery will
eventually succeed. Unexpected failures enter an explicit containment boundary
that preserves evidence, uncertainty, and surviving obligations.

 
*** Recovery states must preserve the kind of uncertainty

Some operational outcomes can be distinguished at one boundary but not
at another. Before an authoritative attempt is initiated, a trusted
provider failure may be a local no-submission result under the contract.
After submission might have occurred, a network timeout, callback
exception or publication loss cannot be converted into the same
no-submission result unless actual command-specific evidence
establishes it. An existing command-record resolver may prove a
disclosed replay without proving current permission to issue a new
write. Current-state reacquisition may show a new claimant without
identifying an earlier Claim command's incorporation.

Each continuation therefore states whether it is:
a guard that *prevents* an effect; a settlement based on authoritative
evidence; a read-only reconciliation; permitted acquisition; a
participant-local presentation/continuity repair; or a compensating
*new* admitted operation. These cannot substitute merely because they
share an exception handler. Failure after successful DOM installation
cannot retract the installed observation; a failure of continuity
restoration keeps a separate continuity obligation.

For an optimistic Claim, a structurally sound required unknown-delivery
path retains the command's original argument/version binding, records
a durable or explicitly qualified recovery owner, checks disclosure
before returning prior results, and allows a separately granted
readback only when its progression and browser-target rights hold.
Neither a generic HTTP 500 nor an optimistic =:rejected= toast
is sufficient handling for unknown incorporation.

A path to a terminal node is not a termination theorem. Liveness depends on the
stated availability, scheduler, permission, resource, and user-action premises.
The application explanation shows those premises next to its progress claims.

 
The application need not promise that an unavailable provider, uncooperative
user or partitioned router will inevitably recover. It must instead
make its liveness contract conditional and testably explicit: which
fairness or availability premises it needs, how long recoverable
command/evidence material is retained, which obligations remain when
those premises fail, and the authorized manual/deferred disposition.
A timeout cannot be used to assert proof of termination, to discard
a prior durable submission, or to make a permanently disabled
required product capability count as completed acceptance.

*** Controlled-defect and positive-path qualification

Construction-time controlled defects deliberately remove *one*
required edge from the actual source-owned assembly and expect a
stable failure at the earliest applicable boundary. A corresponding
valid assembly and fault-injection scenario must exercise the real
continuation and the preservation of authority, uncertainty or
physical installation. Tests that invoke only a helper checker
cannot claim that the deployed managed startup or returned browser
response actually enforces it.

| History | Required earliest legitimate outcome |
|---------+--------------------------------------|
| A valid Claim model, plan, route, sampled time provider and authorized resolver are assembled and successfully exercised. | Admit the candidate; separately show actual effect, participant settlement and physical adoption for product acceptance. |
| Claim requires =:biff.fx/now= but only a differently shaped clock provider is registered. | Reject the construction/provider edge before serving rather than defer a known missing input to the first request. |
| The browser plan requires an unknown-command resolver, but the selected operation assembly has no resolver or retained original binding. | Reject required recovery closure; a present-state card GET is not an automatic substitute for command attribution. |
| A resolver exists but has no real authorized trigger, available owner, or compatible continuation input. | Reject unusable continuation wiring instead of accepting a named function. |
| A valid rendered Claim is attempted after the helper's Membership is revoked. | Preserve structural assembly success, then reject on the current trusted model/transaction guard; do not misdiagnose application preflight failure. |
| A Claim submission might have committed but HTTP settlement is lost. | Preserve =:unknown= and real command binding; continue through qualified reconciliation rather than invent a failed mutation. |
| The durable command record is nondisclosable to the current principal. | Return the admitted nondisclosing outcome; do not leak prior result or relabel it rejected. |
| A granted Refresh was consumed, and another Live advisory arrives. | Preserve new advisory debt; the prior one-use acquisition permission cannot be reused. |
| The acquisition route exists but returns an observation below the required scoped progression. | Do not discharge debt or adopt merely from HTTP success; retry, defer or explicitly block under the declared policy. |
| A fragment subscription is established after a relevant missed change, but nothing new is published. | Require the declared reconnect/fence/replay/reacquisition trigger; a handler waiting only for a future advisory is incomplete. |
| The DOM adoption finishes, then continuity restoration fails. | Report local continuity repair debt; preserve installed observation and authoritative mutation. |
| A valid Claim commits but its response renderer generates a malformed Cancel action. | Reject output delivery at the rendered boundary, not the earlier committed Claim; retain settlement or unknown recovery as appropriate. |
| One required recovery handler is replaced after installation without new admission. | Invalidate affected construction and execution evidence; reject unsupported generation crossing or re-admit the changed path. |
| Recovery queue budget is exhausted while a command may remain incorporated. | Enter typed blocked/deferred/overflow handling and retain applicable evidence; do not discard unknown work as rejection. |
| A checker hits its resource limit without completing a mandatory structural/proof obligation. | Report inconclusive, not established or contradicted, and apply the selected assurance policy. |
| All invalid commands are rejected, but a valid eligible Claim or Reassign is permanently unavailable. | Fail independent positive product acceptance even if negative structural enforcement is correct. |

Negative cases must identify the exact source-declaration change,
expected error/obligation ID, actual production entrypoint or qualified
unit-check boundary, observed absence of a prohibited effect/output,
and recovery/blocked behavior. A rejected build may still own
cleanup of already prepared resources, but it cannot activate an
unchecked candidate.

*** Resource policies are part of admission

Construction and runtime declare limits for model exploration, graph size,
render materialization, response buffering, active executions, recovery queues,
physical remnants, and evidence retention where those resources matter. Limits
have typed outcomes and handling paths.

A resource limit cannot turn an unfinished proof into a successful check, a dropped
advisory into discharged debt, or a lost command record into a rejected command.
Static checking validates the declared policies; runtime enforces their actual
budgets and preserves the appropriate scope of uncertainty.

 
Resource policy also owns work after an HTTP response or assembly generation
retires. The contract specifies whether a command resolver, Live interest,
deferred structured response, worker and physical target is cancelled,
transferred, retained for bounded recovery or reported as unavailable.
A process-local handle cannot silently survive restart as a durable
certificate. Resource exhaustion must never leak an unbounded queue,
promote a stale grant, retry a possibly committed external effect
without an idempotence contract, or expose partially installed
application operations.

A managed profile may select conservative limits to remain usable in a
small deployment and more capable limits for a larger host. It must not
convert a resource-limited checker into a different theorem, omit required
operation/failure classes, or silently weaken the user's chosen
application assurance policy.

** Lifecycle, installation, and supported startup
:PROPERTIES:
:CUSTOM_ID: req-application-lifecycle
:END:

The supported application startup path composes native lifecycle modules under a
qualified integration contract. For a Biff application, that contract names the
selected Biff module/system behavior and the server's handler adoption behavior.
The design does not depend on an unspecified future release automatically
performing Gesso's checks.

Every lifecycle owner has a stable qualified identity, dependencies, start/init
semantics, owned resources, and cleanup behavior. Duplicate IDs, unknown required
IDs, incompatible shared ownership, and required dependency cycles are rejected.
A module is not accepted merely because it uses the expected ID while replacing
the required implementation with a different function.

 
*** Lifecycle identity, resources and independent host choices

The construction retains a *module provenance* relation, not merely an
ordered list of keyword identifiers. Each actual lifecycle module
has a source owner, selected implementation, generation/profile,
required dependency edges, side-effect footprint, resource ownership,
initialization contract, start/stop behavior and compatibility scope.
A built module with the correct =:biff.core/id= but another
=:biff.core/start= implementation is not the admitted module. A
shared XTDB provider, listener, subscription or browser asset reference
needs explicit shared ownership and retirement rather than a
duplicate cleanup callback.

The application derives mandatory Gesso preflight and guarded-output
module requirements from its canonical assembly, while independently
selected Biff and host-specific modules are checked against that
selection. Duplicate IDs, unknown ordering targets, mismatched
implementations, inconsistent provider owners and cycles affecting
required ordering fail before application exposure. A valid module
graph alone is not evidence that the host started the named modules,
installed the anticipated handler, or serves their outputs.

*** Preflight and installation precede application exposure

The required partial order is:

1. obtain and validate the source/configuration and private resources needed for
   construction;
2. close semantic, build, provider, and selected assurance obligations;
3. construct/install the admitted router, response guard, execution/provider
   bindings, workers, and asset references;
4. check their actual required installation relationships;
5. activate the application-serving boundary.

A particular framework may have separate init and start phases. All phases must
respect the exposure rule. Starting an application listener during an earlier
init callback cannot be excused because the named preflight module later appears
first in a start-order list.

There is no universal requirement that preflight be the first module in every
system. Its real dependencies may need private initialization. There is a universal
requirement that no managed application operation is externally available before
its required admission and enforcement bindings are ready.

Health or administration endpoints can have separately admitted scope. They
must not expose unchecked application behavior under a health-check exception.
A listener bound privately or returning only a separately admitted unavailable
response is different from a ready application listener; the profile states its
observable behavior precisely.

 
*** Init-before-start and external-effect fencing

The selected host lifecycle matters. In released Biff 2, all module
=:biff.core/init= functions run before the ordered
=:biff.core/start= phase. Placing the Gesso preflight module first
in the *start* order therefore cannot prove that an initializer
did not already open a network listener, schedule protected
background work, mutate protected XTDB state, or publish a
browser resource under an unchecked configuration.

Initialization required for preflight may allocate private,
non-exposed resources under admitted contracts. An initializer
that creates an effecting resource must have a fence,
disconnected capability, private binding or other independent
guarantee that prevents protected external application behavior
until activation. This applies to scheduled workers, callbacks,
subscriptions and background tasks as much as to HTTP traffic.
An initializer that must perform a durable effect needs its
own authorized transaction/work contract; preflight cannot
retroactively make it private merely by being sequenced later.

The externally observable activation condition is that *every*
mandatory semantic, asset, route, provider, writer, render and
policy obligation needed by the selected managed service has
passed at its respective legitimate boundary. An early open
listener is allowed only if it cannot serve the managed
application before that condition, under a separately checked
unavailable/administrative protocol. A health endpoint is not
an exception permitting unchecked Claim or arbitrary model
effects.

*** The ordinary constructor installs the guarded handler

The application start function derives or enforces the required modules and
ordering. Application authors do not manually remember a preflight ID, wrap one
test handler, or maintain separate checked-dev and unchecked-production entrypoints.

A schematic API sequence is:

#+begin_src clojure
(let [definition (application-definition config)
      candidate (application/prepare! definition)
      installation (application/install-private! candidate host-profile)]
  (application/activate! installation))
#+end_src

The contracts of these calls are substantive:

- =prepare!= admits the semantic/build candidate under its policy; it does not
  report that a server has started.
- =install-private!= consumes that candidate, constructs the actual bindings,
  records owned resources, and runs the relevant installation checks without
  exposing unchecked application operations.
- =activate!= consumes the genuine current installation and completes the declared
  exposure transition; it does not trust a caller-edited accepted flag.

Implementations can combine these calls behind a smaller public interface.
Their phase obligations still hold. A constructor that merely returns an accepted
map without installing the required path does not satisfy the contract.

The final server receives the exact admitted wrapped handler, or a qualified
wrapper composition preserving its contracts. The application can inspect the
actual server/installation relationship to the extent promised by the profile.
Local system-map adoption, observed invocation, and deployed-service adoption
remain separately scoped evidence.

 
*** Concrete Biff installation and serving adoption

The ordinary supported Biff 2 integration must identify its actual
=:biff.ring/handler= owner and the handler consumed by the real
Aleph or equivalent serving module. A canonical module can
check the current =ApplicationAssembly=, require a callable
handler, install a wrapped handler and remove an internal
temporary assembly key. Those actions establish a concrete
local system-map binding, but they do *not* independently
establish that an already-started listener or a different
server module adopted that handler.

Later Biff modules and mutable Vars can replace or invoke
another callable after the checked module ran. An externally
facing server can ignore the conventional handler system key,
and a handler can return raw pre-serialized HTML bypassing the
structured Gesso guard. The finished managed path must prevent
or detect these substitutions within its claimed coverage,
or retain explicit disqualifying deployment premises rather
than reporting unconditional production enforcement.

An actual adoption receipt or qualification may include
the issued handler/route identity, server instance/endpoint,
admitted assembly generation, guard and policy version,
asset serving reference and observed guarded invocation.
A source-issued system map, a caller-provided receipt, or
a single successful test request does not by itself prove
