perpetual adoption or completeness of every serving path.
Controlled faults at the real boundary are required for the
claimed operational scope. Section 07.11 owns that
independent production-path evidence.

*** Request lifetime spans asynchronous completion

At entry, an invocation captures its assembly instance and concrete context. It
resolves route, executor, providers, outcome encoding, render guard, and assets
through those compatible bindings. Asynchronous completion carries this context
explicitly rather than consulting whichever registry became current meanwhile.

An invocation's completion, cancellation, timeout, and transferred work determine
when its assembly/resource references can be released. A handler returning a
future is not necessarily a completed invocation. Streams and workers have
separate declared lifetimes.

Old assembly bindings do not freeze current business authority. Each operation
still checks the current trusted model/authentication premises required by its
contract. If an old assembly or provider profile is revoked, its continued use
requires the declared retirement/compatibility policy, not indefinite reliance
on the fact that a request once acquired a reference.

 
An asynchronous Ring handler's returned value and its completed
response are distinct lifecycle events. Closing the handler's
lexical/dynamic scope when it returns a future, stream or
callback must not release the request's generation, change the
installed guard to a different one, or authorize use of a new
executor/provider accidentally looked up through a global Var.
The request's retained context supplies the checked response
boundary through completion, rejection and cancellation.

Background jobs, Live streams and durable command-resolution
work have their own admission and retirement scopes. Some
obligations transfer across generations or process restarts
using retained durable state; a process-local admitted handle
does not become a durable certificate by serialization.
A retired Request card target cannot be reanimated by an
old callback, and current trusted model authorization is
re-evaluated where an effect requires it. HTTP response
completion alone does not discharge uncertain command
incorporation, post-commit publication or physical DOM
adoption debt.

*** Reload builds a candidate before activation

Development reload and deployment use the same coherence rule. A candidate is
constructed and checked separately from the current admitted assembly. Activation
switches the appropriate new-entry bindings as one admitted transition, using a
compare-and-activate or equivalent mechanism that prevents concurrent reloads
from replacing a newer instance with an older candidate.

The transition covers routes, issued executors, providers, assurance policy,
render checking, asset references, and other relevant realization bindings. It
cannot expose new routes with stale browser assets and an unrelated old report.

In-flight work remains bound to its still-valid assembly or follows an explicit
checked transfer. New invocations use the new instance. Old assets and resolver
contracts remain available for the lifetimes promised by the compatibility and
recovery policy; reference counts alone do not account for sleeping browsers that
are no longer represented by a live server request.

A rejected candidate may leave the prior instance serving only while that instance
remains valid. If a security, backend, or semantic premise has invalidated the old
instance, failed replacement is not permission to keep using it. The application
suspends affected work or follows a declared restricted mode.

Relevant change invalidates dependent evidence. An incremental implementation
can reuse unchanged checked subgraphs and artifacts, but must recheck their joins
into the new root. Cache reuse is justified by complete dependency/applicability
bindings; it is not an assertion that the source looks similar.

 
*** Generation-coherent activation and draining

An activation transition has a single authoritative choice of
the new-entry generation for the selected deployment scope.
It may switch an immutable dispatch/asset/provider composite
by atomic pointer exchange, a short quiescence barrier, or an
equivalent qualified host protocol. Updating several mutable
Vars in sequence without isolating new requests is not
coherent activation. A compare-and-activate check also
prevents an older candidate that finished compiling late
from superseding a newer admitted generation.

The transition records which old requests, streams, workers
and browser clients may continue, which may only resolve
previous commands, and which must be cancelled or migrated
through an explicit compatibility contract. A browser page
rendered under A can fetch its A-specific assets after B is
current; it must not receive an incompatible B bundle at the
same unchecked mutable URL. The retained old serving
reference and command decoder lifetime cannot be inferred
solely from active server request reference counts.

An invalidated security or model premise may require
revocation of an old generation's *future effect rights*
even while preserving its durable command outcome
and authorized reconciliation. Keeping old code running
because B failed preflight is permitted only while A's
own actual predicates and deployment authorization
remain satisfied. The shutdown of A does not authorize
a premature deletion of resources still owned by B.

*** Cleanup preserves ownership and primary failure

Each lifecycle module owns the resources it acquires and any explicitly shared
references. Failed startup retires completed private installations and accounts
for partial acquisition, in dependency-safe order. Cleanup errors are retained
as secondary diagnostics; they do not replace the primary admission failure.

No failed candidate leaves an unchecked application listener or worker active.
Work already transferred to a durable admitted owner remains governed by its
contract. Cleanup cannot erase a committed transaction, acknowledge unfinished
durable work as complete, or cancel a replacement assembly's shared resources.

Shutdown and replacement preserve uncertain command/work obligations through
admitted transfer or durable recovery. Best-effort physical stop follows semantic
retirement; failure to close a socket or release a registry handle does not retain
the old owner's authority to initiate work.

 
A failure is not necessarily all-or-nothing at the physical
level: a module may open a socket and then throw without
returning a completed start result, or a worker may publish
an advisory before an activation attempt is rejected.
The lifecycle contract records partial acquisitions and
side effects as they occur, not only successful module
return values. Failed admission prevents new protected
exposure but must retain cleanup failures, surviving
external effects and transferred durable debt as distinct
diagnostic facts. An already committed domain mutation
cannot be undone by simply calling a stop handler.

Resource teardown is idempotent to the degree declared
by its owner and ordered against shared dependents.
The primary failure cause remains visible, with secondary
cleanup errors and unreleased physical resources attached.
A failed cleanup may demand process fencing, restart or
operator action; it never silently upgrades a failed
candidate into admitted service.

*** Positive and adversarial lifecycle histories

These examples apply to the *real managed constructor* and
selected Biff/Aleph/Live profile. A fake startup map or a
successful stand-alone preflight unit test cannot replace
observed host/module execution where that evidence is required.

| History | Required disposition |
|---------+----------------------|
| Canonical startup validates a real source-derived Claim/Reassign assembly, builds current browser assets, installs the wrapped handler and starts a server that actually consumes it. | Admit and activate only after required phase and adoption checks; real eligible controls and runtime behavior need separate positive evidence. |
| A malformed browser artifact is detected before normal application service. | Reject startup; no protected listener or worker may expose the rejected generation, and privately allocated resources are cleaned or accounted for. |
| The Biff module uses the expected preflight ID but substitutes a different =:biff.core/start= callable. | Reject module identity/correspondence before serving; keyword equality is not implementation provenance. |
| Preflight is first in the ordered Biff start list, but an earlier =:init= function already starts a protected Aleph listener. | Fail the no-exposure contract or require a genuinely unavailable/private fence; first-start ordering does not justify the earlier side effect. |
| A module initializer starts a scheduled raw XTDB writer before admission. | Reject or isolate the protected writer under its own admitted capability; a valid later preflight cannot authorize already-exposed unchecked effects. |
| The checked handler is installed in =:biff.ring/handler=, but the actual serving module captures another callable. | Leave deployed enforcement unestablished or reject activation under strict policy; local system-map equality is insufficient. |
| A later module or hot reload replaces the guarded handler while keeping the original report. | Invalidate the affected installation/serving evidence and refuse protected use until new admission. |
| A valid handler begins under A, then returns an asynchronous response after B becomes current. | Complete under A's retained guard, assets and authorized lifetime or use a separately checked transfer; do not silently serialize under B. |
| Candidate B installs new routes but still references A's incompatible browser assets or provider set. | Reject partial activation; new requests observe a coherent generation, not a mixture. |
| Two reload candidates race and the older finishes after the newer activates. | Compare-and-activate prevents stale overwrite; dependency and phase receipts remain generation-scoped. |
| Candidate B fails validation while a still-valid A is serving. | Preserve A unchanged and retire B's private resources; do not publish B's partial files or workers. |
| Candidate B fails, but A's authorization or security premise has been revoked. | Suspend affected A operations or enter a separately admitted restricted mode rather than retaining obsolete effect rights. |
| A previously served page uses an A-specific asset reference after B activates. | Honor the declared A retention/compatibility policy; never silently substitute B's incompatible runtime. |
| A module acquires a socket and then fails before returning its startup result. | Account for partial physical resource ownership and cleanup; do not claim no resource was started because no result map was returned. |
| A cleanup callback throws while the original preflight failure is being reported. | Preserve the primary failure and separately report cleanup error, leaked resource and required repair. |
| An old request is retired while its Claim might have committed and its response or Live publication was lost. | Preserve durable command resolution and publication debt; lifecycle retirement does not fabricate rejection or undo incorporation. |
| The canonical HTTP guard blocks a malformed Reassign response, while a raw Ring HTML endpoint in the same process bypasses it. | Keep the raw path outside the claimed structured-output coverage or independently qualify it; do not report universal rendering enforcement. |
| A deployment starts healthy and serves an actual valid Claim with authorized reread and browser adoption. | Establish distinct structural, deployed-effect and positive user acceptance evidence; a reject-everything handler is not a completed application. |

Part VII's lifecycle contract applies to a single-node and to
multi-node deployments with the same application-generation
semantics. Additional network nodes, router failover and
distributed activation require separately stated traffic
placement, epoch/fencing, recovery and compatibility premises.
There is no claim that Biff module ordering alone serializes
an entire distributed deployment.

** Production-path enforcement evidence
:PROPERTIES:
:CUSTOM_ID: req-production-path-enforcement
:END:

Checker correctness and production integration require different tests. A checker
can reject malformed input perfectly while the actual application never calls it.
The supported construction therefore provides observable seams for controlled
faults at the real startup, route, effect, and response boundaries.

 
*** Evidence is an observed boundary, not the availability of a checker

A production-enforcement claim identifies the *specific installed
application generation and deployment profile*, its selected
assurance policy and every relevant physical path carrying that
claim. It links:

#+begin_example
source-owned semantic application
  -> admitted plan, artifact and trusted route/executor
  -> actual constructed Biff/Aleph handler and provider
  -> network-facing request/effect/output boundary
  -> observed guarded transaction, response and client adoption
#+end_example

These are different evidence subjects. A valid application report
does not attest the selected server module. A checked handler in
=:biff.ring/handler= does not prove a deployed listener consumed
it. A successful Ring invocation does not prove a remote proxy
uses the same route or serves the same asset bytes. A 200 response
does not prove the authoritative model committed. A correct
browser snapshot does not prove the required command was emitted
from a real control, nor that an earlier command incorporated.

Each test report names its original source, concrete generation,
entrypoint and binding identities, installed dependency/handler
versions, checker or observer mechanism, physical observation
and unresolved host premises. Tests may use isolation and
controlled fixtures, but must state which real layers they
replace. A report containing green flags without source-to-
physical causality cannot become an issued executor, deployment
attestation or transferable certificate.

Each enforcement case records:

- the admitted source/configuration and actual entrypoint under test;
- the controlled defect and the subject/edge it breaks;
- the earliest boundary with enough information to reject it;
- the expected structured diagnostic or typed disposition;
- the prohibited output or physical effect whose absence is observed;
- any already-performed effect or surviving uncertainty that must be preserved;
- a corresponding valid case showing the path remains usable.

 
A controlled mutation starts from a valid source-owned candidate
and changes one specified dependency or installed realization;
the expected failure must be attributable to that mutation.
Changing an unrelated test oracle to reject every request is
not enforcement evidence. Mutation selection includes
*removing the guard itself*: tests which still pass when the
real production enforcement connection is absent have failed
to establish its presence.

Failure evidence is stage-specific. A prevented protected
write requires an actual pre-effect guard and a checked absence
of that effect under the stated physical observation scope.
A mismatch detected after XTDB incorporation or response
delivery is a *post-effect contradiction*, with retained
incorporation/disclosure/recovery obligations, not prevention.
A checker timeout, unavailable observation or incompletely
instrumented host produces an explicit unestablished result,
not an assertion that no effect happened.

A test can inspect an issued handler's identity and observed
local Biff-system invocation, or independently verify a real
network listener/route, or observe a guarded XTDB mutation.
It describes exactly which of those links it established.
Satisfying all of them for one fixture remains bounded
physical correspondence under stated principal, environment,
input and writer assumptions; it does not prove every
arbitrary Clojure handler or all deployment traffic.

A test-only wrapper that rejects before the real entrypoint does not establish
production enforcement. Removing the actual enforcement connection must make the
appropriate integration test fail. The test must distinguish prevented effect,
detected violation after effect, and inability to establish either.

*** Controlled defects exercise actual construction and installation

| Controlled defect | Boundary and required result |
|-------------------+------------------------------|
| Required plan omitted from the source-derived browser build | Build/admission rejects the missing realization. |
| Correct receipt paired with different asset bytes | Asset admission rejects; the candidate does not serve that pair. |
| Correctly named route installed with a different executor | Installation/invocation gate rejects the mismatched binding. |
| Required provider name exists but returns/binds the wrong shape | Static contract mismatch or concrete provider admission rejects at the applicable boundary. |
| Required assurance policy is selected but its gate is omitted | Managed installation/activation fails; a standalone checker test cannot mask it. |
| Render guard removed or an outer guard shadowed | Concrete malformed output cannot pass the managed delivery boundary. |
| Deferred response loses assembly/guard context | Completion rejects or uses the declared safe failure path; it cannot serialize unchecked. |
| Final renderer introduces an anonymous semantic action | Final structured-output checking detects it even if preparation was valid. |
| Post-check middleware changes the protected action | The transformation is rejected, rechecked, or lacks the claimed admission. |
| Undeclared writer appears in the actual covered inventory | Required closed-coverage admission fails; otherwise the affected claim is explicitly limited under its policy. |
| Candidate activation changes only routes and leaves old assets/providers | Coherence check prevents partial activation. |
| Post-commit rendering fails | Malformed output is withheld while incorporation/participant uncertainty remains truthful. |

These defects use isolated fixtures and the supported production constructor.
They do not alter a real user's live data to test failure. The corresponding
assertions observe the actual server/effect/output seam relevant to the claim.

 
*** The production seam must actually fail the negative control

Controlled faults are submitted through the normal managed
startup or actual qualified runtime path, not by calling only
a test-side validator with fabricated route/manifest data.
In particular:

- A source-derived browser build test uses the real generated
  entrypoint and actual emitted bytes. A forged receipt tests
  receipt rejection, not correct compiler semantics or served
  network assets.
- A route/executor test verifies the issued callable and
  *actual* selected method, decoded subject and trusted
  principal. A string-equal route table supplied only to a
  checker does not establish installed dispatch.
- An operation/physical-write test captures the original
  command, guard and transaction identities and reads back
  authorized authoritative state. If the physical submitter
  can be replaced with a function returning a fake committed
  map, the test must not report authenticated incorporation
  without a stronger independent write observation.
- A render test exercises the final checked serialization
  path, including malformed *dynamic* Hiccup and relevant
  HTML/HTMX effective actions. The alternate raw or deferred
  output path is separately qualified or outside the claim.
- A lifetime test distinguishes early Biff module
  =:init= side effects, module =:start= ordering, actual
  host handler selection, a deferred completion, and a
  reload replacing the generation. Preflight's appearance
  first in the start list does not fence earlier init work.
- A writer-coverage test challenges the real effect
  boundary or independently qualified host inventory.
  An operation-ID list checked against another declaration
  list does not prove absence of unregistered raw writers.
- A command/Live test distinguishes actual model commit,
  durable command attribution, post-commit publication,
  baseline/subscription coverage, acquisition permission
  and physical browser adoption. A mocked SSE frame
  establishes neither an emitted invalidation nor delivery.

Every test's failure interpretation states whether it
established rejection of an invalid candidate, rejection
of an invalid invocation, blocked output, observed
contradiction, or an unresolved external premise. Cleanup
and preservation of prior committed work are asserted
where relevant. An invalid candidate must not activate
protected service, but a failed response check cannot
retroactively reject a valid previously committed Claim.

*** Real browser acceptance starts from real controls

Top-level browser acceptance loads the actual generated runtime and operates the
application's rendered controls. It observes the emitted protocol, selected route,
trusted model result, returned evidence, physical installation, and subsequent
authoritative read as required by the capability.

 
A genuine browser case starts with a server-rendered,
source-owned HumanHelp control and its actual compiled
JavaScript, real HTMX events and physical target. It records
a causal chain from the control activation to the command
envelope, selected trusted HTTP route, source-owned model
operation, durable result, authorized acquisition and
installation. A direct HTTP fixture sending an idealized
command remains useful, but is only a server/protocol test.

The browser qualification includes expected loaded artifact
identity, actual URL and asset bytes under the selected serving
profile. The initial HTML and SSE connection provide their
required authoritative baseline/interest relationship.
Multi-client tests exercise remote advisory without granting
automatic Refresh, then an explicit one-use authorized
Refresh that establishes and installs a sufficient current
observation. A lost response or duplicated advisory must
retain command/Refresh debt without inventing command
outcomes or extra acquisition permission.

Direct, same-process Ring tests and a real Chromium/browser
over loopback HTTP/SSE are complementary. A loopback
integration verifies its socket/bridge and observed client
behavior, but does not by itself prove a public deployment's
load balancer, CDN, credential boundary, all writers or
inter-node router failover. The report retains that
qualification rather than attaching one generic
=:runtime-enforced= label to all environments.

It must not repair a missing command field by injecting a valid envelope or
manually dispatching the event the button failed to produce. Such setup is useful
in a lower-level protocol test, whose claim is deliberately narrower.

Acceptance includes valid repetition and concurrent activity, not just the first
successful request. Request-scoped issuance must allow later requests and the
admitted degree of concurrency. Out-of-order completions must preserve separate
invocation/command/target ownership. A one-shot test harness cannot establish a
reusable production route.

 
*** Independent positive product completeness

The tests separately declare the minimum required *real
capabilities* that constitute HumanHelp acceptance: an
eligible creator can create and immediately see a Request;
an eligible helper can Claim; authorized users can Unclaim,
complete and cancel as their models permit; a manager can
Reassign; participants can observe initial state and later
advisory/Refresh behavior under the prescribed ownership
policy. Each capability identifies a positive reachable
scenario, authoritative result, valid control and, where
applicable, physical presentation.

A reduced application can be internally consistent, reject
every malformed operation and display a coherent empty
page while entirely omitting Reassign or Claim. Structural
and negative enforcement tests may pass; the product-
completeness gate must fail. Positive acceptance cannot be
satisfied with a hidden or permanently disabled button,
manually injected protocol message, test-only model callback
or fabricated server response. A test may isolate a trusted
external provider with a qualified fixture, but it must
record exactly which effects and assumptions that fixture
replaced.

Tests also exercise valid *subsequent* operations after one
successful command and at least the concurrency policy
advertised by the application. Two legitimate concurrent
Claim attempts are not supposed to both acquire an
incompatible RequestAssignment. They should instead reach
independent request-local admission, then receive truthful
guarded incorporation, rejection or recovery under the
declared atomicity model. Rejecting one attempt because
a global single-use test slot was already occupied is not
evidence of normal concurrent application usability.

Expected fault diagnostics are asserted specifically. Broadly ignoring console,
page, or request errors would hide the integration failure this layer exists to
catch. Conversely, a deliberate network-loss test need not pretend no diagnostic
should occur.

 
*** Positive and adversarial enforcement histories

The following histories illustrate independent evidence
propositions, not a universal single test fixture:

| History | Required evidence or limitation |
|---------+--------------------------------|
| The installed managed application serves a real eligible Claim control, which commits and is followed by authorized card acquisition and physical adoption. | Trace original source, generated bytes, control, actual route/executor, authoritative write and permitted read; retain assumptions about the tested deployment and physical observer. |
| Removing the actual managed startup/preflight module still lets the test's standalone validator pass. | The production integration test must fail, because the normal startup was not gated. |
| An early Biff =:init= callback starts an unchecked protected worker before preflight's first =:start=. | Detect/fence the exposure; module start ordering alone is not a valid no-exposure proof. |
| A correct checked Biff system map is built, but the actual server captures an older handler. | A local slot report stays local; required deployment adoption fails or remains explicitly unestablished. |
| A locally issued Biff host-adoption handle matches a copied returned system map. | It is not independent server attestation, and cannot be promoted into a production certificate. |
| The browser receives a correctly named JavaScript asset but its emitted bytes differ from the checked receipt. | Reject physical artifact correspondence for the relevant serving boundary. |
| Two valid, independently constructed products exchange an execution handler, Live fragment, or asset while preserving familiar operation IDs. | Reject the mismatched source/realization join; matching names do not justify substitution. |
| A malformed semantic POST loses =:choreo/op= only after final conditional Hiccup rendering. | The actual output guard blocks the anonymous semantic action before delivery, not merely a test-side snapshot scanner. |
| A native detached submitter or second =hx-*= action bypasses a checked button's main transport. | Resolve all supported effective physical requests and reject the unadmitted semantic route. |
| The selected server route decodes Request R2 while the browser command binds Claim to R1. | Reject trusted selector contradiction before the protected model effect. |
| A request's selected provider advertises =:clock= but does not supply the consumed =:biff.fx/now= shape. | Reject at a knowable provider gate; a provider keyword or a later exception is not successful execution. |
| A physical XTDB submitter is replaced by a fake =:committed= result that performs no write. | A 200 or committed map is insufficient; independent authoritative state/transaction attribution is required to claim incorporation. |
| A valid Claim incorporates but the response's Cancel affordance is malformed. | Block invalid output while retaining the real committed command and participant-relative settlement/unknown recovery; do not assert no mutation occurred. |
| A failed settlement leaves the Claim command uncertain while a later card happens to show a helper. | Preserve command attribution as unknown until a permitted command-specific resolver obtains admissible evidence. |
| The Live baseline precedes interest registration and a relevant update occurs between them. | Demonstrate actual fence/replay/reacquisition or retain the no-gap premise; a healthy SSE socket alone does not suffice. |
| A remote client receives duplicated advisories after using its one permitted Refresh. | Do not issue another Refresh grant or discharge fresh advisory debt on the basis of duplicate delivery alone. |
| A deferred response retains an old generation while a new handler and assets activate. | Verify its admitted guard, physical target and compatible retirement path; no silent new-generation splice. |
| A scheduler or raw XTDB path changes protected state without appearing in the registered operation inventory. | Refuse a claimed all-writer enforcement proof unless the physical capability boundary or independent complete inventory covers it. |
| Two consecutive valid Claims on independent Requests are rejected by a shared consumed invocation slot. | Fail the advertised reusable/concurrent route; a one-shot test cannot establish normal operation. |
| An application passes all negative checks but omits the required Reassign control and executor. | Fail independent positive product completeness even if its smaller assembled graph is closed. |
| A Chromium test injects a valid Claim envelope instead of clicking the broken actual button. | Record only a protocol/server fixture success; top-level browser acceptance remains unmet. |
| A network-loss scenario produces its declared command-unknown diagnostic while all unexpected browser errors remain visible. | Assert expected errors precisely and require subsequent permitted resolution; neither a blanket console-error ignore nor an immediate rejection is acceptable. |

Tests exercise the original admission and effect boundaries with
isolated disposable state and explicit failure injection; they
do not corrupt real users' records. The report separates
*prevented effect*, *observed post-effect violation*, *physical
completion*, *current-state read* and *historical command
incorporation*. Known open assumptions, unsupported probes
and test-environment substitutions remain in the provenance
of the reported claim.

Sections 07.12–07.15 must expose these same distinctions
through explanation, diagnostics, acceptance qualification
and the security invariant. Parts VIII–XII retain independent
positive product proofs, formal/model correspondence and
deployment/release assurance. An implementation may make
substantial progress on one layer without being entitled
to the stronger adjacent layer's certificate.

** Application explanation and semantic audit
:PROPERTIES:
:CUSTOM_ID: req-whole-application-semantic-audit-surface
:END:

The application exposes a structured, read-only semantic audit derived from its
actual admitted sources, construction products, and evidence. It supports review
of the correctness-relevant policy without treating a large implementation as
an undifferentiated body of code.

The audit is not a second editable policy registry. Business-rule prose, operation
cards, diagrams, and evidence summaries are projections of the same admitted
subject. Prose explains meaning and rationale; it does not gain mechanical force
by appearing beside a checked predicate.

 
*** Inspection scope and source lineage are part of the artifact

An audit has an identified *subject*: the admitted application generation,
original semantic/source versions, selected operation catalog, assembled
realization/deployment profile, checker versions and evidence dependencies.
Views are derived from those same objects, not from a second registry,
a stale report-shaped map or a source scan that merely found familiar names.
A current, successful assembly report can authorize *describing that assembly*;
it is not itself authorization to execute operations or a proof that an
uninspected model callback implements its descriptive policy.

The root view states, at minimum, which declarations and real sources were
inspected, the admission/checking mechanism, which evidence is only
source-relative, the completeness of each inventory, and the claims not
established. Counts always have an inventory qualifier:

| Count or scope | Permitted interpretation |
|----------------+--------------------------|
| Declared operations and relational rules | Exact members of the selected admitted source catalog, not proof that no other business rules exist. |
| Checked finite state/operation/rule instances | Exercise over the stated initializers, principals, arguments and reachable-state bounds, not all production cases. |
| Observed routes, writers and browser artifacts | Physical observations under the named host/serving scope, not all unobserved entrypoints or future replacements. |
| Open declared structural edges | Failed or unmet edges within the known closed subgraph, not an inventory of human intent. |
| Opaque model callbacks and external effects | Preserved named premises and unsurveyed implementation surface; unknown never means zero. |

An omitted semantic rule that never entered the declared source cannot be
proven absent by successfully checking its smaller catalog. The
source-owned rule catalog, application/operation cards, proof dependencies
and runtime observations therefore retain both their positive *included*
inventory and the relevant completeness/opaque qualifications.

*** Required audit views

| View | Information and required limits |
|------+---------------------------------|
| Business-rule catalog | Stable rule identity, meaning/rationale, formal or opaque contract, source, affected operations, authority, enforcement, and actual evidence. |
| Operation card | Typed inputs, principal/authority dependencies, guards, transition/frame, outcomes, command repetition/disclosure, effects, and recovery. |
| Authorization/disclosure | Current authority sources and policies for invocation, reads, subscription, and prior-result resolution. |
| Domain lifecycle | Actual admitted states and transition relation, generated from semantic definitions rather than guessed from route names. |
| Realization path | Exposed surfaces, plans, assets, routes, actual handlers/executors, providers, acquisition/installation, and serving bindings. |
| Rule/evidence dependencies | Claims affected by a changed rule, operation, implementation, backend profile, or accepted premise. |
| Writer/entrypoint coverage | Declared, installed, observed, classified, excluded, and still-unestablished paths at their actual scope. |
| Opaque-premise report | Each retained premise, its owner/reason, applicability, available tests, and dependent claims. |
| Assurance and exercise | Exact finite bounds, rule/operation/outcome exercise, conditional induction, runtime gates, conformance results, and gaps. |
| Recovery/continuity | Owners and triggers for unknown commands, failed adoption, missed publication, subscription gaps, and version incompatibility. |

A domain lifecycle view uses the operation model's actual enum. It must not rename
HumanHelp's states to superficially similar completed/cancelled labels or infer
terminality from a UI caption.

 
*** Business rules, operations and actual authority

The rule catalog is a normative future capability whenever the application
expresses relevant semantics. For each named rule it records the
source-owned identity, exact proposition or relational terms (when
machine-readable), domain meaning and rationale, affected operations,
authoritative owner, required enforcement site, source-to-implementation
correspondence, and independent evidence or retained premise. A rule that
has a formally stated predicate but no demonstrated XTDB transaction guard
remains a source declaration with an *unestablished physical conformance*
edge, not a production-proved invariant.

For example, HumanHelp Claim's active Membership condition must identify
that the authenticated helper's current Membership in the Request's
Organization is checked at authoritative Claim incorporation. The audit
must distinguish that declared obligation from evidence about the
actual guarded transaction, actor/Request/Organization scope and
interference. A matching rule name, handler name or passing finite
fixture cannot establish current live Membership protection.

Operation cards preserve an executable contract rather than a marketing
summary: typed Request and principal/argument sources, authority,
guards/prestate, transition and frame, command identity and duplicate
handling, authoritative outcomes and disclosure, provider/effect
requirements, physical route/plan/asset, and the permitted acquisition
and recovery paths. A current participant's authorization is determined
by the trusted model and observation context, not by reading a previously
generated audit card. Rendering an eligible or unavailable button does
not change what Claim is allowed to do.

The authorization/disclosure view distinguishes at least *invocation*,
*current Request read*, *subscription/Live interest*, *prior command
result disclosure*, and manager Reassign authority. Sharing a role label
does not establish equivalent permissions. Current user policy and
tenant/Organization context are dynamic model facts, even when the
application has structurally established the existence of their
trusted enforcement bindings.

Where model states and transitions are declared, the lifecycle view
reports their exact internal identifiers and transition relation.
It cannot infer an unexpressed `:completed` or `:cancelled` state
from a UI label, or mark a terminal state because a component hides
its actions. A model exposing no inspectable state relation yields
an explicit unknown/opaque lifecycle view, not an invented diagram.

*** Unknown inventory is not an empty inventory

If a model adapter exposes only a public operation name, the audit cannot infer
its internal predicates or atomic dependency protection. It reports those bodies
as not inspected with their explicit conformance premise. An empty business-rule
list would misleadingly suggest there were no relevant rules.

The same distinction applies to writers, side effects, publication, and policy
branches. Zero unresolved declared edges is not proof of complete human intent
or absence of undiscovered behavior in arbitrary host code.

 
The audit must distinguish three situations that are often mistaken for
one another: (a) a *known complete* catalog with zero entries of a
particular class; (b) a partial catalog containing some inspected
declarations; and (c) an unavailable source whose cardinality is
unknown. A zero count is valid for (a) only within its explicit
closure scope. An empty vector shown alongside =:count :unknown=
in (c) means *no enumerated rules were available to this projection*,
not that the actual application has no rules.

Opaque boundaries remain explicit when registered model functions
can branch on Membership, perform unreported reads, mutate protected
state or publish topics outside the admitted declarative surface.
Where the supported semantic language has precise relational or
state-transition terms, the same audit can enrich those rule cards
with meaningful checked facts. It must not infer that arbitrary
adjacent Clojure was consequently proved equivalent.

Enriching the application with source-owned relational rules or checked transition
terms adds concrete audit coverage. It does not retroactively establish that
uninspected callbacks contain no extra policy. The view distinguishes complete
coverage of a supported construction subset from registered opaque boundaries
and unexamined external behavior.

*** Declared Live overlap is not a transaction dependency proof

Part IV's guard and footprint contracts determine authoritative
dependency meaning; shared Live topics establish presentation impact only.

 
A *dependency* view has typed edges and provenance. A rule-to-operation
edge may be source-declared, derived from the admitted transition
relation, or observed from a specific physical guard. A Live topic
overlap is instead a source-relative *presentation impact* edge.
Operations that touch different protected records can publish
one shared board topic, while two operations that share one guarded
RequestAssignment dependency can legitimately publish different
topics. Reclassifying either relationship as complete transactional
conflict information would mislead application assurance and
incremental invalidation.

For a given changed predicate, model operation, opaque callback,
provider, route, generated plan, artifact or host deployment premise,
the audit can identify *known downstream dependent claims* and
which admission/checker/production evidence must be revisited.
A missing source-ownership edge or an opaque implementation with
unknown side effects creates an open impact boundary; the tool
cannot promise that the listed dependents are complete.
Reusing evidence requires matching original subject, source and
implementation versions, proof/certificate premises, physical
profile and checker semantics, not just equal operation IDs.

*** Explain one operation end to end

A useful explanation of Claim identifies:

1. the exact semantic source, rule dependencies, and operation interface;
2. exposed controls and their selected realization alternatives;
3. projected roles, executable identities, physical handlers, and asset bindings;
4. route/input correspondence and the actual installed executor;
5. provider contracts, invocation gates, and current authoritative guard obligations;
6. model-to-presentation outcome mapping, including repetition and unknown;
7. acquisition, propagation, installation, and recovery paths;
8. assembly/installation identity, policy, evidence applicability, retained premises,
   and unresolved or excluded claims.

The output may show a local issued-handler binding as established while leaving
backend transition refinement conditional on its qualified provider. It may show
finite rule exercise without claiming that every production predicate branch was
executed. Those distinctions are useful information, not deficiencies to hide
behind a single green label.

 
*** Assurance classifications are proposition-specific

A rule's *declared guard binding*, an abstract invariant,
a finite exploration result, conditional induction, the
physical XTDB realization of that guard, the deployed
writer-coverage boundary, and real browser adoption are
different claims. Each report row names its proposition,
source/evidence class, checking mechanism, exact scope,
assumptions, dependencies, proof or observation status,
open contradictions and validity lifetime.

In particular, `assembly-verified` can describe correct
source-owned route/plan/provider structure, while a
model-implementation-conformance proposition remains
`trusted` under an explicitly named premise. A finite
model checking every selected principal/argument pair
does not prove those pairs cover all humans or requests.
A conditional inductive argument does not automatically
establish physical XTDB refinement, all-writer coverage,
kernel soundness or no-gap SSE delivery. A bounded
physical observation cannot be promoted to universal
deployment correctness.

The explanatory surface retains unsupported, inconclusive,
contradicted, open and established evidence at their
individual subjects. Contradiction to one physical
realization cannot be hidden by a successful structural
check of another. Nor can a checked rule be advertised
as exercised when the finite exploration visited no
state in which its source predicate applied.

*** Inspection does not execute or authorize

Explanation reads admitted results and immutable/redacted trace values. It does
not invoke operation callbacks, submit transactions, rerun model builders,
mutate runtime registries, or repair missing edges. Expensive fresh checking is
an explicit separate action whose result has its own identity and scope.

No diagnostic output needs to expose live executor handles, credentials,
principal-sensitive data, or unrestricted command arguments. Redaction reports
what is unavailable rather than fabricating a replacement explanation. Internal
repair detail and client-facing errors can have different disclosure policies.

 
The inspection API must not convert an arbitrary supplied report into
freshly admitted truth. The normal public path re-derives or verifies the
current application assembly and its source dependencies before
producing an audit. A lower-level projection accepting an already
checked report has a strict caller precondition; it is not an
authenticated report verifier in isolation. A private issued executor,
proof/checker handle or live DOM/Request object may be inspected only
through its qualified boundary and is never copied into public
audit output.

A source location may be important for repair but still sensitive.
The selected diagnostic consumer and privilege determine which
source paths, rule literals, principal scopes, commands, tokens
and observations may be disclosed. A redacted field is explicitly
marked redacted/unavailable and cannot be used as evidence
that the hidden dependency is absent. Deterministic view
ordering, stable semantic identity and bounded generation
make comparison and review practical; these are UX
properties, not additional execution authority.

The tool can suggest which *source owner* needs correction,
but it must not automatically rewrite a rule, select a
near-matching operation for dispatch, change a provider
binding, or use a report as a new command. A separate
source correction and admission is required to change
the application's meaning. Sections 07.13–07.14 own
structured diagnostics and full acceptance qualification.

The explanatory surface can show an incomplete candidate's rejected/open
obligations without making that candidate executable. A stale sidecar or trace
mapping must not explain a different executable plan by matching similar names;
Part V's exact correspondence rules apply.

 
*** Positive and adversarial semantic-audit histories

Acceptance exercises the audit through its source-owned
application explanation path. It distinguishes a view of
an admitted candidate from a deployed or behaviorally
accepted system; tests of individual projections have
a correspondingly narrower claim.

| History | Required audit disposition |
|---------+----------------------------|
| A source-owned Claim rule explicitly requires active helper Membership at commit and is connected to an admitted model transition and checked implementation evidence. | Show its exact rule, source, affected Claim, current guard/effect scope, mechanism, relevant assumptions and checked evidence without inventing physical proof. |
| A Claim operation is exposed through a browser plan, HTTP POST, issued executor, typed provider and authorized reread. | Produce an end-to-end operation card with distinct source owners, actual installed/candidate identities, command outcomes and recovery; preserve each edge's assurance class. |
| A legacy model adapter exports only a public Claim name and opaque callback. | Report business rules, authorization predicates, transaction dependencies and lifecycle transitions as not inspected or unknown; an empty returned list is not evidence of no rules. |
| A checked finite relational rule has never matched a source entity in any explored state. | Report that bounded vacuity/exercise fact rather than claiming the business predicate was substantively exercised. |
| An induction proof conditionally preserves an abstract single-owner invariant but host writer inventory is incomplete. | Keep abstract proof evidence and open physical writer/XTDB correspondence as separate propositions. |
| Claim and Cancel both publish =:request/change=, but only their Live topics overlap in the observed source. | Display declared presentation impact; do not infer transaction conflict, common guarded fields or business-rule dependencies. |
| A raw scheduled writer modifies RequestAssignment outside the declared operation registry. | Retain unclassified/unknown physical writer coverage; a closed operation-ID set cannot show complete effects. |
| The selected manager Reassign operation has correct semantic structure but is absent from the installed controls. | Distinguish an available declaration from actual exposure; product completeness cannot be inferred from a valid operation card. |
| An application reports zero declared structural obligations while its opaque model code has uninspected authorization branches. | Show closed declared graph and explicitly unknown model-policy coverage simultaneously. |
| A report-shaped caller map asserts a fully checked rule catalog without a fresh trusted source/assembly. | Refuse to promote copied summary data to current admission, certification or operation authority. |
| A stale browser source map or artifact sidecar names the right operation but belongs to another generated bundle. | Reject/qualify artifact-to-source mapping before displaying it as current provenance; matching names are insufficient. |
| A candidate changes a provider Var, guarded callback or source rule but reuses last generation's green coverage report. | Invalidate affected evidence and re-derive dependent audit views from actual new source/admission. |
| A command has an authenticated historical incorporation while a later Reassign changes the current card. | Preserve independent historical-command and current-state propositions; neither the audit nor the card rewrites the earlier outcome. |
| A limited-privilege caller requests an audit containing private principal or command information. | Disclose only the allowed redacted view, retaining its scope/unknown markers; absence after redaction is not evidence. |
| A UI repair agent sees a nearby valid operation name or provider adapter in the report. | Offer a source-local suggestion only; no automatic semantic substitution, protected invocation or report-to-capability promotion. |
| A real HumanHelp implementation passes structural proof/report checks but cannot execute an eligible Claim or manager Reassign. | Report the established structural evidence but leave independent positive product acceptance failed or open; no universal green badge. |

These cases require concrete original sources and honest
evidence for the selected application and audit level,
not an independently maintained idealized rule document.
Part VIII's real browser product tests and Parts IX–X's
formal/physical proofs can *add* evidence to the
same source-bound audit when justified; a copied
or self-issued report cannot substitute for them.

** Structured diagnostics and repair

Diagnostics identify the failed obligation and its actual owner. Human-readable
messages are rendered from stable structured data; tools should not parse prose
to discover whether the missing edge was a route, provider, asset, or recovery
continuation.

 
*** Diagnose the original proposition and its legitimate detection stage

A diagnostic is a source-bound *explanation of a failed or unfinished
proposition*. It is not a new application semantic fact, a replacement
operation, a trusted executable or a certificate. The ordinary diagnostic
surface derives from the current canonical assembly and actual checker
result; it cannot accept an arbitrary successful caller map as proof that
the inspected source or installed handler is current.

The framework distinguishes a candidate that could not be admitted,
an admitted but not installed construction, a failed actual invocation,
a known post-effect contradiction, and a participant-facing outcome
that remains uncertain. A single generic =:error= or HTTP 500
cannot safely express all of them. In particular, a browser's
reported =:unknown= after Claim settlement loss is not a failed
preflight, an authoritative =:rejected=, or evidence that the
transaction was rolled back.

A stable diagnostic identity includes a *kind* and a scoped
obligation/subject identity. Its generation, semantic source,
route/plan/asset, original command or observed resource
identity, evidence and checker version, and relevant deployment
profile are separately retained when applicable. A copied diagnostic
is valid information about its former subject, not automatically
about a freshly changed generation. Diagnostic vocabulary is
versioned so tools can distinguish renamed public keys from
actually changed failure semantics.

A diagnostic includes, where applicable:

- the error kind and detecting phase;
- operation, projection, route, resource, or claim subject;
- assembly/installation and relevant executable/artifact identities;
- source location that introduced the obligation and source responsible for supply;
- expected relation and actual observed/bound values, within disclosure limits;
- rejected, unsupported, inconclusive, contradicted, or inapplicable status;
- remaining premises and whether any protected effect already occurred;
- mechanically known repair alternatives without automatic substitution.

 
A report also states *which relationship was actually checked*,
which original source supplied each expected condition,
which independent observation (if any) supplied the actual value,
the checker or host trust boundary, and whether the failure
disposition is =rejected=, =open=, =unsupported=,
=inconclusive= or =contradicted= at the specific proposition.
Unobserved means unobserved, not false; copied source declarations
cannot authenticate their own physical adoption.

When a checker emits multiple issues, a deterministic
=first-blocker= is a navigation aid with an explicit priority
rule, not a claim that no other obligations are open. The
full explanation retains the applicable open/assumed/dependent
obligations, subject identity, and whether discovering another
fault requires repairing the first. Stable sort order and
machine-readable paths make diffing repeated diagnosis possible
without creating executable authority.

An illustrative provider error is:

#+begin_src clojure
{:error/kind :incompatible-capability-provider
 :phase :assembly/admission
 :assembly-instance/id candidate-id
 :operation/id :request/claim
 :obligation/id :claim/commit-time-input
 :introduced-by claim-source-ref
 :supplied-by server-binding-source-ref
 :expected {:input-path [:execution-context :biff.fx/now]
            :value-contract :time/instant}
 :actual {:input-path [:execution-context :clock]
          :value-contract :clock/zero-argument-function}
 :suggestions [{:kind :explicit-binding-adapter
                :contract/ref sampled-invocation-time-ref}]}
#+end_src

The suggestion does not install that adapter. Source correction and admission
establish the new binding. Likewise, an unknown =:request/claime= may suggest
=:request/claim= diagnostically but must never be corrected automatically for
execution.

 
The provider example must be interpreted at the *consumer's input
path*. A named =:clock= capability that returns a zero-argument
function is not the =Instant= required at =:biff.fx/now=.
A diagnostic can propose a source-owned sampled-time adapter
when the adapter contract is mechanically known; it must not
invent an implementation, assume the clock is trustworthy,
silently provide a default time, or modify Claim's transaction
semantics. If the provider genuinely failed only at invocation,
the diagnostic identifies that runtime fact rather than
retroactively claiming the builder proved its behavior.

*** Source-local repair is a separate, re-admitted action

Diagnostics describe *candidate actions*, not repairs that have
occurred. Every suggested source correction names the owner
of the declaration that must change, the exact broken relation,
the known alternative interface (if any), the verification
and deployment stages that would need rerunning, and the
extent of evidence that the suggestion itself has. A human
or coding agent may separately choose to edit the source
under normal authorization and version-control rules.
A rebuilt assembly, browser artifact, route and assurance
report then require fresh checking of the changed dependencies.

A repair tool must not treat a near-match operation string
as permission to dispatch it; rewrite a protected role,
tenant or Request selector; add an anonymous HTMX fallback;
substitute a new executable merely because a report names it;
or automatically retry a possibly incorporated command.
Where a domain *compensating operation* is legitimately
needed, it is separately admitted and authenticated under
its own current guards, command identity and effect contract.
No diagnostic callback gains the runtime rights needed to
perform that operation.

A proposed fix can have multiple legal implementations.
The checker explains what is established and what is
unknown rather than guessing a unique implementation from
a plausible name. After source change, it rechecks the
canonical assembly and all dependent generated, installed
and runtime evidence; it cannot simply edit the old
closure report's =:status= field to green.

*** Stable diagnostic families

| Family | Representative distinctions |
|--------+-----------------------------|
| Semantic construction | Unknown operation, duplicate identity, invalid interface, contradictory transition, incompatible realization. |
| Plan/build | Missing plan, wrong plan/operation, stale manifest, asset-byte mismatch, incomplete asset set, unestablished build correspondence. |
| Dispatch/execution | Missing/ambiguous route, selector conflict, wrong issued executor, unsupported route semantics, unclassified writer. |
| Provider/effect | Missing provider, incompatible value or origin, invalid actual candidate, wrong target, unsupported lifetime. |
| Rendering | Missing arguments/basis, anonymous semantic route, implicit downgrade, conflicting attributes, unknown effective context, unchecked response path. |
| Recovery | Missing continuation, incompatible outcome mapping, absent owner/trigger, unsupported retained command contract, unmet acquisition/installation requirement. |
| Installation/lifecycle | Missing gate, wrong actual handler, premature exposure, assembly-instance mismatch, invalid dependency, failed activation/cleanup. |
| Assurance | Unsupported fragment, inconclusive budget, counterexample, inapplicable evidence, unaccepted premise, insufficient coverage. |

These families need stable public identities without requiring this document's
exact keyword spellings. A missing resource and an existing incompatible resource
should not be indistinguishable. Dynamic authorization denial retains its model
outcome and privacy policy; it is not reported as a corrupt assembly.

 
*** Concrete R4 error distinctions remain mandatory

A conforming diagnostic surface can explain the
following independent facts, without requiring
these illustrative keyword spellings as its public API:

| Diagnostic subject | Required distinction and useful evidence |
|--------------------+-------------------------------------------|
| Unknown semantic operation | Original rendered view/source and unknown identifier; admitted operation IDs and safe near matches, with no automatic correction or execution. |
| Missing browser plan | Admitted operation and its exposing role/view exist; the required projected plan is absent. Show candidate plan/manifest scope without claiming semantic rejection. |
| Stale generated artifact | Current source-derived manifest versus actual emitted bytes and current receipt/sidecar. Report exact mismatch and responsible rebuild boundary, never filesystem timestamps as identity. |
| Transport/route mismatch | Differentiate no route, method/protocol mismatch, overlapping/ambiguous route, wrong decoded Request selector and unadopted installed handler. The check uses or qualifies real routing semantics. |
| Anonymous protected HTMX action | Effective concrete method/path, matched semantic route, originating Hiccup/control, and missing operation/basis binding; an unrelated plain GET remains legitimate. |
| Missing or wrong capability | Source operation and consumer input contract (including =:biff.fx/now=), selected actual provider/handler, expected type and observed/declared incompatibility. |
| Missing initial/current acquisition | Logical fragment/owner, required authoritative projection, progression lower bound, permitted trigger and available sources; an SSE route alone supplies neither current knowledge nor a read grant. |
| Missing recovery continuation | Original uncertain command or failure class, required owner/trigger/input, exact resolver/acquisition path and retained uncertainty rather than a fabricated reject. |
| Lifecycle or deployment mismatch | Candidate versus installed generation, actual Biff module/handler, served asset binding, failed gate/cleanup and which physical serving proposition is still unknown. |
| Unsupported or inconclusive assurance | Exact obligation, checker/budget or unsupported language, retained premises and known witness if any; no invented counterexample, passed proof or universal certificate. |

An unavailable, wrongly typed or ambiguous resource must not
be silently classified as merely absent. A known physical
violation must not be relabeled an open proof obligation.
Likewise, an authorization denial for a current
principal and Request remains a typed model outcome,
not evidence that the application graph is corrupt.

A diagnostic must not claim semantic verification succeeded merely because it
reached a later code path. It reports only established evidence. Source summaries,
artifact stamps, and provider declarations can be useful repair facts without
being proofs of their implementations.

 
*** Disclosure, sidecars, and diagnostic noninterference

Source-level internal diagnostics and user-visible response
errors may contain different details under distinct disclosure
policies. A public failure must not leak another principal's
command history, Membership/Organization contents, private
Request identifiers, session material, tokens, executable
handles or unrestricted host source paths. Redaction preserves
explicit =unavailable=/=redacted= markers and the
non-sensitive identity needed to correlate a permitted repair;
it cannot infer that a hidden obligation is absent.

Browser diagnostic sidecars must correspond to the *exact*
generated executable plan and artifact before a source
location or trace is treated as authoritative diagnostic
provenance. An old sidecar with matching operation names
is not a valid map for a changed bundle. Browser
debugging observers are non-authoritative: enabling,
disabling or throwing from the observer cannot change
the semantic trace, adapter effects, resource ownership,
settlement, execution continuation or permission to
perform physical work.

Optional diagnostic probes may be bounded and opt-in
where they execute expensive model checks. Their
failure or timeout is not permission to weaken a
mandatory startup gate, abort an unrelated admitted
command after incorporation, fabricate a passed proof
or suppress a critical runtime error. A diagnostic
system may fail safely while the application's
underlying admitted behavior and obligations remain
as specified.

*** Positive and adversarial diagnostic histories

Acceptance checks stable machine-readable failures
against the actual relevant source/physical
boundaries. A correct looking test report by itself
is not sufficient evidence of installed enforcement.

| History | Required diagnostic or repair disposition |
|---------+------------------------------------------|
| A source-owned Claim has all required plan, HTTP route, typed provider, issued executor and authorized acquisition edges. | Explanation identifies the checked graph and original owners; no failure is invented, and positive usability is tested separately. |
| A rendered control references =:request/claime= while the catalog contains =:request/claim=. | Reject the unknown operation at its legitimate boundary; report known IDs/near match without auto-correcting the invocation. |
| A plan exists for Claim but the current source-derived manifest omits it. | Report missing browser realization, not semantic operation invalidity or an unproven runtime failure. |
| A receipt belongs to the previous generated bundle, though its filename and operation name match the current asset. | Report exact manifest/byte/sidecar mismatch; never trust the stale mapping for source attribution. |
| A route is installed with the wrong method or matches two operations under the actual router's precedence rules. | Distinguish incompatible versus ambiguous route and retain the actual route/source identities. |
| A native form submits anonymously to the protected Claim POST route. | Report effective method/path, semantic-route collision and rendering source; do not turn it into permitted ordinary HTMX. |
| A Claim provider lists =:clock= but the handler requires sampled =:biff.fx/now=. | Report source-owned requirement and incompatible value/input path; a suggested adapter is not automatically installed. |
| A managed fragment has no initial observation or permitted authoritative reread. | Report acquisition owner, required projection/progression and missing permitted trigger; do not call an SSE connection an acquisition. |
| An unknown command has a read-only resolver but no retained ID, authorized trigger or disclosure contract. | Identify the missing continuation binding and preserve unknown incorporation; no generic HTTP error can settle the command. |
| A current authenticated helper loses Membership immediately before Claim. | Preserve successful structural preflight; report the current trusted model rejection without calling it assembly corruption. |
| The real server ignores the checked Biff handler and serves an older raw renderer. | Retain local handler-check evidence but mark deployment adoption/output enforcement unestablished or contradicted where observed. |
| One checker times out while another finds a concrete counterexample. | Preserve the independent inconclusive and contradicted proposition statuses; no single green or generic failed flag erases them. |
| A first-blocker summary names a missing clock, while a second plan/acquisition problem also exists. | Show deterministic first navigation and the remaining open obligation scope; never claim there was only one defect. |
| A copied green report claims physical write coverage and an agent proposes reusing it after provider reload. | Refuse report-as-admission and show invalidated source/implementation dependencies; source must be corrected and re-admitted. |
| A browser observer throws while a valid local execution is running. | Preserve execution effects and resource ownership; observer failure cannot rewrite command outcome or DOM rights. |
| A low-privilege browser receives a diagnostic whose internal version mentions another user's protected command record. | Redact the forbidden record/subject; retain truthful limited scope without leaking prior-result attribution. |
| A Claim has already committed, but response rendering fails on a malformed Cancel action. | Distinguish blocked output from historical incorporation and participant unknown/lost settlement; suggest repair of the renderer, not undo of Claim. |
| A remediation suggestion proposes a replacement handler, while a required external dependency or callable remains opaque. | Show the limits of the suggestion and require source/physical requalification; no fabricated guaranteed fix. |

These histories retain R4's requirement that structured
errors are genuinely actionable. They also reject
"helpful" automatic changes that could silently alter
authorization, operation identity or command repetition.
A source-derived explanation can support both human
and coding-agent repair, but the subsequent edit,
build, admission, deployment and tests remain
ordinary independently authorized work.

** Acceptance, qualification, and change impact

*** The application is usable as well as closed

The three claims in 07.01 are assessed at different boundaries.
This section owns *independent acceptance and qualification*, not
a second Choreo or Request business model. A closed application may
still lack eligible Claim, manager Reassign, initial board knowledge
or one-Refresh adoption. Disabled controls or negative tests
cannot satisfy the positive product profile.

The oracle describes intended observable behavior, not duplicate
executable rules. Disagreements require review rather than
silently rewriting either specification or implementation.

 
*** Three independent gates and a stable product oracle

Acceptance reports separately: (1) structural assembly closure,
(2) enforcement through actual deployed request/effect/output paths,
and (3) the application's promised *positive* behavioral completeness.
Success at one gate cannot mask failure or unsupported scope at another.

The product acceptance profile describes user-visible capabilities and
authoritative outcomes independently of the *current* registry. It is not
a second implementation of the business model. HumanHelp's required
profile includes creator Request creation with immediate visibility;
helper Claim and Unclaim; permitted completion and cancellation;
manager Reassign; relevant board search/sort/filter behavior; initial
authoritative acquisition; and another participant's advisory followed
by explicitly authorized one-use Refresh. Each promised capability
has a positive reachable scenario, real rendered control, actual
model result, and required physical observation, alongside rejection
and unknown-outcome recovery cases.

Deleting Reassign can leave a smaller internally closed application;
it must fail the independently selected product-completeness gate.
A permanently disabled Claim, hidden manager action, synthetic
protocol envelope or reject-all server does not substitute for
usable positive behavior. A disagreement between the independent
product oracle and source-owned execution creates a specification/
implementation review obligation, never automatic rewriting of
the oracle to match the current route table or vice versa.

Tests name exactly which providers, authority, browser, Live,
backend or deployment relationships their fixtures replaced.
A direct trusted-route fixture is useful but cannot satisfy the
real-browser end-to-end requirement by manufacturing the missing
rendered-control-to-command edge.

*** Conformance is bound to actual subjects

Evidence records the source/implementation identity, assembly/configuration,
provider and browser profiles, test/checker version, exercised paths, bounds, and
known limitations. A passing fixture with mocked providers is not evidence that
an unexamined production transaction or subscription implementation conforms.

Each backend profile names the assumptions required by dependent claims, including
atomic dependency protection, command-record incorporation, outcome interpretation,
read progression, retention, and failure/retry semantics where used. A current or
future backend version is qualified against those same assumptions. Detecting a
violation invalidates or blocks the dependent claim; it must not be hidden by a
version update or a stale successful receipt.

 
*** Backend qualification checks actual behavior, not labels

The selected backend profile identifies its exact query, basis,
write, transaction and retry interfaces and expected behavior:
guarded dependency evaluation, transaction-internal prestate,
atomic commit and conflict handling, canonical command-record
co-incorporation where promised, outcome interpretation,
authorized read progression, retention, and failure uncertainty.
Loaded backend/adapter identity, deployment and option surfaces,
tested schedules, checker version, assumptions and independently
unobserved facts are separately recorded.

For XTDB, successfully checking a reviewed 2.2.0-beta1 API,
query/write option keys and one-shot gateway fixture is a
meaningful **interface prerequisite**, but is not proof of
actual internal transaction state, authenticated physical
causality, all production writers or universal abstract-to-XTDB
refinement. A compatibility test may pass while a stronger
atomicity or progression premise remains unproved or is
observed to fail. The corresponding propositions must retain
different results.

Qualification can layer API/interface checks, bounded real
transaction tests with disposable state, guarded source-to-
physical correspondence checks, independently established
host/deployment facts, and stronger future proofs. An
unsupported or changed backend feature does not acquire the
older proof's applicability merely by returning the same
operation IDs or a familiar version label. A strict policy
rejects use of required unqualified behavior before the
protected effect; weaker scopes must be separately selected
and accurately disclosed.

Conformance tests can expose an assumption violation without proving the entire
backend. That is a useful and intended contract. Unknown qualification after a
relevant upgrade remains unknown until the selected admission policy establishes
sufficient applicability; a changed version number is neither proof of failure
nor proof of continued correctness.

 
*** Dependency-specific change impact and evidence reuse

An admitted assembly retains typed dependencies from semantic
rule, initializers, operation families, principal/authorization
contracts, executor and provider closure, routes and actual
writers, browser source and emitted assets, Live acquisition,
backend interface/behavior, deployment and checker/proof policy
to the particular proposition each supports.

| Change | Dependent evidence or behavior to revisit |
|--------+-------------------------------------------|
| Business rule, guard, operation semantics or arguments | Source-model checks, nonvacuity, executor correspondence, role/browser projection and independent product scenarios. |
| Handler, callback, provider or mutable Var | Exact issued implementation, typed input/effect, installation and physical enforcement, even if operation IDs remain unchanged. |
| ClojureScript/compiler, plans, assets or cache/serving policy | Exact built and served bytes, runtime conformance, compatible old-client operation and retained recovery. |
| XTDB backend, adapter, query/write options or semantics | Selected interface, atomicity, physical observation, command history, progression and proof applicability. |
| Biff routes, middleware, server, worker or raw writer | Actual handler adoption, protected writer inventory, effect containment, production checks and cleanup. |
| Live interests, routing, retention or access rules | Initial/subscription gap, reconnect recovery, authorized acquisition and one-Refresh debt. |
| Checker, proof kernel, policy or product profile | Validity of corresponding proofs and assumptions, required checks, and independently authored user capabilities. |

Reuse is permitted only where *all* original source, checker,
implementation, resource, environment and deployment assumptions
relevant to the particular evidence remain applicable. A
stable semantic digest does not freeze an opaque handler's
implementation, an unchanged JS filename does not prove the
emitted bytes, and a passing previous XTDB compatibility test
does not certify a changed backend.

Reverification follows known dependency edges and marks opaque
impact as open rather than pretending a partial dependency
catalog is exhaustive. Incremental checks may reuse untouched
subgraphs but must recheck their joins into the new admitted
generation. A copied green report, process-local handle or
old module/asset receipt cannot promote a newly changed
deployment into the prior generation's authority.

*** Required verification scenarios

The verification strategy covers semantic construction, production enforcement,
and product behavior with appropriately scoped evidence. At minimum, relevant
application profiles exercise:

| Scenario | Evidence sought |
|----------+-----------------|
| Same canonical definition feeds build, startup, render, and tests | Removing or changing an owned declaration affects the actual consuming paths. |
| An opaque builder returns an invalid candidate | The actual candidate is rejected before submission without claiming all builder behavior was proved. |
| Finite exploration reaches its declared bound or exhausts its resource budget | Scope-complete finite results remain distinct from inconclusive computation and unbounded claims. |
| Rule/operation/outcome exercise is vacuous | Required exercise gates reject; the report does not inflate attempted or disabled operations into commits. |
| A copied report or metadata-equivalent function replaces an issued product | Admission rejects the substitution or explicitly establishes a new binding. |
| The server captures an earlier handler while the system map later changes | Installation evidence detects or limits the server-adoption claim rather than trusting the later map. |
| A worker writes state outside the HTTP catalog | Its path is classified and covered, or the dependent closed-world claim fails/remains explicitly conditional. |
| Two valid requests overlap and complete in reverse order | Their scoped capabilities, outcomes, and rendering contexts remain separate and reusable. |
| A deferred/streamed/cached response bypasses the synchronous guard | The selected response contract prevents unchecked managed output or reports the unsupported path. |
| A fragment's effective form/action depends on outer context | Checking uses admitted context or rejects the unestablished interpretation. |
| Old HTML requests assets after a new assembly activates | It receives the bound compatible asset set or follows the declared compatibility failure/recovery path. |
| Artifact, handler, policy, provider, or backend premise changes | Dependent evidence is invalidated/rechecked without mutating an old admission in place. |
| Startup or activation fails after acquiring resources | No unchecked application exposure remains; cleanup and surviving work are accounted for. |
| The response fails after authoritative incorporation | Server knowledge and participant uncertainty remain distinct and recoverable. |
| A disconnected subscriber misses relevant changes | Initial/reconnect acquisition closes the required gap without needing a new advisory to arrive. |
| A required user capability is removed while the remaining graph closes | Independent product acceptance fails. |

Formal checks, controlled-defect tests, observed execution correspondence, and
real-browser acceptance are complementary. A unit test of a report shape cannot
replace evidence that the actual handler or browser edge is used. A successful
request cannot establish every route or every possible schedule.

 
*** Qualification matrix and controlled positive/negative tests

| Evidence level | Required positive control and adversarial limitation |
|----------------+-----------------------------------------------------|
