| Source and finite model | Original rule/operation/outcome coverage with nonvacuous positive and rejected branches, plus source-mutant and bound-exhaustion cases. |
| Inductive and formal | Exact abstract invariant, transition catalog, proof/checker version and retained premises; unmodeled writers or undecided proof remain open. |
| Source-to-implementation | Real issued executor, route, typed provider, browser plan and generated asset joined to admitted sources; equal-name substitutions fail. |
| Physical backend | Actual guarded XTDB write, command record, current observation and progression under selected profile; changed backend/atomicity premises invalidate. |
| Production serving | Biff/module/handler, network traffic, emitted HTML and served JS actually use checked paths; removing the real guard fails. |
| Browser and Live | Real rendered control and compiled JS/HTMX submit, authorized settlement/reread, Live advisory/Refresh and physical DOM adoption; uncertain delivery retains debt. |
| Product completeness | Explicit required Create, Claim, Unclaim, completion, Cancel and Reassign capability success; deleting one fails regardless of smaller assembly closure. |

Each test states its scope, original sources, concrete checker and
backend/host, selected actor/argument/schedule, applied fault,
observed results, bounds and unestablished premises. It checks
a corresponding *valid* behavior. An intercepted fake committed
map cannot prove physical XTDB incorporation; a direct injected
protocol command cannot prove a button worked; a local Biff
system map does not attest a separately deployed listener.

*** Additional positive and adversarial histories

| History | Required classification |
|---------+-------------------------|
| Real eligible Claim and manager Reassign controls trigger admitted guarded operations and authorized card adoption. | Positive product cases, separate from structural or deployment proof. |
| The operation registry deletes Reassign and all remaining preflight checks pass. | The independent product profile fails despite closed structural subset. |
| A disabled Claim is accompanied by a manually injected ideal protocol command. | Route fixture may pass; rendered control/browser acceptance fails. |
| Two clients receive remote advisory after Claim; the second uses one explicit Refresh. | Test initial knowledge, advisory debt, one-grant acquisition and installed physical observation. |
| Reviewed XTDB API/option checks pass but a transaction atomicity premise fails. | Preserve interface success and fail/open the stronger behavioral proposition. |
| A new backend version changes query/write options after preparation. | Refuse affected operation until requalification; no inherited stale receipt. |
| A source report is edited to assert verified, or a private issuance handle is copied. | Neither issues proof, admission or physical transaction authority. |
| A rule changes but retains operation ID =:request/claim=. | Recheck dependent models, physical executor, browser and product evidence. |
| New JavaScript bytes are served under an unchanged filename or a CDN returns stale bytes. | Fail exact serving-currentness claim until bound to admitted assets. |
| A scheduled raw XTDB writer is missing from the registered operation catalog. | Complete writer coverage remains unestablished or prohibited by actual capability boundary. |
| Static Hiccup passes while dynamic rendering emits a malformed semantic POST. | Actual output guard must block or production enforcement remains open. |
| Claim commits, then its response fails and the client retries. | Preserve historical command ID, incorporation and authorized recovery without fictitious rejection. |
| A subscriber misses a change between initial read and interest registration. | Require fence/replay/permitted reacquisition or leave no-gap claim open. |
| Two independent requests overlap and finish in reverse order. | Preserve separate invocation, owner, target and command scopes. |
| A later module replaces the checked Biff handler after an earlier success receipt. | Invalidate deployed-adoption evidence and re-admit or restrict service. |
| An abstract model passes safety, but manager Reassign never becomes enabled. | Record abstract safety and failed nonvacuous/product coverage separately. |
| A model checker times out or an external physical witness is unauthenticated. | Report inconclusive or conditional evidence, not a universal certificate. |
| A feature passes negative and structural checks but the real browser cannot activate it. | Fail real-browser/product completeness despite green isolated tests. |

Application qualification grants no new business authority.
Current principal and Membership, RequestAssignment state,
guarded transactions and disclosure of recorded commands
remain with their trusted model/runtime owners.

The suite includes positive controls for each rejection gate. Rejecting all
requests, never exposing a control, or disabling concurrency universally is not
an acceptable way to satisfy the intended application's behavioral requirements.

** Whole-application security and construction invariant

Preflight establishes the stated structural relationships and selected assurance
conditions. It does not confer a principal, disclose a protected result, authorize
a transaction, or establish that a mutable world still satisfies a prior guard.
Those premises are checked at the trusted boundary that owns them.

 
*** Trusted authority is an explicit boundary, not metadata

The canonical construction may establish that an operation has one admitted
name, typed arguments, generated plan, physical transport and trusted server
executor. It must not replace the authenticated principal or current model
authorization with a browser argument, role label, stored card, copied proof
report, or prior successful preflight. The server resolves every protected
operation through its own installed and current trusted registry.

| Source of information | Authority it may establish |
|-----------------------+----------------------------|
| Rendered control, plan digest, basis, command metadata or browser certificate | A request for a particular semantic action or a participant-relative observation; **no** principal authentication, permission, transaction or disclosure authority. |
| Trusted request ingress | Valid method/route/envelope, decoded subject, authenticated principal/tenant and correct issued executor binding; **not** indefinite business permission. |
| Public authoritative model operation and guarded transaction | Current domain guard, permissible effect and authoritative result under the selected XTDB/backend premises. |
| Durable command record and resolver | Command-specific historical incorporation or an explicitly unresolved/nondisclosable state under the *original* binding and a current trusted disclosure predicate; **not** permission to issue a new mutation. |
| Application assembly, artifact receipt or host installation evidence | Structural/build/serving correspondence at its qualified subject and generation; **not** an operation or data-access capability. |
| Formal proof, finite-model report, checker diagnosis or runtime observation | The exact proved, bounded, observed, open or assumed proposition with its scope; **no** automatically conferred authority beyond the independent trusted execution boundary. |

Untrusted values may guide selection only after they are decoded, normalized,
validated and matched to the trusted route/operation/subject contract.
Inconsistent Request IDs in path and command arguments, a forged principal,
a wrong tenant, an invalidly replayed command ID, or a purported assembly
certificate supplied by the client cannot win a conflict with trusted
context. Protected result disclosure, including history of a command that
has already incorporated, is evaluated under its own current authorization
policy, not the policy used when the command was originally issued.

The browser can forge local metadata, operation names, command bytes, certificates,
and assembly IDs. Trusted ingress and model operations remain secure without
assuming that the browser follows the admitted implementation. Conversely, server
construction controls accidental misuse by trusted host code; a hostile JVM with
reflection or arbitrary bytecode replacement is outside that claim unless an
additional isolation mechanism is explicitly supplied and qualified.

 
*** Threat model and effect containment

Gesso's structural contracts are designed to prevent accidental and
misconfigured bypass in cooperating application/server code and to
remain safe against a malicious or stale browser request. They do not
by themselves sandbox arbitrary trusted application code, a compromised
JVM, reflection, hostile classloading, administrator-level access to the
XTDB process, or an independent writer with unrestricted database
credentials. Claims covering such adversaries require separately
qualified process isolation, physical write capability restriction,
deployment authentication or independent complete writer evidence.

The protected write domain and its allowed writer policy are named.
A route registry that lists every declared Choreo operation cannot
establish that no scheduler, initializer, migration, worker, raw XTDB
client or external writer can mutate the same protected state. A
host-supplied writer inventory is useful conditional evidence, but its
completeness and ability to constrain actual physical effects remain
separate propositions. Stronger all-writer invariants must be enforced
at the actual capability boundary or depend on explicitly justified
complete deployment/physical-writer premises. Hidden writers are
not excluded by matching operation IDs or a successful local proof.

The same principle governs model authorization: an application-supplied
callback that claims to enforce active Membership is not automatically
equivalent to a transaction-internal guard. Correctness of the declared
business rule, the admitted abstract transition, the real executable
guard, the physical XTDB prestate and commit, and every interfering
writer require separately applicable evidence. A finite example of
Claim safety or conditional induction can establish an important
abstract fact without proving all deployed transactions respect it.

A structural report, artifact receipt, process-local handle, proof certificate,
and runtime observation each has a defined role. None silently acquires the
others' authority. Production evidence is applied only to its actual subject,
scope, assumptions, and current applicability.

 
*** No credential promotion across lifecycle, evidence or time

Each issued effect right has a checked owner, operation, principal scope,
source generation, physical target, permitted use and retirement contract.
Source/assembly closure cannot mint that right merely by returning a
copyable report. An issued request-local callable cannot be copied as a
portable credential or reused by another invocation without its own
admission. A browser-issued one-Refresh permission is deliberately
distinct from the existence of an advisory or the ability to connect
to an SSE stream; a consumed grant cannot be revived by replay.

Construction, installation, actual network serving, current invocation
authorization, successful authoritative incorporation, permitted
readback, physical DOM installation and subsequent participant
continuity remain independent statements. When a Claim commits but
its response is lost, its incorporation does not disappear: the
participant remains =:unknown= until command-specific evidence
authorizes a different settlement. When the card is updated and a
later Reassign changes current state, that observation does not
rewrite historical incorporation. A failed response renderer cannot
turn a prior committed mutation into rejection; a later observer
cannot serve as a retroactive pre-effect guard.

Generation changes preserve the original binding of already issued
commands, qualified old-client asset/plan compatibility and declared
recovery work. They do not preserve an obsolete principal's right to
initiate new protected effects. An old callback cannot silently
borrow a new handler/provider or a retired browser target. An
initializer that opened a listener or writer before preflight
cannot be excused by placing the checker first in a later Biff
=:start= ordering. New protected traffic is admitted only
through the selected, actually adopted generation and its
applicable physical/effect/security gates.

Single-node and distributed realizations are constrained by the
same security and semantic invariants. Multi-node routing, interest
advertisement, failover, replay and invalidation duplication require
additional consistency, isolation and liveness premises; a
router's locally missing interest is not authority to omit
a remote participant's permissible recovery. Advisory Live
delivery alone never authorizes a protected data read, and
missing messages never prove the participant is up to date.

The whole-application invariant is:

#+begin_quote
One source-owned definition yields an admitted semantic and physical realization
under an explicit assurance policy. Every required operation, effect, output,
observation, and recovery edge has a compatible current binding, and the actual
installed paths enforce the required checks before their protected actions.
Construction, artifact, installation, invocation, and physical-completion facts
remain distinct. Missing structural edges reject rather than silently weaken
meaning; opaque application logic retains explicit contracts and premises.
Admitted assembly instances remain coherent through build, serving, asynchronous
work, reload, and retirement. Declared closure, production enforcement, and
independent product completeness are separately evidenced, and authority remains
with the trusted runtime/model boundaries that own the relevant current facts.
#+end_quote

 
*** Conditions for interpreting the invariant

The quotation is a **normative end-state property**, not a certificate
that a particular Gesso commit or arbitrary Clojure application
currently satisfies it. Its "every required" quantification applies
to the *truthfully covered* operation, effect, writer, product and
deployment scope under the selected assurance policy. It cannot
prove unknown writers absent or make a smaller operation catalog
satisfy broader HumanHelp capabilities. To assert it of an admitted application
generation =A= and its specified protected effects, the evidence
must account for all the following conditions:

1. The source-owned catalog and its independently selected
   positive application requirements are identified; required
   operations, rules and recovery cases are nonvacuously covered.
   Unknown or opaque business rules remain declared premises,
   not implicitly absent.
2. Semantic operations, browser controls/plan, exact generated
   artifacts, actual routes, trusted model calls, physical
   providers, protected writers, final output, observation and
   recovery all have appropriately checked bindings. A
   structurally known missing edge prevents admission, rather
   than downgrading a managed operation to anonymous HTMX.
3. The installed startup, actual handler, guarded transaction
   path and relevant response/asset serving mechanisms enforce
   those checks in the qualified deployment. Local system-map
   equality and source-relative diagnostics do not establish
   physical serving or writer completeness.
4. Each attempted effect is checked against *current* trusted
   authentication, authorization, model guards, command
   binding and transaction assumptions at its legitimate
   authoritative boundary. The invariant must continue to
   hold under all covered relevant concurrent writers, not
   only the operation that the user clicked.
5. Protected output, prior-command disclosure, Live interest,
   one-Refresh acquisition, physical adoption and old
   command resolution respect their own permissions,
   progression and lifetime, including ambiguous delivery,
   postcommit failures and generation turnover.
6. Relevant changed sources, providers, checkers, plans,
   backend assumptions or deployed wiring invalidate
   dependent evidence. Bounded finite checking,
   conditional induction, host observations, compiler
   premises, actual backend behavior and production
   deployment are never collapsed into one green claim.
7. Independent real user acceptance demonstrates required
   positive Create/Claim/Unclaim/Cancel/complete/Reassign
   and advisory/Refresh behaviors as applicable; a
   structurally closed, successfully rejecting but
   functionally empty application does not qualify.

A qualified invariant is about the actions and physical
deployment scopes it actually covers. Fairness, continuous
connectivity, backend correctness, correct application
business rules, distributed recovery and hostile trusted
processes require separately named assumptions or proofs.
A finite model checker can prove an invariant for its
admitted finite model; the complete real application
guarantee additionally needs correct mappings and
coverage for all claimed physical effects.

*** Security and construction falsification histories

Tests select the original source-owned application,
intentionally change one structural or physical edge,
and observe its legitimate real boundary. Valid positive
cases remain independently required.

| History | Required result and security interpretation |
|---------+---------------------------------------------|
| An authorized helper uses the real Claim control, and the current model incorporates the guarded transaction with permitted readback. | Structural, trusted-effect, participant and physical adoption evidence remain separate; valid Claim must stay usable. |
| The browser forges =:principal= or Membership role in a Claim payload. | Trusted ingress/model ignore that authority claim and enforce current authenticated principal and tenant. |
| A Request R1 Claim envelope is sent to the installed R2 Claim route. | Reject contradictory normalized selectors before protected effect; do not choose the more convenient untrusted field. |
| The browser sends a copied ApplicationAssembly, valid artifact receipt or alleged proof certificate to skip server checks. | Reject authority promotion; actual installed server and current model requirements remain mandatory. |
| A command ID that previously incorporated is replayed with a different operation, arguments or principal. | Reject incompatible binding or withhold disclosure; do not authorize a new mutation or reveal a protected historical result. |
| A correctly bound old command result is requested by a principal lacking current disclosure permission. | Return the authorized nondisclosing disposition, not the old outcome or a fabricated rejection. |
| Claim's declared active-Membership rule passes a finite check but the issued XTDB callback omits the real current guard. | Keep the abstract result separate; fail/open physical model-enforcement correspondence and relevant product acceptance. |
| A worker using raw XTDB privileges alters RequestAssignment outside the registered route catalog. | Reject complete-writer/security claims absent an actual shared capability restriction or independently complete interference proof. |
| A current generated browser asset is checked locally but a different bundle is served to an old page. | Reject or qualify exact serving/generation correspondence; source receipt alone is insufficient. |
| Biff's preflight starts first in ordered =:start=, while a previous =:init= has already exposed protected work. | Fail the no-unchecked-exposure condition or require a real pre-activation fence. |
| A valid Claim commits, but its HTML response is malformed and never delivered. | Retain authoritative incorporation and participant =:unknown= until admissible command resolution; output rejection is not transaction rollback. |
| An SSE advisory arrives twice after a one-use Refresh grant was consumed. | Preserve advisory debt without granting unauthorized repeated acquisition or adoption. |
| A Live router fails while a new subscriber's interest was not yet known to its replacement. | Require qualified fence/replay/reacquisition coverage or report an open no-gap premise; a silent stream is not fresh knowledge. |
| A server-side diagnostic report is copied from generation A and submitted as generation B's admission proof. | Refuse report-as-capability; recheck original sources, installed bindings and applicable changed premises. |
| The managed application has no usable manager Reassign, although its reduced semantic graph and guards pass. | Structural success may stand; independent positive product completeness fails. |
| A runtime checker is unsupported or times out while all route/asset declarations look correct. | Retain unsupported/inconclusive mandatory obligations under the selected policy; no automatic downgrade or universal certificate. |

These histories are requirements for future qualified
implementations and tests, not assertions of a freshly
completed Gesso test suite. Their scope and independent
acceptance must remain visible in the application's
semantic audit and explanation surface.

*** Part VII completion is not automatic acceptance

Finishing the fifteen sectional R5.1 source reviews
establishes only editorial progress. Whole-Part-VII
reconciliation must separately inspect internal
duplication and contradictions, cross-part interfaces,
the complete R4 preservation inventory, and consistency
of the revised final invariant with its construction,
browser, model and deployment premises.

Independent reviewed-candidate acceptance then evaluates
the resulting published part and its original sources.
Neither step grants whole-application certification to
Gesso or HumanHelp. Parts VIII–XII and full-plan review
retain their separate outstanding requirements.
* Part VIII — HumanHelp proving application
:PROPERTIES:
:CUSTOM_ID: part-08-humanhelp-proving-application
:PART_REVISION: 08-20261110
:END:

This part specifies a complete proving application for the contracts in Parts
I–VII. HumanHelp supplies real domain rules, authenticated users, persistent
Requests and assignments, a useful board, concurrent browsers, and recoverable
failures. It must demonstrate that the assembled path works, rather than merely
that its components can each return a successful check.

This is a normative application design. Requirements describe the system to be
built; they are not assertions that the corresponding implementation or proof
already exists. The selected product policies are stated here so that browser
behavior has an independent acceptance oracle. A remaining unresolved product
contract is identified explicitly and cannot be counted as completed.

Examples use illustrative construction and inspection notation. They do not
introduce a second public API alongside production model and Gesso contracts.
In particular, a plain map containing an operation, evidence reference, or
successful verdict is not an issued executor, admitted observation, or permit.

** Purpose, scope, and independent claims

The fifteen reviewed units specify one application, not fifteen
independent implementations. 08.01–08.03 own its production semantics,
application identity and independently required user capabilities;
08.04–08.07 own adopted board knowledge, local Create, remote
advisory/one-use Refresh and user interaction; 08.08–08.10 join
authenticated authority, Live, command recovery, concrete routes,
assets and host lifecycle; 08.11–08.14 own assurance/test oracles,
structural enforcement, connected evidence and resource limits;
08.15 owns joint acceptance. Parts IV–VI own generic command,
progression and physical-effect semantics, and Part VII generic
application assembly. None of these overlapping views creates a
second Request machine or operation registry.

The immediate application is the HumanHelp example UI, backed by the production
=net.humanhelp.site.model.*= models. The eventual production UI may consume the
same contracts. Its completion is a separate product milestone; the example
must not depend on that unfinished interface to supply essential behavior.

The example owns integration and presentation. It does not own a parallel Request
store, a simplified Membership policy, a substitute assignment model, or a
browser-specific interpretation of Request states. Development fixtures create
valid production entities and enter through declared initialization paths.

Three claims must be reported separately:

| Claim | HumanHelp evidence |
|-------+--------------------|
| Declared closure | One application definition connects required operations, plans, routes, providers, acquisitions, rendered actions, and recovery paths. |
| Production enforcement | Actual serving, dispatch, model invocation, transaction submission, and browser effect boundaries enforce the admitted contracts. |
| Behavioral completeness | Independent user scenarios succeed through real controls and persisted production semantics. |

An application can be closed after accidentally deleting Reassign. A model can
be correct while the browser never sends its command. A browser can display
success while no authoritative assignment exists. Each must fail the claim it
violates; none is repaired by a green result in another column.

HumanHelp is a broad reference consumer. It exercises authentication, creation,
all required lifecycle operations, selective adoption, search, sort, visibility,
details, continuity, response interaction, disconnect/reconnect, and concurrent
use. A single Claim demonstration is a necessary vertical slice, not the whole
application.

*** Generic mechanisms and application policy

Gesso supplies operation identity, projection, semantic admission, managed effect
ownership, authority and observation boundaries, scoped progression, application
closure, evidence classification, and recovery composition. HumanHelp supplies
Request eligibility, Organization and Membership policy, assignment meaning,
board ordering, and the choice to defer remote changes until Refresh.

HumanHelp failures can justify a generic improvement when they expose a reusable
missing obligation or enforcement boundary. A missing way to preserve unknown
command outcomes is such a gap. A wrong rule about who may reassign a Request
is a HumanHelp model defect. Gesso must not acquire HumanHelp business rules to
make a reference application pass.

 
*** The proving UI is the selected real application, not a parallel demo

During this integration milestone, the global =/app= entrypoint actually
selects =net.humanhelp.example.app= through the application's normal
routing and startup path. The incomplete =net.humanhelp.site= UI is *not*
another acceptance implementation and need not be finished to demonstrate
this reference application. Eventually it may consume the same production
model and Gesso contracts; its completion is independently scheduled.

The boundary is strict in both directions. Production
=net.humanhelp.site.model.request.core= and the relevant public
Organization, Membership and User model APIs own their persistent facts,
eligibility and guarded transitions. The model-owned
=net.humanhelp.site.model.request.choreo= coordinates those *public*
operations and exports semantic browser capabilities. The example
provides board/query composition, views, routes and user interactions,
but cannot invent an easier RequestAssignment schema, mutate an
example-only Request store or implement authorization in a card
component. A broken production transition is repaired in its
production owner; replacing it with a sample mutation to make
Chromium green is an invalid migration.

The physical browser participant =:helper= in the current Request
choreography is not evidence of actual helper Membership: the same
signed-in participant can display requestor and manager affordances.
Its trusted authority role, the authenticated principal, selected
target helper, physical server host and current model guard remain
distinct. Example request inputs and generated browser operation
metadata cannot supply the principal or bypass current Organization
and Membership checks.

Development fixtures bootstrap genuine production User,
Organization, Location and relevant Membership/assignment
relationships through declared model/initialization paths.
A fixed example Organization or Location used by a selected
fixture is *not* a substitute for tenant-scoped authorization
or complete production capability coverage. Tests identify
their fixture and actor assumptions, and exercise the real
public production model rather than a mock that merely returns
a plausible Request card.

** One application definition and actual installation

HumanHelp has one source-owned application definition. It composes production
model operations and choreography with concrete browser and server realizations,
physical routes, acquisition scopes, views, assets, capabilities, and the chosen
assurance policy. The constructor returns the admitted application used by
startup, rendering, dispatch, and inspection.

Tests call that constructor with explicit fixture dependencies. They do not
maintain a second operation registry or a shadow assembly. Product acceptance
remains independent: its list of required capabilities cannot be generated solely
from whatever operations happen to remain in the application definition.

 
*** Product scope must not be confused with a closed lifecycle slice

The application has multiple overlapping but nonidentical inventories.
The model-owned operation catalog identifies what the production model
can execute. The browser-plan registry identifies the lifecycle
operations currently exposed through one client projection. The
application's complete protected effect/writer scope includes
other sources such as Create, initialization and background work.
The independently selected HumanHelp product profile defines
what a *complete proving application* must make usable.

A structural checker can validly close a six-operation browser
lifecycle slice — Claim, Unclaim, mark on the way, Complete, Cancel
and Reassign — without thereby having checked Request Create,
authentication, read authorization, search, details, selectable
response interaction, all model writers or positive end-to-end
product behavior. The finished application must *compose* its
distinct Create operation and every other required protected
capability into appropriate route, trusted model, effect,
rendering and acceptance evidence. Its report states what was
included, intentionally separate or still unqualified, never
advertising a partial fragment as a fully admitted product.

The acceptance oracle is independently selected and includes
the full required-capabilities contract in 08.03, not merely the
set of current browser plan keys. Removing manager Reassign from
a plan may leave a smaller graph that passes its own checks;
that must still fail the independent product gate. Likewise
a green lifecycle preflight is not evidence that a real
Create dialog produces a persistent Request with immediate
creator-local visibility.

*** Source responsibilities

The following names locate responsibilities; they do not require that every
application use exactly this file decomposition.

| Owner | Responsibility |
|-------+----------------|
| =net.humanhelp.site.model.request.*= | Request and RequestAssignment meaning, lifecycle rules, public reads and writes, command disposition, authoritative changes. |
| Production Organization, Membership, and User models | Their own entities, association and eligibility rules, permitted public projections, and relevant operation contracts. |
| Production Request choreography | Distributed operation contracts, projected roles, semantic operation identities, outcome and recovery branches. |
| =net.humanhelp.example.board= | Authorized read composition and pure presentation over adopted observations; no independent lifecycle policy. |
| Example Request-card component | Render prepared production affordances and adopted facts; provide stable card identity and continuity slots. |
| Example Refresh component | Render pending, refreshing, failed, and disconnected states; issue an explicit adoption request. |
| =net.humanhelp.example.live= | Scope routing, subscription policy, query/projection contracts, acquisition and installation integration. |
| Example optimistic integration | Application presentation choices bound to generic projected plans and effect ownership. |
| Example routes and app composition | Physical dispatch, trusted context construction, issued executor bindings, startup and host installation. |
| Example application-preflight integration | Invoke and explain the canonical constructor and selected admission policy; no separate semantic registry. |
| Example views | Page composition, dialogs, local options, accessible feedback, details, and declared managed render surfaces. |

Late renderer resolution can break a namespace dependency cycle. It cannot allow
a renderer to escape admission or be silently replaced after its binding has
been checked. Reload creates a new candidate assembly and adopts it coherently
under Part VII.

 
Source ownership also distinguishes *public-model* calls from
private implementation reuse. Cross-model decisions use
the owning model's =*.core= API and required guarded
dependencies; the example must not reach into another
model's =domain=, =fx= or =graph= internals to create a
more convenient eligibility path. The Request Choreo
coordinates the same public operations; it cannot
embed a competing set of Organization or Membership rules.

A concrete route declares which trusted callable it actually
uses, which semantic operation it exposes, what principal and
Request selector it receives, and which physical model/
transaction and authorized acquisition follow. A view
that displays a semantic capability cannot silently
downgrade to an anonymous HTMX POST because its optimistic
basis is missing. A raw writer or alternate Ring route
outside the plan inventory remains relevant to the
protected-effect scope; a report of zero declared
uncovered writers cannot prove that actual writers are
absent.

*** A concrete construction path

The supported path performs these steps:

1. Load production definitions and explicit configuration, including the runtime
   profile, board policy, trusted capabilities, and assurance requirements.
2. Resolve the operation catalog, semantic declarations, opaque host contracts,
   choreography projections, and required acquisition/recovery continuations.
3. Derive browser plans and the manifest from that source; build the generated
   bootstrap and exact asset set under the qualified compiler/build profile.
4. Bind physical dispatch to the issued server realizations and the trusted
   context/provider mapping. Include relevant non-HTTP writers in the scope of
   the application claims.
5. Admit concrete view preparation and render boundaries, query scopes, Live
   declarations, effect implementations, and product-specific adoption policy.
6. Apply the selected structural and assurance gates, preserving unresolved
   premises and the actual scope of each result.
7. Install the admitted handler and runtime resources into the serving host;
   expose ordinary service only after the required initialization succeeds.

The serving host must actually consume the checked handler. Merely returning
one from a helper or storing it in a system map does not establish adoption by
a running server. Tests observe the installed entrypoint and exercise it.

 
The example application route selected globally, the canonical
application constructor, emitted browser artifact, guarded HTML
output and physical server startup are *joined deployment facts*.
A build script and a runtime may share a source declaration yet
load different JavaScript bytes, or a Gesso module may install
a checked =:biff.ring/handler= while an alternate server captures
a different callable. Those are distinct failed/unsupported
evidence claims, not successful application installation.

On Biff 2, all module =:init= functions can run before ordered
=:start= functions. Mandatory preflight must therefore fence
protected listener, scheduler, writer and public operation
effects even when private initialization is allowed. The
actual Aleph server must consume the admitted handler before
ordinary service; a later handler/asset/provider replacement
invalidates the affected evidence. No startup policy may
pretend a successful check rolls back a mutation that already
committed or resolves a command whose response disappeared.

Test setup and the running application use the *same*
construction owner and original production model definitions.
Controlled defects remove a real required operation,
route, provider, plan, artifact or acquisition edge and
must fail the corresponding gate. A test-only duplicate
assembly remaining green after the production constructor
breaks is not valid acceptance evidence.

*** Assurance is explicit and useful

HumanHelp uses the full host language. Pure functions, FX composition, ordinary
Clojure and ClojureScript, and opaque integration code remain available. The
application identifies the contracts on which its claims depend and proves the
parts supported by the selected semantic fragment.

The admission profile must require structural closure and the applicable issued
callable/plan bindings. For operations represented by the source-owned relational
construction, it also requires their declared invariant checks, rule exercise,
and operation/outcome coverage. Conditional induction is required where the
application claims that stronger result; a finite exploration result is not
renamed an induction theorem.

Unsupported operation semantics must be declared as opaque premises with an
owner, effect/dependency interface, and conformance obligations. The admission
policy explicitly accepts or rejects those premises for the claimed application
invariant. It must not make an incomplete model look total by omitting the opaque
operation from writer coverage.

For example, a proof of unique active primary assignment may depend on the
Request command implementation, initialization, collaborator/reassignment writers,
and the qualified transaction adapter. A theorem about the finite abstract
operation catalog alone does not establish the corresponding physical database
invariant.

The permanent executable semantic core governs admitted transitions. A proof
checker or later small proof kernel checks a specified class of proof evidence.
Neither replaces HumanHelp's transaction boundary or current authorization.

 
*** Positive and adversarial assembly histories

The following scenarios exercise the same production-backed
example selected by =/app=. Structural checks, actual
production enforcement and independent product outcomes
are reported as different propositions.

| History | Required result and evidence scope |
|---------+------------------------------------|
| The selected example creates a Request through the production model; its creator immediately sees the committed Request under a qualified read basis. | Verify the real Create route, trusted requestor, production persistence, progression, visible rendered control and local adoption; passing lifecycle-plan preflight alone is insufficient. |
| A valid helper uses the actual Claim card and the public production model incorporates the guarded assignment. | Trace model-owned choreography, issued HTTP executor, authenticated principal, guarded commit and authorized acquisition; do not treat a green browser map as a domain write. |
| The same browser is a requestor on one Request and an authorized manager on another. | Its physical Choreo participant can be shared while the trusted model evaluates distinct current actor and target permissions. |
| An example Claim handler writes an example-only RequestAssignment or directly imports another model's private FX helper. | Reject semantic/source ownership as unproven or incorrect; the example may not replace production RequestAssignment or authorization meaning. |
| A fixture supplies a valid Organization ID but no applicable active Membership for the actor. | Current production authority rejects the protected action; fixed fixture values and rendered capabilities cannot grant Membership. |
| An assembly checker includes all six lifecycle browser plans but omits Create, an actual raw writer or another promised product operation. | Report exact checked lifecycle scope; reject a full product/all-writer claim and fail independent missing-capability acceptance. |
| A lifecycle operation ID is removed from the real production browser declaration while an independently rebuilt test registry still includes it. | Tests must use the real constructor and expose the omission rather than pass a shadow assembly. |
| The named route and operation exist but the deployed Aleph handler uses a different callable from the checked system-map slot. | Retain structural evidence but leave production serving/adoption unestablished or contradicted. |
| A Biff =:init= starts a protected writer/listener before the checked startup's ordered =:start=. | Fence its external effects or fail the protected no-exposure contract; first-in-start is insufficient. |
| A valid operation commits, then its response renderer fails or network settlement disappears. | Preserve authoritative incorporation and command-specific unknown/recovery debt; never fabricate rollback or new-command permission. |
| A test injects a correct Claim protocol directly while the actual button never submits. | Treat it as a bounded protocol test, not positive real-control browser/product acceptance. |
| The source/asset/handler generation changes while a pending card response or command resolver still refers to the prior generation. | Preserve declared retained owner/compatibility and real rights, or explicitly block/reconcile; never silently splice a new executor into old work. |

An eligible Create and Claim scenario must be demonstrated
in addition to controlled invalid cases. Subsequent 08.xx
sections own the full Request lifecycle, selective board
adoption, one-Refresh policy, response-flow choice and
concurrency matrices; this initial assembly section does
not redefine their domain policy or pretend those
end-to-end capabilities have passed independent acceptance.

** Production model truth and public operation boundaries

A Request belongs to its production Organization and Location. Its helper
relationship is represented by production RequestAssignment semantics. The UI
must not replace those facts with a convenient =helper-id= field or infer the
whole lifecycle from whether one optional field is present.

The canonical Request states for this application are =:open=, =:claimed=,
=:on-the-way=, =:done=, and =:cancelled=. Display text such as “Completed” may
label =:done=; it must not introduce a competing persisted =:completed= state.
Public predicates and prepared projections provide state meaning to presentation.

 
*** Production aggregate, state vocabulary, and source authority

The production Request and RequestAssignment are separate persisted entities
forming one model-owned Request aggregate. A Request owns Organization,
Location, requestor, content and lifecycle identity. A primary or collaborator
RequestAssignment owns its helper, role, active/ended state, provenance and
history. An active primary assignment is not interchangeable with a
convenient =:request/helper-id= view field, a provisional label or the
browser's selected target.

The public =request.core= predicates and snapshots, not example component
conditionals, determine =:open=, =:claimed=, =:on-the-way=, =:done= and
=:cancelled= and the assignment relationships each permits. Terminal
completion and cancellation close the assignments required by the production
operation; Reassign preserves a lawful historical end of the previous
primary and creation of the new primary in one protected operation.
Collaborator writes, Request editing, initialization and Organization/
Membership changes remain within the relevant invariant/writer scope
even when this proving UI does not expose each as a dedicated control.

Use public =net.humanhelp.site.model.request.core=,
=membership.core=, =organization.core= and =user.core= semantics
for cross-model decisions. The production =request.choreo= layer
coordinates these public operations; neither it nor the example
may independently reimplement private =domain=, =fx= or =graph=
policy to win a race against the public model.

*** Atomic dependencies, not a sequence of reassuring reads

A lifecycle handler may parse inputs, authenticate, prepare context, and perform
advisory reads. The public production operation remains responsible for the
resolve-or-incorporate protocol in [[#req-atomic-authoritative-transition]].

For a new Claim, the protected dependency set includes the targeted Request,
its Organization/Location association as required by policy, the actor and
selected helper where distinct, effective Membership, Organization policy,
relevant assignment facts, and command exclusion. The ownership change,
assignment changes, command result, and required durable publication intent
are established at the declared atomic boundary.

The actual set follows the production rule. If eligibility depends on a related
entity or on the absence of another active assignment, that dependency must be
protected too. Guarding only the Request document is insufficient. Conversely,
the example should not invent unrelated dependencies merely to make a diagram
appear comprehensive.

Separate reads of Request, Membership, and Organization followed by an unguarded
write leave a race. Rechecking only the rendered card's revision leaves a race.
A transaction plan must preserve every relevant dependency through the qualified
submission mechanism, including absence or query dependencies where required.

 
*** Guard construction and physical correspondence are different claims

The admitted Claim plan has a source-relative obligation to protect
the aggregate snapshot, current operational Organization/Location
scope, selected target's active eligible Membership and relevant
role/skill assignment, and (for manager-assisted Claim) the actor's
current supervisor/administrator authority. It additionally excludes
active assignments as a *cardinality/absence* condition. The exact
dependency footprint is determined by the real model policy,
not by a hand-authored audit approximation.

Gesso's generic transaction representation may combine
=:commands= (Request/RequestAssignment mutations),
=:guards= (versioned dependency evidence),
=:assertions= (including set-level absence/cardinality)
and =:changes= (semantic changes for Live). These
are different kinds of obligations: guarding each observed
assignment is insufficient by itself when a new matching
assignment could appear. The Request aggregate concurrency
root and required relevant absence assertions must be
honored by the selected XTDB transaction semantics.

The *model planner* may have a well-formed protected plan
while the *physical backend* still requires independent
qualification for transaction-internal evaluation,
assertion atomicity, contending writers, post-commit
progression and actual submission/observation provenance.
An optional finite proof of the source-owned rule does
not authenticate every XTDB attempt. Likewise,
calling =model.tx/transact!= is not proof that unregistered
maintenance writers cannot bypass Request invariants.
The application can qualify the bounded real transaction
behavior it has observed without calling that evidence
universal linearizability or a complete-writer certificate.

The browser's previously adopted basis =X17= is an
authoritative *scoped observation frontier*, not the
Request's revision, a global snapshot of all HumanHelp
state, or an automatic stale-command veto. Unrelated
commits may advance the database while Claim remains
valid; a relevant Membership/assignment change must be
reconsidered by the model and guarded at incorporation.

*** Actor, target helper, and command identity

The authenticated principal comes from the trusted request/runtime context.
Browser fields, rendered capabilities, certificates, selected personas, and
knowledge of a UUID do not establish that principal.

A target helper can be a legitimate domain argument. Reassign requires target
selection; a production Claim variant may permit a manager to claim for another
eligible helper. That argument does not replace the actor. The model checks the
actor's authority to select the target and the target's eligibility atomically.
The basic Claim control in this proving UI means “claim for myself”; any separate
manager-assisted variant is labelled and tested as such.

Before the first possible send, the admitted command boundary supplies a stable
=:gesso/command-id= and binds it to the operation/interface, canonical arguments,
authority domain, and principal. A declared mapping may expose that value as
=:command-id= at the public model boundary. Retries preserve the binding.

The HumanHelp domain argument =:request-id= denotes a Request. Transport
correlation uses =:http-request-id= or =:transport-request-id=. Execution,
resource instance, board owner, assembly/deployment, and command identities stay
distinct. One generic “generation” field cannot stand in for all of them.

 
*** Request actor, target, scope, and trust separation

For the ordinary =:request/claim= control, *claim for myself*
binds target helper to the currently authenticated actor
within the trusted operation, not from a posted =:helper-id=.
A distinct manager-assisted Claim may legitimately supply
a different =:helper-id=, but the authoritative model must
protect both the actor's **exact** supervisor or
administrator role at the applicable Location and the
chosen target's separate helper eligibility. HumanHelp
does not grant manager authority merely by a role-name
hierarchy or by the browser using the one physical
=:helper= choreography participant.

Reassign likewise must not equate an actor's permission
to choose a target with the target's eligibility to
hold the new assignment. Relevant Organization
scope, Location, current Membership, active role
assignments and declared skills are model dependencies.
A target-helper picker can narrow options for UX;
it cannot authorize a protected transaction.

A route must reconcile the normalized path Request ID
with the semantic command's Request argument. A
separately chosen target/helper/skill cannot replace the
trusted principal or ownership context. A valid
operation capability or browser-chosen principal
identifier is inert presentation data. Public
model authorization and its current protected
dependencies determine the actual transition.

*** Resolve an existing command before applying new-command guards

A compatible repetition checks the retained command record's binding and current
permission to disclose its outcome. It returns the permitted historical result
without incorporating again. The fact that the Request is now claimed does not
justify rejecting a retry of the successful command that claimed it.

A new command must pass the current commit guard. Concurrent compatible attempts
must not both establish a new incorporation. Incompatible reuse is a typed
protocol failure. A failed physical attempt is not automatically a definitive
command rejection when another delivery of that command may still succeed.

Command retention, exclusion after result expiry, recovery across interface
versions, and disclosure after role changes follow Part IV. The browser may not
create a new identifier merely to make an unresolved operation appear retryable.
A command-recovery record and a current Request read answer different questions.

 
*** Historical incorporation requires an actual selected implementation

The complete target protocol is *resolve or incorporate*:
a trusted server obtains an authoritative record for the
original typed command binding (principal, operation,
canonical argument set, interface/authority domain and
stable command ID), verifies current disclosure rights,
and returns the recorded result when repetition is
compatible. An unresolved original command never becomes
permission to mint a fresh ID merely because a timeout
occurred or the current Request looks claimed.

For new incorporation, the command record/exclusion
and Request/RequestAssignment guarded mutations must
share the qualified atomic boundary. An existing
record must be effectively immutable for the selected
retention contract. Record expiry must not permit
duplicate logical incorporation while an old retry
can still arrive; the operation must define exclusion,
compatibility or manual reconciliation through that
lifetime. Retried transport attempts can reach another
Aleph node without changing their semantic identity.
A later current-policy or principal-role change may
forbid disclosure of a previously successful result
without reversing the historical commit.

This is a **required finished-system protocol**, not
an assertion that every current `request.core` call
already persists command ID and outcome. Current
production public Request operations expose
transaction =:commit/status= and progression; their
model transaction success is not, by itself, a
durable same-command replay certificate. Gesso's
source-level command-record helper is experimental
construction with a trusted disclosure/lookup
assumption, not an installed HumanHelp
exactly-once service. The application must connect,
qualify and test that mechanism before claiming
the stronger recovery property.

*** Outcome and presentation contracts

| Model evidence | Presentation and recovery obligation |
|----------------+--------------------------------------|
| =:committed= with permitted success evidence | Settle the bound operation as =:accepted=; install only the observations the result or a follow-up acquisition justifies. |
| =:already-incorporated= with a permitted successful recorded outcome | Use the same accepted successor without another mutation or duplicate publication intent. |
| =:rejected= with authoritative command disposition | Follow the rejection branch and permit the declared scoped reacquisition; preserve any undisclosable details. |
| =:commit-unknown= | Keep command disposition unknown and invoke the bound reconciliation path. |
| Malformed input, incompatible reuse, invalid credentials, or disclosure denial | Use its declared typed handling; do not invent a domain rejection or reveal a protected prior result. |

A replayed success is historical. It does not prove that the helper still owns
the Request after later Unclaim or Reassign. The UI may say that the command
succeeded while displaying a newer permitted card observation with a different
current assignment.

A timeout does not mean rollback. A publication failure after a known commit
does not erase that commit. The server can know =:committed= while a disconnected
browser knows only =:unknown=. A lost response is resolved with authoritative
command-specific evidence, not by guessing from a fresh card that another actor
could have produced.

 
*** Distinguish the current model API from the intended protocol layers

The present public Request operation reports
=:commit/status :committed= and, when available,
a composable authoritative =:progression=. The
current Request choreography checks that committed
result and constructs its own protocol-v3
=:confirmed= authority projection. These are
different *interfaces* from the Part IV
=:committed= / =:already-incorporated= /
=:rejected= / =:commit-unknown= command
disposition taxonomy and from the browser's
=:accepted= / =:rejected= / =:unknown=
presentation. A correct adapter preserves
the evidence required for each mapping;
matching words or a generic 200/500 response
do not supply the missing durable record.

For the initiator, a direct correlated success can
justify an explicitly scoped card acquisition or
adoption if it meets the protocol's trust and
progression requirements. A remote browser may
receive only an advisory and is not automatically
entitled to reread the board; one-user-Refresh
remains a separate grant. Validating a current
card can supersede provisional display even
while command-specific historical attribution
remains unknown.

A post-commit error in HTML generation,
publication or response delivery cannot
reinterpret the actual Request/RequestAssignment
commit as rollback. If physical storage reports
an uncertain write, neither the model nor
participant may invent a definitive rejection
until admissible authoritative evidence settles
the bound command. Recovery has a real retained
owner, trigger, authorization, progressive read,
expiration and explicit blocked/manual state
when automatic resolution is not possible.

*** Positive and adversarial model-boundary histories

Acceptance exercises the production source/physical
path and the relevant trust boundary. It does not
substitute copied maps or idealized isolated model
fixtures for a real deployed operation.

| History | Required model/command/presentation disposition |
|---------+-------------------------------------------------|
| An authorized helper claims a genuinely open Request through the real public model. | Request becomes =:claimed= and an active primary RequestAssignment is atomically established; a justified progression permits the matching authoritative read. |
| Two distinct eligible helpers submit different Claims from the same observed open state. | At most one establishes that open-to-claimed primary transition; the other cannot create a second active primary through a stale read. |
| A missing active assignment appears between Request snapshot read and commit. | The active-assignment absence assertion and aggregate protection reject or re-evaluate rather than allow two active primary assignments. |
| A helper's Membership or Location role becomes invalid after an advisory read but before incorporation. | The actual protected authority dependency blocks the new Claim despite the old enabled browser button. |
| A manager selects another eligible helper under the same Request Location. | Guard the manager actor's exact supervisor/admin scope and the target's distinct current helper/skill eligibility, with correct assignment provenance. |
| A browser forges =:principal=, =:helper-id=, selected role or a browser certificate. | Do not grant helper or manager authority; the trusted model binds actual actor and independently checks any legitimate target. |
| A route targets Request R2 while the bound semantic command specifies R1. | Reject the conflicting normalized Request identity before protected mutation. |
| A permitted current Claim arrives with observed basis X17 after unrelated XTDB commits to X23. | Do not reject merely because X17 is old; the model evaluates its actual currently protected dependencies. |
| Claim modifies Request but the primary assignment assertion or insert fails. | The qualified atomic boundary leaves no partially claimed Request or orphan active primary. |
| The public production Claim returns committed Request and assignment with progression, but no durable record for command C42. | Classify successful model mutation and current read evidence honestly; do not claim proved historical C42 replay/deduplication. |
| C42 is delivered twice with identical principal, arguments and operation, with an authoritative disclosed record retained. | Resolve the second delivery to its historical permitted result without reapplying the Request mutation or duplicating durable publication intent. |
| Another principal reuses C42 or a later retry changes C42's Request/target/helper arguments. | Reject incompatible binding or prohibit disclosure; no new effect under the borrowed command ID. |
| C42 is incorporated, then Reassign changes the current helper and C42 is retried. | A permitted replay still reflects C42's historical result while the fresh Request snapshot reflects the later Reassign. |
| The command record is absent at a lookup basis that cannot rule out pending C42 incorporation. | Remain unresolved; absence alone neither proves rejection nor permits a fresh same-intent command. |
| A previously authorized principal loses permission to see C42's result. | Enforce current disclosure rules without leaking retained binding, Request or result. |
| A successful Claim commits and HTML rendering or Live publication fails. | Preserve the committed model truth; participant can remain =:unknown= until permitted command-specific recovery. |
| A physically unregistered writer bypasses the Request lifecycle API to change active assignment rows. | Retain the incomplete-writer/physical correspondence premise; a complete declared operation catalog does not prove global safety. |
| A browser shows “Claimed” provisionally but the real model rejects or no persisted active primary exists. | Provisional presentation may be rolled back or superseded, but a final accepted product result cannot be DOM-only success. |

These histories are required behavioral targets,
not claims that HumanHelp's current `dev`
branch passes the complete durable-command
or real-browser matrix. Section 08.03 owns
the worked Claim control and positive
product oracle; 08.04–08.09 own the
cohort, adoption, continuation and recovery
details. Parts IV and VII govern protocol
outcome types and real assembly/production
enforcement, and Parts IX–XII retain
independent formal/physical proof.

** Required user capabilities
:PROPERTIES:
:CUSTOM_ID: req-humanhelp-required-capabilities
:END:

The following obligations are independent of the assembled operation list.
Conditional unavailability under production policy is legitimate; permanent
unavailability or omission of a promised capability is not.

| Capability | Positive user interaction | Independent authoritative or observable result |
|------------+---------------------------+-----------------------------------------------|
| Authentication | Sign in as a real eligible fixture user. | Reads and writes bind to that principal; a second context has a separate session. |
| Create | Enter valid Request content in the real dialog and submit. | One Request in the selected authorized Organization/Location, correlated command outcome, and prompt creator-local visibility. |
| Claim | Eligible helper clicks Claim on an open Request. | Production claimed state and the proper active primary assignment. |
| Unclaim | Eligible current helper releases a claimed Request. | Production open state and assignment termination required by the model. |
| Mark on the way | Eligible current helper acts on a claimed Request. | Production =:on-the-way= state and its required lifecycle facts. |
| Complete | Eligible helper completes a claimed or on-the-way Request. | Production =:done= state and closure of the active assignments required by policy. |
| Cancel | Eligible requestor cancels an allowed active Request. | Production =:cancelled= state and required assignment closure. |
| Reassign | Authorized manager chooses a legitimate different eligible helper and confirms. | Production replacement of primary responsibility and correct assignment history. |
| Refresh | User explicitly adopts current board information. | A qualified scoped observation is installed, with only covered obligations discharged. |
| Search and options | User changes search, creation order, mine-first, unclaimed-first, or terminal visibility. | Deterministic presentation of the adopted cohort without unrelated remote adoption. |
| Details and continuity | User opens details, edits allowed local input, and survives permitted updates. | Correct disclosed information and bounded restoration of compatible local interaction state. |
| Response interaction | User completes the separately selected response-flow contract. | Its independent product outcome, as required below. |
| Recovery | User encounters rejection, uncertainty, disconnect, or stale application state. | An honest status and a usable declared path to recover under the stated availability assumptions. |

The production model owns exact eligibility. These descriptions do not authorize
an actor who lacks current Membership or whose Request state changed. Positive
fixtures satisfy policy through real production relationships; negative fixtures
change one relevant premise and assert the corresponding outcome.

 
*** Independent user-capability oracle and positive controls

This table is a *separately selected product requirement*, not a census
of the current browser plans or a generated registry of admitted operations.
Every promised capability has its own positive reachable scenario using the
real selected =/app= surface and public production models. Its fixture
establishes legitimate current User, Membership, Organization, Location,
Request and RequestAssignment relationships without bypassing a guarded
operation. The expected model effect and observable UI are independently
specified; the test does not rewrite the oracle when a handler or button
is removed.

A capability may be hidden, disabled, or rejected in a legitimately
ineligible state. The same operation must remain *usable* in a separate
eligible state. Structural closure, refusal of invalid requests, and
absence of console exceptions cannot satisfy a product capability
whose button never submits or whose state never commits.

The product oracle separates (a) rendered affordance and browser input,
(b) trusted transport and production model operation, (c) committed
Request/assignment and permitted command-outcome evidence,
(d) authoritative acquisition and physical installation,
and (e) relevant local/remote presentation continuity.
An isolated source, server, or browser fixture may establish
some of these; it must report its narrower scope.

The full product acceptance also covers the broader response-flow decision,
real authentication, creator-local Create, multi-client advisory and one
user-Refresh, search/order/filter, details/continuity, and unknown/reconnect
recovery. Passing a six-operation lifecycle gate does not qualify those
other capabilities. The explicitly selected response-flow contract remains
a genuine pending product decision until chosen and independently tested;
the evaluator may not silently accept either absence or a substitute
unrelated workflow.

Reassign is not a hidden model function with a permanently disabled button. Its
UI must provide target discovery/selection, visible validation, confirmation,
and a tested eligible path. Target search reveals only permitted User projections
and is revalidated at commit. “Take over” is not silently treated as a synonym
for Reassign; if exposed, its actor and target policy must be explicitly bound.

Additional model operations, including Edit and collaborator management, remain
inside the relevant writer/invariant coverage even when this stage does not
promise dedicated example controls for them. Excluding a control is different
from pretending that the writer cannot affect the shared database.

 
*** Lifecycle operations share one user-to-model path

For Claim, Unclaim, Mark on the way, Complete, Cancel and Reassign,
the positive case begins at the *actual rendered enabled control*.
The source-owned semantic operation must retain its identity across
the generated plan, loaded browser artifact, HTMX request, trusted
route, public model operation, guarded outcome, settlement, scoped
acquisition and final DOM. A missing optimistic basis, plan or
route rejects the managed action rather than silently converting
it to an anonymous POST. A terminal removal follows authoritative
membership/absence semantics, not a speculative view-side decision.

A present target-helper selector is necessary but not sufficient for
Reassign. Target candidates are permitted User projections with an
explicit target choice and confirmation. Trusted model authority must
separately recheck the current actor's manager role, the target's
Membership/helper/skill eligibility and the protected Request's
current assignment at commit. A dropdown or physical =:helper=
browser role does not grant model permission.

The canonical real Chromium scenario may exercise Claim, Unclaim,
Claim again, Mark on the way, Complete, owner Cancel and manager
Reassign with distinct legitimate fixture Requests. Positive
acceptance additionally checks each operation's negative/concurrent
case and fresh persisted result. One all-green happy trajectory
alone cannot establish the behavior under stale Membership,
competing commands, lost settlement or a permanently unavailable
network. Section 08.12 owns the full independent test architecture.

** Worked vertical slice: Claim

Alice is an authenticated helper with effective Membership in the Request's
Organization. The board has adopted an authorized observation of Request R17 as
open. The prepared Claim control carries its unconditional semantic operation
identity and the concrete realization data its plan needs.

 
*** Admission and observation before Alice clicks

Alice's card has a Request identity =R17=, an adopted authoritative
Request/assignment projection and a scoped XTDB observation frontier
=X17=. The latter is neither the Request's revision nor a guarantee
of database currentness. The page also has a live executable
browser-plan/artifact binding, rendered action and target/owner
identity; a server-issued certificate or metadata copied into
the page does not grant authority.

The test locates the actual enabled Claim control in rendered
=GET /app= and follows the generated script/HTMX path. It
must not manually create, inject or edit
=__gesso_live_optimistic_command=, silently synthesize a
browser command in the HTTP fixture, or use an example-only
Request store. A separately named lower-level HTTP fixture
*may* manufacture the wire command to inspect server/model
behavior, but it is never promoted into proof of this
browser-to-command edge.

The real route binds its normalized Request selector to
the command arguments, rejects a mismatch, and obtains
Alice's authenticated User identity from trusted context.
The physical browser participant =:helper= is not evidence
that Alice has effective helper Membership; the current
production model guard establishes that independently.

1. Alice clicks the actual control. The admitted browser plan binds command C42,
   its operation/arguments, execution owner, and presentation target. The bridge
   supplies the wire protocol; the test or page author does not handcraft it.
2. A provisional “Claiming…” state may appear. It is owned by that execution and
   does not establish authoritative assignment or disable another user's model
   operation.
3. The installed route resolves the exact admitted server realization. The
   trusted boundary authenticates Alice, validates the command envelope and its
   interface mapping, and invokes the public production operation.
4. Resolve-or-incorporate recovers an existing compatible result or protects the
   complete current guard and atomically incorporates C42. A new Claim cannot
   succeed if the relevant current policy denies it.
5. The outcome mapping settles accepted, rejected, or unknown as justified. An
   accepted result authorizes only its declared card/result acquisition and
   installation, not a fresh whole-board membership query.
6. Physical installation completion records adoption and retires superseded
   provisional rights. Late callbacks from the old target/execution cannot
   restore its speculative card or apply a second settlement.

 
*** Distinguish authority, delivery, and a successful browser test

A positive browser Claim test observes the generated command's exact
operation, Request argument, stable logical command identity,
execution/physical target, route and supported observed basis.
It then correlates the trusted production result and any
authoritative progression-bearing response with a permitted
card acquisition and actual installed DOM. A fresh authorized
reread or reload verifies that the Request and *primary*
RequestAssignment persist. A provisional badge alone does
not qualify success; neither does seeing a 200 response
whose body was never installed.

The first eligible claim transition changes the persisted
Request and primary assignment together. A rival new Claim
with another command cannot create a second active primary;
an open-state Request guard without the active-assignment
absence/cardinality assertion is insufficient. A model-defined
rejection for invalid current Membership or an already
claimed Request is legitimate *runtime behavior*, not
application assembly corruption.

There are three distinct settlement contexts: the public
=Request core= result with =:commit/status= and transaction
progression; the trusted current protocol-v3 optimistic
server's =:confirmed= result with a justified projection;
and the finished-system Part IV command taxonomy
=:committed=, =:already-incorporated=, =:rejected=,
=:commit-unknown= with browser =:accepted=, =:rejected=,
=:unknown=. Their mappings are explicit, not inferred
from an HTTP status or equal-sounding strings. In
particular, the present source-backed Claim route does
not establish durable historical replay of C42 merely
by generating a protocol command ID. The Part IV
same-transaction command-record/retention and
disclosure mechanism remains a separate required
implementation and qualification.

If Bob concurrently claims R17 with a different command, at most one new Claim
can establish primary ownership from the eligible open state. In a fault-free
run with both outcomes delivered, the other command receives the appropriate
authoritative rejection. When outcome delivery is deliberately lost, unknown is
a valid intermediate participant state and reconciliation is required.

If C42 commits but its response is lost, Alice's retry preserves C42 and its
binding. It does not fail solely because R17 is now claimed. If a later Reassign
has changed R17, a permitted replay can still report C42's historical success;
the fresh card must reflect the distinct current observation.

If the result response fails render validation after commit, the invalid output
is blocked. The commit remains real. Diagnostics and recovery must keep those
facts separate rather than pretending preflight rolled back the transaction.

A checked semantic certificate can justify admitting the Claim plan under its
premises. Separate evidence establishes installed dispatch and current atomic
enforcement. Returning that certificate from the browser creates no Membership,
principal, current Request state, or permission to disclose the command result.

 
*** Positive and adversarial capability histories

The following histories are acceptance *obligations*, not
assertions that every scenario has passed in the running
application. Each retains the source-owned business
policy and selected product profile.

| History | Required positive or failure result |
|---------+------------------------------------|
| An eligible signed-in helper clicks the actual Claim button on an adopted open Request. | Browser generates C42, trusted production Claim commits one Request and active primary assignment, justified card installation occurs and fresh reload retains the mutation. |
| A lower-level integration test posts a manually encoded valid command while the actual Claim button is disabled or broken. | Credit trusted route/model fixture only; fail independent real-browser positive acceptance. |
| Alice's card lacks a justified XTDB observed basis though Claim is still a semantic operation. | The managed control is unavailable or structural/render validation rejects the missing binding; no anonymous HTMX fallback. |
| Two eligible helpers race to claim the same open Request using distinct commands. | At most one open-to-claimed incorporation succeeds; rejected or uncertain competitors keep typed outcomes and no second active primary. |
| An unrelated XTDB transaction advances X17 to X23 before Alice clicks. | No automatic stale-command rejection; the real model evaluates protected current Request and Membership dependencies. |
| Alice's active Membership is revoked after a valid card was rendered. | Trusted Request model rejects the new Claim with no partial assignment despite the old visible affordance. |
| Claim commits but its response or canonical Hiccup rendering fails. | Model truth remains committed; participant retains unknown/uncertain settlement and authorized command-specific recovery, not fictitious rollback. |
| C42's response is lost; Alice retries with the same binding after the Request became claimed. | The *finished* resolve-or-incorporate path returns a permitted historical result without replaying the mutation; a current implementation lacking durable records must not claim that guarantee. |
| C42 succeeds and a later legitimate Reassign replaces the current helper. | C42's permitted historical replay still reports its old incorporation; fresh authorized acquisition reports current new helper. |
| The browser reports a claimed card optimistically but no authoritative active primary assignment exists. | Do not accept DOM-only success; rollback/supersede provisional presentation and fail the positive product result. |
| Alice Unclaims after a successful Claim and follows the rendered Unclaim control. | End the active primary assignment and reach the model-defined open state, then confirm by fresh authorized read. |
| A helper clicks Mark on the way and later Complete from legal current states. | Verify real production =:on-the-way= and =:done= transitions, required assignment continuation/closure and persisted reload. |
| An eligible requestor Cancels a separate Request. | Confirm the model-defined =:cancelled= result and ended assignments without borrowing helper-only authority. |
| A manager selects a different eligible helper in the real Reassign menu. | Require browser-generated selected-target command, trusted manager/target guards, historical assignment end, new active primary and persisted reload. |
| A nonmanager sees a forged Reassign action or a stale selector includes an ineligible helper. | Rendered options cannot grant permission; trusted Request model rejects unauthorized/ineligible target without partial Reassign. |
| A full lifecycle browser test passes while Create, login, local search, Refresh or details never work. | Preserve the bounded lifecycle success but fail the broader independently selected HumanHelp product profile. |
| A remote connected browser receives advisory after Alice's Claim. | Do not silently adopt new remote data; preserve advisory debt and the separately permitted one-user-Refresh acquisition. |
| A refresh/acquisition returns an older card after a newer justified installation. | Preserve the newer scoped observation and participant owner; late callback cannot overwrite canonical state. |
| An already consumed one-use Refresh grant is paired with a duplicated SSE advisory. | Duplicate invalidation cannot manufacture another user read grant or erase unresolved advisory obligations. |
| Browser session for the helper is absent or forged, despite a syntactically valid C42. | Trusted boundary rejects principal substitution; neither operation metadata nor certificate supplies authentication. |
