| Terminal visibility | =:done= and =:cancelled= are hidden/shown within adopted membership without changing database state |
| Details/focus/scroll | Compatible same-identity replacement preserves declared continuity; target retirement or lost read permission cannot resurrect private DOM |
| Rapid input, stale callbacks | Later local edits and justified installations dominate stale search/option/continuity callbacks |
| Remote lifecycle change to visible R | Existing adopted R fields remain until the specified user-approved Refresh or authorized actor-specific read |
| SSE disconnect/reconnect | Lost interest/coverage is reported and recovered within the selected mechanism; reconnect never silently grants remote adoption |
| Duplicate/retired events | No duplicate protected effect, obsolete target resurrection or foreign recipient disclosure |
| Response flow | The independent response interaction product contract must be selected and passed; an unresolved decision remains an acceptance blocker |

All remote/local cases use at least two independently authenticated
browser contexts, preferably distinct principals, with independently
verified sessions, permission scopes and actual network connections.
A pair of pages sharing one mutable auth fixture is not enough.
Cross-Organization and cross-Location tests challenge both payload
disclosure and metadata/count/interest leakage. The test distinguishes
a user-local option from a server-side query change: where a
new authoritative collection query is actually required, it needs
its own authorization and scoped read/adoption permission; it
cannot be smuggled in as mere presentation search.

*** Fault, recovery and environmental qualification

| Fault or changed premise | Required evidence and safe result |
|--------------------------+-----------------------------------|
| Failure before actual submission | No new authoritative effect; typed local failure and permitted new admission |
| Submission with lost result | C42 remains unknown until exact authorized command-specific evidence; current card read alone cannot attribute C42 |
| Known commit, failed rendering/transport | Persistent transition remains; invalid output blocked and actor has qualified acquisition/recovery |
| Crash after commit before Live publish | Transaction-coupled durable publication intent or the explicitly chosen tested alternative closes the declared recovery path |
| Live delivery gap or reconnect | Interest/grant fencing, scope and basis recovery; no accidental automatic adoption |
| Result lookup denied/expired | No protected disclosure; denial/retention expiry is not evidence of rejection |
| Fragment read timeout/partial/error | No invented complete authoritative absence, and no false Refresh-debt discharge |
| Partially installed OOB/multi-target response | Per-target physical completion and repair rights; no claimed atomic multi-target adoption |
| Older network/optimistic callback | Retired E42/T1 cannot overwrite newer justified installation or restart old plan |
| Deployment A to B while client A persists | Matching assets/compatible protocol or declared reload/retirement; no mixed-generation actuation |
| Wrong installed Biff handler or receipt | No protected service with unsupported assembly; paired valid startup still succeeds |
| Membership/Organization change in flight | Proper current guards, read/disclosure revocation and usable permitted recovery |
| Unknown/extra physical writer | Coverage obligation remains open; it cannot borrow the declared operation's proof |
| Changed XTDB/HTMX/compiler qualification | Dependent proposition requalified, blocked or honestly reported unsupported, never silently left certified |

Fault injection records the exact boundary and ordering: before send,
after send/before transaction, after commit/before response, after
commit/before publication, read-success/swap-failure, owner retirement
and browser reload. It must not replace a real backend/handler with a
fake transition while claiming physical refinement. Fault-free tests
must not tolerate synthetic unknown outcomes; fault tests must not
convert unknown to rejection. Automatic retry budgets, retention
horizons, user recovery affordances and resource cleanup are
separately observed.

Unexpected console/page/network failures and unrelated non-2xx
responses fail the test. The fixture may accept an *expected* typed
fault only in the case that injected it, with exact operation/subject,
first enforcing boundary, permitted outcome and current poststate.
Blanket suppression of 4xx/5xx, all timeouts, or all exceptions
would conceal a broken product path. Negative cases pair with
a valid, eligible positive so "reject everything" cannot pass.

*** Evidence ledger, suite composition and completion

The finished HumanHelp acceptance report connects the real
production assembly, generated browser manifest/build receipt,
physically served asset, authenticated sessions, rendered controls,
browser-created commands, installed Ring route/handler, XTDB
transaction/readback evidence, actual SSE/HTMX/OOB effect events,
current adopted frontier and independent product outcomes. Each
reference has its source, version, trust boundary, observation
scope and limitations. It must not use a copy of one green
preflight result as evidence of all these independent edges.

The suite reports distinct statuses for domain/model, bounded
semantic checking, backend qualification, declared and actual
writer coverage, structural/render rejection, installed-host
adoption, real browser lifecycle, full two-client board/Refresh,
failure/reconnect, and independent response-flow requirements.
A partial pass is reported as partial. A missing positive
capability, unqualified real writer, untested physical join, or
still-unselected response-flow contract prevents full HumanHelp
product acceptance, even when every available test passes.

A future strengthened Gesso checker can produce more of the
required oracles automatically from one source-owned application,
but it cannot silently generate the independent HumanHelp
business intent or prove physical causality from unchecked
report-shaped maps. Part IX owns compositional certification;
Part X owns the proof/refinement correspondence conditions.
Section 08.13 details deterministic structural rejection,
while 08.14–08.15 join deployment evidence and final
acceptance gates. Their work remains open until demonstrated,
not declared complete by this section.
** Structural rejection and production enforcement

The HumanHelp proving application must demonstrate *selective*,
source-derived rejection: an invalid operation, construction,
rendered action, runtime invocation or physical continuation is
rejected at the first boundary that actually has enough trusted
evidence to reject it, while a nearby legitimate HumanHelp action
remains executable. A clean report is not an execution credential.
Passing a test by rejecting every operation is a failure of the
independent positive product contract.

The finished system does not solve this by maintaining a second
example-owned operation registry, a hand-copied route inventory, or
checker fixtures that silently substitute for the production
application. The production Request model, Request Choreo, concrete
HumanHelp routes, actual server realization, Live acquisition
graph and generated browser artifact are the sources from which the
canonical assembly and its checks are derived. Tests intentionally
damage *one* of those real sources or one installed boundary, then
exercise the same checker, renderer or dispatcher used in service.

*** Admission stages and first enforcing boundaries

The selected assurance policy assigns each check to the earliest
boundary at which its actual evidence is available. Static
construction may decide a missing typed operation or route; it
cannot invent the future authenticated principal or the current
Request/assignment prestate. Concrete rendering can inspect the
supported actual Hiccup/HTMX/native form coordinates; it cannot
prove that an arbitrary future script emits no other request.
The trusted route can bind untrusted input to the selected operation
and real actor; the production model and guarded XTDB transaction
decide commit-time business eligibility. A physical adapter can
deny an obsolete target's effect only while it owns the actual
admission/installation boundary.

| Stage | Evidence and responsible rejection |
|-------+------------------------------------|
| Source/semantic construction | Unknown operation, invalid role or impossible plan, undeclared required recovery, or unclosed operation/source dependency |
| Application assembly | Missing required browser plan, trusted executor, route, provider, publication or authoritative acquisition edge; route/operation ambiguity or contradictory server binding |
| Build and deployment admission | Invalid source→generated-plan→artifact receipt/bytes relation, unsupported compiler/runtime profile, stale or mismatched physically served asset, or incompatible application generation |
| Actual structured-render/serialization | Enabled but unprepared action, missing required observation, anonymous collision with a reserved semantic route, conflicting effective request coordinates, or unsupported output outside the selected enforced profile |
| Trusted HTTP/command ingress | Malformed protocol, method/path/subject/operation mismatch, forged identity, incompatible command binding or denied required disclosure |
| Current model and transaction | Changed Membership/Organization/Request eligibility, conflicting primary assignment, failed current guard, qualified duplicate/exclusion result, or invalid domain transition |
| Browser effect and acquisition | Unauthorized collection expansion, ungranted Refresh, invalid progression, retired subscription/target/execution or stale physical rollback |
| Host installation and execution | Invalid or replaced checked handler, unsupported Biff start order, unmediated writer, mismatched runtime capabilities or discovered coverage gap under a mandatory policy |
| Postcommit observation/recovery | Qualify the actual outcome, preserve unknown and repair obligations, never reclassify an already committed Request as precommit rejection |

A checker must not move a failure earlier by assuming facts it has
not observed. Nor may the application defer a statically detectable
missing route until the first user clicks Claim. If an error
appears after a real commit, the responsible boundary blocks
invalid output or later effects and initiates recovery; it cannot
retroactively deny the successful transaction.

*** Controlled defects in one actual production construction

Each defect fixture starts with the ordinary real HumanHelp
application constructor and its source-owned production Request
Choreo/route/Live declarations. The test removes, substitutes or
changes one declared edge *before* the relevant check, or exercises
a specified post-admission physical replacement. The remaining
sources stay real so failure is attributable to the selected
defect. The test records the original and changed source/generation,
first rejecting boundary, typed diagnostic and prohibited effect;
the paired valid case is run through the same boundary.

| Controlled defect | Required result and positive counterpart |
|-------------------+------------------------------------------|
| Unknown =:request/claime= or valid operation with incompatible role | Source or preparation reports unknown/mismatched operation and originating view; genuine Claim remains admitted |
| Missing Claim browser plan or incompatible plan/role | Assembly reports the exact required realization; no fallback anonymous =hx-post=; matching generated Claim plan works |
| Missing route, method mismatch, duplicate ambiguous route or route points to Cancel | Assembly/installed dispatch rejects the actual unresolved or contradictory operation/route/Request binding; valid Claim route reaches the intended server |
| Missing current-time, trusted actor, transaction, seed or qualified read provider | Statically absent capability fails before serving; a dynamically unavailable provider fails at trusted invocation without unauthorized mutation; supplied valid provider works |
| Missing initial board acquisition, fragment/stream route, settlement or denied-disclosure recovery | Admission reports the missing required path; declared incomplete dynamic condition cannot strand a pending operation; intact acquisition and recovery succeed |
| Missing exact browser artifact, stale plan stamp, wrong bytes or forged receipt | Supported build/start/serve check rejects with expected and actual artifact lineage; rebuilding and serving the actual matching bytes succeeds |
| Enabled action missing required =:observed-basis= or canonical operation identity | Real preparation/rendering rejects or presents an explicitly admitted unavailable/alternate control; a qualified enabled Claim is rendered correctly |
| Ordinary HTMX/native form submits to protected Claim route | Actual supported output scanner catches anonymous method/path collision; trusted route separately rejects missing semantic protocol; normal read-only form and real managed Claim remain legal |
| Form owner/submitter overrides or keyword/string duplicated request attributes | Actual effective method/path and ambiguous attributes cannot evade the selected structured check; equivalent nonambiguous canonical form passes |
| OOB/error/deferred/cached rendering bypasses the guard | Serving boundary rejects unsupported managed output or supplies the same actual serialization check; valid deferred or ordinary response under its declared profile is served |
| Forged browser principal, Request retargeting or valid-plan command on wrong lifecycle route | Trusted route ignores client identity as authority and refuses incompatible operation/subject; correct authenticated command reaches public Request core |
| Incompatible C42 reuse or lost C42 result | Current permitted command resolution rejects binding reuse and preserves unknown delivery; exact permitted replay does not reincorporate |
| Unqualified advisory used to adopt remote R or repeated one-use Refresh | Live/acquisition effect admission refuses unauthorized membership/permission use; a separate genuine permitted Refresh succeeds |
| Stale E1/T1 callback after newer T2 or removed target | Final physical effect gate refuses installation/rollback; current T2 and authorized continuation remain intact |
| Correct preflight report but different Ring handler actually served | Startup/host adoption blocks the selected protected deployment claim; canonical installed handler can serve the valid page |
| Omitted/false read-only background writer or unrestricted XTDB capability | Mandatory writer-coverage claim stays open or deployment blocks; separately issued covered writer succeeds within its admitted scope |
| Source removes Reassign from model, Choreo and generated checks | Independent product acceptance fails even though the reduced declared catalog is closed; eligible real Reassign succeeds in the positive fixture |

A defect that changes several facts at once is not an oracle for
which one should have failed first. The test either isolates them
or reports their causal ordering and the evidence available to
each boundary. A failure at an earlier supported gate can make
later gates inapplicable; it does not demonstrate those later
gates would work or reject correctly. The positive counterpart
is necessary to exclude a permanently disabled or
reject-everything application.

*** Physical rendering and both directions of protection

For HumanHelp managed lifecycle routes, the *producer* and
*consumer* protections are complementary. Supported actual
pre-serialization structured rendering cannot emit a live
anonymous action to a protected route, even when its HTML
looks like an ordinary button. The trusted receiving handler
cannot execute such an action even if a malicious client
manufactures it, the served markup was not produced by
HumanHelp, or a later JavaScript sends it. Neither guard is
permission for the other to be absent from the declared
protection profile.

Rendering checks the actual expanded concrete occurrence,
including conditional affordance selection, target identity,
effective HTMX inheritance, native form owner/action/method and
submitter overrides, supported OOB destinations and plan/basis
preparation. A disabled-looking control with a still-active
request route is not a valid disabled control. Missing
observed basis is not silently converted to a guessed Request
revision, wall-clock time, anonymous normal POST or inferred
authorization. The application selects only an expressly
admitted unavailable/alternative state or rejects the render.

The selected Hiccup/serialization mechanism has a finite
language and a physical boundary. An inspector that receives
canonical Hiccup cannot certify pre-serialized HTML,
arbitrary JavaScript-produced requests, future middleware
substitution, deferred work outside its guard, or bytes
served by a different handler. Those paths require a
connected enforcement mechanism, explicit disallowance
under the admitted profile, or an honestly narrower claim.
A passing snapshot render does not establish universal
dynamic-output coverage. Unchecked raw HTML is not cured
by adding a success-shaped value to the assembly report.

If an output check rejects *before* sending a protected
command, the positive oracle establishes that no protected
mutation was submitted. If it rejects a response after a
previously committed Claim, the mutation remains authoritative:
the correct oracle is blocked invalid output, preserved
command/outcome evidence and permitted authoritative repair.
It is wrong to assert Request remains open merely because
a postcommit response-render guard failed.

*** Trusted actor binding and command disposition

For a routed Claim(R17), the trusted boundary uses the
authenticated current principal and the concrete route's
operation/Request selection. The browser-supplied
=:principal=, target-helper string, role name, client ID,
plan stamp, command identity and reported basis are data
to verify, not an authorization token. Route-selected
Claim cannot perform Cancel, reach R18, invoke an
arbitrary Clojure callable or bypass the current
production Request/RequestAssignment/Organization/
Membership/Location guards.

A malformed command, invalid transport and incompatible
binding can be rejected *before domain invocation*. A
well-formed authenticated command may instead fail a
model-defined current eligibility rule after trusted
execution begins. That is a legitimate domain rejection,
not necessarily an application-assembly fault. A
commit followed by lost outcome remains uncertain to
the participant until qualified command-specific
reconciliation; timeout, denied disclosure and missing
historical lookup are not evidence of model rejection.
A duplicate exact binding is resolved under the
selected durable-command protocol; an incompatible reuse
must not obtain another user's historical result.

The test checks separately for absence of prohibited
model invocation, absence of new transaction
incorporation, absence of unauthorized disclosure,
and absence of stale physical installation. These
are different postconditions. A checked route that
refuses Claim before invocation should not be
credited with proving every conceivable concurrent
database writer obeys the same invariant.

*** Runtime installation, source identity and report integrity

Gesso's canonical managed Biff/Aleph path must install
the actual checked Ring handler *before* admitting
protected HTTP requests. The exact
=application-handler-module= object is part of the
native module collection once; its required qualified
module ID is first in the declared Biff start order.
The startup checker rejects a missing/duplicated
module, a forged module carrying the correct ID,
a non-ID component-function start sequence,
a mismatched current assembly or noncallable
Ring handler. The selected Aleph adapter must
serve the resulting handler, not an older Var or
different unwrapped function.

The host admission evidence is invalidated by later
handler/module/route/asset replacement unless the
replacement is admitted and checked under the new
generation. If a server intentionally uses raw Ring
responses, off-process writers or a separate
HTTP entrypoint, the production policy must
enforce or exclude them explicitly rather than
inherit the canonical wrapper's limited guarantee.
A current in-memory report does not prove which
callable the deployed server actually installed.

ApplicationAssembly and checking reports are
derived from the original source objects, verified
identity and current underlying artifact; arbitrary
Clojure maps are not capabilities. A caller must
not gain authority by copying a passing report and
changing =:valid?=, =:errors=, =:analysis= or an
assembly field, swapping an operation registry,
adding a favorable proof badge or using a stale
content-identical replacement provider. Genuine
reconstruction/rechecking is required when the
selected source, host callable, compiler receipt,
actual served asset or admission generation
changes. Even a well-formed checked report is
descriptive of its stated scope and never by
itself permission to perform a protected effect.

A structural preflight can check known supplied
writers and enforcement edges; it cannot discover
every process with direct XTDB access by
enumerating the registered Biff modules. The
assurance report distinguishes declared,
enumerated, physically observed and proven
restricted paths. An unclassified writer remains
an open mandatory condition or blocks
installation under the selected policy. It
cannot be hidden by relabeling a descriptor as
read-only or reporting an uninspected inventory
as empty.

*** Dynamic failure completeness and recoverability

Static admission does not guess future transaction
results or assume every GET, SSE stream and
subscription will succeed. It must nevertheless
establish an allowed continuation or recovery
policy for each dynamic condition that can strand
a managed command or adopted board obligation:
missing/expired observation, authoritative
rejection, submitted-but-unknown transaction,
unavailable disclosure, lost subscription, failed
fragment reread, partial DOM/OOB installation,
obsolete plan or target, exhausted retry budget,
and unavailable trusted provider.

Each continuation identifies its owner, permissible
current authority/read scope, bounded retry or
user action, release of obsolete physical rights,
and what evidence can terminate uncertainty.
An invalid assembly is rejected if it has no
declared legal recovery route for a required
uncertain branch, even when a particular test
happens to succeed. A permitted explicit
degraded path is named and reflected in the
assurance claim; the system must never silently
turn a semantically protected lifecycle command
into anonymous HTMX or turn participant unknown
into rejected.

Recovery and static safety are reported
separately: correctly preventing an unsafe
stale swap is a safety success, while eventual
convergence depends on declared provider
availability, scheduling fairness, retention
and (for explicit Refresh) permitted user
action. Runtime denial may therefore preserve
visible pending/advisory debt rather than
fabricate completion.

*** Structured diagnostics and acceptance

Each rejection supplies stable machine-readable
category, precise proposition, original source
or physical occurrence, application generation
where relevant, operation/route/target subject,
expected versus actual relation where safe,
first responsible enforcement boundary,
and whether the effect was already submitted
or committed. Diagnostics may report unknown
rather than an invented yes/no; errors from
domain guards and from assembly incompatibility
retain distinct types and recovery contracts.

The diagnostic audience determines allowed
detail. Redact authenticated credentials,
full command bodies, private Request content,
unverified tenant identifiers and protected
read/query results. Useful developer-local
explanations may show source paths, selected
operation names, mismatch categories and
safe route templates; they must not leak
cross-Organization information to a browser
or untrusted requestor.

#+begin_example
Positive and adverse — one real production boundary:
  Good Claim(R17): canonical constructor, installed handler,
    enabled bound control, trusted principal, guarded commit,
    authorized readback and browser settlement all succeed.
  Missing Claim plan: same source construction with only
    required plan removed -> preflight rejection, no fallback.
  Paired valid case still succeeds after restoring the plan.
#+end_example

#+begin_example
Adversarial — anonymous request and forged principal:
  A real Hiccup/native form inherits the protected Claim POST,
    but lacks managed operation/protocol metadata.
  Supported final render check rejects its emission.
  Independently a forged external POST supplies :principal Mallory
    and incompatible Claim/R17 wire values.
  Trusted ingress does not execute as Mallory or mutate R18.
#+end_example

#+begin_example
Adversarial — postcommit output failure:
  C42 validly commits Request R17 + primary assignment.
  A later output renderer fails structural enforcement.
  The invalid response is not delivered, but XTDB commit persists.
  Recovery obtains qualified current state and historical
    C42 outcome separately; the server never reports "not committed"
    merely because its HTML response was blocked.
#+end_example

#+begin_example
Adversarial — startup identity and escaped writer:
  The browser receipt and ApplicationAssembly check successfully.
  HumanHelp supplies a noncanonical Biff module/incorrect order,
    or Aleph invokes a different unwrapped Ring handler.
  Service admission refuses the installed-boundary claim.
  A background raw XTDB writer outside the checked module catalog
    leaves global writer closure explicitly unproved.
#+end_example

HumanHelp's structural rejection gate exercises
the production preflight constructor, actual
rendered responses and installed host path
against controlled defects: unknown operation;
missing/mismatched plan, route or server;
missing provider and initial acquisition;
anonymous native form and HTMX action;
forged/mismatched command; stale asset;
handler/module mismatch; unauthorized
advisory/Refresh; retired effect; hidden writer;
and required capability removal. Each case
has a paired usable positive through the
same enforcing boundary, a precise typed
diagnostic and an appropriately scoped
no-prohibited-effect oracle.

A negative fixture that passes only because
the app never starts, no browser control
exists, all requests are rejected, or a
fake checker is used is insufficient. The
complete product still requires the real
HumanHelp Chromium lifecycle and two-client
board/Refresh behavior of 08.12. Section
08.14 joins connected evidence and operational
limits; this section specifies enforcement; independent acceptance must
establish whether the selected build actually passed the tests.
** Connected evidence and operational limits

HumanHelp is useful as evidence for Gesso only when its real
production model, assembled semantic operation, browser command,
installed host, authoritative effects, Live advisory and adopted
presentation can be related without inventing unobserved edges.
The completed application exposes connected evidence for at least
Claim, Create with selective adoption, Reassign with genuine target
selection, and explicit one-use Refresh. It does not construct a
parallel example-owned witness registry that could agree with
itself while the running application uses different sources.

Connected evidence does not mean that one large success map,
identical operation names, a common digest or passing tests
automatically prove causality. Every link states which
source-owned relation, verified construction, qualified physical
observation, authenticated receipt, or still-open premise
supports it. The claim remains no stronger than its weakest
required, unestablished connection.

*** Claim-specific evidence and its ownership

Each end-to-end report identifies its *subject*: exact HumanHelp
source and ApplicationAssembly generation, Request/actor scope,
selected operation and assurance policy, physical runtime and
backend qualification, observation interval, and the independently
required product outcome. An audit view is derived from those
subjects; it is not a credential, an execution grant, or a
surrogate for verifying the present caller and protected effect.

| Link in the chain | Required provenance and boundary |
|-------------------+----------------------------------|
| Production source | Exact public Request/RequestAssignment operation, relevant Organization/Membership dependency declarations, owned transition and contract version |
| Admitted application | Choreo/plan, checked operation/route/acquisition construction, known missing or opaque edges, and application-generation identity |
| Actual served control | Authenticated viewer and permitted scope, concrete rendered command identity, effective action/target and inspected supported HTML form/HTMX transport |
| Browser execution | Generated/served asset identity, C42 user intention, local execution E42, transport attempt H1, target T1 and applicable resource generations |
| Trusted ingress | Actual installed Ring/Reitit handler and trusted principal, selected Request/operation, protocol/binding validation and capability providers |
| Domain incorporation | Guarded Request/assignment transition, qualified XTDB transaction evidence, exact command record where the durable profile promises it, and truthful committed/rejected/unknown outcome |
| Publication and delivery | Source-derived invalidation or transaction-coupled intent, authorized scope, publish attempt, recipient subscription/receipt or a specifically visible evidence gap |
| Acquired authority | Scoped read permission, actual basis and completeness, operation-specific observation and any qualified absence |
| Physical settlement/adoption | Issued install permission, current target/generation, actual swap/continuity completion, adopted membership and fields, and remaining Refresh/command obligations |
| Assurance conclusion | Each established proposition, evidence mechanism, physical/test scope, accepted premises, untested boundaries and current applicability |

This report is a directed, typed chain, not a chronology guessed
from log timestamp order. A browser HTTP 200 cannot authenticate
a model transaction. An XTDB readback at a later basis cannot
by itself identify which command caused its values. A matched
command-record value does not establish that every outside
writer was observed; a returned command outcome does not prove
the browser installed it. A Live publish receipt cannot prove
recipient delivery or adoption. Independent evidence must
actually join across the selected edges.

When a test or diagnostic sees only an in-process callback or
caller-reported observation, the report says so and preserves
the original trust boundary. In particular, a checked Gesso
report/fingerprint is not a transferable proof certificate,
and an observation attached to a copied Request/actor map
does not become authenticated by the map's shape. Claims
involving uninspected external writers, compiler semantics,
hidden data sources or opaque policy functions remain
conditional or open under the selected assurance policy.

Reports for developers and operators retain useful
diagnostic context but redact sessions, private Request
content, credential/command bodies and tenant-scoped
identities unless their audience is specifically authorized.
Correlators and structural fingerprints do not themselves
grant result disclosure. A principal or access-policy change
may invalidate further acquisition even when the historical
command remains incorporated.

*** Connected HumanHelp journeys

Claim establishes a positive route from a real eligible
button through browser-generated C42 and trusted route to
production Request and primary assignment incorporation.
It separately establishes permitted current reread and
a physically installed settled card after provisional
ownership retires. A lost H1 response is not negative
transaction evidence: its participant branch remains
command-outcome unknown until exact authorized historical
correlation, while a fresh Request read may independently
repair visible state.

Create/selective adoption establishes that local creator S
receives its own correlated authoritative result while
already-connected viewer B learns of remote S only as
advisory debt. If B has an earlier remote R pending and
creates its own local T, T may be adopted without R or
R's pending debt being silently consumed. The evidence
records the actual creator-specific transaction and
reread, each viewer's independent session, authorized
advisory scope, and the before/after adopted cohort.
It does not call a broadcast or toast an authoritative
card installation.

Reassign establishes legitimate distinct actor and
target-helper identities, current relevant Membership,
Organization/Location and Request guards, model-defined
ending of the previous primary assignment and creation
of exactly one new primary. It then connects the real
target selector, browser command, trusted route, transaction,
qualified readback and displayed result. An old candidate
who loses eligibility between display and commit must
not be counted as a valid successful Reassign.

Explicit Refresh establishes the one-use action/grant
that permits a scoped remote acquisition, the captured
required advisory obligations, the actual read result,
qualification of the returned progression/scope and
physical installation of the admitted projection. Only
requirements actually covered by that successfully
adopted result are discharged. A newer advisory,
uncovered scope, failed read, partial OOB installation,
obsolete response or lost permission retains its
specific obligation or justified unknown status.
No self-perpetuating successor read or passive SSE
event inherits a fresh grant merely from a previous
Refresh attempt.

#+begin_example
Positive — four connected journeys:
  Helper A clicks rendered Claim(R17) -> browser C42 / E42 / H1.
  Trusted Request model commits guarded Request+assignment.
  Actual authoritative reread and installation settle R17.
  Creator A adds S; viewer B receives advisory but not S's card.
  Manager M selects eligible target H2 and reassigns R17.
  B explicitly Refreshes; only the qualified acquired scope
    installs and only actually covered debt is discharged.
  Each edge retains its distinct source and physical witness.
#+end_example

These histories are independently testable but not one
universal serial execution. Joined claims require actual
identity, scope, predecessor/successor and temporal
relations; four individually plausible snapshots do not
automatically form a contiguous physical history.

*** Safety, uncertainty and progress are distinct claims

The following are safety properties: no double primary
assignment under the specified guarded writer set;
no unauthorized command or scope disclosure; no
anonymous lifecycle route downgrade; no unpermitted
automatic adoption; no retired E42/T1 continuation
overwriting a newer installation; no loss of uncovered
Refresh obligations through a successful-looking HTTP
response. Their evidence can be finite, conditional
inductive, runtime enforcement or bounded observed
physical behavior, but those mechanisms are named
separately.

Progress propositions have different conditions. If
Live transport is available with the declared fairness
and recovery strategy, relevant advisory may eventually
reach an interested active browser. If the authoritative
provider is available, permitted Refresh may acquire
current data. If the user never takes the explicitly
required Refresh action, a stale adopted board is
allowed indefinitely; the UI must still explain the
pending condition and expose the action. A transient
unavailable provider, denied disclosure, expired
command record or permanent network partition does
not falsify a promise whose *premises* explicitly
exclude that situation; it does prohibit claiming
unconditional eventual convergence.

A publication failure after committed Request mutation
does not reverse the mutation. The primary durable
publication profile requires transaction-coupled intent
recorded with the business transition and an
at-least-once worker/recovery protocol with stable
work identity, duplicate-safe delivery, restart,
backoff, retention and a visible escalation policy.
A simpler selected user-Refresh/periodic-reconciliation
profile makes a narrower liveness claim and tests its
actual recovery conditions. An in-memory callback,
successfully registered subscription or best-effort
postcommit push cannot claim the stronger durable
crash-to-publication guarantee.

Similarly a stable C42 identity is not guaranteed
historical exactly-once behavior unless the chosen
backend profile provides qualified atomic
command-record/domain-effect incorporation and
exact-binding replay. Current Request state and C42
historical attribution are different acquisitions.
Transport timeout, missing lookup, expired retention
and unauthorized disclosure remain unknown or
undisclosable where appropriate. A cleanup function
cannot turn that uncertainty into rejection.

*** Resource limits, backpressure and debt accounting

The installed application publishes actual resource
budgets and owners as part of its named deployment
profile rather than implying unbounded queues or
infinitely retryable work. At minimum its limits cover:

| Resource | Required capacity and overload semantics |
|----------+-------------------------------------------|
| In-flight fragment acquisitions | Per logical fragment/request-generation bound; allowed coalescing and obsolete-transport cancellation; no duplicate ungranted remote Refresh |
| Pending successor requirements | Bounded representation retaining scopes, covered/unknown knowledge and joinability of actual progression; incomparable bases cannot be ordered by timestamp or max ID |
| Advisory debt | Per-viewer/scope bounded storage or safe compaction to a coarser "updates/continuity unknown" obligation, never silent forgetting of missed distinct requirements |
| Publication intent and delivery | Queue size, worker ownership, retry/backoff, retention, failed-work escalation and durable handoff where promised |
| Command outcome recovery | Receipt/index retention, context/disclosure restrictions, retry rate/work horizon and honest expired/undeterminable result |
| Browser-owned effects | Bounded live timers, listeners, transport handles, installed optimistic generations, retained continuity snapshots and retired-but-not-yet-cancelled resources |
| Local presentation | Board cohort/page size, number of visible cards, detail/focus/scroll captures, drafts and permitted in-memory history |
| Diagnostic evidence | Bounded, redactable and access-controlled records with useful provenance retained long enough for the selected claim, not unlimited raw browser/transaction logs |

Resource limits are not solely performance goals. An
exhausted acquisition slot must not silently authorize
an extra read; an overflowing advisory queue must not
discard the only evidence of remote change; and evicting
an unresolved command receipt must not invent a known
terminal outcome. Safe coalescing may combine equivalent
obligations or use a qualified coverage join. Where
requirements cannot be safely joined, the runtime retains
a bounded coarse unknown/debt state with a permitted
full-scope repair path and visible explanation. One
queue slot bounds stored work, not the semantic number
of unfulfilled obligations it represents.

Overflow handling identifies its effect on safety,
fairness and progress. Repeated hot scopes cannot
indefinitely starve an unrelated permitted Refresh
or a queued authoritatively correlated local result
under a claimed fair profile. Dropped jobs report
their loss/unknown coverage through the designated
owner. If the selected profile has no durable queue,
the evidence must not pretend pending in-memory work
survives process restart.

#+begin_example
Adversarial — advisory overload:
  Distinct remote R1 and R2 requirements accumulate while
    viewer B is offline; the fine-grained budget fills.
  Coalescing may retain a scope-wide "possibly changed" debt
    and require explicit authorized complete Refresh.
  It may not erase R1, declare B current after R2 delivery,
    or install remote cards without an explicit grant.
#+end_example

*** Resource retirement and ownership transfer

Cleanup first *revokes semantic permission* for the old
execution, request, target, subscription, grant or
continuity slot; it then attempts physical abort,
listener removal, timer clearing, XHR/SSE release
and continuity snapshot disposal. Physical abort is
best effort. An old asynchronous callback that
arrives after cleanup cannot regain rights because
its generation has been retired, even if the browser
or network library cannot cancel it.

Release is idempotent under duplicate completion,
nested removal, aborted transport, unsuccessful
cleanup and application shutdown. Exact owners are
registered, so removing one card's interest does
not accidentally close a shared SSE connection
still serving another authorized subscriber.
Partial cleanup failure is diagnosed and bounded;
a detached DOM node or callback is not silently
treated as harmless if it retains a reachable
protected effect capability.

An uncertain C42 result, pending durable publish
intent or unfulfilled Refresh/advisory debt may
outlive its original physical card/target. Before
disposing the old owner, the runtime transfers
the still-valid semantic obligation to a declared
recovery owner (possibly an authorized server-side
index). That transfer preserves only the minimal
qualified command reference and scope; it does
not resume E42, re-grant a one-use Refresh, preserve
disallowed private content, or override a new
principal's access restrictions. Expired retention
produces an honest recovery limit.

Startup, shutdown, rolling generation replacement,
logout, permission revocation, browser navigation
and disconnect all have declared retirement and
handoff behavior. Cleanup must be testable both
after a normal successful operation and after
each partial failure path. A clean empty pending
resource map is insufficient evidence of no
leaked native listener or wrong-installed
physical target; the test checks the actual
supported shell/host resource boundary.

#+begin_example
Adversarial — late physical completion:
  E1 uses T1 and an in-flight H1; then a newer
    authoritative card installs into T2.
  Semantic retirement revokes E1/T1 installation rights.
  H1's abort fails and callback eventually completes.
  The runtime drops E1's now-unauthorized effect; it
    cannot restore T1, change T2 or clear unrelated debt.
  If C42 remains unknown, the recovery owner retains
    its qualified historical inquiry independently.
#+end_example

*** Connected fault evidence and failure attribution

The application exercises at least these ordered
negative histories against its actual boundaries:

| History | Safe conclusion and observation |
|---------+---------------------------------|
| Invalid pre-submit operation | No protected command submitted; construction/route diagnostic names the first real rejection boundary |
| Submitted C42, lost HTTP result | Historical outcome unknown to browser; no fabricated rollback or new C43 replay; authorized command-specific recovery remains |
| Commit, then response-render failure | Request/assignment truth persists; invalid output rejected; permitted reread and historical result are distinct |
| Commit, then publication crash | Durable intent replays under the selected primary profile or an explicitly weaker alternate recovery path is exercised; no false "delivered" claim |
| Advisory received but no permission to adopt | User sees pending indicator; no unauthorized remote collection acquisition/installation |
| Refresh returns partial or stale coverage | Only actually installed, qualified covered obligations discharge; newer/uncovered debt remains |
| Reassign with policy change in flight | Current guard prevents obsolete target incorporation; no partial primary-assignment transition |
| Installed T2, late E1 rollback | No stale physical restoration even if transport cancellation fails |
| Restart with old A page and new B | Incompatible effects retire or request qualified reload; old C42 may be reconciled independently under current authorization |
| Unenumerated raw XTDB writer | Physical-writer coverage remains unknown/open or fails selected admission; declared catalog cannot conceal it |

The report distinguishes "expected rejection occurred",
"no forbidden effect was observed through the
qualified mechanism", "qualified absence established",
and "not observed or still unknown". Lack of a log
line, a passing timeout assertion or a successful
build receipt is not a proof of non-execution.
A bad browser response cannot undo a previously
successful transaction. Fault injection exposes
the precise point before submission, after
submission, after commit, before publication,
during acquisition or during physical install;
it does not mock away the real effect and then
claim physical correspondence.

*** Retiring obsolete migration state and classifying defects

The final HumanHelp proving surface uses production
=net.humanhelp.site.model.*= semantics and the
single admitted example construction. It has no
parallel demo Request store, competing example
authorization state machine, alternate "visible
revision" treated as XTDB authority, duplicate
route/operation catalog, anonymous lifecycle
fallback, stale CSS producer, or compatibility
code that silently changes the supported
Choreo/Biff/HTMX contract. Legitimate
presentation-local option/draft state remains;
it is not a competing source of Request truth.

Removing obsolete files, tests and resources
happens only after the replacement path and
required positives are established. Repository
history and a short reason/replacement record
make the removal auditable without making a
temporary cleanup checklist part of the
timeless product semantics.

When HumanHelp testing discovers a problem,
the evidence identifies its ownership:
a missing reusable representation/closure
property is a *generic Gesso gap*; wrong
example routes, assets, or application
composition are *HumanHelp integration
defects*; wrong lifecycle/Organization
policy is a *production HumanHelp model
defect*; changed XTDB, HTMX, Biff,
browser or network behavior is an
*external/runtime premise failure* requiring
requalification. A generic framework rule
is introduced only when the discovered
need is reusable, not merely because the
example exposed a bug.

Completion evidence is generation- and
profile-specific. The HumanHelp app's
positive behaviors, negative enforcement,
resource bounds, durable or weaker recovery
profile, live publication, physical writer
coverage and open premises are reported
separately. Part VIII §08.15 specifies
their joint completion conditions. Parts IX
and X own the broader compositional proof
and implementation-refinement claims; their
open premises cannot be silently discharged
by a connected HumanHelp trace.
** Completion gates

HumanHelp is the proving application for the finished Gesso design,
not a permanently privileged demonstration or a convenient subset
of the currently working UI. Completion requires a coherent
installed production-backed application and independent evidence
that its promised user capabilities work under the selected,
qualified substrate. The gates are normative acceptance
obligations; neither their presence in this document nor a green
source-derived assembly means that the current implementation
has already met them.

An acceptance claim names its exact application source and
admitted generation, code/build/artifact identity, deployed
handler and browser assets, authentication and disclosure
profile, relevant XTDB/Biff/HTMX/CLJS versions and configuration,
tested actor/Request/Organization scope, operational
assumptions, known opaque boundaries, and observed evidence.
It is invalidated or narrowed when any required binding,
source, runtime, writer coverage or provider contract changes
without applicable requalification. A partial result is
reported as partial, with the independent failed, missing,
conditional or untested gates still visible.

*** Non-vacuous gate set and independent acceptance

The fourteen gates below are distinct obligations, not
fourteen names for a single passing source check.
Each has at least one eligible positive and its applicable
negative/fault case; completed checks must exercise the
*real* enforcing or user-facing boundary rather than an
uninstalled fixture or a copied result.

| Gate | Acceptance obligation |
|------+-----------------------|
| 1. Production model authority | Request creation and lifecycle mutations use public production Request and related User, Membership, Organization/Location semantics; current guarded Request/RequestAssignment transactions and actor/target policy produce the model-defined outcomes, including actual duplicate and unknown-command handling. |
| 2. One admitted application source | Choreo, role-local plans, routes, server operations, trusted providers, Live/acquisition, concrete rendering and checking consume one source-derived ApplicationAssembly. Tests inspect that construction; they do not manufacture a second implementation whose internal consistency hides production drift. |
| 3. Installed host and writer adoption | The actual serving Biff/Aleph handler and protected mutation paths use the admitted construction and declared capabilities; the selected policy qualifies relevant outside writers and exposes unknown writer coverage rather than assuming registration is exhaustive. |
| 4. Current browser and asset correspondence | Generated plans, build manifest/receipt, actual served JavaScript and dependent assets, client bootstrap and deployment generation agree under the selected qualification. Incompatible, stale or forged bindings fail before they can authorize protected effects. |
| 5. Claim end to end | A genuine rendered enabled Claim control generates its own command in the actual browser, reaches the trusted route, commits the guarded Request/primary assignment and settles physically; fresh authorized read and reload confirm persisted truth. |
| 6. All lifecycle capabilities | Claim, Unclaim, Mark on the way, Complete, Cancel and Reassign each have an independently eligible browser-originated success; Reassign uses real authorized target selection, and each has meaningful current-policy denial, concurrency and applicable recovery evidence. |
| 7. Rich-board product behavior | Real Create, creator-local visibility, adopted-cohort search and sort, both priority toggles, terminal options, details, accessible status, focus/scroll continuity and the independently selected response interaction behave as the declared HumanHelp product contract requires. |
| 8. Selective multi-client adoption | Distinct authenticated users/contexts demonstrate that remote creation and remote lifecycle changes, including already-visible cards, remain advisory until explicit permitted Refresh or a separately admitted local-result/recovery acquisition; local incorporation cannot adopt unrelated remote members or erase their debt. |
| 9. Explicit Refresh correctness | A user action creates a bounded scoped one-use read/adoption grant; actual authoritative observation and installed coverage justify precisely the discharged requirements, with protected handling of later advisories, stale responses, partial swaps and retry. |
| 10. Fault and recovery behavior | Lost/unknown command outcomes, already-incorporated replay, failed acquisition/installation, postcommit publication crash, lost SSE continuity, deployment changes and retired callbacks take the declared safe and usable recovery paths, with truthful uncertainty and bounded resource ownership. |
| 11. Structural and runtime enforcement | Controlled malformed operation, assembly, plan, route, provider, render, native-form/HTMX action, protocol, asset, handler, and physical-effect cases reject at their first real applicable boundaries; paired valid production cases remain usable. |
| 12. Semantic and assurance evidence | Application/business invariants, finite/conditional proof scopes, initial states, complete declared operations, independent required capability coverage, source-to-issued-execution bindings, interference and opaque premises are described accurately; unqualified physical writers and missing refinements are not certified by a generated report. |
| 13. Qualified physical substrate | Selected Biff lifecycle, HTMX/SSE browser adapter, CLJS/compiler/artifact supply, XTDB guards/absence/progression, authentication, publication/recovery and actual resource behavior satisfy the assumptions needed for each claimed gate, or the claim remains explicitly conditional/open. |
| 14. Independent real-browser acceptance | Chromium/Playwright uses the installed service and generated runtime with genuine controls, sessions and requests, current model readback after reload, meaningful two-client scenarios, deterministic backend races and narrow fault expectations; deleting a required capability or suppressing unexpected failures makes this gate fail. |

R4's eleven original completion gates are preserved in
this more explicit partition: semantic-route exclusion,
runtime adoption, artifact currentness, real Claim, the
full lifecycle, rich board, multi-client behavior,
production-constructor tests, malformed fixtures,
Chromium tests and supported Biff/Gesso substrate.
Extra gates make recovery, explicit Refresh,
source/physical proof and dependency qualification
visible rather than assuming they follow from a
green browser test. The original gates do not
become optional simply because they now have
different numbering and clearer ownership.

*** Product contract decisions, profiles and exclusions

The required user capabilities are independent of
the current implementation's registered operation
list. Removing Reassign from Request Choreo and
from the derived finite machine does not make
the reduced application acceptable if HumanHelp
still promises Reassign. Permanently disabling
all Claim actions is likewise not an acceptable
way to satisfy negative tests. A particular
Request may legitimately deny a command under
current model policy while another eligible
fixture satisfies the positive capability.

The selected remote-lifecycle adoption decision
at [[#decision-humanhelp-remote-lifecycle-adoption]]
requires explicit Refresh for ordinary remote
creation *and* lifecycle changes, including a
Request that was previously visible. That
choice is normative. A locally correlated
settlement or permitted affected-Request
recovery read has its own narrower grant;
neither silently grants remote collection
adoption. Loss of authenticated authority is
a separate safety transition: protected
projection and future trusted access are
revoked according to the supported client
contract, rather than delayed to honor a
user's Refresh preference.

The independent response-flow requirement
at [[#decision-humanhelp-response-flow]]
must be selected by HumanHelp product authority,
with actor eligibility, intent, source/model
owner, input, disclosure, observable success,
persistence/external effects and adverse
recovery behavior. A working Claim is not
automatically proof of the intended response
interaction. If HumanHelp expressly chooses
"respond by claiming", its own versioned
product contract and real user acceptance
must establish that this fulfills the complete
promise; otherwise the response-flow gate
remains open. No new messaging model,
provider or contact-disclosure policy is
invented solely to close a checklist.

The primary strong publication/recovery
profile at 08.08 requires a qualified
transaction-coupled publication intent and
its durable at-least-once recovery worker.
A selected weaker periodic-reconciliation
or user-Refresh profile has different
liveness and crash guarantees and must be
accepted as an explicit product/deployment
choice with its own tested behavior and
disclosed limitations. It cannot silently
borrow the primary profile's durable
delivery or timely notification claim.
Exactly the same discipline applies to
command history retention, backend writer
coverage, Live continuity, application
generation pinning and external effects.

An unsupported extension may be excluded
only by a precise declared boundary that
does not undercut an independent required
HumanHelp capability. For example, a
profile excluding arbitrary JavaScript
requests still protects actual managed
HTML and trusted lifecycle ingress;
the exclusion does not justify bypassing
the real Claim button or its server route.
Unknown or unsupported is not "passed".

*** Whole-path safety, evidence and causality

A completed HumanHelp Claim has a real
actor and Request, source-owned semantic
operation and browser plan, eligible
rendered affordance, actual compatible
served runtime, browser-generated command,
route-selected trusted executor, qualified
guarded transaction, truthful outcome,
scoped current read and physically
settled adopted result. The evidence chain
identifies each of these as an actual
binding, observed effect or explicitly
accepted premise. A successful UI
animation alone cannot establish
authoritative mutation.

Create with selective adoption, a
legitimate target-helper Reassign and
the one-use Refresh journey likewise
need connected positive outcomes.
Multiple plausible snapshots do not
prove one adjacent execution history;
the report must connect command,
transaction, actor, read and physical
installation with adequate correlation
and trusted provenance. A matching
model abstraction does not establish
that every physical XTDB writer refines
it. An exactly matching browser
manifest cannot prove arbitrary
compiled JavaScript correct.

A meaningful negative acceptance
states whether the forbidden request
was never emitted, denied at trusted
ingress, rejected by current model
policy, excluded atomically by XTDB,
or prevented from physically
installing. These are distinct
claims. A valid commit followed by
failed HTML/OOB delivery remains
committed and requires authorized
recovery; postcommit output failure
cannot be credited as a precommit
domain rejection. A lost command
response may leave the historical
outcome unknown even if the current
Request state is freshly observed.

The desired final invariant includes
both safety and qualified progress.
A retired callback cannot reinstall
obsolete DOM or consume one-use
Refresh permission. Unknown C42
must have its declared bounded
recovery/disclosure path; if the
evidence horizon expires, honest
indeterminacy is permitted. An
already-connected viewer whose
remote board has changed may
remain on older adopted content
indefinitely when the chosen
policy requires an explicit
Refresh the user never performs.
The pending advisory, safe action
and scope of its coverage remain
visible as the user-facing
progress contract; automatic
remote adoption is not introduced
to manufacture convergence.

*** HumanHelp evidence and release decisions

For each gate the independent acceptance
record gives a state such as satisfied
under a named profile, conditional on
enumerated premises, open/untested or
failed; it does not collapse these
into one green "complete" label.
It records the source, code/asset
and host identity, test suite and
actual execution results, adversarial
coverage, responsible owner,
assumptions and expiration or
requalification triggers.
A passing test *definition* is
not proof it was executed, and a
caller-reported observation is not
authenticated by a report digest.

The final installed HumanHelp application
must have real independently authenticated
multi-client browser contexts, matching
source-to-host and source-to-asset
evidence, genuine production model
transactions, actual target/adoption
observations and fault outcomes at
their claimed boundaries. The real
host's ability to serve unrelated
ordinary routes does not excuse
missing managed-operation enforcement.
All proposed positive and adverse
capabilities must be tested with the
actual qualified backend/adapter when
the gate requires physical evidence.
The suite must not ignore unexpected
console errors, failed HTTP requests,
domain exceptions or missing assets
by an overbroad diagnostic waiver.

No earlier or later proof-certificate
claim is created merely by satisfying
these HumanHelp product gates.
Parts IX and X own compositional
certification and stronger
implementation correspondence;
Parts XI and XII own release and
roadmap coherence. HumanHelp's
function is to exercise those
reusable Gesso interfaces and
surface counterexamples, not to
introduce HumanHelp-specific
semantics into the proof kernel.
The source-derived assembly may
be called closed for its admitted
scope while wider writer coverage,
physical refinement or independent
business correctness remain open.
Such a result is useful but is
not full HumanHelp completion.

#+begin_example
Positive — eligible joined acceptance:
  Two distinct authenticated HumanHelp clients start
    with a qualified production Request cohort.
  A's real Claim reaches guarded Request/assignment commit;
    a fresh reload confirms actual model truth.
  A creates S, and B receives an authorized advisory
    without automatically adopting S.
  Manager M reassigns R17 to an eligible target helper,
    with exactly one active primary after commit.
  B explicitly Refreshes and installs the scoped authority;
    only covered advisory requirements are discharged.
  Independently, every required lifecycle and selected
    response-flow capability passes its positive case.
  The installed source, asset, host, model and physical
    evidence support each claim under the named profile.
#+end_example

#+begin_example
Adversarial — green reduced application is incomplete:
  Remove Reassign and its matching plan from the source.
  All remaining declared structural and finite checks pass.
  Independent HumanHelp capability acceptance fails:
    a promised eligible Reassign is unavailable.
  A copied assurance report cannot change that result.
#+end_example

#+begin_example
Adversarial — partial success and unqualified recovery:
  Genuine Claim commits with a correct RequestAssignment.
  Response delivery fails; C42 history is still unknown
    to the browser, although current Request truth can be read.
  Publication intent is only an in-memory callback.
  The application may report committed Request truth and
    bounded best-effort Live, but not durable crash recovery.
  If response flow is unselected, full product acceptance
    remains open independently of Claim's success.
#+end_example

** HumanHelp proving-application invariant

#+begin_quote
The finished HumanHelp proving application consumes the
authoritative =net.humanhelp.site.model.*= public production
semantics for User, Membership, Organization, Request and
RequestAssignment. One canonical, source-owned
ApplicationAssembly binds Request Choreo, its actual
browser plans/assets, concrete trusted routes and server
operations, required capabilities, Live/acquisition and
rendered affordances to the installed Biff/Aleph
application generation. It does not maintain a competing
example Request store, business-rule machine, revision
frontier or operation registry.

Every enabled lifecycle action retains its exact
source-owned semantic identity and is executable only
through an admitted generated browser and trusted
production model boundary. Missing optimism, observation,
route, plan or authorized recovery never silently
degrades to an anonymous lifecycle POST. Actual Claim,
Unclaim, Mark on the way, Complete, Cancel and Reassign
are available in independently eligible cases and
remain subject to current authenticated actor/target,
Organization/Membership, Request state and guarded
Request/RequestAssignment transaction semantics.
Historical incorporation, authoritative rejection,
uncertain delivery and currently displayed Request
truth are separate propositions.

One user's correlated confirmed Create or lifecycle
result may promptly update only the permitted local
Request/card and membership scope. Remote creation and
remote lifecycle changes, including those to an
already-visible Request, remain advisory until a
separate explicitly permitted Refresh or affected-
Request recovery acquisition. Search, sort, terminal
options, drafts, response interaction, details and
continuity operate on justified adopted content
without inventing authoritative collection membership.
A one-use Refresh establishes the actual scoped
observation, installation and coverage needed to
discharge its corresponding debt; a stale response,
failed swap, unrelated local result or reconnect
cannot erase uncovered or later obligations.

Each protected execution, target, transport,
subscription, grant and recovery owner has bounded
resources and current physical effect rights.
Retirement prevents obsolete callbacks from
installing or rolling back newer justified state.
Actual model commits are not undone by failed
notification or rendering, and unknown outcomes
and disconnected interest gaps follow their
declared qualified recovery rules.

Independent HumanHelp product intent and real
multi-client Chromium/browser, public model,
XTDB/host, negative-boundary and physical
observation evidence establish only their
properly scoped conclusions. Formal finite
checks, conditional abstract proofs, source
admission, operational qualification and
deployed correspondence never impersonate
one another. Full acceptance requires every
promised capability—including the separately
selected and tested response-flow experience—
and the applicable safety, recovery, evidence
and substrate gates to be satisfied for the
identified application and runtime profile.
#+end_quote

This is the Part VIII *target-system invariant*,
not an assertion that current HumanHelp or
Gesso source, existing test definitions or an
R5.1 editorial review has already certified
the physical application. Further whole-Part
VIII and whole-plan reconciliation may sharpen
cross-part terminology, assumptions and
proof obligations without changing the
independent product acceptance principle.
* Part IX — Compositional certification
:PROPERTIES:
:CUSTOM_ID: part-09-compositional-certification
:PART_REVISION: 09-20261108
:END:

This part specifies how Gesso checks, composes, and preserves assurance about the
semantic artifacts and applications defined in Parts I–VIII. It makes the
certification boundary concrete: which judgments are checked, what evidence can
establish them, how dependencies are derived, and what remains conditional on
runtime enforcement or an explicitly accepted contract.

The specification describes the intended system from its foundations. It does
not assert that every judgment or correspondence mechanism is implemented. A
supported certification profile has an executable contract and conformance suite;
an unsupported judgment cannot be made available by giving it a reassuring name.
Operational admission, compositional certification, external formal assurance,
and multi-node deployment retain their separate scopes.

A certification profile names the exact propositions it promises, its source
and implementation subjects, authorized assumption classes, concrete admission
stage, required evidence and observable rejection behavior. A lower profile
can remain useful when a stronger judgment is unavailable; it is not an
implicit substitute for a requested stronger profile. Full application
assurance additionally needs the independent product, physical writer,
authenticated execution and deployment obligations owned by later parts.
A checked abstract theorem about an issued plan never authorizes a database
commit or proves the current browser has installed that plan.

Examples use ordinary data notation. Unless explicitly described as executable
source for a named language, their purpose is to expose a contract. Writing a
certificate-shaped map, matching a fingerprint, or displaying an accepted report
does not cross an admission boundary.

** Governing compositional contract
:PROPERTIES:
:CUSTOM_ID: req-compositional-certification
:END:

A downstream claim may rely only on propositions actually established by its
checked dependencies and on assumptions explicitly admitted by its selected
policy. Every premise retains its subject, scope, applicability, and evidence
class. Neither a namespace's reputation nor an upstream artifact's general
“verified” label supplies a missing proposition.

In particular, the downstream consumer must identify the *specific*
required proposition, the upstream exported guarantee, its type and subject,
and any still-open premise. A matching proof object is insufficient when its
schema, rule source, declared operation catalog, application generation,
actor/subject binding, executable lowering or selected runtime contract has
changed. Exact source identity is a change detector; compatible evolution
must have its own checked relation and cannot be assumed from equal names.

Judgment results distinguish rejected construction, an accepted unconditional
judgment within a stated formal model, a checked conditional derivation, a
finite bounded result, a trusted/opaque assertion, and a runtime-observed
fact. A passed conditional abstract checker never becomes an unconditional
proof merely because all required source files were present. A composed
judgment inherits the applicable open premises and trust of its required
dependencies; it does not average them into a stronger green status.

Certification concerns a claim about a subject. It is not a universal property
of a namespace, function, application, or certificate object. A rule can be well
typed while its business meaning is wrong. A choreography can have a checked
projection while its server realization violates the model contract. A finite
model can preserve an invariant while an omitted physical writer breaks it.

The certified construction path must make these distinctions inspectable and
make unsupported substitutions fail before the protected downstream construction
or effect. It must also remain useful: declarations and public model contracts
are authored once, and Gesso derives the routine identities, obligations,
dependency edges, proof candidates, and diagnostics.

The checked construction path must begin from the real source-owned
declarations and the selected application/host graph, not an auditor's
second hand-maintained list of "approved" operations. Every exported
judgment has a specified coverage obligation over its relevant language:
terms, branches, required operations, relationships, message contracts,
effects, initial states and declared termination/recovery cases as needed.
A checker may establish closure for its *inspected* subset; it cannot infer
that arbitrary Clojure bodies, raw XTDB capabilities or external processes
contain no uninspected business-policy writer.

Source completeness and intended product meaning are separate obligations.
An internally consistent machine that has removed HumanHelp Reassign may
pass the remaining derivations while failing the independent product
capability oracle. An omitted rule, dependency or protected writer cannot
be excused by a proof DAG that correctly checks every submitted node.
The scope of a failed or unknown coverage check must remain visible in
both the certification decision and the next downstream diagnostic.

*** Full-language applications remain first-class

Ordinary Clojure and ClojureScript remain available under
[[#req-full-language-construction]]. A closed proof language is a tractable
reasoning fragment, not a replacement application language. Arbitrary algorithms,
libraries, recursion, effects, and opaque policy functions can participate through
declared contracts on the same managed construction path.

An opaque component identifies its inputs, results, effects, relevant state
and authority dependencies, implementation binding, and the assertions on which
dependent claims rely. Purity, determinism, termination, or bounded resource use
are required only when the claimed property needs them. A callback's type or
name cannot establish those properties.

The framework proves supported surrounding properties even when one component is
opaque. For example, command identity preservation, required result variants,
unchanged frame fields, and retired-effect exclusion need not all depend on the
truth of an Organization policy predicate. A conclusion that does depend on that
predicate's implementation remains explicitly conditional on its contract.

Unsupported proof syntax is rejected by that proof profile. It is not silently
executed as host code, silently replaced by an assumption, or used to downgrade
a requested strong build. The author may deliberately bind a supported opaque
contract or select another profile; the resulting claim and accepted premises
must be visible.

A policy predicate that decides permission, disclosure, ownership, lifecycle
transition or command incorporation must be accounted for in the semantic
subject, through a checked dependency, a runtime-enforced condition or a
named opaque contract. If Gesso discovers an unmodeled decision in the
implementation subset it actually inspects, it reports a semantic-policy
escape with the affected proposition and repair choices. Silence while
examining only a structured rule AST is not evidence that hidden policies
do not exist in an uninspected Clojure body. Human-facing policy rationale
and independent tests can challenge whether the *right* rule was declared;
neither automatically becomes a theorem in the proof kernel.

Opaque contracts remain useful at the edge of a narrower theorem: Gesso may
still establish command identity, result-variant coverage or frame safety
that do not depend on the opaque implementation. Claims that *do* depend
on the predicate's truth, purity, termination, current actor or database
consistency inherit its specified proof or trust premise. The requested
assurance profile determines whether that open premise is permissible.

*** Three semantic responsibilities

| Responsibility | Contract |
|----------------+----------|
| Executable semantic core | Defines and executes admitted application transitions and abstract effects from current state and input/events. |
| Proof kernel | Checks derivations in a small, closed inference language under explicit premises. It creates no runtime fact or transaction authority. |
| Dedicated semantic checker | Establishes a specified judgment such as rule typing, dependency closure, projection admissibility, or exact finite exploration under its own stated checking contract. |

These responsibilities support one *canonical semantic vocabulary*
but expose three different acceptance paths. The executable core interprets
admitted transitions and effects, with runtime enforcement for current
principal, transaction and physical resource rights. The proof kernel
checks closed derivations over named propositions and premises; a derivation
supplied by the compiler does not become true because the compiler generated
it. A dedicated checker can establish a well-defined alternative judgment
without pretending it was checked by the proof kernel. Each result records
which checker/source version and trusted mathematical or interpreter
assumptions it depends on. Testing the kernel against itself is not an
independent soundness oracle.

#+begin_example
One source-owned HumanHelp Claim:
  Request model declares current actor, Request, assignment and
    Organization/Membership dependency contracts.
  Gesso derives a guarded operation, Choreo projection and the
    applicable proposition/coverage obligations.
  A small proof checker may establish a conditional abstract
    invariant for the declared transition subject.
  A concrete XTDB/host boundary separately checks the current
    guarded write and independently permitted disclosure.
  Browser installation establishes its own target/generation effect.
  A certificate-shaped map cannot substitute for any of those steps.
#+end_example

These responsibilities can share canonical terms and versioned primitive
semantics. They must not develop competing meanings for the same construct.
Sharing code does not prove correctness, however, and it is not independence
when a test oracle simply invokes the checker being tested.

The canonical semantic definitions are executable specifications: accepted term
schemas, interpretation, judgment inputs and outputs, side conditions, and
negative cases. They may be implemented in focused namespaces such as
=gesso.assurance.rule*= and =gesso.assurance.proof.*= and the Choreo semantic
modules. A logical =gesso.semantic= surface, if exposed, organizes those contracts;
it must not create a parallel interpreter or require a wholesale namespace move.

*** Certified admission, composition, and failure behavior

Certified construction is a checked *boundary*, not a shape convention.
After a stage requires an admitted semantic interface, its supported public
consumer must not accept an unexamined map with copied =:verified?=,
=:proof-status= or subject digest as a replacement. Appropriate
implementations include private issued handles, checked constructors and
freshly validated certificate references; the design does not require
nominalizing every ordinary Clojure value. Ordinary cooperating use must
not accidentally cross a required certification gate.

The construction sequence is conceptually raw declaration, normalization,
elaboration, complete obligation generation, appropriate checking,
qualified certificate/admission, downstream composition and installed
realization. Not every profile requires a proof-kernel certificate, but
every claimed stage must have its own actual checked admission. A failing
required obligation yields no value of that *certified* artifact class;
an intentionally partial/conditional diagnostic is a different
artifact whose status cannot masquerade as fully admitted.
The first boundary with enough evidence reports an exact typed failure
and the downstream artifacts not issued.

A dependency graph may have recursive executable behavior, but its
justification relation cannot use a cycle of certificates that establish
each other's premises. A recursive theorem needs a specifically checked
inductive, guarded or fixed-point rule. A certificate's exported semantic
interface contains only the guarantees permitted for downstream use,
together with its assumptions, evidence class and applicability scope.
It is not permission to inspect arbitrary private implementation data
and silently promote it to a proposition.

Proof sidecars, checked reports and trace diagnostics are allowed to decide
*build-time admission*. Once the executable meaning has been admitted,
optional proof data cannot mutate its actual transition relation or grant
new runtime authority. Source/plan identity accompanies the issued artifact,
but that identity alone is not proof of matching Clojure, XTDB, browser
