   established derivation steps;
   forward/circular references
   and fabricated prior-step
   conclusion are rejected.
7. The complete original source
   and normalized formula denote
   the same supported proposition;
   a dropped premise, altered
   atom or forged typed context
   cannot inherit the proof.
8. A finite independent truth
   valuation matches a supported
   source step; truncation or
   over-budget enumeration is
   incomplete, not proof of
   all valuations.
9. Formal S0/S1 applies to every
   supported rule/formula shape
   under its premises; one
   checked instance or sample
   catalog is not promoted
   to universal soundness.
10. The source-level Clojure
    checker accepts an admitted
    derivation under its exact
    grammar; a deliberately
    faulty parser or
    normalizer admits the
    wrong original subject
    and fails S2.
11. The typed-atom bridge
    agrees over its qualified
    source-binding domain;
    an opaque Membership
    or Organization-policy
    atom is not marked
    universally true from
    finite examples.
12. The trusted issuer
    rechecks current
    original-source
    obligations and the
    genuine proof;
    a copied successful
    report or stale
    assembly/certificate
    cannot mint a new
    current proof.
13. An external proof
    artifact with exact
    statement, axioms,
    backend and checker
    is reverified in
    the declared
    admissible scope;
    changed axioms,
    malformed proof,
    unsupported syntax
    or exit-code-only
    success cannot
    create the claim.
14. A valid abstract
    Claim proof may
    coexist with an
    independently
    qualified physical
    implementation
    witness; an
    unguarded actual
    XTDB writer is
    not made safe
    by the kernel
    theorem.
15. Retired browser
    owner/resource
    cannot mutate
    a reused target;
    proof-term
    reuse or matching
    artifact ID
    is not
    effect-time
    permission.
16. Genuinely eligible
    HumanHelp Claim
    and the other
    independently required
    lifecycle/product
    positives remain
    executable; a
    reject-all source
    machine is not
    accepted as a
    completed product.

Each case names the original source,
selected proof checker and
quantified domain, exact
positive control and mutant,
first rejecting or enforcing
boundary, actual evidence
class, remaining premises
and independently observed
effect where physical
correctness is claimed.
A theorem that is
still open or a
tool run that was
not performed
must be reported as such.

**** Order later formal targets by the trust gap they eliminate

After the propositional theorem and its concrete
checker-binding work, expand only where a
specific original-source judgment and transfer
edge can be defined. Appropriate later
subjects include:

- typed-rule evaluation and semantic
  preservation of proposition
  normalization/atom meaning;
- guarded-transition consequence
  and simultaneous assignment/
  presence-aware frame rules;
- source-complete conditional
  induction and exact certificate
  premise substitution;
- role-local knowledge/provenance
  and protected authority
  non-escalation;
- conservative progression/
  observation algebra and
  requirement discharge;
- global-to-local Choreo
  projection and portable
  executable-plan lowering;
- browser adapter/resource
  refinement and selected
  physically enforced
  authorization/XTDB
  transitions.

Theorem selection is driven by
the original operation language,
the size of the remaining
trusted base, independent
counteroracles and real
correspondence needs.
A formal theorem for one
closed calculus cannot
automatically cover arbitrary
host-language conditionals
or all multi-node schedules.
The aspiration is high
assurance of the original
source and deployed
application, without
forcing developers to
author formal syntax or
pretending the full
general-purpose Clojure
runtime has been proved.
*** Finite exploration and abstraction

Finite exploration can expose a genuine semantic counterexample, establish a
property *exactly for one complete finite model*, or supply a bounded
conformance check of an implementation. These are three different evidence
classes. To transfer a finite-model theorem beyond its enumerated domain, Gesso
must provide a separately justified abstraction/refinement relation from the
original admitted source to that model, and a further implementation relation
for the actual production execution if the claim concerns XTDB, transport or
the browser. A finite test does not become an unbounded proof because the
software is deterministic or its sampled observations match.

The finite subject is derived from the canonical Gesso model, Choreo or
browser-adapter semantics admitted under Parts I–IX. It retains exact
source-generation, operation/initialization and invariant obligations,
policy choices, source-derived reader/guard/frame semantics and open premises.
Developers should not have to construct a second handwritten formal app with
rules that merely resemble the runtime. An intentionally simplified
independent test model may be useful, but its results are explicitly
test-relative until the original-source correspondence is justified.

**** Exact finite claims: closure, totality and vacuity

An exact-finite result records the following as the *complete, closed
model under examination*:

| Required element | Exact claim boundary |
|------------------+----------------------|
| Initial states | Original admitted initial-condition/initializer relation, all selected starting states and their eligibility/inhabitation checks |
| State and input domains | Each field's type, absence/present-nil interpretation, enum values and representative or exhaustive status, including identity and collection bounds |
| Operations | Independently source-derived complete original operation IDs, guards, typed inputs, simultaneous writes, frames, outcome/failure/unknown transitions and environmental steps |
| Transition semantics | Admitted enabled steps and successor relation, stuttering, scheduling, terminal/deadlock treatment and whether rejected operations are transitions or errors |
| Property | Exact invariant, deadlock-freedom, eventuality or trace obligation, its quantifiers, scope and any fairness or environmental premises |
| Exploration | Reachable-state/edge coverage, generated-vs-pruned states, cutoff, visited-state equivalence, trace/history handling, bounds and result kind |
| Evidence | Checker/translator version, canonical input, actual outcome/counterexample, original source location, independent oracle and open abstraction/production bridges |

An exhaustive result requires the whole reachable graph of *that* finite
model under its declared transition relation, not merely all states up to a
search depth or all choices returned by an unverified event generator.
A BFS/DFS exploration may use state deduplication only when its equality
or quotient is sound for the specific state/trace property. In particular,
merging distinct histories because their current map happens to match
can discard command-history, fairness, previous assignment or in-flight
physical callback distinctions relevant to the theorem.

A depth limit, state cap, edge cap, missing choice, unexpected exception,
unsupported operation, unavailable dependency or timeout makes the selected
exhaustiveness claim *incomplete*. It does not become a proof of absence of
counterexamples. An actual reproduced counterexample to an adequately
specified finite model can still be reported even if exploration did not
finish; it must carry the actual trace and scope, not a fabricated
"complete" status. A potential deadlock is distinguished from a declared
terminal state, a blocked environmental step and a liveness violation.
An empty initialization set makes a universal invariant trivially true;
that is not sufficient positive evidence that the application works.

For source-relative induction, the finite oracle can enumerate selected
prestates and operation inputs and check base and step preservation without
exploring only reachable states. It still must name whether each domain
contains *all* values of the declared type or only representatives.
Enums and Booleans may have complete finite domains under the
given versioned interface; integers, strings, UUIDs, timestamps,
dependency depths and arbitrary sequences usually do not.
Checking all input combinations over a representative set is exact
for *that set*, not proof that no omitted value changes an operator's
semantics. A finite model with every guarded operation disabled
can look safe while missing required positive Claim, Unclaim or
manager Reassign behavior.

**** Safety transfer requires the right simulation relation

Let C denote the original/concrete semantic transition system, A
the finite abstract system, R a relation from relevant C states
to A states, and P_C/P_A the corresponding safety predicates.
The intended *concrete-to-abstract* safety transfer needs:

#+begin_example
Initial coverage:
  for every admitted concrete initial state c0,
    there exists abstract initial a0 with R(c0, a0).

Step simulation:
  whenever R(c, a) and a relevant concrete step c --e--> c',
    there is a permitted finite abstract trace a ==e==> a'
    (possibly with justified hidden/stuttering steps),
    with R(c', a') and preserved required observations.

Property reflection:
  for every related (c, a), P_A(a) implies P_C(c).

Then an A invariant over all its reachable states transfers to
related C reachable states, under the stated relation and premises.
#+end_example

The quantifiers and direction matter. Showing that each abstract step
can be mimicked by one convenient concrete execution does *not* establish
that every concrete execution is represented. Likewise, mapping each
concrete state to some abstract state without checking its successors
does not establish safety transfer. A proper abstraction may
*overapproximate* concrete behavior and therefore admit spurious
abstract counterexamples. A finite abstract violation is an actual
failure of the chosen abstract property, but need not be realizable in
the original semantics or in a deployed browser/XTDB execution;
concretization and relation inspection decide the stronger attribution.

For *production* safety, a second relation must qualify the actual
installed code, original source version, authorized backend prestate,
all relevant writers, transport/DOM effects and failure semantics.
An abstract source theorem does not authenticate the route, model
caller, physical transaction or browser mutation. A single
real-world event can correspond to multiple abstract steps, but
that stuttering/partial-order permission must not hide an
unauthorized write, stale DOM adoption or additional active
primary assignment.

**** A bounded slot is not a bounded history

Logical browser active/queued slots, request concurrency and
selected finite state projections do not bound command identifiers,
resource or effect instance IDs, history length, attempt count,
provider bases, user inputs, dependency depth, retired metadata,
in-flight network requests or physical DOM side effects.
Gesso must either prove a state/data bound *under actual scheduling
and retention premises* or choose a sound abstraction for each
unbounded dimension; it cannot infer finite-state completeness
from one bounded queue setting.

Equality-class or symmetry reduction of opaque IDs is often
preferable to arbitrarily choosing UUID 1–4. The abstraction
must retain every equality and inequality relation relevant to
guards, callback ownership, command replay, identity freshness,
reused DOM IDs and noninterference between owners. An old resource
A and active B may be represented by classes =:old= and =:current=,
but two outstanding callbacks to *different old identities* cannot
always be merged without proving the property ignores their
difference. Fresh allocation can change the class partition.
Recycling an old ID or aliasing two logical commands changes the
transition relation unless ruled out by a source/protocol premise.

An unbounded collection may admit a cutoff or data-independence
proof, but that theorem must justify the cutoff for the
particular property and all supported transitions. A finite
representative Request/RequestAssignment model with two helpers
can expose a one-primary race; it does not prove
arbitrary number of helpers or all admin/migration writers
without the required symmetry, cardinality, operation-catalog
and physical-refinement arguments.

**** Resource ownership: a local abstraction with an explicit limit

The following executable example isolates one ownership predicate. It uses
opaque resource and effect identities and an active phase. Identity equality
and phase are checked again at the point of mutation. It is not the complete
Part VI adapter: execution ownership, plan compatibility, authority scope,
observation coverage, and batch completion remain additional conditions there.

#+begin_src clojure
(defn owned-effect? [state callback]
  (and (= :active (:resource-phase state))
       (some? (:resource-instance state))
       (= (:resource-instance state) (:resource-instance callback))
       (some? (:effect-id state))
       (= (:effect-id state) (:effect-id callback))
       (= :awaiting-effect (:effect-phase state))))

(defn ownership-observation [state callback]
  {:active? (= :active (:resource-phase state))
   :same-resource? (and (some? (:resource-instance state))
                        (= (:resource-instance state)
                           (:resource-instance callback)))
   :same-effect? (and (some? (:effect-id state))
                      (= (:effect-id state) (:effect-id callback)))
   :awaiting? (= :awaiting-effect (:effect-phase state))})

(defn abstract-owned-effect? [observation]
  (and (:active? observation)
       (:same-resource? observation)
       (:same-effect? observation)
       (:awaiting? observation)))

(def resource-a
  {:resource-phase :active
   :resource-instance :fixture/resource-a
   :effect-id :fixture/effect-a
   :effect-phase :awaiting-effect})

(def callback-a
  {:resource-instance :fixture/resource-a
   :effect-id :fixture/effect-a})

(def resource-b
  (assoc resource-a
         :resource-instance :fixture/resource-b
         :effect-id :fixture/effect-b))

(assert (owned-effect? resource-a callback-a))
(assert (not (owned-effect? resource-b callback-a)))
(assert (not (owned-effect? (assoc resource-a :resource-phase :retired)
                           callback-a)))
(assert (not (owned-effect? (assoc resource-a :effect-phase :completed)
                           callback-a)))
(assert (= (owned-effect? resource-b callback-a)
           (abstract-owned-effect?
            (ownership-observation resource-b callback-a))))
#+end_src

The four Boolean observations support a local predicate comparison. They are
not by themselves a finite transition system. A finite abstraction for the
whole adapter must also specify allocation, identity freshness, replacement,
retirement, queues, and adversarial late events while preserving the necessary
equality relationships. It must account for two callbacks that alias the same
identity and callbacks that do not. Collapsing all old identities into one name
without preserving the relevant relations can change the modeled behavior.

The final-mutation requirement follows even before a universal abstraction
proof exists: callback A may pass its first check, be deferred, and arrive at
mutation after resource B has replaced A. The shell must evaluate ownership
against B at that moment. Retaining the earlier Boolean =true= is not permission.
The same distinction applies when a completed effect has consumed its phase but
a duplicate callback arrives.



**** From four Boolean observations to a complete browser machine

The preserved Clojure example above has four *local predicate*
observations: active resource, equal resource instance, equal effect ID
and awaiting-effect phase. They demonstrate the Boolean equivalence
of =owned-effect?= and =abstract-owned-effect?= for the specific
constructed inputs; they do not enumerate all reachable adapter
states or prove the concrete-to-abstract relation. In particular the
four Booleans do not encode how an execution acquires ownership,
what happens when targets are replaced, how effects are scheduled,
or whether the shell rechecks permission at the physical mutation.

A full finite adapter subject would also model, as needed by the
selected claim:

- creation/allocation and freshness of resource, execution and
  effect identities; permitted alias relationships and changes
  across target reuse, plan replacement and owner retirement;
- normalized callback delivery, duplicates, delay, loss,
  cancellation failure and physical requests remaining after
  semantic retirement;
- current plan and application generation, installed asset/route
  and target compatibility, active/queued logical slots, effect
  phases and bounded or abstracted retained metadata;
- authoritative observation frontiers, provisional/confirmed
  command ownership, permission to acquire, and the different
  physical events for transport completion versus DOM install;
- multi-target HTMX/OOB partial completion, repair, abort,
  continuity ownership and current effect-time revalidation;
- environment/adversary choices that must be included to
  warrant a universal claim over the declared scheduling scope.

The finite model should retain a stable *logical* command C42
independently of physical attempts H1/H2 and current resource A/B.
Conflating those identities could make a late response look like
a valid result of a new command. An optimistic current card is
also not an authenticated statement of C42's durable
incorporation. The transition relation must preserve these
distinctions rather than assuming every successful HTTP
response is a current authorized DOM adoption.

The physical browser requirement can be falsified by a precise
interleaving:

#+begin_example
A is the current resource; effect F from A is pending.
A callback for F arrives and passes callback-entry checks.
The callback is deferred before its managed DOM mutation.
A retires; new resource B adopts the same target DOM ID.
The deferred A callback resumes.
At the physical mutation boundary A no longer owns the target.
The shell must reject A's mutation even if its earlier check passed.
#+end_example

The originally preserved predicate rejects this case *only when
evaluated against the current B-owned state at the mutation point*.
A cached earlier =true= is not a permission lease. The
browser adapter can model that admission; a theorem about
the real shell additionally needs actual code/HTMX/DOM
effect-time correspondence, physical scheduling and
installed artifact currentness. This also applies to a
completed effect that receives a duplicate callback
after its awaiting phase is consumed. For a batch,
successful installation of one target does not prove
every other target adopted.

**** Liveness needs divergence, fairness and permission premises

Finite safety and finite liveness require different claims.
An abstract safety simulation can hide arbitrarily many
internal steps while preserving protected invariants. A
progress/termination theorem additionally needs to show
that the relation does not admit an infinite concrete
divergence that the abstract model silently skips.
Fairness assumptions must refer to the actual relevant
scheduler, participant, provider, delivery or
recovery mechanism; a bounded test depth does not
establish them.

A fairness-sensitive model must identify which actions
are enabled, which remain continuously or repeatedly
enabled, what strong/weak fairness applies and whether
environment or user actions are assumed. The declared
property is specific—for example, a retained qualified
command result becomes observable when authorized
recovery is repeatedly attempted under sufficient
provider availability. That is not the same as claiming
every network partition heals, every user presses Refresh
or every provisional UI state settles automatically.
Under HumanHelp's selected remote-advisory policy,
a remote board's actual acquisition is conditional
on *user-granted* scoped Refresh; SSE delivery does
not authorize background collection reading.

Finite cycle detection can identify a lasso violating
an explicitly encoded fairness/liveness obligation
in the selected model. If the model is cut at depth
N, a finite sequence with no terminal state is not
in itself proof of infinite divergence. Conversely,
a reachable terminal path does not prove all fair
runs eventually reach it. For a concrete liveness
transfer the abstraction must preserve applicable
fairness, enabledness and non-divergence,
not only a Boolean ownership invariant.

**** Evidence categories and reproducible adversarial acceptance

An assurance report should explicitly identify:
the original source and selected abstraction generation,
the exact finite domains and whether they are exhaustive,
initial and transition catalogs, property/temporal
meaning, complete-vs-bounded exploration status,
checker/tool options, evidence origin, reachability/
deadlock/fairness interpretation, original source
locations of violations and open simulation,
concretization and production-enforcement premises.
A copied finite result is not issuer-controlled proof
or a current deployment authorization. Section 10.12
owns the reusable evidence-package lifecycle.

The following paired checks distinguish the strength
of each conclusion:

1. A complete declared Boolean/enum domain is explored;
   one omitted enum variant invalidates exhaustive coverage.
2. Nonempty valid initial states and a genuinely enabled
   positive Claim exist; empty Init or reject-all
   operations cannot pass whole-product acceptance.
3. Every original operation and selected environment
   step appears; removing Unclaim, Reassign or a
   relevant competing writer invalidates the
   corresponding source/physical completeness claim.
4. All reachable states/edges in a finite model are
   exhausted; a depth/node/edge cap is labelled
   incomplete rather than counterexample-free.
5. Source base/step enumeration respects absent
   versus present nil and simultaneous writes;
   conflation or sequential assignment produces
   a discriminating independent-oracle mismatch.
6. A valid symmetry/equality abstraction
   preserves current-vs-old callback relationships;
   collapsing distinct alias classes or fresh
   allocation incorrectly changes an observable
   outcome.
7. A complete source/abstract initial and
   transition simulation implies the named
   concrete safety property; state mapping
   without step simulation is rejected.
8. A deliberate abstract overapproximation
   produces a scoped counterexample; it
   cannot be reported as a physical XTDB
   or Chromium incident without concretization.
9. Competing helper C42/C43 commands are
   represented distinctly and at most
   one primary can incorporate under
   the claimed atomic model; merged
   command IDs falsely erase the race.
10. A valid A callback mutates a current
    target when fully authorized; a
    deferred A callback after B replaces
    it must fail at *effect time*.
11. Duplicate callback and completed
    effect cannot reuse a consumed
    permission; a cached initial
    =true= cannot grant a second
    DOM mutation.
12. Real multi-target partial installation
    retains incomplete/repairable
    outcome; one target HTTP 200
    cannot qualify full-batch
    authoritative adoption.
13. A finite lasso under justified
    fairness can refute selected
    progress; a depth-limited
    prefix is not an infinite
    liveness counterexample.
14. A fair authorized recovery
    is conditional on retention,
    availability and appropriate
    user action; it cannot
    silently force remote Refresh
    or assume network healing.
15. A finite source-level transition
    result is reported as bounded;
    copied diagnostic or
    controlled physical observation
    cannot be promoted to
    original-source theorem
    or actual host authority.
16. A selected abstraction backed
    by a checked step/property bridge
    can justify the corresponding
    quantified safety domain;
    a finite sample without the
    bridge retains its finite-only
    evidence status.
17. Real browser execution agrees
    on the exercised supported
    resource/effect mutation case;
    a CLJC adapter-model pass
    does not itself prove that
    Chromium and HTMX executed
    the same physical schedule.
18. Positive HumanHelp creator-local
    and explicitly user-authorized
    remote adoption remain possible;
    a model that hides these
    required cases is not a
    complete application witness.

Each case specifies source identities, finite/abstract
universe, exact bounds and declared fairness,
positive execution, adversarial change, first
checking or physical boundary, independent
observable result and still-open assumptions.
Correct source rejection is not evidence that an
unmediated physical writer was prevented.
A finite checker timeout remains incomplete;
an unknown physical outcome remains unknown;
neither may be marked as an exhaustive safe run.

The final standard is *finite proof with honest
scope* and *generalization only through a
justified relation*. A small abstract state
machine is valuable when it covers the right
behaviors, not because its state count is small.
*** Reproducible formal evidence and maintenance

A formal or source-checked result is usable only when its *exact claim,
scope, origin, assumptions, inputs and applicability* can be reconstructed.
The evidence package is a versioned, inspectable record of what was actually
checked, not an independent source of application semantics, an executable
permission, or a transferable certificate merely because it contains a
fingerprint or successful status. Gesso derives it from the original admitted
source and trusted checker/issuer boundary; application developers do not
hand-maintain parallel formal declarations.

Two enduring questions must be answerable separately: *Is this theorem still
valid for the same semantic subject under the same premises?* and *Does the
currently installed application still satisfy the correspondence and
environment premises needed to use it?* A source-level proof can survive a
route replacement while its production applicability fails. A physical
observation can become stale without disproving the underlying theorem.
No evidence record, regeneration operation or failed tool run silently
upgrades one kind of claim to another.

Part IX governs the actual proof judgments, original-source requirement
closure, premise substitution and issuer-controlled admission. Sections
10.01–10.11 identify the formal theorem, physical realization and exact-finite
abstraction obligations. This section defines their reproducibility,
dependency/revocation and deployment-applicability lifecycle; 10.13
separately owns trust-base and backend-assumption qualification details.

**** Evidence package: identify the proposition and the actual result

An evidence package has a closed, versioned schema appropriate to its selected
claim category. For every applicable entry it records:

| Element | Required binding and interpretation |
|---------+-------------------------------------|
| Claim | Exact proposition/temporal property, quantifiers, domain, observation alphabet, selected assurance profile and evidence class |
| Original source | Actual admitted model/rule/operation/Choreo subject, normalization and identity versions, complete original operations, initializers and source-required obligations |
| Formal subject | Generated translation/extraction version, normalized definitions, declared axioms, explicit abstraction and proof/refinement direction |
| Method | Kernel/derivation checker, model exploration, independent oracle, external proof system, controlled physical observation or qualified runtime enforcement, without conflating them |
| Reproducibility | Exact checker/translator/toolchain/dependency versions, meaningful flags, solver options, bounds, fairness, seeds, resource budgets and supported input encodings |
| Result | Observed success, counterexample, rejection, inconclusive, unsupported, timeout, environment failure or not-run, plus real logs/trace references where permitted |
| Premises | Used and still-open assumptions, trusted external contracts, discharged source obligations, provenance of discharge and explicit nonclaims |
| Dependency closure | Exact semantic/interface and proof dependencies, checker/issuer dependencies, currentness and invalidation relationships |
| Production applicability | Installed callable, route/worker, model, assets, runtime/resource generation, backend/credential domain and actual correspondence evidence where claimed |
| Evidence custody | Trusted issuer/checker origin, how inputs/results were acquired, immutable artifact identity, validation/import rules, authorized access and redaction boundary |
| Recheck lifecycle | Owner, triggering changes/contradictions, failed or stale disposition, dependent claim invalidation and permitted recovery/requalification path |

A theorem proof and a model-checking run have different semantics even when
both finish successfully. An external backend result that exhausted its state
space, a finite typed-rule sample, a source-rechecked kernel derivation, a
process-local transaction witness and an observed Chromium DOM effect each
establish only their own named claim. A report must not compress their
distinct conclusions into a common =:certified?= boolean or make several
incomplete witnesses add up automatically to universal soundness.

For exhaustive finite evidence, include the *entire declared finite machine*:
types and optional presence, initial states, complete operation/environment
relation, enabledness, abstract identity quotient, state/edge bounds,
reachability and deadlock treatment. Record whether actual exploration was
complete. For unbounded claims, include the separately checked abstraction,
simulation, induction or external metatheorem required for that conclusion.
Timeout, budget exhaustion, failed external checker and an unrun gate do not
mean “no counterexample.” An independently observed model counterexample can
remain a valid *scoped failure* even if wider exploration terminates early.

**** Reproducibility means rechecking the right original source

A replay starts from the authenticated original semantic subject and its
required proof/profile obligations, regenerates or independently validates
the formal subject, and checks the exact claim under the recorded definitions
and assumptions. It does not trust a cached positive report as input to its
own validation. Canonicalization must represent all meaning-changing parts:
type, field presence, ordered expression and proof-step operands, nominal
atom/role/operation IDs, interface, dependencies, abstraction, admitted
primitives, relevant versions and assumptions.

Structural identity is not denotational equivalence. A hash of a normalized
EDN interface establishes an identity for those canonical bytes under
the stated encoder and collision assumptions; it does not establish that an
opaque Clojure function implements the interface, that an XTDB node executed
a particular transaction, or that the served browser bytes came from the
claimed build. Conversely, an irrelevant comment, formatter change or
metadata field omitted under a *proved/defined canonicalization contract*
need not invalidate an unchanged semantic theorem. The consumer must not
choose arbitrary fields to omit merely to preserve a stale cache hit.

The replay procedure must distinguish three reproducibility targets:

1. *Semantic replay:* same admitted source meaning, exact proof statement,
   valid abstract evidence and open premises, even when nonsemantic build
   details change.
2. *Artifact replay:* deterministic or explicitly qualified reproducible
   generation of formal/compiled artifacts, with relevant compiler, codec,
   dependency, target/runtime, optimization and asset-manifest inputs.
3. *Physical replay/observation:* a newly acquired, qualified observation at
   the actual running model, backend, authenticated handler/worker and browser
   effect boundary. This need not reproduce the same physical history;
   it establishes only the stated new physical applicability/behavior.

A bitwise identical formal artifact need not result from every valid rerun if
the selected backend has nondeterministic output. In that case a small trusted
checker may validate the same theorem independently and the package records
the actual seed, ordering, checker version and evidence identity. If the claim
requires bitwise reproducibility of emitted assets or provenance of the exact
deployed executable, then nondeterministic rebuilding is not an excuse to
accept different unverified bytes. A stored digest is useful as an integrity
index only when the artifact was acquired from a trusted source and the
expected digest is authenticated at the consuming boundary.

External theorem-checking code, formal definitions, axioms, imports,
normalization, backend version and proof rules are part of the relevant
trusted base unless independently justified. A successful CLI exit status
is not by itself a proof. A generated checker result may carry a checked
proof term, a genuinely re-executed finite trace or a named conditional
provider assumption, but the package must say which.

**** Evidence origin, portability and proof-authority boundaries

Gesso distinguishes *descriptions* of evidence from *issuer-controlled
admission* of evidence. Ordinary maps, saved logs, Git objects, labels,
summaries, copies of proof reports and matching fingerprints remain
descriptive unless a trusted current checker/consumer validates their
actual contents and binding. A process-local, registry-backed proof handle
can be authoritative for the particular source-relative local check under
its trusted-JVM threat model; serializing its printed representation
does not make it a portable certificate or cross-process security token.

A durable proof artifact may be retained, moved between processes or
reused across releases only under a separately specified authenticated
revalidation, signed-attestation or trusted publication/import contract.
If signatures are used, the key, signer, trust/revocation, validity scope,
payload schema and bytes covered must be defined. Signing that a map was
written does *not* prove its theorem is valid, its model source is current
or its claimed backend execution occurred. Rechecking a sound proof term
against current definitions can be stronger than trusting the signature of
a fallible checker, but only within the actually established trust base.

A qualified theorem can be imported without rerunning its expensive
derivation for every HTTP request when the exact immutable premise and
dependency lifecycle supports reuse. Runtime authorization, actor/tenant
membership, command replay/retention, protected reads, transaction prestate
and effect-time browser ownership are *not* permanently discharged by
that reuse. Logical premise substitution is also not a way to clone a
one-Refresh user grant, one-shot transaction attempt, resource lease or
actual principal capability.

Source- and production-based reports should be inspectable without
publishing protected raw Request, Membership, Organization, command ledger,
SQL parameters, document contents, session credentials or private browser
state. The evidence store can retain authorized access-controlled
artifacts while a copyable diagnostic exposes redacted subject handles,
claim categories, bounded counters, stable failure reasons and permitted
source spans. A privacy-safe redaction must not change the semantics of a
supposedly exact checked subject; the trusted checker uses the protected
original and the viewer receives a separate nonauthoritative explanation.

**** Dependency-aware validity, applicability and revocation

The dependency graph separates semantic claims, checked proof rules,
conditional assumptions and *physical applicability* rather than
containing one undifferentiated whole-release checksum.

| Dependency change or observation | Appropriate consequence |
|----------------------------------+-------------------------|
| Meaning-changing original rule, model interface, operation set, initializer, invariant or proposition | Invalidate affected original-source theorem and dependent proof/admission, then recompute required obligations |
| Checker rule, parser, normalizer, proof kernel, formal axioms or translation semantics changes | Revalidate/reprove affected checker/formal trust and the source-to-encoding correspondence, even if an old artifact's string digest still matches |
| Codec, target platform, compiler/lowering or generated executable changes | Requalify dependent executable/physical correspondence; an unaffected abstract theorem may remain valid |
| Installed route, callable/Var, worker, browser asset, resource generation or backend client changes | Reestablish current deployment adoption and effect/transaction boundary; a pure theorem is not automatically false |
| Backend version/configuration/isolation, writer credentials, topology or external provider contract changes | Requalify the affected external/physical premises under the actual new environment |
| Accepted trusted assumption is revoked, contradicted or expires | Retract the dependent claim's applicability or restore an explicitly justified replacement premise; do not erase its dependency |
| New observed counterexample contradicts a claimed formal theorem or qualified implementation relation | Classify and investigate the specific theorem/bridge, block unsupported stronger claims, preserve reproducible evidence and notify affected consumers |
| No relevant dependency changes under verified canonicalization and lifetime | Reuse only the unaffected claim and its valid supporting premises, without inferring fresh physical authority |

Dependencies include the actual *original-source-required* obligations,
not merely a structurally consistent user-submitted proof DAG. The graph
must distinguish a theorem's used named premises, an application's required
but still open capability/acceptance conditions, and the provider facts
whose continued truth the consumer needs. If a provider's proposition
only implies a narrower consumer assumption, the substitution is checked
directionally and the provider's still-open premises propagate.

Revocation and replacement operate on applicability, not history revision.
A once-correct theorem does not become a false historical claim simply
because the deployed XTDB version or Biff handler changed. Its *use*
for that current system is suspended until the new correspondence is
qualified. If the theorem's own proof rule or source meaning was invalid,
the theorem's evidence must instead be retracted or rechecked at that
level, with dependent results appropriately invalidated. A stored C42
command's actual committed outcome likewise is historical application
data; invalidating a proof cache does not rewrite it.

A compatible semantic interface may allow a pure proof to be reused
through a checked directional equivalence/refinement bridge, including
its assumptions. A mere matching friendly operation name, same shape,
old certificate, copied fingerprint or source file path does not
supply such a bridge. Changed opaque implementation can leave a
source proof intact while its implementation obligation reopens.
For source or runtime changes outside a theorem's proven dependency
closure, avoid needless rechecking when that lack of dependency is
actually justified, not simply inferred from a filename or build cache.

**** Admission, deployment and failure-aware requalification

For a selected strong construction profile, required evidence must be
present, correctly issued, current and within its qualified scope
*before* the protected application/operation is admitted or an
effect requiring it is permitted. Unavailable external prover,
unsupported subject, invalid import, lost proof artifact, stale
premise, failed backend qualification or incomplete evidence
yields a typed failure/open status; it does not silently downgrade
to an opaque rule, mark an assumption discharged or issue a
certificate from cached descriptive metadata.

An outage of the external theorem tool need not retroactively
invalidate a still-current independently checked immutable theorem
under an explicitly defined lifecycle. It can prevent *new*
strong-profile admissions and required rechecks. Whether a running
deployment may continue serving depends on its own previously
admitted generation, currentness, assumed environment and
runtime enforcement policy. A change that revokes a needed
current model/server authorization still prevents the relevant
protected effect at the actual effect boundary, regardless
of theorem-cache health.

A deployment rollout can temporarily serve different generations
or route a participant to a host with different assets. Each
claim identifies the actual process/host and loaded artifact
generation for which it applies, or a proven compatibility
relation covering the mixed versions. A prior successful
startup check does not guarantee subsequent route/worker
replacement, remote-node credentials, browser cache
or direct XTDB writer remains constrained. Multi-node
deployments use the *same* application semantics as one
node, with additional physical topology, routing,
writer, outbox replay, registration-frontier and
failover premises rather than a new proof language.

A maintenance operation may be explicitly privileged, but it
must state its protected effects, source/operational contract,
effect on invariants and the requalification required before
stronger dependent evidence resumes. Migrations and initializers
are not outside the model solely because they do not arrive
through HTTP. An incomplete/unknown physical writer census
cannot be replaced by a green source proof report.

For each failed/retracted claim, preserve a useful typed
diagnostic: the specific first blocker, original source/proof
subject, evidence class, premise or physical boundary owner,
current versus stale generations, safe reproduction
instructions and an actionable requalification requirement.
Do not turn a timeout into an observed counterexample,
a failed post-submit read into a known rejection, or a
post-effect mismatch into prevention of an already occurred
effect.

**** Paired acceptance for reproducibility, reuse and staleness

The following controls must be fixed before the acceptance
campaign, including original source, actual evidence issuer,
selected profile, positive case, adversarial mutation,
first enforcing boundary and independently observable
result where a physical effect is claimed:

1. The same canonical semantic source replays to a
   qualified exact theorem; a changed original guard
   cannot reuse the old semantic cache entry.
2. Source reordering that is explicitly nonsemantic
   retains defined canonical identity; reordering
   meaningful formula operands or proof steps
   must change the affected subject.
3. A real independent checker validates an admitted
   proof under its actual stated axioms; a
   “proved” flag or exit-code-only copy is rejected.
4. A complete finite-domain oracle records true
   exhaustive coverage; a timed-out, truncated or
   unsupported run remains incomplete, not
   counterexample-free.
5. A valid source-relative certificate can be
   reused while source and graph remain current;
   copied EDN, forged process-local handle
   and stale dependency graph cannot gain admission.
6. A declared assumption that is still needed
   propagates to the consumer; an apparently
   matching provider report cannot
   silently discharge it.
7. Revoking a qualified provider or current
   backend premise blocks dependent production
   applicability; an unaffected pure theorem
   need not be declared mathematically false.
8. A changed checker rule or normalizer forces
   affected independent proof validation even
   when the generated theorem bytes happen
   to be identical.
9. A changed Biff handler/worker or loaded
   browser asset reopens its physical binding;
   a source proof remains scoped to its
   actual original semantic subject.
10. A controlled installed gateway/XTDB
    observation supports only that acquired
    call/result/readback scope; copied
    node identity or matching ledger cannot
    prove full write causality and all writers.
11. A new legitimate helper with current
    Membership may Claim under the actual
    public model; an old proof artifact
    cannot authorize a revoked helper.
12. A compatible H2 replay preserves
    durable historical C42 incorporation;
    re-running the formal checker
    does not grant a fresh command write
    or rewrite a known outcome.
13. An authorized browser resource
    may perform its currently permitted
    DOM effect; an old certificate or
    resource-instance ID cannot grant
    an effect after owner retirement.
14. A staged multi-node rollout
    uses qualified exact
    host/asset/provider identities;
    merely matching the source
    hash on incompatible served
    executable generations is
    insufficient.
15. A redacted public diagnostic
    exposes the correct claim and
    first blocker without private
    Request/command data; a raw
    credential or sensitive trace
    is not published as evidence.
16. An actual semantic contradiction
    invalidates relevant affected
    claims under the chosen owner;
    a different external solver
    outage is classified as
    unavailable, not a
    falsified theorem.
17. A changed migration or direct
    external writer is either
    formally/physically included,
    constrained or retained as
    open; a returned empty
    inventory does not
    establish complete coverage.
18. Eligible Claim, Unclaim,
    Reassign and selective
    user-authorized Refresh
    remain independent
    product positives; a
    fail-closed proof gate
    cannot claim whole-app
    acceptance by rejecting
    all operations.

Each case records whether evidence was actually obtained, whether
the result proves a finite/abstract theorem or only selected
physical behavior, all remaining premises and its exact
invalidation conditions. A copied report, stale fingerprint
or successful explanation is never a permission to commit
an XTDB transaction, disclose a protected document,
replay a command or mutate a retired DOM target.

The maintenance invariant is *exact proposition,
honest evidence, current applicability*. Changed
systems should not invalidate everything
indiscriminately, but no change that affects a
claim's meaning or enforcing boundary may be
hidden behind a convenient cache hit.
** Trusted computing base, security boundaries, and failure modes
:PROPERTIES:
:CUSTOM_ID: req-trusted-system-boundaries
:END:

Every claim identifies its trusted base. The logical trusted base, physical
execution dependencies, security boundary, and availability premises overlap
but are not identical. Listing every library without indicating which claim
depends on it is insufficient.

*** The assurance ledger

The root ledger identifies the executable semantic core, proof kernel, semantic
checkers, normalizers, elaborators, lowerings, runtime gates, build process,
external checkers, and implementation or dependency versions in scope. It joins
these to original obligations, accepted evidence, application assertions,
external assumptions, and enforcing boundaries.

For a physical claim, include the actual serving process's assembly identity,
installed handler binding, artifact manifest, backend connection identity, and
relevant runtime configuration under their stated trust contracts. An identity
is recorded only where it has been acquired or verified appropriately. A value
copied from caller metadata is labeled as claimed, not observed.

The ledger exposes which claims are conditional, unsupported, stale, refuted, or
blocked by profile requirements. It preserves the reason and first boundary of
failure without leaking protected inputs, command records, document contents,
credentials, or raw provider exceptions into public diagnostics.

Source size and namespace inventories help focus review. They are not proof of
soundness. A small explicitly described kernel is valuable because it reduces
the surface requiring trust and analysis, not because short code is inherently
correct.

**** Claim-indexed trusted base and independent observation

The root ledger is a dependency view over individual exported guarantees,
not one repository-wide "verified" flag. Each entry names its original
semantic subject and source obligation, precise proposition, checker or
physical witness, version and issuer, open premises, affected application
operations, enforcing boundary and currently applicable deployment scope.
An inventory that cannot enumerate its claimed original-source or physical
writer universe reports an open completeness obligation, not an empty set.

The ledger makes five different categories of dependency inspectable:

- *Logical*: executable semantics, proof rules, source-to-obligation
  derivation, elaborator, normalizer, proof checker and independent verifier.
- *Execution*: the actually issued executor, lowering, installed handler,
  browser adapter/effect interpreter, build and loaded output correspondence.
- *Security*: principal authentication and session binding, protected
  read/write/subscription admission, disclosure, credentials and capability
  origin where relied upon.
- *Environment*: backend isolation, atomicity, read consistency, code
  execution, transport, process failure, persistence, clocks and any
  fairness/liveness assumptions used by that particular theorem.
- *Evidence*: proof object or checked derivation, exact finite exploration,
  installed-assembly check, runtime enforcement, independently observed
  physical result, test, application assertion or still-trusted premise.

Reports distinguish =machine-proved=, =kernel-checked=,
=exact-finite checked=, =assembly-verified=, =runtime-enforced=,
=tested=, =asserted= and =trusted= rather than upgrading them by
aggregation. They also expose =unknown=, =unsupported=, =incomplete=,
=stale= and =refuted= at the relevant scope. A source fingerprint or
serialized assurance report has no authority to mint its own proof.
Conditional root guarantees retain every relevant unproved premise
transitively; one central opaque premise may outweigh many checked
derivations. Evidence-class counts and namespace sizes are review aids,
not a confidence score or theorem.

**** External-boundary inventory assigned to actual claims

The following are candidate trust premises, not blanket assumed truths.
For each applicable family the ledger names the exact behavior depended
upon, version/configuration, checking or observation method and owner:

| Boundary family | Behavior the particular claim may rely on |
|-----------------+-------------------------------------------|
| JVM, Clojure and third-party libraries | Primitive values, evaluation, concurrency, exception and memory behavior |
| CLJS, JavaScript engine and browser | Portable values, DOM and effect timing, resource lifecycle and stale-callback rejection |
| HTMX, SSE, Aleph/Ring and network | Actual route and response emission, session/request origin, reordering, loss, duplication and reconnect |
| Authentication and protected disclosure | Trusted principal binding, command arguments, authorization and guarded read/subscription results |
| XTDB and production adapter | Transaction guards, conflicts, atomic write footprints, query basis, codecs and provider time |
| Host, OS, storage and clocks | Persistent state, restart, failure, process replacement, delivery and time/fairness assumptions |
| External proof tools | Checker/kernel, input language, proof import, axioms, options and sound interpretation |
| Semantic/build pipeline | Normalization, compilation, lowering, asset manifest, emitted plan and loaded-byte correspondence |
| Cryptographic and identity mechanisms | Canonicalization, collision assumptions, signer origin, key lifecycle and credential secrecy |

An external proof kernel may be a logical trusted premise; the browser
runtime is a separate physical premise. Conversely, a mathematical
theorem can remain valid when the deployed browser or backend becomes
unqualified. An opaque Clojure callback remains outside the closed
logic until its specified conformance is independently established.
A malicious browser is untrusted in the modeled web contract; hostile
code already holding unrestricted server JVM/database authority is a
different threat model requiring separate isolation. Observation by
a caller-supplied host, node or registry enumeration does not attest
the deployed physical boundary. Identify separately the trusted
issuer, acquired evidence and what is merely copied metadata.

The release-level ledger is the union of claim-specific dependency
closures and the original-source coverage obligations. It can report
rejected, stale and unobserved claims without exposing document values,
command records, credentials, private principal details or raw
exceptions through public diagnostics. Subsequent admission and
runtime gates enforce the requisite premises; the ledger by itself
does not issue a certificate or authorize an effect.

*** Backend assumptions are qualified contracts

The goal is not to prove all of XTDB. The goal is to state exactly which backend
behaviors the application's claims use, qualify the concrete backend and adapter
combination against those behaviors, and invalidate dependent applicability when
that qualification no longer holds. This follows
[[#req-backend-assumption-qualification][Part I]].

Each assumption record contains:

- a stable proposition and the scope of the operations relying on it;
- the backend product and exact version or justified compatible version range;
- the adapter, client, query or transaction subset, codecs, topology, and relevant
  configuration;
- its source of justification and evidence classification;
- the executable qualification cases and their expected semantic outcomes;
- the recorded observations and known limits of those cases;
- invalidation triggers, responsible owner, and the admission/runtime response.

**** Qualification attaches to a selected lowering, not an entire product

The qualification relation connects four independently justified links:
(1) the original Gesso operation/invariant/writer catalog and its
backend-dependent propositions; (2) the selected production lowering,
guard/predicate and declared physical write/read footprint; (3) a
test against the actual selected backend and adapter with an independent
acceptance oracle; (4) evidence that the claimed installed process
uses that qualified lowering. Completing only one link cannot
discharge the others. A controlled test node is not automatically the
deployed node, and observing equal records at one read basis is not
proof of transaction-internal prestate or causality.

The qualification fixture must record the positive legal operation,
the adversarial mutation or interleaving, expected semantic result,
physical observations and the backend API behavior being challenged.
Independence is relative to the property: reusing the very same
faulty guard or adapter to generate both expected and observed results
is a shared-bug risk. Active write tests run on an isolated test
backend; after a potentially submitted transaction, failures of
diagnostic acquisition cannot authorize automatic retry.

A timeout, environment refusal, unsupported query construct, missing
witness, insufficient contention or ambiguous provider return is
=incomplete= or =inconclusive= at the required scope, not a passing
qualification. A reproduced contradiction is =refuted=. Every
observation identifies which phase, basis, issuer and environment
actually supplied it, plus the limits of that observation.

Qualification tests must use the production lowering and actual backend boundary
for the claim in question. A fake adapter that returns expected statuses tests
the fake, not backend semantics. Conversely, backend tests do not establish that
all production writers use the tested lowering.

The qualification contract covers the behaviors actually used:

| Assumption | Required challenge cases | Consequence of failure |
|------------+--------------------------+------------------------|
| Guard and mutation share the promised atomic semantics | Concurrent conflicting changes; guard failure; no partial promised writes | Dependent atomic-transition claim cannot be admitted |
| Physical replacement preserves the declared frame | Concurrent edits outside business fields; added/absent/null fields; unsupported values | Reject the lowering or strengthen its guard/update mechanism |
| Relationship and absence constraints hold | Competing inserts, reassignment, association changes, duplicate command deliveries | Dependent uniqueness, authorization, or deduplication claim fails |
| Provider outcome means what the adapter reports | Submission/return/exception distinctions; abort; lost reply; restart and reconciliation | Preserve uncertainty unless authoritative evidence resolves it |
| Read basis and coverage have the declared meaning | Lagging readers; pinned multi-query projections; insufficient progression; reconnect | Refuse false discharge or authoritative-currentness claims |
| Required intent survives commit failure windows | Crash before commit, after commit before dispatch, during retry, and after acknowledgment | Narrow or reject the claimed publication-recovery guarantee |
| Revision discipline supports a history claim | Competing writers, delete/recreate, restoration, and numeric exhaustion | Do not claim ABA exclusion without the complete discipline |

**** Real-backend positive and adversarial qualification pairs

The selected qualification profile must include relevant paired tests
rather than merely collecting successful unit-test counts:

| Positive boundary observation | Adversarial challenge and required outcome |
|-------------------------------+--------------------------------------------|
| Eligible guarded Claim changes authoritative ownership | Competing assignment or Membership change cannot be defeated by a stale external pre-read |
| Command and domain writes incorporate together | Duplicate command ID or a failed assertion cannot produce a half-committed history |
| Qualified full-document update preserves declared frame | Concurrent unrelated insert/remove, absent/present-nil or nested field change exposes inadequate field guards |
| Protected absence/uniqueness transition admits only one primary | Two competing inserts or association changes must not both satisfy an assumed uniqueness predicate |
| Result and physical query have a documented relation | ID-only submit, execute return, failed assertion, exception and lost response preserve their distinct uncertainty |
| Pinned observation matches tracked domain and command records | Independent pre/post snapshots and co-observed records never automatically prove internal read basis or specific causality |
| Qualified read reaches the requested basis | Lagging reader or echoed caller token must not be reported as observed authoritative freshness |
| Compatible command resolution is disclosure-authorized | Revocation, switched principal or arguments must not leak past results or resubmit historical intent |
| Required publication intent survives committed failure windows | Crashes before commit, before dispatch, during retry and after acknowledgment must meet the promised recovery contract |
| All covered writers preserve a version discipline | Raw writer, delete/recreate ABA, restoration and numeric overflow challenge global history claims |
| Supported codec preserves exact value meaning | Absent/nil, unsupported values and schema changes may not silently modify guard/frame interpretation |
| Selected backend/adapter configuration is qualified | Changed provider, driver, topology, codec or transaction form cannot silently inherit incompatible evidence |

The oracle must distinguish *pre-effect enforcement* from detecting an
already committed violation after the fact. An observed transaction
key, command record and document at a common basis do not by themselves
prove which submitted command caused the state. One tested schedule
does not establish universal isolation, all-writer confinement or
an unbounded refinement theorem. The bounded tested result and every
still-open transfer premise remain visible.

Provider time semantics are explicit. Valid time, system or transaction time,
application domain revision, and a basis sufficient for progression are not
interchangeable. A transaction receipt that establishes one does not fabricate
the others. A read option must be qualified for the actual provider version;
returning the caller's requested token in response metadata is not evidence
that the read satisfied it.

The tests must distinguish a property violation from an unavailable environment
or inconclusive run. A passed finite corpus is tested evidence under the named
external premise, not proof that every backend defect will be detected. No
finite suite can guarantee discovery of every future incompatible behavior.
The operational guarantee is that relevant changes and observed contradictions
invalidate qualification and trigger its declared response; the evidence report
must not promise omniscient detection.

*** Qualification is enforced, not merely documented

Build/startup checks the selected backend profile and required qualification
identity. Changing the backend, adapter, transaction shape, relevant codec,
configuration, or topology requires the applicable requalification. A compatibility
range is allowed only with an explicit justification; a floating dependency
version cannot silently inherit the old result.

When a required premise is known to be violated, the affected guarantee is no
longer applicable. The selected strict profile blocks new affected mutations or
admission and exposes the failure. It may preserve safe reads or unaffected
operations where their premises still hold. It must not silently downgrade the
same requested claim to “tested.”

**** Qualification state, claim scope, and the first enforcing gate

The selected application assurance profile identifies the *required*
backend, original-source, runtime and installed-artifact premises for
each operation and each exported guarantee. Qualification is not a
permanent attribute of a dependency name: it is evidence applicable to
a versioned backend, selected lowering, operation and installed assembly
under explicitly scoped conditions.

At build, startup and the actual protected execution boundary, the
affected claim is classified from current evidence and current known
premises. A required qualification that is unavailable, unsupported,
stale, inconclusive or known to be contradicted cannot be substituted
with a test receipt, copied success flag, historical certificate or a
weaker profile while continuing to claim the same guarantee. A strict
profile must reject admission or a *new* dependent physical effect
before the boundary it claims to protect. Unaffected operations or
safe disclosures may remain available only when their own dependency
closures and authorizations are satisfied. The decision explains the
first failed premise and permitted recovery path without disclosing
protected model state.

The precise gate is part of the proof obligation: a startup report
that is no longer current at request time, a check after an irreversible
write, or a handler wrapper that is bypassed does not show prevention
by the real enforcing path. Relevant configuration, handler, backend
qualification, installed plan or credential changes require the
corresponding revalidation and coherent replacement/retirement of
dependent issued execution capabilities. Source fingerprints and
version stamps detect changes within their declared scope; they do not
discover unobserved external mutations or authenticate the live host.
A deliberate lower-assurance application mode may be offered as a
different requested profile with its own explicit claims and owner
consent. It is never a silent fallback from mandatory certification.


An operational incident may require reconciliation of already submitted commands.
Stopping new submissions does not undo past commits or turn in-flight outcomes
into rejections. Command evidence and admitted recovery paths remain available
under their own authorization and safety contracts. A pre-existing theorem can
remain valid as a conditional statement while its failed production premise is
reported as unsatisfied.

*** Runtime authority survives every formal boundary

The browser is permitted to send arbitrary bytes. It may forge command-looking
maps, DOM, headers, semantic IDs, certificate-looking objects, roles, principal
fields, basis tokens, and resource references. Server authority still comes
from trusted context and current public model policy.

**** An untrusted request cannot carry authority across boundaries

For Claim, the browser may submit a believable command ID, existing
Request ID, old principal ID, a cached permit, a current-looking
progression token, and a well-formed proof report. Each remains
untrusted request data. The actual server derives the current
authenticated principal from its trusted session boundary; resolves
the named operation and target through admitted registry and model
paths; validates semantic argument and command identity bindings;
and protects dynamic eligibility dependencies in the *actual*
authoritative incorporation boundary, not only a preparatory read.

Historical command resolution is a separate branch: a compatible
recorded command may yield a permitted result only after current
disclosure authorization. Revocation after an already incorporated
effect does not erase history, but neither does historic success
authorize another incorporation or another principal's disclosure.
An inaccessible, absent or ambiguous historical record may leave
the effect unknown. A copied old permit, a browser-supplied principal,
or a changed request handler cannot transform that uncertainty into
authority.

The threat model records which runtime code, modules and database
credentials are trusted. Neither compiled JavaScript, HTML attributes,
client validation, a stamped plan, nor a certificate-like map is
authority over protected server writes or reads. Public interfaces
must reject same-shaped self-declared “certificates”; persisted
evidence is inert until independently checked and admitted for the
current source, premise, issuer and assembly. A matching checked
route/affordance only proves its bounded construction relation, not
that every direct entrypoint and privileged writer is mediated.


Trusted registries resolve operations; protected reads, command lookups, and
subscriptions are authorized at their actual boundaries. Artifact signing may
establish origin or integrity under its key assumptions. It does not establish
semantic correctness or authorize a principal. A checked rendering path does
not replace endpoint authorization when the rendering is bypassed.

The transport contract also owns request-origin controls, input limits,
authentication/session handling, and protected-data disclosure. A theorem about
modeled non-escalation is not a proof of the entire web stack. Hostile code with
arbitrary JVM introspection or direct database credentials is outside an ordinary
cooperating-process capability model unless a separate isolation mechanism is
part of the stated threat model.

Local opaque handles and captured function identities prevent common accidental
substitution and forged report use. They are not a JVM sandbox, persistent
revocation service, or defense against arbitrary modification of trusted code.
A weak registry's garbage collection is not semantic retirement. Persisted data
re-enters through validation; it does not regain issuance merely by preserving
a printed identifier.

*** Hashes, compatibility, and installed artifacts

A recomputed digest binds specified bytes or normalized content under its
canonicalization and collision assumptions. A copied digest string does not.
Neither proves the proposition associated with the bytes.

An unchanged browser asset can still have stale evidence if a required semantic
dependency changed. Conversely, a newly built compatible artifact need not
invalidate every interface theorem. Exact artifact identity, semantic interface
compatibility, and assembly applicability are checked separately according to
Parts VII and IX.

**** A stale-but-byte-equal example

The following is an illustrative *pure Clojure data comparison*, not
an artifact validator, cryptographic check, trusted certificate API or
proposed callable interface:

#+begin_src clojure
(let [cached {:artifact/id "sha256:91b..."
              :membership :semantic/membership-M18
              :assembly :assembly/H42}
      current {:artifact/id "sha256:91b..."
               :membership :semantic/membership-M19
               :assembly :assembly/H43}]
  [(= (:artifact/id cached) (:artifact/id current))
   (= (select-keys cached [:membership :assembly])
      (select-keys current [:membership :assembly]))])
;; => [true false]
#+end_src

Even if the bytes were independently verified and the old browser
asset genuinely still matched, its proof about M18 cannot simply
serve a changed M19-dependent claim in assembly H43. The checked
semantic dependency closure and the current installed assembly are
separate obligations. Conversely, a newly emitted asset may preserve
a semantically compatible interface without requiring every
unaffected abstract theorem to be proved again. Both directions
require a *checked* compatibility decision, not string equality.


The browser build receipt binds canonical manifest input, trusted compiler
identity, emitted plan registry, and actual output bytes. Startup verifies the
asset that will be served. A manifest string embedded by an arbitrary emitter
is not proof that its JavaScript implements the plan. The compiler and runtime
remain named premises unless separately justified by correspondence evidence.

The serving process must adopt the final checked handler, not a retained earlier
closure. A local system-map assignment or router certificate is evidence about
that inspected binding; the deployed-handler claim requires the actual server
handoff. Deferred response bodies and streams retain the appropriate assembly
and output-validation scope through emission. Versioned assets and protocol
compatibility follow the coherent activation and retirement rules of Part VII.

*** Circular trust, shared bugs, and assertion inflation

An operation cannot prove its own implementation by declaring its desired
postcondition. A certificate cannot count itself as its dependency. Recursive
semantics require an explicit sound fixed-point or induction rule, not a cycle
of mutually approving reports.

**** Issuer discipline, forged reports, and proof-dependency cycles

A map such as the following is a counterexample to unsound public
admission, not a valid certificate:

#+begin_src clojure
{:semantic-id :example/request-claim
 :valid? true}
#+end_src

A public checked operation must not be issuable merely by matching
these field names. Issuance checks the original admitted source,
independent mandatory obligations and declared proof derivation
through the relevant checker under its stated trust assumptions.
An opaque process-local handle can enforce ordinary cooperating-code
identity and lifetime boundaries, but is not a signature, JVM sandbox,
durable revocation service, or protection against privileged runtime
tampering. A copied serialized report, retained weak-reference key,
or restored printed handle does not reissue authority. A durable
package is imported as inert input and rechecked for its claimed
source, type, version, premises and admissibility before use.

Dependency graphs must have source-complete required obligations and
an acyclic *justification* relation. A certificate cannot be its own
evidence, and two certificates cannot discharge each other by a
cycle of asserted equivalences. Legitimate recursion requires a
separately checked fixed-point or induction rule with its soundness
premise made explicit. A proof of projection cannot assume precisely
the projection-preservation judgment it is supposed to establish.
A theorem under open source/authorization/backend premises remains
conditional even when the internal derivation is perfectly valid.


Source-rechecking, independent negative examples, mutation tests, independently
implemented checks, external formalization, and actual-boundary integration
challenge different failures. They should remain separate mechanisms. Two
wrappers around the same faulty predicate do not become independent evidence
because they produce different report types.

Original obligations remain visible. A report must show which root guarantees
depend on each asserted or trusted premise. One central opaque premise may
matter more than dozens of small checked facts. Required evidence cannot be
removed from the ledger or made optional merely because the current checker
cannot establish it.

Semantic fingerprints need both negative and positive controls: meaning-changing
mutations must invalidate the applicable claims, while harmless source or
formatting changes should preserve compatible interfaces. Under-approximation
admits stale meaning; over-approximation encourages unnecessary proof churn.

*** Sidecar noninterference and required gates

Optional proof trees, theorem metadata, debugging traces, and diagnostic sidecars
must not become inputs to production transition decisions. For the same admitted
plan, initial state, and event stream, their presence or absence must not change
the semantic result. Failure of optional reporting must not invent a commit,
rejection, or effect permission.

Required admission checks are different: they determine whether construction or
execution is permitted under the selected profile. Their failure may prevent
admission. Runtime authorization and currentness checks likewise enforce real
premises. Noninterference does not require bypassing either kind of gate.

**** Observable noninterference and enforceable failure semantics

For identical admitted source, accepted inputs and environmental
event history, switching optional diagnostic/proof-tree/trace
sidecars on or off must preserve semantic transitions, emitted
authoritative commands, execution identity, and the resulting
authoritative outcome. Diagnostic code may record redacted
observations but cannot inject an extra transition, alter a guard,
modify an effect payload, perform an additional submission, or
reinterpret an already-started transaction's uncertainty as
rejection. If an observer fails *after* an effect might have been
submitted, the authoritative status may remain unknown to that
observer; neither an automatic retry nor a false rejection follows.

An intentionally required admission checker is not an optional
sidecar. Its failure must block the relevant protected action at
the specified pre-effect gate. Likewise, a current authorization
or read/disclosure check is a real execution premise, not mere
diagnostic metadata. Optional reports may fail independently
without claiming that required checks were skipped or that
authoritative work was undone.

**** Paired enforcement, forgery, and noninterference controls

The finished system must make each relevant boundary independently
challengeable, with its real positive case and forbidden alternative:

| Admitted positive case | Adversarial case and required boundary |
|------------------------+----------------------------------------|
| Qualified selected XTDB backend admits eligible guarded Claim | Changed/failed mandatory backend premise blocks new dependent Claim before its write |
| Current authorized principal uses an admitted operation | Forged principal, role, token, command binding or certificate map grants no server authority |
| Compatible historical command is disclosed by current policy | Revoked disclosure or changed argument cannot leak record or cause re-incorporation |
| Original source and valid issued proof are freshly checked | Copied report or same-shaped map cannot mint an issued value |
| Acyclic source-complete proof dependencies justify a conclusion | Self-reference, mutually circular certificates and omitted required premise reject |
| Versioned artifact is verified against the serving bytes and current closure | Same digest claim with changed semantic dependency/assembly cannot reuse stale authority |
| A fresh checked handler is actually installed and invoked | Retained old handler, raw route or direct writer is not silently certified by the checked route |
| Rechecked semantic fingerprints preserve valid compatible changes | Relevant rule/premise mutation invalidates; irrelevant formatting alone need not cause proof churn |
| Optional diagnostic sidecar reports one underlying operation | Disabled, throwing or reordered diagnostic cannot create a second write or change settlement |
| Required audit/publication is part of the operation contract | Treating it as droppable optional telemetry fails the operation-specific gate |

Positive controls establish nonvacuous permitted work, not merely
successful rejection. These are prospective verification contracts;
runtime/XTDB/browser tests in Part X 10.15 must reach the claimed
physical boundary with independent effect observations and preserve
unsupported, timeout and unknown classifications distinctly.


If durable audit or publication is required for the operation's semantics, it is
an explicit operation obligation with a failure contract, not an optional
sidecar. Required effects cannot be hidden as diagnostics and then discarded
under a noninterference rule.

** Validation through the real enforcing boundaries

Formal and concrete evidence are complementary. Retain unit and property tests,
exact finite checks, portable-runtime conformance, real browser integration,
backend qualification, installed-application acceptance, and multi-node fault
scenarios where their claim depends on physical deployment.

*** The validation ladder has independently owned claims

The validation ladder comprises complementary mechanisms, not a
single regression-test success state. A complete release record identifies
which obligation each layer challenges and the original subject from which
that obligation was derived:

- *Unit and property tests* examine value, state transition, elaboration,
  normalization and invalid-input behavior; they cannot authenticate the
  production shell merely by invoking a pure function.
- *Proof checker and model/finite-state runs* establish their precise source,
  inference, finite-domain, abstraction or bounded-counterexample result.
  An incomplete exploration and a genuinely exhaustive finite result are
  different, even if both find no counterexample in visited states.
- *JVM/Node and CLJS portability tests* check actual shared semantics,
  codecs and error classification across the supported runtimes. Matching
  results are tested correspondence for the selected inputs, not universal
  source/physical equivalence.
- *Real Chromium integration* exercises the emitted, verified production
