  browser asset, HTMX extension, EventSource, actual HTTP/SSE and DOM effect
  timing; a mocked adapter or synthetic browser event has narrower scope.
- *Actual Biff/XTDB integration* exercises the checked handler, issued
  operation, selected guarded lowering, real provider, authoritative writes,
  durable command record and acquired readback. A locally checked Ring
  object does not establish deployment through the serving socket.
- *Application acceptance* uses the actual HumanHelp public models and
  user-visible Claim, recovery, notification and selective Refresh actions;
  a toy Request, injected browser command or successful HTTP status is not
  a substitute for that vertical composition.
- *Multi-process acceptance* adds independent processes, shared authoritative
  persistence, command-resolution portability, interest routing and the
  selected failure topology. Part X 10.16–10.19 own its concrete design;
  a two-label single JVM is not two physical hosts.

Evidence may be reused only for the exact propositions, versions and
qualified premises it establishes. The reported release outcome separates
admitted semantic theorem, tested implementation correspondence, actual
installed effect enforcement and current backend/host qualification. A
failed test identifies the likely owner of the repair—original rules,
semantic implementation, lowering, build/shell, policy, backend assumption
or application assembly—without altering a theorem to hide an
implementation or environmental defect.


An acceptance case records its admitted assembly and artifact, input and fault
schedule, expected semantic result, first enforcing boundary, actual observation
origin, and remaining assumptions. A negative test must reach the boundary it
claims to test. A test-only wrapper that rejects earlier is not evidence that
the production gateway, endpoint, or browser mutation gate enforced the rule.

*** Evidence fixture, independent oracle, and classification

For each required guarantee the acceptance fixture records the original
Gesso source location and operation/invariant ID; expected state and
allowed outcomes; exact issued assembly and loaded asset; principal,
command and transaction/attempt bindings as permitted by disclosure;
provider and adapter versions; controlled input/fault schedule; first
*real* enforcing boundary; independent observations of both the
authoritative state and any forbidden physical effect; and every open
trust, coverage or fairness premise.

The expected result must come from the declared semantic obligation,
not be reverse-engineered from the same adapter under test. Independent
observations may use a second read path, a controlled database query,
receipt/ledger inspection, forbidden-effect counter, or a browser
user-visible oracle, with the independence and provenance limitations
recorded. A test that asserts a wrapper's earlier rejection cannot
claim the later production gateway rejected; a report computed only
from supplied expected values cannot authenticate the physical
transaction. When a source mutation changes semantics, record the
*first* mandatory boundary expected to refuse it and challenge that
boundary directly.

Run a valid positive control through the same tested boundary, not
merely a separate fixture. A reject-all implementation can pass many
negative cases; it cannot pass the matching positive control. Likewise
a "no forbidden write observed" verdict requires credible coverage of
the actual write surface and observation interval, not an empty
test-local counter with uninspected direct writers.

Outcomes are typed: =passed= under a precise scope, =counterexample= or
=refuted= with an actual witness, =rejected-as-designed=,
=unsupported=, =incomplete=, =unavailable=, =timed-out= and
=commit-unknown= when submission may already have occurred. A
deliberately rejected malformed declaration is not a counterexample
to an admitted model; a finite search cutoff is not a positive theorem;
an unrelated console/network error is not an expected injected
failure. Keep exact counterexample event order, identity, basis,
observation origin and the point where semantic/physical evidence
diverged, while redacting protected inputs and credentials from
public reports.


*** Required mutation and positive-control pairs

| Mutation or failure | Expected enforcing boundary | Positive control |
|---------------------+----------------------------+------------------|
| Change a proof premise or dependency after issuance | Certificate currentness and required-closure admission | Unchanged immutable closure remains reusable |
| Copy a successful report into a new map | Issuer or persistence revalidation | Original source is rechecked and legitimately issued |
| Append a physical write after canonical lowering | Owned gateway payload and footprint check | Exact admitted transaction reaches the provider |
| Change an unguarded field before a replacement write | Qualified frame/guard contract | Independent safe fields are preserved by the selected mechanism |
| Supply a stale principal or Organization association | Trusted invocation and atomic current-policy guard | Authorized compatible self-claim succeeds |
| Retry an incorporated Claim after Request becomes claimed | Binding and permitted recorded-result branch | Same command returns its allowed historical outcome |
| Lose one attempt while another delivery commits | Command-resolution boundary | Outcome remains unknown until sufficient command evidence arrives |
| Replace a resource after callback admission but before mutation | Final physical effect gate | Current owned effect can install and complete |
| Break actual server adoption while retaining a checked router object | Installed production-entrypoint validation | Real request reaches the issued handler and gateway |
| Change provider version or relevant adapter semantics | Qualification applicability gate | Qualified supported configuration admits the same operation |
| Exhaust the finite checker before exploration completes | Evidence result classifier | Completed exhaustive run reports its exact bounds |
| Supply an unsupported host function to a closed rule checker | Closed-language admission | Explicit opaque contract remains usable under a permitted profile |

The mutation corpus covers source obligations and their actual
derivatives independently. Examples include omitted operation or
invariant, mutated guard/read dependency, dropped frame or uniqueness
predicate, stale certificate or source closure, forged issued handle,
changed plan/compiler asset, missing route/writer adoption, and an
unchecked direct or deferred writer. Rejecting an invalid *declared*
proof graph is not proof that a later physical raw XTDB write cannot
bypass a production admission gate.

Where a positive result depends on a callback, do not assume an
opaque Clojure function behaves as its declarative summary. Challenge
the callback at its supported use-site or retain a named conformance
premise. Where an observed result depends on backend behavior,
recheck the selected qualified provider boundary, not a fake return
map. An accepted source claim is not a universal security/availability
claim, and a tested production slice need not refute a valid abstract
theorem when its host implementation fails.


Positive controls establish useful acceptance, not just rejection. The test
suite must also preserve a known formal counterexample, an incomplete exploration,
and an unsupported feature as distinct statuses. “Nothing unsafe happened” is
not enough if the intended operation never executed.

*** Physical concurrency and failure windows

Backend scenarios must include competing commands, repeated delivery of one
command, policy changes between preparation and commit, changed relationship
members, and concurrent writes outside the nominal business fields. The
transaction tests inspect authoritative outcomes and state under the declared
provider contract, not only HTTP status codes.

*** Physical Claim and command failure-window matrix

Tests involving authoritative mutations use concurrent requests that
genuinely reach the selected physical gateway. Force contention with a
barrier *after each request acquires its own prestate and issued
capability* where that is the scenario. Observe what each submission
actually did, which transaction committed or asserted, whether the
document frame survived, and whether the command record and domain
write share the promised all-or-nothing outcome. A post hoc comparison
of two HTTP 200 responses is insufficient.

Required schedules distinguish:

- guard failure and successful same-version conflict control;
- competing Claim and Membership/Organization association changes;
- interleaved unguarded changes outside business fields, including
  absent/nil, whole-record replacement, relationship/absence and
  writer-footprint differences;
- duplicate delivery of *one logical command* versus two genuinely
  different commands and separate submission-attempt identities;
- crash/exception before physical submission, after a successful
  transaction but before the Ring response, and during later
  readback or command-resolution observation;
- already-incorporated compatible replay under current disclosure
  versus new incorporation, revoked permission or incompatible
  argument/target binding;
- a fresh *authorized* request after a resolved conflict versus
  prohibited reuse of the consumed one-shot writer; and
- outbox publication before/after commit, dispatch, receipt and
  retry under the promised delivery/gap-recovery contract.

A lost response after successful submission is not a rejected
transaction; an observation failure cannot request an automatic
second submission. The test independently inspects the durable
physical record to distinguish the *actual test oracle's knowledge*
from what the browser or request caller is entitled to know. A
currently claimed Request does not establish which command caused
the claim, and a matching transaction ledger/readback may be
co-observation without proven causal correspondence. Time/basis,
writer completeness and actual installed-handler scope must be
qualified separately. Even a successful controlled embedded-XTDB
contention test does not certify all backend schedules or external
direct writers.


Browser scenarios include reordered callbacks, duplicate completion, failed
abort, resource replacement, deferred mutation, insufficient observations, stale
plans, and partial installation repair. Expected network or console failures in
fault injection are asserted precisely; unrelated failures still fail the case.
A successful portable test does not substitute for the real HTMX or browser
lifecycle event that the shell normalizes.

*** Browser and user-level delivery schedules

A real-browser fixture must load the same checked runtime bytes and
HTMX/SSE versions selected by the installation being claimed. It
drives actual user actions and physical event delivery instead of
injecting only already-normalized adapter events. Adversarial cases
include SSE duplication, reconnect/loss, delayed or reordered
fragment response, overlapping POST/GET, aborted request that still
completes, stale callback after resource retirement, DOM root
replacement, optimistic settlement after rejection or uncertainty,
a deferred side effect whose owner changes before mutation, and
partial installer failure followed by allowed repair.

Use both semantic adapter traces and observed DOM/network state:
selected item, focus/scroll continuity, pending marker, refresh
affordance, stable behavior-owning root, current/advisory/canonical
progression and actual server-refetched HTML. A browser trace that
retains a stale pending state, silently adopts a remote advisory
revision, sends a second command, or installs an effect under a
retired resource fails the appropriate obligation. Deliberately
expected network/console errors must be identified by type and
fault schedule; new or unrelated failures remain failures. Portable
CLJS tests and mocked HTTP fixtures are useful separate layers, not
evidence that native HTMX lifecycle events were normalized correctly.

For HumanHelp, complete acceptance starts from real production
model operations, routes and protected public policy, covers the
actual Claim/unclaim/take-over/done/cancel life cycle and independent
multi-client visible state, and preserves the distinction between a
creator's immediate result and another viewer's advisory update plus
explicit Refresh. A browser-only demo, a fabricated positive
command, or a reachable-looking checked route does not close this
application-wide guarantee.


Host scenarios include concurrent independent requests and any supported deferred
execution. They must demonstrate that one request's identity, writer capability,
result, or admission limit cannot be silently inherited by another. Thread-bound
APIs that intentionally exclude deferred work must reject it clearly rather than
claiming it was mediated.

*** Independent host isolation and closure limits

Concurrent checked Biff requests must not share request-local writer
issuance, principal context, one-shot permit, current target, result
or admission budget. Test controlled overlap, queue saturation,
timeout/exception cleanup and sibling-request isolation. If a scoped
writer is deliberately synchronous/thread-bound, deferred callbacks
and off-thread use reject before an effect rather than inheriting a
previous request's permit. A post-dispatch host report may detect a
mismatch after irreversible work; it cannot certify that the write
was prevented.

Production adoption is checked separately from an in-process system
map: show that the actual listener dispatches through the final
checked handler, that real HTTP invocations reach their intended
operation and guarded writer, and that the serving JS/fragment/stream
corresponds to the admitted assembly. Deliberate bypass tests should
challenge raw Ring responses, retained pre-mediation handlers,
background/worker/migration/admin writers and separate XTDB
credentials under the application's declared supported universe.
The result may correctly be =open= for uninspectable external
writers; absence from the surveyed host registry is not proof of
absence from the deployment.

Run completion also records negative controls for the test harness
itself: missing backend, never-executed action, empty generator,
untriggered race, absent browser asset, unsupported physical
interface, and timed-out test. These do not pass due to vacuity. A
scope-qualified failed oracle may block production admission if it
is required by the selected assurance profile, without conflating
that gate with optional logging or undoing an already committed
effect.


No single passing history establishes universal refinement. These tests make
premises falsifiable, exercise real boundaries, and provide reproducible
regressions while the report retains their scope.

** Multi-node realization and authoritative rendezvous
:PROPERTIES:
:CUSTOM_ID: req-multi-node-realization
:END:

Multi-node deployment changes physical placement. It does not create a second
authority model, a second command meaning, or automatic permission to adopt
remote state.

*** One semantic machine under physical placement

Single-process and multi-process Gesso are *realizations of the same*
admitted application. The original model rules, public operations,
command-resolution outcomes, Choreo roles, knowledge obligations, browser
progression and adoption policy do not acquire a separate distributed
meaning. What changes with placement is which physical process,
transport, backend, interest router and resource instance realizes each
part of that same contract.

The distributable implementation therefore has two independently
checked relationships:

- *Semantic preservation*: every selected distributed operation,
  settlement, invalidation, acquisition and effect corresponds to an
  admitted single-machine behavior, including rejection, unknown
  outcomes, stuttering and permitted nondeterminism.
- *Physical qualification*: the actual installed hosts, writer paths,
  authoritative backend, request/session bindings, transport and
  routing/recovery mechanisms satisfy the named assumptions required
  for that correspondence under the declared topology and failures.

The semantic machine does not become correct merely because two
nodes agree with one another. A local reporter's assertion that it
used the shared database, a matching application fingerprint or a
successful load-balanced request is not evidence of all relevant
physical entrypoints, current authorization, writer confinement or
a general distributed refinement theorem.


*** Roles, principals, authorities, and hosts remain distinct

A role is a choreography role. An actor realizes that role under a principal and
context. An authority owns specified authoritative facts or operations. A host
is a physical process that may realize an authority projection for an invocation.
None of these identities is interchangeable.

The identity contrast is:

#+begin_example
choreography role:   :request-authority
original host:       web-node A
replacement host:    web-node C
semantic authority:  [:authority :request R]
#+end_example

These symbols illustrate different identity categories, not a
special topology API or an assertion that node A owns authority.
The same principal may have different actor instances in separate
tabs, and separate HTTP requests may realize the same logical command.
A host/process identity and an admitted assembly generation likewise
must not be substituted for an execution, principal, authority or
resource-instance identity.


A Claim sent through host A and retried through host C retains its bound
=:gesso/command-id= and public operation meaning. Each delivery may have a new
=:http-request-id= and attempt identity. Host C must authenticate its own
invocation, validate the existing command binding, and use the shared authoritative
command-resolution mechanism. Node-local caches cannot establish cross-node
deduplication.

The retention contract names the period and scope in which replay is supported.
A deleted command record cannot silently make an old command identifier a fresh
intent. The protocol must either preserve sufficient tombstone/exclusion evidence,
use an enforced expiry or epoch contract that rejects expired reuse, or narrow
the claimed retry guarantee explicitly. A client must not work around uncertainty
by allocating a new command identifier for the same pending intent.

Physical relocation cannot reconstruct an intent whose binding was never retained.
A current-state read at host C may establish the Request's present state while
leaving the originating participant's command outcome unknown.

*** Command identity, compatibility, and retention across hosts

The original operation and command binding remains stable across
host movement only when its actual retained evidence survives:
authority/namespace and target, principal, operation, immutable
semantic arguments, command identity, retained outcome and any
applicable compatibility or expiry discipline. An HTTP delivery
may have a new transport-request ID, and each physical submission
has its own attempt identity and one-shot capability lifetime.
Neither the new host nor a repeated caller-provided command ID
confers fresh authorization.

For a retry through C, the current trusted session/principal and
protected result disclosure must be re-established. A compatible
*recorded* command is resolved without incorporating again; a new
command requires its own current authoritative eligibility and
transaction-time guards. Duplicate concurrent deliveries of one
command must not both create a new durable effect, under the
qualified atomicity and retained-record assumptions. A changed
principal, target, operation or argument binding cannot claim the
old result. Missing, expired, inaccessible, or indeterminate
evidence cannot silently become a new command or rejection.

The retention guarantee states its supported time horizon,
namespace, archival/tombstone or expiry mechanism, and treatment
of old commands after node replacement or backend restoration.
A finite record TTL without enforceable reuse exclusion does not
provide indefinite deduplication. A replaced database incarnation
or restored old snapshot does not automatically continue the old
command history merely because its authority label or IDs match.

An origin host may fail before submission, after an unobserved
submission, after commit but before HTTP settlement, or after
result publication. Those are different participant-knowledge
states. The successor can return a recorded historical outcome
only after acquiring sufficient trusted command-specific evidence;
reading a Request's present state alone cannot establish the
identity or outcome of Alice's lost command. A process-local
attempt journal, response object or callback is not a portable
cross-host authority credential.


*** The selected ordinary topology is deliberately small

The baseline multi-node realization uses:

- at least two independently running application processes behind a request
  distributor that can route a retry or reconnect to another process;
- one qualified authoritative backend deployment shared by those processes;
- durable publication intent stored atomically with the model operation where
  the application requires post-commit notice recovery;
- a dispatcher and advisory distribution path that can reach interested
  sessions on either application process;
- shared or otherwise compatible authentication, command resolution, protocol,
  artifact, and assembly-compatibility contracts.

These are responsibilities, not a required list of infrastructure products. A
separate broker is warranted only when the selected delivery contract needs it.
Multiple processes and a shared database are sufficient to test meaningful host
replacement; a single process with two labels is not.

*** Minimal physical realization without prescribing products

A practical first deployment may use two Aleph/Biff processes,
a request distributor such as HAProxy, shared qualified XTDB
persistence, and a cross-host invalidation transport such as Valkey.
A durable log such as Redpanda or another broker is optional and
justified only by the selected acknowledgment, replay or routing
contract. These are illustrative integration choices,
not Gesso protocol requirements, mandatory infrastructure, or
proof that the deployment works.

The implementation should first express these responsibilities
through stable Gesso semantic, writer, publisher, registration and
transport interfaces. An in-process implementation and a
multi-process implementation must satisfy the same application
contract. A later Rust router or another transport implementation
is an optimization or independently qualified adapter, not an
excuse to change application semantics or force authors to write
a separate multi-node protocol.

Different nodes may concurrently run compatible but nonidentical
assembly generations during a rolling deployment. The selected
version-compatibility contract must identify admissible old/new
operation, command record, credential/session, browser artifact,
wire-format, progression, interest-registration and recovery
behavior. If compatibility is not established, new admission
or adoption is blocked, or a defined retirement/reacquisition
path is used. A retained old route, writer callback or browser
resource cannot silently cross the compatibility boundary.


The topology qualification identifies concrete services, versions, transport
configuration, credentials, failure model, and consistency assumptions. A backend
being shared does not prove that two read paths have identical freshness.
For that topology, the root ledger records at least:

- actual *distinct* host/process identities, deployed final
  handler/worker generation, serving sockets and writer entrypoints;
- the shared authoritative backend's real incarnation, version,
  transaction/consistency contracts, writer domain and connected
  credentials, including external/direct writers where in scope;
- the request distributor's routing and failure behavior, what
  session authentication can be reconstructed at a replacement
  host, and how clock/host-health observations are qualified;
- actual command-record retention, historical outcome readback,
  compatibility and disclosure, not just process-local one-shot
  evidence;
- distributed publication, interested-recipient routing,
  registration/replay/gap detection, authorization, and which
  observations are durable versus advisory;
- supported concurrent and mixed-generation admission, failure
  detection, bounded recovery/retirement and liveness/fairness
  premises, with the first enforcing or observation boundary for
  every exported guarantee.

The current authoritative read may be served through a different
XTDB client or host context. A successful query is not proof
that the requested progression frontier was satisfied, and
token metadata echoed from a request is not an authenticated
observed basis. A qualified insufficient read preserves the
browser's outstanding debt and recovery path. Provider system
time, transaction ID, domain revision and an SSE cursor are not
one interchangeable global sequence.

*** Invalidation routing is a realization, not a second authority

An authoritative database change, a durable publication intent,
an expanded Gesso Live invalidation, a router-forwarded notice,
a subscriber's admitted advisory and a domain-participant message
are different facts. In particular, an invalidation means that
relevant authority may have advanced and a later acquisition
must respect its scope/progression. It does *not* mean the client
received a choreography message, that protected content may be
disclosed, or that a browser may automatically adopt new state.

Indexed local interests may be extended across nodes by one or
more routers. Hierarchical/coarse filters, replicated interest
views, interleaved routing assignments, and conservative
republication are possible realizations; none is prescribed by
the semantic model. Any selected topology must specify how
interest registration becomes effective, which host/router has
enough knowledge to avoid excluding an interested recipient,
what happens when that knowledge is stale or a router fails,
and how a missed notice is detected or conservatively recovered.
An independently healthy backup router is insufficient if it
has not acquired the relevant interest or replay frontier.
Router process health alone cannot certify complete routing
state.

Because invalidations do not command a domain mutation,
duplicate or unnecessarily broad *authorized* advisories may
be acceptable when coalesced without losing required progression
or violating privacy and load constraints. This permits
conservative recovery without logging one completion receipt
per recipient for every broadcast. But retransmission cannot
repair a missed publication or registration race unless a
qualified retained source, fence, replay or gap detection
mechanism provides the necessary evidence. Neither a dropped
notification nor a long silence is proof that no relevant
change occurred. The exact outbox/registration and subscriber
contracts belong to 10.17; direct, semantically meaningful
participant routing belongs to 10.19.

The minimal multi-host contract must also preserve tenant and
principal scope: interested routes do not grant permission to
read a Request, and a topic or advisory payload cannot leak
protected identities, values or counts merely because it
contains no document body. Reauthentication, disclosure
checks and resource ownership still apply at receiving hosts
and browsers.

*** Placement-specific fault boundaries and evidence

A real multi-host acceptance cannot be performed by renaming
two objects inside a single JVM. The test harness must be able
to stop one physical process while a second continues, route
new requests independently, force a qualified lagging read,
change shared authorization state, observe committed command
records, and exercise notice loss or an incomplete registration
frontier. It must record which process, backend and transport
actually supplied each observation.

At minimum, challenge a same-command retry through a surviving
host, concurrent duplicate submissions, lost original response,
backend incompatibility, command-retention expiry, stale
interest/router knowledge, router replacement, interrupted
rollout, and one authorized cross-host Refresh. Pair each with
a successful ordinary operation rather than passing a
reject-all or never-delivered implementation. 10.17–10.19
own the detailed publication, HumanHelp two-host schedule,
ephemeral-message contrast and complete acceptance matrix.

Safety is required during permitted interruptions: do not
invent commits, successful deliveries, authorized disclosures,
progression or UI adoption. Conditional liveness requires
explicit assumptions about backend availability, surviving
routes, retry/replay retention, eventual dispatch, current
authorization and (for HumanHelp remote adoption) a permitted
user Refresh. A partition that prevents those premises
cannot be used to claim eventual progress. This is a named
open guarantee, not a reason to weaken the single-node safety
laws.


Qualified progression checks still apply at each host.

*** Durable facts are the ordinary rendezvous

For HumanHelp's ordinary cross-user work, Alice submits a public authoritative
operation, its durable state and command result are incorporated, and a durable
outbox intent supports advisory publication. Bob's session may receive an
advisory through another host. That advisory records a possible need to acquire
new authority; it does not carry permission to adopt protected domain content.

The durable-state contrast is an illustrative semantic path:

#+begin_example
Alice browser -> host A -> guarded Request/Claim operation
                             |
                durable Request + command result + outbox intent
                             |
                  cross-host advisory distribution
                             |
Bob browser <- host C <- authorized scoped notification
    |
explicit Refresh -> qualified authorized authoritative reread
    |
current browser resource -> permitted adoption batch
#+end_example

A Request and its assignment are the durable rendezvous, not an
in-memory suspended choreography on A. None of these arrows alone
proves the next step: an advisory is not permission to read, an
observed Request state cannot attribute Alice's lost command,
and an acquisition is not an installed browser view.

Bob's explicit Refresh authorizes a board acquisition under the current
principal, scope, required progression, and Part VIII policy. Host C reads the
qualified authoritative projection. The browser admits the response under its
current resource ownership, then installs and records adoption only when the
required batch completion succeeds.

The durable Request and assignment facts are the rendezvous. Ordinary Claim,
Reassign, lifecycle updates, and later reads do not require a persistent
participant-message process or a suspended choreography stack for every user.
The public model contracts and short choreographies connect those interactions.

*** Source-derived publication and atomic recovery obligations

An admitted authoritative operation declares the eligible semantic
changes and scopes that require later notification. A primary domain
change need not depend on which browser interests were known in the
writer's process at commit time: an ephemeral interest cache is
not a complete inventory of future subscription/recovery needs.
The exact protected operation/writer catalog from original source
must be related to its production effect and publication-intent
generation; observing one well-behaved writer does not close
unregistered or external write paths.

Where the selected application promises recovery of required
post-commit notice, the model effect, durable command outcome where
applicable and durable outbox intent are incorporated atomically
under the qualified backend contract, or through an independently
justified equivalent that cannot lose a required intent after
commit. An attempted command whose outcome is unknown cannot be
used to invent a success advisory or automatically resubmit the
effect. Publication failure after a known commit cannot undo it.

Each durable intent binds an independently issued identity,
applicable original operation, authorized scope, semantic
notification purpose, versioned encoding and source-qualified
progression requirement. Command ID, outbox ID, provider basis,
domain revision, transport cursor and browser resource are
distinct. The outbox records the minimum required scope/notice
material, not a snapshot of private Request/User data that
bypasses future read authorization. A separately declared
best-effort notification may omit durable intent only if loss
is genuinely permitted by its weaker application contract.


*** Outbox dispatch and advisory recovery have separate guarantees

The outbox record establishes durable publication intent, not delivered notice.
The dispatcher claims pending work through a qualified concurrency mechanism,
retries failures, and records completion according to the chosen publication
acknowledgment contract. A crash after publish but before recording completion
may duplicate publication. Receivers must handle duplicates without duplicating
commands or inventing progression.

A durable outbox identifier, command identifier, provider progression requirement,
and subscriber cursor serve different purposes. One may be related to another
by checked evidence; they are not the same token.

*** Dispatch ownership and delivery evidence boundaries

The dispatch state machine names pending, claim/lease, attempt,
accepted-by-distribution, completion, retry and retention. A
qualifying lease/fencing or comparable concurrency contract
prevents a stale worker from illegitimately completing a task
taken over by a surviving worker. Lease clocks and transaction
assumptions are qualified rather than inferred from process
health. A dead host cannot strand publication intent solely in
a process-local callback.

The selected acknowledgment must say whether it is a log append,
broker acceptance or other durable distribution-boundary event.
A send timeout after possible acceptance is not proof of failed
delivery: retry may duplicate the *advisory*. The receiver's
idempotent/coalescing logic must preserve the strongest required
scope/progression debt without issuing another domain command.
A publication attempt, broker acceptance, router forwarding,
SSE write, browser receipt, current authorized reread and
completed DOM adoption are different evidence classes.

| Stage | What its observation establishes |
|-------+----------------------------------|
| Domain commit | Authoritative state and qualified required intent exist |
| Dispatcher claim | Worker owns one temporary publication attempt |
| Distribution acknowledgment | Named broker/log/router boundary accepted notice |
| Router forwarding | Candidate interested host/session route was selected |
| SSE/HTTP write | Transport attempted delivery, not browser reception |
| Browser advisory admission | Potential-change debt was registered |
| Authoritative acquisition | Current permission and provider basis allow a candidate |
| Adoption batch | Current owned resource installed the permitted candidate |

Ordinary advisory recovery need not store a persistent per-recipient
completion record for every send: conservative redelivery is
permitted under authorized scope, load, progression and retention
bounds. A claimed at-least-once *browser* delivery guarantee
would need stronger recipient acknowledgment/replay evidence.


The selected delivery contract is at least once to its named distribution
boundary under dispatcher availability and retry premises. It must state whether
that boundary is a durable log, broker acknowledgment, or another qualified
acceptance point. It must not describe this as at-least-once delivery to every
browser unless retention, recipient acknowledgment, replay, and authorization
actually establish that stronger claim.

Outbox draining alone does not close a subscriber's registration gap. If a notice
was published before a new interest became effective, a live-only subscriber
may miss it. The baseline subscription protocol therefore establishes a fence
or equivalent qualified handshake relating initial observation, registered
interest, and replay/gap evidence. A gap is recorded even if no advisory arrives.
Reconnect carries the same obligation; silence is not evidence of no change.

*** Registration fences, late interests and router failover

An initial board read followed by registration can miss an
intervening update. Registering first and then reading is
sufficient only if effective registration and the observation's
coverage are related by a qualified fence or equivalent handshake.
A supported protocol relates the authorized first observation,
effective interested-recipient registration, retained event
interval and replay or conservative reacquisition. If provider
and router use different sequence coordinates, a checked bridge
must relate them; equal-looking counters/timestamps are not
evidence of the same frontier.

A change committed just before a new interest was learned must
not disappear solely because no earlier browser listener existed.
Likewise a silent dropped notice, late interest update, restarted
host, expired cursor, changed filter or reconnect either has
qualified event coverage or produces explicit gap/recovery debt.
A safe alternative to full replay is conservative authorized
reacquisition, subject to HumanHelp's explicit Refresh policy
and the selected user-action/recovery contract. Silence is not
evidence that the subscriber is current.

Routers may use indexed interests, replicated filter views,
coarse/fine hierarchies or interleaved ownership. None is required
by the semantic model. A healthy replacement router with an
outdated interest view is not evidence of routing completeness.
The selected contract must identify registration ownership,
effective propagation, filter/version exchange, failure
detection, retained publication source, and how undercoverage
is avoided or recorded. Overdelivery or duplicate descriptive
invalidations may be cheaper than precise per-recipient
acknowledgments, but only when scope privacy, bounded fanout
and progression composition hold. Merely replaying events for
interests remembered by a failed host cannot recover interests
the surviving router never learned.

A *change event*, a durable publication intent, an expanded
Live invalidation, a broker notice and a Choreo participant
message have different meanings. Invalidations do not carry
permission to mutate authoritative state, and must not be
silently upgraded into participant-message receipts or UI
adoption. The exact direct-message contract belongs to 10.19.


Interest filtering is an optimization over authorized scope. It must either
avoid missed relevant changes under its stated contract or expose conservative
gap/recovery evidence. Stale interest registration, dropped transport messages,
retention expiry, or node loss cannot be treated as proof that the user's view
is current.

*** Recovery guarantees and independent fault oracles

Safety is unconditional relative to the declared trusted
boundaries: lost, delayed, duplicated or misrouted notices
cannot authorize a protected read, manufacture an incorporated
command, erase unknown command status, invent an observed basis
or silently install remote model changes. Publication and
subscription progress are conditional on required retention,
working backend, surviving dispatcher, available distribution
path and retry fairness. Browser receipt adds connectivity and
current scope; HumanHelp remote adoption additionally depends
on explicit permitted Refresh. A partition or revoked
permission cannot be called a violated unconditional liveness
promise.

| Positive control | Adversarial control |
|------------------+---------------------|
| Atomic Claim commits state, command and outbox intent | Host dies after commit before publication; intent survives |
| Replacement worker dispatches pending publication | Dead host-local callback was the sole publisher |
| Broker/log acknowledges at declared boundary | Timeout after possible accept is mislabeled no-delivery |
| Receiver coalesces repeated scoped notice | Duplicate publication triggers a second Claim |
| Subscriber registers with qualifying fence/replay | Commit between first read and effective interest is silently missed |
| Backup router recovers or conservatively detects uncertainty | Healthy router with stale filter drops notice without gap |
| Expired replay cursor yields recovery debt | Silent reconnect is declared current after retention expiry |
| Sufficient authorized reread on C clears covered debt | Token echo or lagging read claims a frontier not observed |
| Explicit Refresh permits one candidate acquisition | Advisory alone auto-adopts protected Request content |
| Scope-minimal notice reaches authorized destination | Cross-tenant topic or counts leak via routing |
| Publisher eventually reaches named boundary under fairness | Partition is misreported as unconditional browser delivery |
| Compatible recorded command is disclosed on retry | Lost HTTP response causes a new domain incorporation |

The future tests use actual independent host, provider and
transport boundaries with positive controls; in-process source
inspection alone cannot establish this multi-node contract.


Advisories and interest topics can themselves disclose protected information.
Their payloads and scope references are minimal and authorized; routing membership
does not grant permission to read the underlying Request. A notice may carry an
opaque progression requirement without revealing protected content or counts.

*** HumanHelp preserves explicit Refresh across hosts

Part VIII selects explicit Refresh for both remote creation and remote lifecycle
changes to already visible cards. This policy is settled for this plan; only the
separate response-flow product contract remains unresolved there.

Remote advisories may update scoped outstanding debt or indicate a recovery gap.
They do not automatically fetch and adopt a new board. Own-command outcomes and
the specifically permitted local rejection/unknown recovery paths remain the
exceptions defined in Part VIII. Those exceptions do not authorize unrelated
membership changes or clear unrelated remote debt.

*** The selected product contract and distinct permissions

This is a selected *HumanHelp* application policy, not a
general change to Gesso Live's choreography semantics. The
authoritative model may commit remote Create, Claim, Unclaim,
Take-over/Reassign, On-the-way, Complete or Cancel on another
host. The resulting scoped invalidation records potential
outstanding authority that Bob could choose to acquire;
it never grants a domain read or installs a changed card.
Both remote creation and lifecycle changes to a card Bob
already sees require explicit Refresh for ordinary
collection-content adoption.

The two independently permitted local continuations are
narrower than a global Refresh:

- Alice's own accepted command can adopt its *correlated*
  authorized result and the declared selective affected-card
  or membership change, subject to physical installation and
  current ownership. It cannot clear unrelated board advisory
  debt or pretend that a later individual-card observation
  refreshed the whole cohort.
- A rejected or indeterminate local command can perform its
  specifically admitted affected-Request recovery read. This
  can disclose a current state caused by someone else where
  current authorization permits, but cannot add unrelated
  collection members or convert unknown command attribution
  into a historical success/rejection claim.

Initial page acquisition, user Refresh, an own-command result,
and a scoped conflict-recovery read carry different grants
and coverage claims. A browser can still display a stale
Claim button before an explicit Refresh, but its invocation
must pass *current* protected model eligibility and cannot
assume the displayed owner or Membership is authoritative.
The separate HumanHelp response-interaction product choice
in Part VIII remains unresolved; completing this two-host
Claim case does not certify that product journey.


One Refresh grant authorizes one board acquisition under that contract. It does
not schedule an automatic successor read when a newer advisory arrives during
the request. A user action explicitly coalesced under the permitted policy is
accounted for as that action, not invented by the scheduler. An actually newer
qualified observation may discharge additional covered debt where the scoped
progression relation proves it sufficient.

*** Refresh grants, adversarial arrivals, and scoped debt

One permitted Refresh issues one board acquisition with a
stable scope, resource ownership, optional previously observed
progression requirements and a bounded lifecycle. If a newer
advisory arrives while the acquisition is pending, it records
separate or composable scoped debt; it does not silently
schedule a successor GET or confer a new user grant. Only a
new explicit Refresh/Retry action, or user action explicitly
coalesced under the admitted policy, may issue the relevant
additional acquisition. If the *already issued* qualified
read returns a sufficiently newer coherent observation, it
may discharge newer debt that is actually proved covered.
Mere chronological arrival, a greater-looking token or a
matching Request UUID is not such proof.

A command outcome, invalidation, provider read basis, SSE
cursor, board-cohort membership, per-card observation and
successful HTMX installation are distinct evidence. Debt
merging preserves organization/location/projection and
progression-compatibility boundaries; unrelated or
incomparable requirements remain separate. When retention,
coalescing budget or replay coverage is insufficient, report
typed unknown/gap debt rather than dropping it or declaring
the board current.

Search, sort, mine-first, unclaimed-first, terminal-visibility
and card expansion operate on the *adopted* bounded cohort
under Part VIII's local presentation contract. They cannot
trigger an undisclosed remote collection reacquisition just
because the visible board has newer advisory debt. A
successful local action may selectively update the affected
card and legitimate membership without upgrading the entire
adopted-cohort basis.


A board observation must be coherent across Request, primary assignment, and
permitted User projection at its declared provider context. A lagging host that
cannot satisfy the required progression returns insufficiency and preserves
recovery. It must not echo the requested basis as if it had observed it. A
successful HTTP response is not evidence that the required frontier was reached.

*** Qualifying one coherent board candidate

A complete-board acquisition binds the current trusted
principal and allowed Organization/Location, source-owned
cohort and completeness contract, RequestAssignment primary
membership, Request statuses, permitted User projections,
query temporal context and finite collection bounds.
These relations must be observed at one qualified common
provider basis or carry independent evidence sufficient to
justify the advertised coherence. A series of unrelated
reads on an advancing database is not a complete snapshot
because the last response happened to return HTTP 200.

An insufficient or lagging read through C must preserve the
original debt and typed retry/repair affordance. The
server must not fabricate sufficiency by echoing a requested
frontier into its response. A complete authorized current
board can establish current cohort membership; an individual
Request recovery read cannot. A missing Request in an
incomplete, denied, truncated or differently scoped result
does not establish authoritative absence. Counts are facts
about the *adopted* cohort, not the latest global database.

The browser treats the received candidate as *not yet
adopted*. The current resource instance, authenticated
scope, acquisition grant, nonregressing progression and
permitted installation batch must agree. For HTMX OOB
toolbar and collection changes, physical target installation
and batch completion are distinct from HTTP receipt. A
failed or partial swap retains unsettled adoption debt and
uses the declared compensation/repair protocol without
claiming that an older owner regained rights. A delayed
callback, aborted-but-completed request or replaced DOM
resource cannot install a stale candidate, even when its
domain Request ID is still valid.


No acquired board is adopted if its resource is retired, its scope is no longer
permitted, or it would regress newer locally installed authority. Installation
of toolbar, collection, and associated evidence follows the adoption-batch
contract, including repair after partial failure. Reconnect and host replacement
do not waive that contract.

A known authorization-context change retires the affected protected projection
and subscriptions according to their lifetime contract. It cannot erase data
already disclosed to an offline browser. Protected rereads and subscription
renewal still require current authorization at the replacement host.

*** Context changes outrank remote-adoption preference

Logout, switched principal or Organization, revoked read
permission and replacement of the admitted board scope
are trusted context/lifetime transitions, not ordinary
remote Request advisories. They retire incompatible
subscriptions, grants, pending installations, provisional
effects and protected projections according to the
supported-client contract. An in-flight request created
for Bob's prior Organization cannot install its late
response into the new identity's board. Historical
command-result disclosure requires its own *current*
principal and permission; reconnect to a different host
does not inherit Alice's old browser settlement rights.

No framework can retract protected bytes already copied
by an untrusted or offline client. The enforceable boundary
is current server-side read, stream, command, historical
result and recipient/OOB-drain authorization, plus
retirement of controlled client resources. An advisory
topic or count must not reveal otherwise protected
Request, helper or Organization facts.


*** A concrete two-host failure schedule

The schedule's authoritative and browser facts must be
observed at different physical boundaries. In particular,
an outbox publication does not confirm Bob's SSE receipt,
Bob's SSE receipt does not authorize Refresh, and an
authorized acquisition does not prove a DOM adoption.
The Alice/host-A and Bob/host-C flow is the reference scenario. The steps below require a
*qualified* shared backend, distinct running host processes,
actual current sessions, and the installed Gesso/HTMX/SSE
browser path for an end-to-end acceptance claim. A two-host
fixture drawn as one JVM with two labels does not establish
this physical guarantee.


The following schedule exercises distinct facts; it is an acceptance scenario,
not a proof that every deployment execution behaves this way.

| Step | Authoritative or transport fact | Permitted participant conclusion |
|------+---------------------------------+----------------------------------|
| 1 | Alice's bound Claim reaches host A | Submission may proceed; no commit is inferred from arrival |
| 2 | Guarded Request, primary assignment, command result, and outbox intent commit | The authoritative command is incorporated |
| 3 | Host A dies before delivering Alice's response or dispatching the outbox | Alice may still have =:commit-unknown=; the commit remains durable |
| 4 | A dispatcher on another surviving process publishes the retained intent | Notice reaches the declared distribution boundary; browser receipt is separate |
| 5 | Bob receives a valid scoped advisory through host C | Record debt; do not automatically adopt the remote lifecycle change |
| 6 | Alice reconciles or replays the same bound command through host C | After binding and disclosure checks, return the permitted recorded result |
| 7 | Bob presses Refresh and host C obtains sufficient coherent authority | Acquire a candidate observation; current browser admission and installation remain necessary |
| 8 | Bob's current resource successfully installs the admitted batch | Record the permitted adoption and discharge only justified covered debt |

*** Failure cuts, correct negative conclusions and recovery

| Fault point or race | Required observation and forbidden shortcut |
|---------------------+----------------------------------------------|
| A fails before reaching the physical write boundary | No commit inferred from intent; reissue only under the qualified command protocol |
| A submits but the transaction result is lost | Alice keeps =:commit-unknown= until command-specific retained evidence resolves it |
| A commits but dies before HTTP result or outbox dispatch | Durable domain, command result and required publication intent survive; absence of response is not rejection |
| Outbox is forwarded twice or acknowledgment is lost | Bob may see duplicate advisory debt, never a second Claim or automatic board adoption |
| Notice was emitted before Bob's interest became effective | Registration fence, replay or explicit gap/authorized recovery; stream silence is not currentness |
| Router fails with stale interest knowledge | Replacement repairs coverage or records uncertainty; healthy process alone is insufficient |
| Bob's previous Refresh is pending when another notice arrives | Retain uncovered newer debt; do not schedule an automatic successor acquisition |
| C returns a lagging or noncoherent board | Reject insufficiency as a candidate for the claimed scope, even when HTTP succeeded |
| Bob changes Organization or logs out during the read | Retire incompatible owner; drop the old response and recheck server-side disclosure |
| Browser swaps toolbar but fails collection installation | Keep batch/adoption incomplete and repair within current resource lifetime |
| Bob's DOM resource is replaced while an old callback is pending | Old callback/effect cannot mutate the new resource or restore stale continuity |
| Alice resolves C42 through C after concurrent new domain activity | Historical C42 attribution and current Request content are acquired separately |
| C42 cannot be disclosed after Membership revocation | Nondisclosure is correct; never guess rejection or reveal another user's history |
| A Remote Request is created while Bob searches adopted cards | Search changes only adopted presentation; new Request appears only after an admitted Refresh or own-result rule |

The positive control for each case includes a real eligible
operation and, where the policy permits, a subsequent
successful authorized acquisition and installation.
A reject-everything handler, empty subscriber fixture,
untriggered process fault or stale synthetic adapter trace
is not evidence of the relevant production guarantee.
Gesso's underlying model checker can explore abstract
schedules, but physical two-host correspondence also
requires real independent host, provider and browser
observations with their versions, scope and open premises
recorded.


Variants lose the advisory, expire a cursor, duplicate publication, reject a
lagging read, change Membership, or replace Bob's resource between receipt and
mutation. Each variant must preserve its unresolved obligations until the
appropriate evidence and permission exist. Host C's ability to read the current
Request does not by itself attribute Alice's command.

*** Direct participant routing is an explicit extension

An ephemeral feature can have different semantics. For a typing indicator, the
meaningful event may be an admitted participant-message receipt, with no durable
business fact to reread. Its contract must say so instead of borrowing the
Request invalidation protocol.

*** Contrasting ephemeral typing-message contract

The durable HumanHelp Claim example in 10.17–10.18 has a
current authoritative Request to reread. An ephemeral
typing indicator can instead depend on a specific
*admitted participant-message receipt* from one choreography
execution. The receiver cannot reconstruct that event
merely by querying the latest Document, nor may a
database-update advisory substitute for the message.

The following Clojure data illustrates this contrast.
The compact data below retains the semantic fields without
claiming that a routing namespace, function or physical
transport implementation is thereby specified:

#+begin_src clojure
{:message/intent {:message/id :illustrative/message-M
                  :kind :collaboration/typing
                  :document/id :illustrative/document-D}
 :contract {:delivery :best-effort
            :durability :ephemeral
            :duplicates :permitted
            :late-message :discard
            :sender-binding :authenticated-principal
            :recipient-binding :current-collaboration-route
            :authorization :current-document-membership
            :semantic-effect :recipient-observed-admitted-message}}
#+end_src

These are *schematic* bound identity placeholders and
declarative requirements, not runnable sample API calls,
authentication evidence, or checked physical admission.
The same browser-supplied message ID, kind and Document ID
do not authenticate its sender, designate permitted
recipients, or assert actual receipt. The trusted host
must bind sender and recipients from current authenticated
and authorized collaboration state, and the receiving
host/session must independently admit the routed message
for its current principal, role, execution, scope and
resource owner.

A Gesso Choreo =:communicate= transition is the global
semantic declaration; endpoint projection produces
role-local send/receive obligations. Actual physical
routing must refine the declared message/receipt events.
Projection may establish who is supposed to know what;
it cannot infer that a remote process actually delivered
the envelope, that a browser saw it, or that a protected
session was authorized at delivery time. A transport
adapter supplies those distinct, source-linked
correspondence witnesses.


A minimal typing contract binds sender identity through authentication, resolves
recipients from current authorized collaboration scope, limits payload, defines
message and execution correlation, admits receipt under the recipient's current
resource, and specifies best-effort delivery, duplicate handling, and expiry.
The UI effect still passes its final ownership gate. Loss is permitted by that
best-effort contract; persistent replay is not automatically useful for an
expired typing signal.

*** Physical correlation, delivery, and admission

Distinguish message identity, choreography execution,
role-local send occurrence, transport attempt, broker
acknowledgment, recipient-side receipt and actual UI
effect. A best-effort transport may lose or duplicate an
envelope. A duplicate with the *same admitted delivery
identity* must not execute the same role-local semantic
receive twice within its declared deduplication scope;
different declared messages must not be collapsed just
because their payloads or Document selector match.
Where a protocol explicitly tolerates repeated typing
indications, idempotence still must not mint fresh
sender knowledge, permissions or authoritative content.

Receive admission checks intended recipient and
execution/role correlation, complete required payload
shape, authenticated sender provenance from the trusted
routing boundary, current Document membership, compatible
plan/protocol generation, expiry, and current resource
ownership. A message for a retired or replaced browser
target cannot reuse a newer target's rights. If a sender
loses membership before the relevant trusted send
boundary, old browser intent is not grandfathered.
If permission is revoked between routing and receipt,
the chosen current-disclosure/recipient-admission policy
decides what may still be shown; an old broker queue
does not override it.

No router-supplied sender ID, recipient selector,
proof-looking map, claimed host identity or timestamp
is independently authoritative merely because its
syntax matches a declared type. Security and disclosure
must be re-established through actual trusted
installation boundaries. Recipient-scoped delivery
cannot reveal private Document existence, membership or
typing activity to a different tenant or session.
Malformed, oversize, unsupported, replayed under an
incompatible generation, and mistargeted envelopes have
typed rejection/ignore behavior under the selected
protocol; none may grant an alternative authoritative
operation.


If expiry uses clocks across hosts, the contract names the clock and skew
assumptions, or uses a receiver-local lifetime with appropriately narrower
meaning. A timestamp alone does not prove that a remote message is fresh. A
broker's acknowledgment, transport delivery, admitted receipt, rendered indicator,
and domain commit are distinct events.

*** Expiration, optional durability, and non-interchangeable receipts

Typing is a useful example precisely because its
best-effort loss is allowed and a missed transient UI
effect need not be recovered by durable authoritative
reread. The bounded lifetime is scoped to the chosen
sender/recipient contract. If clocks across hosts
are compared, issuer, offset/skew and admissible
expiration behavior are trusted premises. An opaque
receiver-local timeout can implement a narrower
lifetime without assuming synchronized wall clocks.
A stale but syntactically valid typing message is
discarded; a late duplicate cannot resurrect a retired
resource or start a new execution.

If a product later requires guaranteed receipt, this
is a different explicit choreography/message
contract: durable retained message identity,
recipient-specific authorization and admission,
receipt acknowledgment, deduplication horizon,
replay/gap and retirement behavior, and the
appropriate fairness/availability premises.
Broker durability, a publish acknowledgment, a
websocket/SSE write, participant semantic receipt,
and displayed indicator remain different events.
Even a durable routed message is not an
authoritative Request commit unless an explicitly
admitted domain operation performed that commit.


Stronger direct-message guarantees require explicit persistence, recipient
admission, acknowledgment, deduplication, retry, retirement, and version
compatibility contracts. Infrastructure reuse is allowed; semantic conflation
is not. Direct participant routing must not redefine ordinary authoritative
convergence or bypass protected-data authorization.

*** Assured endpoint correspondence without a second application

Gesso developers continue to define one ordinary
Choreo and its public model/admission rules. The
framework's projected plans and internal proof/checking
machinery derive role knowledge and message obligations;
developers do not hand-maintain a second Quint/TLA/
Recife description of the physical router.

A multi-node evidence path relates original
=:communicate= source, checked endpoint projection,
per-role execution state, trusted sender binding,
issued routed envelope, physical delivery attempt,
current authenticated recipient admission, and
the exact participant receipt/host effect. Each
edge is individually qualified. The current
portable realization harness can exercise deliberate
message drop/reorder and role-local behavior, but
a deterministic in-memory queue is not a
cross-host authenticity, confidentiality, delivery
or resource-ownership proof.

The selected direct-message adapter can reuse
infrastructure chosen for Live advisories, but
distinct queues, subjects, admission/disclosure
rules, acknowledgments and failure semantics
remain explicit. The app's ordinary durable
Request-convergence guarantee must not depend on
a participant typing indicator arriving.


*** Multi-node assumptions and acceptance

The root assurance graph includes actual host replacement, backend qualification,
writer coverage, command retention, outbox recovery, dispatch acknowledgment,
interest registration, replay/gap detection, and current authorization contracts.
It also includes old/new assembly compatibility and browser artifact availability
across rolling activation. Merely sharing a database or load balancer establishes
none of these joins.

*** Source-to-physical acceptance evidence

Whole-application assurance names the original
operations, relevant writers, participant messages,
hosts, browser resources, routes, installed asset
versions, exact admission profiles, and physical
backend/transport identities. A successful isolated
send/receive projection test or one load-balanced
HTTP request does not close this application scope.

A required positive case traverses the *actual*
installed producer, transport and consumer path,
with two independently running processes where
cross-host behavior is claimed. Its adversarial
companion challenges the first enforcing boundary
for the specific promise, and records independent
observable effect/receipt state. A diagnostic
report containing matching fabricated host labels
or supplied expected outcomes is not physical
correspondence evidence. The suite must record
source-linked observed, tested, assumed,
inconclusive and refuted portions separately.


The multi-node acceptance suite uses real process and transport boundaries and
must include:

- mutation through one host becoming authoritatively observable through another;
- compatible retries through a different host, including concurrent deliveries;
- loss before submission, after possible submission, after known commit, and
  after publication but before dispatch acknowledgment;
- duplicate and reordered advisories with preserved scoped debt;
- initial-subscription and reconnect gaps, including a silent missed notice;
- expired replay retention and explicit recovery without false currentness;
- remote creation and lifecycle change remaining unadopted until permitted
  Refresh, with own-command exceptions exercised separately;
- insufficient progression at the replacement host without false discharge;
- Membership or scope loss affecting reads, command-result disclosure, and
  subscription renewal;
- concurrent independent request contexts without capability or identity leakage;
- incompatible plan or assembly replacement following the declared retirement
  and recovery path;
- eventual successful recovery once the named availability, permission,
  retention, and user-action premises hold.

*** Paired distributed and direct-message failure controls

| Positive boundary case | Adversarial or forbidden outcome |
|------------------------+----------------------------------|
| One authorized sender's typing reaches a current admitted recipient | Forged sender, recipient or Document selector cannot disclose or install |
| Choreo send and receive correlate within one execution | Same event label in a different execution cannot satisfy receipt |
| Best-effort typing message displays under current owner | Message for a retired browser resource cannot mutate its replacement |
| One scoped delivery ID is admitted once under its contract | Transport duplicate cannot manufacture a second semantic receipt |
| Recipient's current membership permits the indicator | Revocation before current receipt gate cannot silently retain admission |
| Supported receiver-local expiration discards late typing | Spoofed remote wall clock cannot prove freshness across hosts |
| Declared best-effort loss leaves no claimed recipient receipt | Broker enqueue alone cannot count as delivered or rendered |
| Qualified stronger durable-message profile supports required replay | Expired or absent replay evidence cannot be called guaranteed receipt |
| Committed Request on A is acquired by permitted read on C | Message routing cannot become a second authoritative Request owner |
| Same bound command resolves after host replacement | Replayed HTTP attempt cannot create a second committed domain effect |
| Durable outbox recovers a crash after authoritative commit | Dead worker cannot permanently strand required publication intent |
| Interest registration fence/replay closes initial gap | Healthy router with stale filters cannot silently drop advisory coverage |
| Remote HumanHelp update waits for explicit permitted Refresh | Typing, SSE or advisory arrival cannot auto-adopt remote board truth |
| Lagging C read preserves scoped outstanding debt | Echoed progression token cannot certify a current coherent snapshot |
| Mixed old/new compatible plan versions follow checked admission | Unqualified wire/asset/assembly generation cannot silently inherit rights |
| Concurrent independent requests preserve principal/permit isolation | One request's writer, client, receipt or command result cannot leak |
| Selected real host fault is observed under declared topology | Two in-JVM labels or untriggered crash cannot prove failover |
| Liveness under named surviving topology and user action is met | Partition, denied disclosure or no user Refresh cannot be promised unconditional convergence |

This matrix supplements the multi-node inventory
below and the 10.16–10.18 contracts. Positive cases
prevent a reject-all implementation from appearing
safe, while fault-injection and trace evidence
show where the physical system first departed
from admitted semantics. An unexecuted test is an
open obligation, not certified coverage.


The report separates safety during interruption from progress once those premises
hold. If current authorization no longer permits result disclosure, the suite
expects nondisclosure rather than assuming eventual command attribution. If
explicit Refresh never occurs, the remote-adoption liveness claim is not enabled.

Persisting arbitrary suspended choreography machines remains a separate facility
with persistence, migration, ownership, and recovery contracts. Ordinary long
waits use durable model state and later short choreographies. Multi-node support
does not require converting those waits into serialized process stacks.

** Formal correspondence and system-boundary invariant

#+begin_quote
A claim applies to production only through its stated representation, checking,
or refinement relation and the continued applicability of its premises. The
executable semantic core, proof kernel, dedicated checkers, external formal
checker, physical gateways, and deployed entrypoints have distinct obligations.
Source-derived coverage, observed execution, trusted backend behavior, and
universal theorems are not interchangeable evidence.

Full host-language implementations remain available through explicit contracts.
Finite checking remains finite unless a justified abstraction transfers it.
Physical guards and writes enforce current authority; certificates do not.
Known commits remain commits despite delivery loss, while participants preserve
unknown outcomes until permitted authoritative evidence resolves them.

Every relevant backend or implementation change triggers the appropriate
qualification and correspondence checks. Multi-node placement changes hosts,
not authority, command meaning, resource ownership, or HumanHelp's adoption
policy. The root report preserves the evidence class, scope, assumptions,
applicable identities, enforcing boundary, and unresolved obligations of each
claim.
#+end_quote

*** Interpret the invariant as a claim-specific transfer judgment

The closing rule is conditional and typed: *claim C about
source subject S applies to installed production subject P
only when each required interpretation, original-source
coverage, admissible proof, implementation refinement,
runtime enforcement and environment assumption for that
exact C,S,P has been established under the selected
scope*. If a mandatory edge is unknown or refuted, the
abstract theorem may still be true; its corresponding
production or completion claim remains conditional,
unsupported or rejected by the selected strict profile.
A matching name, digest, code shape or HTTP response is
never a substitute for the missing edge.

| Claim edge | What must actually be established | What it does not grant |
|------------+----------------------------------+------------------------|
| Original source to obligation | All relevant declared initializers, operations, business invariants, actors, writers and product requirements are represented without silently narrowed coverage | Correctness of arbitrary opaque Clojure or undiscovered deployed writers |
| Source to semantic/formal subject | Versioned normalization, interpretation, abstraction and proof dependencies preserve the precise source proposition | A handwritten convenient specification substituted for HumanHelp |
| Proof or finite result | Genuine issuer/checker run, exact quantifiers/bounds, source premises and an admissible derivation or witness | Universal theorem from a bounded test or a copied successful report |
| Semantic to runtime transition | Directional refinement with stated abstraction, visible events, stuttering/failures, source/effect and message correlations | A converse simulation or liveness property not separately proved |
| Runtime to protected authority | Installed authentic principal, guarded atomic writer, trusted read/disclosure and physical effect-time admission | Authority from browser data, a certificate label or a process-local diagnostic |
| Physical provider and topology | Qualified selected XTDB/backend, codecs, actual installed handlers/writers, host/broker/asset identities and recovery assumptions | All-schedules provider theorem or all external direct writers from one node's observation |
| Client acquisition and adoption | Current scope/permission, genuinely sufficient provider basis, active resource and completed browser installation | Canonical truth from an advisory, echoed token, SSE send or HTTP 200 |
| Release and application acceptance | Every required product capability, independently selected policy, positive/adversarial test and deployment gate for the named milestone | Automatic completion of other milestones or future deployments |

This is an *obligation map*, not a prescribed public map API or evidence that the listed checks have passed.
Original-source completeness is judged against the
source's full declared requirements, not the smaller
catalog returned by an elaborator or a conveniently
successful subset of tests. A required obligation
omitted from the assembled application remains owed.
An externally authored proof language is optional
internal framework machinery; normal application
authors continue to use Gesso/Clojure declarations.

*** Evidence remains precise under composition and change

Evidence classes must remain distinct at the root:
proved or checker-admitted conditional theorem,
exact-finite result, tested correspondence,
physically observed enforcement, runtime
assumption, application assertion, unsupported,
unknown, stale and refuted are not interchangeable.
A derived proof inherits every relevant admitted
premise, trusted inference rule, external checker
assumption, backend condition and coverage gap.
The assurance graph does not promote open premises
to proved merely because many other nodes passed.
A copyable report, signed-looking payload, source
fingerprint or issued abstract certificate does not
authenticate the current installed server or replace
its live authorization checks.

For a safety invariant, the claimed quantifier
and transition universe include the necessary
initialization, legal steps, relevant conflicts
and writer/dependency closure. A real execution
may conform through a declared directional
abstraction with hidden local steps; byte-identical
state traces are not automatically necessary.
Conversely, finite exploration, a sampled physical
schedule or one causal-looking readback cannot be
called an unbounded proof of transaction or
browser refinement. Noninterference of optional
observation sidecars is not evidence that mandatory
runtime guards were applied.

Liveness is separate. Any eventual-command,
publication, convergence, participant-message or
HumanHelp adoption conclusion names availability,
fairness, durable retention, connectedness,
current authorization, replay/gap recovery and
the *user's explicit Refresh where required*.
Safety remains required during supported partitions
and delivery uncertainty without pretending the
liveness antecedents hold. A known committed
effect cannot be relabeled rejected when its
response, notice, readback or diagnostic fails.
An indeterminate command remains unknown until
authorized command-specific evidence settles it;
current Request state does not retrospectively
identify the successful command.

A relevant source, invariant, backend implementation,
physical writer, proof assumption, compiler, browser
asset, assembly generation, authenticated context,
transport, retention or deployment topology change
invalidates or requalifies exactly the dependent
claims. An independently checked compatible
replacement can retain valid abstract theorems;
an unchanged byte digest cannot preserve a
claim whose semantic dependency or live boundary
has changed. Failure to *observe* an external
change is a named assurance limitation, not
proof that it did not occur.

*** Proof hardening and multi-node experiments may proceed iteratively

Complete multi-node productionization is *not* a
prerequisite for strengthening the executable semantic
core, its proof obligations or source-relative theorems.
Conversely, a small real two-process experiment may
expose an unstated transaction, observation, routing,
identity or failure assumption before the corresponding
formalization is considered mature.

The supported feedback loop is: admit the current
versioned semantic source; check its obligations;
exercise a bounded real deployment; independently
classify observed counterexamples and unsupported
physical edges; repair the actual source semantics,
implementation or assumption contract under its
proper owner; regenerate and rerun the dependent
checks. A finding in the physical realization must
not be concealed by weakening a formally true
requirement, and a changed semantic rule must not
inherit an incompatible old theorem. Small physical
tests remain tested evidence, never proof of all
deployments. The semantic authority is never
derived from the host conducting the experiment.

This iterative development permission does not
collapse the four separate release milestones
below or bypass Part XI's selected candidate,
installation and activation requirements.

*** Four independent completion milestones

A release or progress report must never claim one
milestone solely because a different one succeeded:

| Milestone | Positive scope | Still separate |
|-----------+----------------+----------------|
| Operational application success | The supported real product capabilities and user-visible workflows work under named deployment and test conditions | Compositional certification, external proof and cross-node failure coverage |
